    using var command = new MySqlCommand("select id, name, price, currentstock, minimumstock from articles", connection);
    using MySqlDataReader reader = command.ExecuteReader();
    Console.WriteLine("Content of the table [articles]:");
    while (reader.Read())
    {
        Console.WriteLine($"  {reader.GetInt32(0)} {reader.GetString(1)} {reader.GetDecimal(2)} {reader.GetInt32(3)} {reader.GetInt32(4)}");
    }
}

// an article: a row of the [articles] table
record Article(int Id, string Name, decimal Price, int CurrentStock, int MinimumStock);

Results:

> dotnet run adonet-06.cs
Database connection string: [Server=localhost;Port=3306;Database=dbarticles;User=root;Password=]

Insertion without a transaction...
6 row(s) modified
article [article, 100] inserted
Database access error (Duplicate entry 'article' for key 'articles.UNQ_NAME')
Content of the table [articles]:
  7 article 100.00 10 1

Insertion inside a transaction...
1 row(s) modified
article [article, 100] inserted
transaction rolled back (Duplicate entry 'article' for key 'articles.UNQ_NAME')
Content of the table [articles]:
  • Line 11: an array of two items with the same name, [article]. The uniqueness constraint [UNQ_NAME] on table [articles] prevents both from existing in the database at the same time: inserting the second one will trigger an exception thrown by the DBMS and relayed by the connector. To demonstrate the effect of a transaction, the two items will be inserted in two ways:
    • first, outside of any explicit transaction. Since MySQL is in autocommit mode, each insertion is performed within an implicit transaction. The first record will be inserted, but the second will not;
    • then within an explicit transaction encompassing both insertions. Because the second insertion will fail, the first will be rolled back: ultimately, no insertions will be made;
  • lines 15–26: the table is cleared, then both items are inserted without an explicit transaction. Since we know the second insertion will throw an exception, it is caught by a [try] / [catch]; finally, the table is displayed;
  • lines 28–32: The same sequence is repeated, but with an explicit transaction. This time, the exception is handled in the [InsertArticlesInTransaction] method;
  • line 40: the insertion method without a transaction. It uses two methods: [CreateInsertCommand] (line 80), which creates the parameterized insertion command, and [InsertArticle] (line 92), which assigns values to the parameters and executes the command;
  • line 52: the method for inserting within a transaction:
    • line 57: the transaction is created with the isolation level [ReadCommitted], as specified in the 2008 course. It belongs to the connection. The [using] statement ensures that it is rolled back—and thus canceled—if it has not been committed;
    • line 62: the command is placed within the transaction. This line is mandatory: with MySqlConnector, a command executed on a connection that has a transaction in progress—without specifying that transaction—throws an [InvalidOperationException];
    • Lines 63–65: the inserts;
    • line 68: everything went well: the transaction is committed, and the inserts are permanently added to the database;
    • Line 74: An insertion failed: the transaction is rolled back. The explicit [Rollback] is not strictly necessary, since releasing the uncommitted transaction would roll it back anyway, but it makes the code clearer.

In the results:

  • Line 5: displayed by command [delete]: there were six rows in the table;
  • line 7: the exception caused by the second insertion. The message indicates that the constraint [UNQ_NAME] on table [articles] was not satisfied;
  • line 9: the table is not empty: the first record was inserted;
  • line 12: displayed by command [delete]: there was one row in the table;
  • Line 13: The first insertion was successful… within the transaction;
  • line 14: the message displayed when the transaction fails;
  • line 15: the table is empty: the transaction’s [Rollback] rolled back the first insertion.

docs.title: 10.7. The ExecuteScalar method
docs.text:
Among the methods of the [DbCommand] class, there was the following:

NameTypeRole[ExecuteScalar]Mexecutes a SQL [select] command that returns only a single result, such as [select count(*) from articles].

More specifically, [ExecuteScalar] returns the first column of the first row of the result, in the form of an [object?]. The program [adonet-07.cs] demonstrates a few uses of this:

#:package MySqlConnector@2.4.0

// the ExecuteScalar method
using MySqlConnector;

const string ConnectionString = "Server=localhost;Port=3306;Database=dbarticles;User=root;Password=";

try
{
    // the single values returned by selects
    object? averagePrice = ExecuteScalar(ConnectionString, "select avg(price) from articles");
    Console.WriteLine($"Average price of the articles = {averagePrice} (type {averagePrice?.GetType().Name})");
    object? nbArticles = ExecuteScalar(ConnectionString, "select count(id) from articles");
    Console.WriteLine($"Number of articles = {nbArticles} (type {nbArticles?.GetType().Name})");
    object? name = ExecuteScalar(ConnectionString, "select name from articles where price = (select max(price) from articles)");
    Console.WriteLine($"Most expensive article = {name} (type {name?.GetType().Name})");
    object? missing = ExecuteScalar(ConnectionString, "select name from articles where price > 10000");
    Console.WriteLine($"Article over 10000 euros: {missing ?? "null"}");
    object? empty = ExecuteScalar(ConnectionString, "select max(price) from articles where price > 10000");
    Console.WriteLine($"Maximum price beyond 10000 euros: {empty} (type {empty?.GetType().Name})");

    // conversion of the result into the expected type
    decimal average = Convert.ToDecimal(averagePrice);
    int count = Convert.ToInt32(nbArticles);
    Console.WriteLine($"Rounded average = {Math.Round(average, 2)}, count = {count}");
    // a direct cast fails: count returns an Int64 (long) and not an Int32 (int)
    int n = (int)nbArticles!;
    Console.WriteLine($"n = {n}");
}
catch (Exception ex) when (ex is MySqlException or InvalidCastException)
{
    Console.WriteLine($"{ex.GetType().Name} : {ex.Message}");
}

// execution of a select that returns a single value
static object? ExecuteScalar(string connectionString, string query)
{
    using var connection = new MySqlConnection(connectionString);
    connection.Open();
    using var command = new MySqlCommand(query, connection);
    return command.ExecuteScalar();
}

Results:

> dotnet run adonet-07.cs
Average price of the articles = 271.666667 (type Decimal)
Number of articles = 6 (type Int64)
Most expensive article = bow (type String)
Article over 10000 euros: null
Maximum price beyond 10000 euros:  (type DBNull)
Rounded average = 271.67, count = 6
InvalidCastException : Unable to cast object of type 'System.Int64' to type 'System.Int32'.
  • Line 36: The program’s [ExecuteScalar] method opens a connection and executes the query using the command’s [ExecuteScalar] method;
  • line 11: the average price of the items. The C# type of the result depends on the SQL type of the value: the average of a [DECIMAL] column is a [decimal] (line 2);
  • line 13: the number of items. MySQL returns an integer of type [BIGINT], which becomes a [long] ([Int64]) in C# (line 3);
  • line 15: the name of the most expensive item, a string. The query contains a subquery, enclosed in parentheses;
  • line 17: if the query returns no rows, [ExecuteScalar] returns [null] (line 5);
  • line 19: if the query returns a row with the SQL value [NULL] (the maximum of an empty set), [ExecuteScalar] returns the object [DBNull.Value], which is displayed as an empty string (line 6). We must therefore distinguish between two cases: no row ([null]) and a value of [NULL] ([DBNull]);
  • lines 23–24: To obtain the result in the expected type, we use the methods of the [Convert] class, which can convert a [long] to a [int];
  • line 27: a direct type cast fails because the object is a “boxed” [long]: it can only be unboxed to its exact type. The 2008 program wrote [(int)ExecuteScalar(…, "select count(id) from articles")]: this worked with SQL Server Compact, whose [count] yields a [int], and would fail with MySQL (line 8). This is an example of the peculiarities of DBMSs that the generic connector does not hide.

docs.title: 10.8. Asynchronous methods
docs.text:
Chapter 9 showed that input/output operations must be asynchronous in applications that serve many users (servers, web services) or that have a graphical user interface: while a SQL command is executing on the server, the application thread must not be blocked. All methods of ADO.NET that communicate with the DBMS have an asynchronous version, which returns a task ([Task], [Task<T>], or [ValueTask]) and accepts an optional [CancellationToken]:

ClassSynchronous methodAsynchronous method[DbConnection][Open], [Close], [BeginTransaction][OpenAsync], [CloseAsync], [BeginTransactionAsync][DbCommand][ExecuteReader], [ExecuteNonQuery], [ExecuteScalar], [Prepare][ExecuteReaderAsync], [ExecuteNonQueryAsync], [ExecuteScalarAsync], [PrepareAsync][DbDataReader][Read], [NextResult], [Close][ReadAsync], [NextResultAsync], [CloseAsync][DbTransaction][Commit], [Rollback][CommitAsync], [RollbackAsync]

The ADO.NET objects also implement the [IAsyncDisposable] interface: they are released using [await using] (C# 8), which calls their [DisposeAsync] method. The program [adonet-08.cs] uses these methods:

#:package MySqlConnector@2.4.0

// the asynchronous versions of the ADO.NET methods
using System.Data.Common;
using System.Diagnostics;
using System.Runtime.CompilerServices;
using MySqlConnector;

const string ConnectionString = "Server=localhost;Port=3306;Database=dbarticles;User=root;Password=";

// the data source: it makes (already open) connections to a same database
await using var dataSource = new MySqlDataSource(ConnectionString);

try
{
    // 1 - an update statement, inside a transaction
    await using (MySqlConnection connection = await dataSource.OpenConnectionAsync())
    {
        await using MySqlTransaction transaction = await connection.BeginTransactionAsync();
        await using var command = new MySqlCommand("update articles set price = price * 1.1 where price < @price", connection, transaction);
        command.Parameters.AddWithValue("@price", 200);
        int nbRows = await command.ExecuteNonQueryAsync();
        await transaction.CommitAsync();
        Console.WriteLine($"{nbRows} price(s) increased by 10 %");
    }

    // 2 - a select whose rows are returned as they are read
    await foreach (Article article in GetArticlesAsync(dataSource))
    {
        Console.WriteLine(article);
    }

    // 3 - a single value
    await using (DbCommand command = dataSource.CreateCommand("select sum(price * currentstock) from articles"))
    {
        decimal stockValue = Convert.ToDecimal(await command.ExecuteScalarAsync());
        Console.WriteLine($"Stock value: {stockValue} euros");
    }

    // 4 - a query blocked by another transaction, cancelled after one second
    // the [blocking] transaction modifies article no. 1 and does not end: the row stays locked
    await using MySqlConnection connection1 = await dataSource.OpenConnectionAsync();
    await using MySqlTransaction blocking = await connection1.BeginTransactionAsync();
    await using (var command1 = new MySqlCommand("update articles set currentstock = currentstock - 1 where id = 1", connection1, blocking))
    {
        await command1.ExecuteNonQueryAsync();
    }
    // another connection wants to modify the same row: it must wait for the end of the [blocking] transaction
    using var cancellation = new CancellationTokenSource(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(1));
    var stopwatch = Stopwatch.StartNew();
    try
    {
        await using DbCommand command = dataSource.CreateCommand("update articles set price = price * 2 where id = 1");
        await command.ExecuteNonQueryAsync(cancellation.Token);
    }
    catch (OperationCanceledException ex)
    {
        Console.WriteLine($"{ex.GetType().Name} after {stopwatch.Elapsed.TotalSeconds:F0} s : {ex.Message}");
    }
    // the [blocking] transaction has not been committed: it is undone when [blocking] is released
}
catch (MySqlException ex)
{
    Console.WriteLine($"Database access error ({ex.Message})");
}

// the articles of the table, returned one by one (asynchronous stream)
static async IAsyncEnumerable<Article> GetArticlesAsync(MySqlDataSource dataSource,
    [EnumeratorCancellation] CancellationToken token = default)
{
    await using MySqlConnection connection = await dataSource.OpenConnectionAsync(token);
    await using var command = new MySqlCommand("select id, name, price, currentstock, minimumstock from articles", connection);
    await using MySqlDataReader reader = await command.ExecuteReaderAsync(token);
    while (await reader.ReadAsync(token))
    {
        yield return new Article(reader.GetInt32(0), reader.GetString(1), reader.GetDecimal(2),
            reader.GetInt32(3), reader.GetInt32(4));
    }
}

// an article: a row of the [articles] table
record Article(int Id, string Name, decimal Price, int CurrentStock, int MinimumStock);

Results:

> dotnet run adonet-08.cs
3 price(s) increased by 10 %
Article { Id = 1, Name = bike, Price = 500.00, CurrentStock = 10, MinimumStock = 5 }
Article { Id = 2, Name = pump, Price = 11.00, CurrentStock = 10, MinimumStock = 2 }
Article { Id = 3, Name = bow, Price = 600.00, CurrentStock = 4, MinimumStock = 1 }
Article { Id = 4, Name = arrows - set of 6, Price = 110.00, CurrentStock = 12, MinimumStock = 20 }
Article { Id = 5, Name = diving suit, Price = 300.00, CurrentStock = 8, MinimumStock = 2 }
Article { Id = 6, Name = diver's oxygen tanks, Price = 132.00, CurrentStock = 10, MinimumStock = 5 }
Stock value: 12550.00 euros
OperationCanceledException after 1 s : Query execution was interrupted
  • Line 12: a data source [MySqlDataSource], a class derived from [DbDataSource] (.NET 7). It is created once and for all with the connection string and then provides connections and commands. In an application, this is what is registered in the dependency injection container, rather than the connection string. Since it manages the connection pool, it is released at the end of the program, here via [await using];
  • lines 16–24: an update command within a transaction:
    • line 17: [OpenConnectionAsync] returns an already open connection. Opening a connection is a network operation: it is asynchronous. The [await using (…) { … }] block releases the connection upon exit;
    • lines 19–23: the transaction is created, the command [update] is executed by [ExecuteNonQueryAsync], and the transaction is committed by [CommitAsync]. Note the three-parameter constructor of [MySqlCommand]: request, connection, transaction;
  • Lines 68–76: a method that returns the records as an asynchronous stream, [IAsyncEnumerable<Article>] (C# 8, Chapter 9):
    • [ExecuteReaderAsync] executes the query, then [await reader.ReadAsync(token)] reads the rows one by one. [Read] can indeed wait for the network: the reader receives the rows from the server in batches;
    • [yield return] returns each record to the calling code as soon as it is read, without waiting for the entire table to be read: a [select] that returns one million rows does not use more memory than a [select] that returns ten;
    • The connection, command, and reader are released when the stream is finished (or abandoned by the calling code);
    • the [[EnumeratorCancellation]] attribute allows the calling code to pass a cancellation token via [GetArticlesAsync(dataSource).WithCancellation(token)];
  • Line 28: The calling code iterates through the stream using [await foreach]. The results show that the three prices below 200 euros were increased by 10%;
  • lines 33–37: [dataSource.CreateCommand] creates a command that will open its own connection (and close it); it returns a [DbCommand]. [ExecuteScalarAsync] returns the unique value;
  • lines 40–58: canceling a request:
    • lines 42–46: An initial connection starts a transaction that modifies item No. 1 but does not commit it. The DBMS has locked the modified row until the end of the transaction;
    • line 49: a cancellation source that will cancel its token after one second (Chapter 9);
    • line 54: a second connection attempts to modify the same row. It must wait for the first transaction to complete… which it will not do. After one second, the token is canceled: MySqlConnector then instructs the server to abort the request (command MySQL [KILL QUERY]), and [ExecuteNonQueryAsync] throws an [OperationCanceledException] (line 10). Without the cancellation, the request would have waited for the lock timeout of MySQL—50 seconds by default—and then failed;
    • the transaction [blocking] is never committed: it is rolled back when [blocking] is released, at the end of block [try].

Asynchronous versions offer no benefit to a small console program that performs one task at a time: they do not make a request any faster. However, they are the standard in server applications, such as ASP.NET Core web services (Chapter 13), which serve many users simultaneously.

docs.title: 10.9. Batch Execution
docs.text:
Each command execution involves a round trip between the application and the server. When multiple SQL commands need to be executed, they can be sent to the DBMS in a single exchange, in the form of a batch. .NET 6 added the abstract classes [DbBatch] and [DbBatchCommand] to ADO.NET: a batch is a list of commands, each with its own text and parameters, executed by a single call. MySqlConnector implements them using the classes [MySqlBatch] and [MySqlBatchCommand]. The program [adonet-09.cs] uses them:

#:package MySqlConnector@2.4.0

// the batch API (DbBatch, .NET 6): several SQL statements sent to the DBMS in a single exchange
using MySqlConnector;

const string ConnectionString = "Server=localhost;Port=3306;Database=dbarticles;User=root;Password=";

try
{
    await using var connection = new MySqlConnection(ConnectionString);
    await connection.OpenAsync();
    Console.WriteLine($"The connector can execute batches: {connection.CanCreateBatch}");

    // 1 - a batch of three update statements, each with its parameters
    await using var batch = new MySqlBatch(connection)
    {
        BatchCommands =
        {
            new MySqlBatchCommand("insert into articles(name, price, currentstock, minimumstock) values(@name, @price, 5, 1)")
            {
                Parameters = { new MySqlParameter("@name", "canoe"), new MySqlParameter("@price", 800) }
            },
            new MySqlBatchCommand("update articles set currentstock = currentstock + @addition where currentstock < minimumstock")
            {
                Parameters = { new MySqlParameter("@addition", 10) }
            },
            new MySqlBatchCommand("delete from articles where name = 'pump'"),
        }
    };
    int total = await batch.ExecuteNonQueryAsync();
    Console.WriteLine($"Total number of modified rows: {total}");

    // 2 - a batch of two selects: one reader, two successive results
    await using var batch2 = new MySqlBatch(connection)
    {
        BatchCommands =
        {
            new MySqlBatchCommand("select name, currentstock from articles where currentstock < minimumstock + 5"),
            new MySqlBatchCommand("select count(*), sum(price * currentstock) from articles"),
        }
    };
    await using MySqlDataReader reader = await batch2.ExecuteReaderAsync();
    Console.WriteLine("Articles to watch:");
    while (await reader.ReadAsync())
    {
        Console.WriteLine($"  {reader.GetString(0)} : {reader.GetInt32(1)}");
    }
    // moving to the next result
    await reader.NextResultAsync();
    await reader.ReadAsync();
    Console.WriteLine($"{reader.GetInt64(0)} articles, stock value: {reader.GetDecimal(1)} euros");
}
catch (MySqlException ex)
{
    Console.WriteLine($"Database access error ({ex.Message})");
}

Results:

> dotnet run adonet-09.cs
The connector can execute batches: True
Total number of modified rows: 3
Articles to watch:
  bow : 4
  arrows - set of 6 : 22
  canoe : 5
6 articles, stock value: 17200.00 euros
  • Line 12: The [CanCreateBatch] property of [DbConnection] indicates whether the connector can execute batches. With a connector that cannot, the generic method [connection.CreateBatch()] throws a [NotSupportedException];
  • Lines 15–27: A batch of three update statements. The batch is constructed using object and collection initializers: the collection [BatchCommands] receives three [MySqlBatchCommand] objects, the first two of which have their own parameter collection [Parameters]. Each command in the batch has its own parameters, even if they share the same name as a parameter from another command;
  • Line 30: The three commands are sent and executed in a single exchange. [ExecuteNonQueryAsync] returns the total number of modified rows: one insertion ([canoe]), one update (the stock of arrows, which is below the minimum stock), and one deletion ([pump]);
  • lines 34–39: a batch of two [select] commands;
  • line 42: the batch is executed by [ExecuteReaderAsync], which returns a single reader for both results;
  • line 49: after reading the rows of the first result, [NextResultAsync] moves the reader to the next result.

The same effect could be achieved by writing multiple SQL commands separated by semicolons within a single command, which MySqlConnector accepts. However, the parameters for all commands would then be mixed together, and this syntax is not accepted by all DBMSs; the batch API is the standard form specified by ADO.NET.

docs.title: 10.10. Sample Application - Version 6
docs.text:
Let’s revisit the example application [Tax]. The latest version, version 5, was discussed in Chapter 6. It was a three-tier application whose [dao] layer retrieved its data from a text file, a JSON file, or its own code, and whose layers were integrated via a dependency injection container. We modify the [dao] layer so that it retrieves its data from a MySQL database:

The 2008 course (Version 7) reused the [ui] and [business] layers from the previous version by recompiling their source code into a new solution, and integrated the layers with Spring.NET. We reuse the Version 5 projects as-is, via project references, and write only the new parts: the [dao] layer and the program that integrates the layers.

docs.title: 10.10.1. The database
docs.text:
The tax brackets are stored in the [brackets] table within a MySQL database named [dbtaxes], created by the [sql/dbtaxes.sql] script:

-- creation of the database [dbtaxes] of the application [Tax] (version 6)
-- execution: mysql -uroot < dbtaxes.sql

-- the script is written in UTF-8
SET NAMES utf8mb4;

-- the database is recreated on each execution of the script
DROP DATABASE IF EXISTS dbtaxes;
CREATE DATABASE dbtaxes CHARACTER SET utf8mb4 COLLATE utf8mb4_0900_ai_ci;
USE dbtaxes;

-- the table of the tax brackets (2004 scale on 2003 income)
CREATE TABLE brackets (
    id      INT PRIMARY KEY AUTO_INCREMENT,
    limits  DECIMAL(10,2) NOT NULL,
    coeffr  DECIMAL(6,3) NOT NULL,
    coeffn  DECIMAL(10,2) NOT NULL
);
INSERT INTO brackets (limits, coeffr, coeffn) VALUES
    (4962, 0, 0),
    (8382, 0.068, 291.09),
    (14753, 0.191, 1322.92),
    (23888, 0.283, 2668.39),
    (38868, 0.374, 4846.98),
    (47932, 0.426, 6883.66),
    (0, 0.481, 9505.54);

-- a user specific to the application, who only has rights on the database [dbtaxes]
CREATE USER IF NOT EXISTS 'admtaxes'@'localhost' IDENTIFIED BY 'pwdtaxes';
GRANT ALL PRIVILEGES ON dbtaxes.* TO 'admtaxes'@'localhost';
  • Lines 13–17: The table [brackets] has four columns: the primary key [id], generated by the DBMS, followed by the three columns [limits], [coeffr], and [coeffn], which represent a tax bracket of type [DECIMAL]: these are amounts and coefficients that must be accurate. The 2008 script used type [DOUBLE];
  • lines 19–26: the seven brackets of the 2004 tax schedule for 2003 income, used since the beginning of the course (this is an exercise: the tax schedule is not up to date). The brackets are inserted in ascending order of their thresholds, and the [id] column reflects this order;
  • lines 29–30: creation of a user MySQL [admtaxes], with password [pwdtaxes], who is granted full permissions ([GRANT ALL PRIVILEGES]) on all objects in the database [dbtaxes] ([dbtaxes.*]), and only on those objects. The application will run as this user rather than as the administrator [root]: if the administrator’s password were to be compromised, only the database [dbtaxes] would be at risk. [IF NOT EXISTS] allows the script to be run multiple times.

The script is executed by the administrator:

> mysql -uroot < dbtaxes.sql

then we verify that the user [admtaxes] has access to the brackets (the [-p] option alone prompts for the password, which is not displayed as it is typed):

> mysql -uadmtaxes -p -t dbtaxes -e "select * from brackets"
Enter password: 
+----+----------+--------+---------+
| id | limits   | coeffr | coeffn  |
+----+----------+--------+---------+
|  1 |  4962.00 |  0.000 |    0.00 |
|  2 |  8382.00 |  0.068 |  291.09 |
|  3 | 14753.00 |  0.191 | 1322.92 |
|  4 | 23888.00 |  0.283 | 2668.39 |
|  5 | 38868.00 |  0.374 | 4846.98 |
|  6 | 47932.00 |  0.426 | 6883.66 |
|  7 |     0.00 |  0.481 | 9505.54 |
+----+----------+--------+---------+

docs.title: 10.10.2. The TaxV6 solution
docs.text:
Version 6 is a solution consisting of three projects, located in the [10-adonet/TaxV6] folder:

csharp-oct-2026/
  06-architectures/TaxV5/             version 5, reused
    Tax.Dao/                            entities, ITaxDao interface, implementations of version 5
    Tax.Business/                       [business] layer
    Tax.Ui/                             [ui] layer (Dialog class) and program of version 5
  10-adonet/
    sql/
      dbtaxes.sql                       database creation script
    TaxV6/
      TaxV6.slnx
      Tax.Dao.MySql/                    library: the new [dao] layer
        Tax.Dao.MySql.csproj
        Dao/
          MySqlTax.cs
          DbTax.cs
      Tax.Tests.MySql/                  MSTest tests of the new [dao] layer
        Tax.Tests.MySql.csproj
        MSTestSettings.cs
        MySqlTaxTests.cs
      Tax.Ui.MySql/                     executable: integration of the layers
        Tax.Ui.MySql.csproj
        Program.cs
        appsettings.json
        appsettings-db.json
        appsettings-base.json
        appsettings-server.json
        appsettings-query.json

It was built using the following commands, entered in the [TaxV6] folder:

> dotnet new classlib -n Tax.Dao.MySql -o Tax.Dao.MySql
> dotnet new console -n Tax.Ui.MySql -o Tax.Ui.MySql
> dotnet new mstest -n Tax.Tests.MySql -o Tax.Tests.MySql
> dotnet new sln --format slnx -n TaxV6
> dotnet sln TaxV6.slnx add Tax.Dao.MySql Tax.Ui.MySql Tax.Tests.MySql
> dotnet add Tax.Dao.MySql reference ../../06-architectures/TaxV5/Tax.Dao
> dotnet add Tax.Dao.MySql package MySqlConnector --version 2.4.0
> dotnet add Tax.Ui.MySql reference Tax.Dao.MySql ../../06-architectures/TaxV5/Tax.Business ../../06-architectures/TaxV5/Tax.Ui
> dotnet add Tax.Tests.MySql reference Tax.Dao.MySql ../../06-architectures/TaxV5/Tax.Business

The solution file contains only the three new projects:

<Solution>
  <Project Path="Tax.Dao.MySql/Tax.Dao.MySql.csproj" />
  <Project Path="Tax.Tests.MySql/Tax.Tests.MySql.csproj" />
  <Project Path="Tax.Ui.MySql/Tax.Ui.MySql.csproj" />
</Solution>

The command [dotnet build TaxV6.slnx] also compiles the Version 5 projects referenced by these projects.

Here we see the value of a layered architecture and class libraries. In 2008, the DLL files in the [business] and [ui] layers of version 5 contained the name and version of the DLL file from the [dao] layer with which they had been compiled, and their source code had to be recompiled to make them work with a new [dao] layer. Here, the [business] and [ui] layers only recognize the [ITaxDao] interface, defined in the [Tax.Dao] project in version 5; the new layer [dao] implements this interface in a new project. No lines of code from version 5 are modified.

docs.title: 10.10.3. The [dao] layer
docs.text:
The project file [Tax.Dao.MySql.csproj] is as follows:

<Project Sdk="Microsoft.NET.Sdk">

  <PropertyGroup>
    <TargetFramework>net10.0</TargetFramework>
    <ImplicitUsings>enable</ImplicitUsings>
    <Nullable>enable</Nullable>
  </PropertyGroup>

  <ItemGroup>
    <!-- the entities and the ITaxDao interface of version 5 -->
    <ProjectReference Include="../../../06-architectures/TaxV5/Tax.Dao/Tax.Dao.csproj" />
  </ItemGroup>

  <ItemGroup>
    <!-- the ADO.NET connector of MySQL -->
    <PackageReference Include="MySqlConnector" Version="2.4.0" />
  </ItemGroup>

</Project>
  • Line 11: The reference to project [Tax.Dao] in version 5, which contains the entities ([TaxBracket], [TaxException]) and the interface [ITaxDao]. The path is relative to the project folder;
  • Line 16: the MySqlConnector connector.

The class [MySqlTax] implements the interface [ITaxDao]:

using Entities;
using MySqlConnector;

namespace Dao;

// a [dao] layer that reads the tax brackets from a MySQL database
public class MySqlTax : ITaxDao
{
    // error codes specific to this implementation
    public enum ErrorCodes { Access = 101, Data = 102 }

    // the default query: the brackets must be returned in increasing order of the limits
    public const string DefaultQuery = "select limits, coeffr, coeffn from brackets order by id";

    // tax brackets
    public TaxBracket[] TaxBrackets { get; }

    // constructor: the brackets are read once and for all
    public MySqlTax(string connectionString, string query = DefaultQuery)
    {
        List<TaxBracket> brackets = [];
        try
        {
            using var connection = new MySqlConnection(connectionString);
            connection.Open();
            using var command = new MySqlCommand(query, connection);
            using MySqlDataReader reader = command.ExecuteReader();
            // one bracket per row of the result: limit, coeffR, coeffN
            while (reader.Read())
            {
                brackets.Add(new TaxBracket(reader.GetDecimal(0), reader.GetDecimal(1), reader.GetDecimal(2)));
            }
        }
        catch (MySqlException e)
        {
            // database access error: we wrap it in a TaxException
            throw new TaxException("Error accessing the tax brackets database", e) { Code = (int)ErrorCodes.Access };
        }
        catch (Exception e) when (e is InvalidCastException or ArgumentOutOfRangeException)
        {
            // a missing column, of incorrect type or with a NULL value
            throw new TaxException("The tax brackets of the database are incorrect", e) { Code = (int)ErrorCodes.Data };
        }
        // an empty table is also an error
        if (brackets.Count == 0)
        {
            throw new TaxException("The database contains no tax bracket") { Code = (int)ErrorCodes.Data };
        }
        TaxBrackets = [.. brackets];
    }
}
  • line 7: the class [MySqlTax] implements the [ITaxDao] interface from version 5: a read-only [TaxBrackets] property (line 16);
  • line 10: error codes specific to this implementation, modeled after those of [FileTax] and [JsonTax]: 101 (the code used in the 2008 course) for a database access error, 102 for incorrect data;
  • line 13: the query that returns the brackets. The [order by id] clause is important: the [business] layer expects the brackets in ascending order of their bounds, and a [select] without a [order by] returns the rows in an order that SQL does not guarantee (the 2008 query omitted it);
  • line 19: the constructor receives the connection string and the query, which has a default value (optional parameter, C# 4). As in the 2008 version, the brackets are read once and for all in the constructor: the [dao] layer is a singleton in the application, and the database is not queried again afterward. Since a constructor cannot be asynchronous, the read operation uses the synchronous methods of ADO.NET;
  • lines 24–27: the connection, the command, and the reader, as in the previous examples;
  • lines 29–31: each row of the result becomes a [TaxBracket] object: [reader.GetDecimal(i)] reads column number i as a [decimal];
  • lines 34–37: a database access error is encapsulated in a [TaxException] with code [Access], just as [FileTax] and [JsonTax] did with input/output errors. The [ui] layer does not need to be aware of exceptions from MySqlConnector;
  • lines 39–42: a query that returns fewer than three columns ([ArgumentOutOfRangeException]), a column whose value is [NULL], or a non-numeric type ([InvalidCastException]): the data is incorrect;
  • lines 45–47: an empty table is also a data error;
  • line 49: the list is converted to an array by a collection expression.

docs.title: 10.10.4. Tests for the [dao] layer
docs.text:
The 2008 course tested the [dao] layer with NUnit. As in Chapter 6, we use MSTest. The test project references the new [dao] layer and the [business] layer from version 5:

  <ItemGroup>
    <!-- the MSTest testing framework -->
    <PackageReference Include="MSTest" Version="4.0.2" />
  </ItemGroup>

  <ItemGroup>
    <!-- the tested [dao] layer and the [business] layer of version 5 -->
    <ProjectReference Include="../Tax.Dao.MySql/Tax.Dao.MySql.csproj" />
    <ProjectReference Include="../../../06-architectures/TaxV5/Tax.Business/Tax.Business.csproj" />
  </ItemGroup>

The test class is as follows:

using Dao;
using Entities;
using Business;
using MySqlConnector;

namespace Tests;

// tests of the [dao] layers MySqlTax and DbTax (the database [dbtaxes] must exist)
[TestClass]
public class MySqlTaxTests
{
    // the test database
    private const string ConnectionString = "Server=localhost;Port=3306;Database=dbtaxes;User=admtaxes;Password=pwdtaxes";

    // the brackets read from the database are those of the "hardwired" version
    [TestMethod]
    public void SameBrackets()
    {
        TaxBracket[] reference = new HardwiredTax().TaxBrackets;
        CollectionAssert.AreEqual(reference, new MySqlTax(ConnectionString).TaxBrackets);
        CollectionAssert.AreEqual(reference,
            new DbTax(MySqlConnectorFactory.Instance, ConnectionString, MySqlTax.DefaultQuery).TaxBrackets);
    }

    // the [business] layer of version 5 with the new [dao] layer
    [TestMethod]
    [DataRow(true, 2, 60000, 4282)]
    [DataRow(true, 3, 60000, 2959)]
    [DataRow(false, 0, 60000, 11519)]
    public void CalculateTax(bool married, int nbChildren, int salary, int tax)
    {
        ITaxBusiness business = new TaxBusiness(new MySqlTax(ConnectionString));
        Assert.AreEqual(tax, business.CalculateTax(married, nbChildren, salary));
    }

    // nonexistent database (or forbidden to the user)
    [TestMethod]
    public void MissingDatabase()
    {
        TaxException e = Assert.ThrowsExactly<TaxException>(
            () => new MySqlTax(ConnectionString.Replace("dbtaxes", "dbtaxesunknown")));
        Assert.AreEqual((int)MySqlTax.ErrorCodes.Access, e.Code);
        Assert.IsInstanceOfType<MySqlException>(e.InnerException);
    }

    // unreachable server
    [TestMethod]
    public void UnreachableServer()
    {
        TaxException e = Assert.ThrowsExactly<TaxException>(
            () => new MySqlTax(ConnectionString.Replace("3306", "3399")));
        Assert.AreEqual((int)MySqlTax.ErrorCodes.Access, e.Code);
    }

    // query that returns only two columns
    [TestMethod]
    public void IncorrectQuery()
    {
        TaxException e = Assert.ThrowsExactly<TaxException>(
            () => new MySqlTax(ConnectionString, "select limits, coeffr from brackets"));
        Assert.AreEqual((int)MySqlTax.ErrorCodes.Data, e.Code);
    }

    // query that returns no row
    [TestMethod]
    public void NoBracket()
    {
        TaxException e = Assert.ThrowsExactly<TaxException>(
            () => new MySqlTax(ConnectionString, "select limits, coeffr, coeffn from brackets where id < 0"));
        Assert.AreEqual((int)MySqlTax.ErrorCodes.Data, e.Code);
    }
}
  • Line 13: The tests use the database [dbtaxes], which must have been created by the script [dbtaxes.sql]. These are therefore no longer unit tests in the strict sense—which would test a class in isolation—but rather integration tests: they verify that the [dao] layer works with the DBMS;
  • Lines 17–22: The brackets read from the database (by [MySqlTax], then by the [DbTax] class described below) are identical to those in the "hard-coded" version [HardwiredTax]. [CollectionAssert.AreEqual] compares elements one by one using its [Equals] method; the [record struct] method compares properties. Note that the [decimal] values read from the database have two decimal places ([4962.00]), whereas those of [HardwiredTax] have none ([4962]): for the type [decimal], these two values are equal;
  • lines 27–33: the [business] layer from version 5 calculates the expected taxes using the new [dao] layer;
  • lines 38–43: a nonexistent database causes a [TaxException] with code [Access], which encapsulates the original [MySqlException] exception;
  • lines 48–51: an unreachable server (no server is listening on port 3399) also causes an access error;
  • Methods [IncorrectQuery] (line 57) and [NoBracket] (line 66): a query that returns only two columns, or that returns no rows, causes a [TaxException] with code [Data].

Running the tests yields the following results:

> dotnet test --logger "console;verbosity=normal"
Test run for bin/Debug/net10.0/Tax.Tests.MySql.dll (.NETCoreApp,Version=v10.0)
VSTest version 18.0.2 (x64)

docs.title: 10.10.5. Integrating the layers
docs.text:
The [Tax.Ui.MySql] project contains the program that integrates the layers. Its project file is as follows:

<Project Sdk="Microsoft.NET.Sdk">

  <PropertyGroup>
    <OutputType>Exe</OutputType>
    <TargetFramework>net10.0</TargetFramework>
    <ImplicitUsings>enable</ImplicitUsings>
    <Nullable>enable</Nullable>
  </PropertyGroup>

  <ItemGroup>
    <!-- the new [dao] layer -->
    <ProjectReference Include="../Tax.Dao.MySql/Tax.Dao.MySql.csproj" />
    <!-- the [business] and [ui] layers of version 5, unchanged -->
    <ProjectReference Include="../../../06-architectures/TaxV5/Tax.Business/Tax.Business.csproj" />
    <ProjectReference Include="../../../06-architectures/TaxV5/Tax.Ui/Tax.Ui.csproj" />
  </ItemGroup>

  <ItemGroup>
    <!-- dependency injection container and reading of a JSON configuration file -->
    <PackageReference Include="Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection" Version="10.0.12" />
    <PackageReference Include="Microsoft.Extensions.Configuration.Json" Version="10.0.12" />
  </ItemGroup>

  <ItemGroup>
    <!-- the configuration files are copied next to the executable -->
    <None Update="appsettings*.json" CopyToOutputDirectory="PreserveNewest" />
  </ItemGroup>

</Project>
  • line 12: the new layer [dao];
  • lines 14–15: the layers [business] and [ui] from version 5. The [Tax.Ui] project is an executable, but a project can reference an executable as a library: we use its public class [Dialog]. Its configuration files are also copied to the output folder, but those from the [Tax.Ui.MySql] project, which has the same name, replace them;
  • Lines 20–21: the dependency injection container and configuration reading, as in version 5.

The configuration file [appsettings.json] is as follows:

{
  "ConnectionStrings": {
    "dbtaxes": "Server=localhost;Port=3306;Database=dbtaxes;User=admtaxes;Password=pwdtaxes"
  },
  "Dao": {
    "Implementation": "MySqlTax",
    "Query": "select limits, coeffr, coeffn from brackets order by id"
  }
}
  • Line 3: the connection string for user [admtaxes] to database [dbtaxes];
  • line 6: the implementation of the [dao] layer;
  • line 7: the query that returns the brackets. Including this in the configuration allows you to use a different database—even one with tables or columns that have different names—without modifying the code.

The program [Program.cs] is the one from version 5, with the exception of the registration of the [dao] layer:

using System.Data.Common;
using Dao;
using Entities;
using Business;
using Microsoft.Extensions.Configuration;
using Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection;
using MySqlConnector;
using Ui;

// the configuration file: appsettings.json by default, or the one passed as an argument
string configFile = args.Length > 0 ? args[0] : "appsettings.json";

// the ADO.NET connectors usable by the DbTax implementation
DbProviderFactories.RegisterFactory("MySqlConnector", MySqlConnectorFactory.Instance);

// integration of the layers
ITaxBusiness business;
try
{
    // reading the configuration, next to the executable
    IConfiguration config = new ConfigurationBuilder()
        .SetBasePath(AppContext.BaseDirectory)
        .AddJsonFile(configFile, optional: false)
        .Build();
    string implementation = config["Dao:Implementation"] ?? "MySqlTax";
    string connectionString = config.GetConnectionString("dbtaxes")
        ?? throw new TaxException("The connection string [dbtaxes] is missing from the configuration");
    string query = config["Dao:Query"] ?? MySqlTax.DefaultQuery;

    // registration of the layers in the container
    var services = new ServiceCollection();
    // the [dao] layer: the implementation is chosen by the configuration
    services.AddSingleton<ITaxDao>(_ => implementation switch
    {
        "MySqlTax" => new MySqlTax(connectionString, query),
        "DbTax" => new DbTax(DbProviderFactories.GetFactory(config["Dao:Connector"] ?? ""), connectionString, query),
        _ => throw new TaxException($"Unknown implementation [{implementation}] of the [dao] layer")
    });
    // the [business] layer: the container will pass it the [dao] layer
    services.AddSingleton<ITaxBusiness, TaxBusiness>();

    // creation of the container, then of the [business] layer (and therefore of the [dao] layer)
    ServiceProvider provider = services.BuildServiceProvider();
    business = provider.GetRequiredService<ITaxBusiness>();
}
catch (Exception e)
{
    // display of the error and end of the program
    Dialog.DisplayError(e);
    return 1;
}

// the dialog with the user: the [ui] layer of version 5
Dialog.Run(business);
return 0;
  • line 14: the registration of the MySqlConnector connector, used by the [DbTax] implementation described in the following paragraph;
  • lines 26–28: the connection string and the query, read from the configuration. The absence of the connection string is an error; the query has a default value. Note the operator [??] followed by an expression [throw] (C# 7);
  • lines 33–37: the [dao] layer is a [MySqlTax] (or a [DbTax]), created using the connection string and the query;
  • line 54: the Version 5 dialog box, unchanged.

Execution with the [appsettings.json] file:

> dotnet run
Tax calculation parameters in the format: Married (y/n) NbChildren Salary, or nothing to stop: y 2 60000
Tax=4282 euros
Tax calculation parameters in the format: Married (y/n) NbChildren Salary, or nothing to stop: y 3 60000
Tax=2959 euros
Tax calculation parameters in the format: Married (y/n) NbChildren Salary, or nothing to stop: n 0 60000
Tax=11519 euros
Tax calculation parameters in the format: Married (y/n) NbChildren Salary, or nothing to stop:

Here are the course reference values: 4,282 euros for a couple with two children, 2,959 euros for a couple with three children, and 11,519 euros for a single person without children, with an annual salary of 60,000 euros.

With the file [appsettings-base.json], whose connection string refers to a database named [dbtaxesunknown]:

> dotnet run -- appsettings-base.json
Exception chain:
----------------------------------------
Entities.TaxException: Error accessing the tax brackets database
----------------------------------------
MySqlConnector.MySqlException: Access denied for user 'admtaxes'@'localhost' to database 'dbtaxesunknown'
----------------------------------------

The user [admtaxes] has rights only to the database [dbtaxes]: MySQL denies access to any other database, whether it exists or not (line 6).

With the file [appsettings-server.json], whose connection string specifies port 3399—on which no server is listening (this is what would happen if a MySQL server were stopped)—:

> dotnet run -- appsettings-server.json
Exception chain:
----------------------------------------
Entities.TaxException: Error accessing the tax brackets database
----------------------------------------
MySqlConnector.MySqlException: Unable to connect to any of the specified MySQL hosts.
----------------------------------------

With the file [appsettings-query.json], whose query requests only the columns [limits] and [coeffr]:

> dotnet run -- appsettings-query.json
Exception chain:
----------------------------------------
Entities.TaxException: The tax brackets of the database are incorrect
----------------------------------------
System.ArgumentOutOfRangeException: ordinal ('2') must be less than '2'. (Parameter 'ordinal')
Actual value was 2.
----------------------------------------

In all three cases, the [dao] layer encapsulated the original exception in a [TaxException], which was displayed by the [Dialog.DisplayError] method in version 5, and the program terminates.

docs.title: 10.10.6. Change the database
docs.text:
The [dao] layer [MySqlTax] uses the classes from the MySqlConnector connector. If you switch DBMS, you must write a new [dao] layer… or use the generic connector, as the [dao] layer from the 2008 course did: This is the role of the [DbTax] class in the [Tax.Dao.MySql] project:

using System.Data.Common;
using Entities;

namespace Dao;

// a [dao] layer that reads the tax brackets from any database
// it only knows the abstract classes of ADO.NET: the connector is given to it by its factory
public class DbTax : ITaxDao
{
    // error codes: the same as those of MySqlTax
    public enum ErrorCodes { Access = 101, Data = 102 }

    // tax brackets
    public TaxBracket[] TaxBrackets { get; }

    // constructor: the connector's factory, the connection string, the query that returns the brackets
    public DbTax(DbProviderFactory factory, string connectionString, string query)
    {
        List<TaxBracket> brackets = [];
        try
        {
            using DbConnection connection = factory.CreateConnection()
                ?? throw new InvalidOperationException("the connector cannot create a connection");
            connection.ConnectionString = connectionString;
            connection.Open();
            using DbCommand command = connection.CreateCommand();
            command.CommandText = query;
            using DbDataReader reader = command.ExecuteReader();
            while (reader.Read())
            {
                brackets.Add(new TaxBracket(reader.GetDecimal(0), reader.GetDecimal(1), reader.GetDecimal(2)));
            }
        }
        catch (DbException e)
        {
            throw new TaxException("Error accessing the tax brackets database", e) { Code = (int)ErrorCodes.Access };
        }
        catch (Exception e) when (e is InvalidCastException or ArgumentOutOfRangeException)
        {
            throw new TaxException("The tax brackets of the database are incorrect", e) { Code = (int)ErrorCodes.Data };
        }
        if (brackets.Count == 0)
        {
            throw new TaxException("The database contains no tax bracket") { Code = (int)ErrorCodes.Data };
        }
        TaxBrackets = [.. brackets];
    }
}
  • line 17: the constructor receives the connector factory, the connection string, and the query. The code uses only the abstract classes from [System.Data.Common]: it does not contain the name of any DBMS;
  • Lines 22–27: The connection is created by the factory (the expression [throw] handles the theoretical case of a factory that would return [null]), and the command is issued by the connection;
  • line 34: the base exception for all connectors.

The configuration file [appsettings-db.json] selects this implementation and the connector [MySqlConnector]:

{
  "ConnectionStrings": {
    "dbtaxes": "Server=localhost;Port=3306;Database=dbtaxes;User=admtaxes;Password=pwdtaxes"
  },
  "Dao": {
    "Implementation": "DbTax",
    "Connector": "MySqlConnector",
    "Query": "select limits, coeffr, coeffn from brackets order by id"
  }
}

and the program [Program.cs] creates the layer [dao] with the factory registered under this name:

        "DbTax" => new DbTax(DbProviderFactories.GetFactory(config["Dao:Connector"] ?? ""), connectionString, query),

Execution:

> dotnet run -- appsettings-db.json
Tax calculation parameters in the format: Married (y/n) NbChildren Salary, or nothing to stop: y 2 60000
Tax=4282 euros
Tax calculation parameters in the format: Married (y/n) NbChildren Salary, or nothing to stop:

To use a SQL Server database (or PostgreSQL), all you need to do is:

  • create the brackets table in a SQL Server database, for example, a table named [data] with columns [data1], [data2], and [data3]—as the 2008 course did to highlight the benefits of placing the query in the configuration;
  • to add the package [Microsoft.Data.SqlClient] (or [Npgsql]) to the project [Tax.Ui.MySql];
  • register its factory in [Program.cs]: [DbProviderFactories.RegisterFactory("Microsoft.Data.SqlClient", SqlClientFactory.Instance)] (or [DbProviderFactories.RegisterFactory("Npgsql", NpgsqlFactory.Instance)]);
  • write a configuration file similar to [appsettings-db.json]:
{
  "ConnectionStrings": {
    "dbtaxes": "Server=localhost;Database=dbtaxes;User Id=admtaxes;Password=pwdtaxes;TrustServerCertificate=True"
  },
  "Dao": {
    "Implementation": "DbTax",
    "Connector": "Microsoft.Data.SqlClient",
    "Query": "select data1, data2, data3 from data order by id"
  }
}

Only MySQL is installed on the machine used to write this course: we did not run this configuration. The layers [business] and [ui] and the class [DbTax] do not need to be modified: only the connector’s configuration and registration change. Note that the query for [DbTax] has no parameters and uses only standard SQL functionality: this is what allows it to be executed by any DBMS. A more feature-rich [dao] layer (searches, updates) would quickly reach the limits of the generic connector described above: this is where an ORM such as Entity Framework Core takes over.

docs.title: 10.11. Conclusion
docs.text:
This chapter has covered database access in connected mode using ADO.NET:

  • a DBMS-specific connector (MySqlConnector for MySQL) provides the classes [XxxConnection], [XxxCommand], [XxxDataReader], and [XxxTransaction], derived from the abstract classes [DbConnection], [DbCommand], [DbDataReader], and [DbTransaction] from [System.Data.Common];
  • a connection is opened as late as possible and closed as early as possible by a [using]: the connection pool makes this practice inexpensive;
  • [ExecuteReader] executes a [select] and returns a reader that is traversed row by row with [Read]; [ExecuteNonQuery] executes an [insert], [update], or [delete] and returns the number of modified rows; [ExecuteScalar] returns a single value;
  • Errors are [DbException] ([MySqlException] for MySqlConnector);
  • external values are always passed via parameters, never concatenated to the query text, which protects against SQL injection;
  • transactions ([BeginTransaction], [Commit], [Rollback]) ensure that a sequence of commands is atomic (SQL);
  • asynchronous methods ([OpenAsync], [ExecuteReaderAsync], [ReadAsync]…) and [await using] are standard in server applications; batches ([DbBatch]) reduce the number of exchanges with the server;
  • the generic connector ([DbProviderFactory], [DbProviderFactories]) makes the code independent of the DBMS, within the limits of each DBMS’s specific characteristics.

Version 6 of the [Tax] application demonstrated that, thanks to the layered architecture, switching from a file to a database requires only writing a new [dao] layer and modifying the configuration. The next chapter will create a seventh version of this layer using Entity Framework Core, which generates the SQL commands itself.

To learn more:

  • the ADO.NET documentation: ADO.NET (written for the .NET Framework, but the concepts and classes in [System.Data.Common] are the same);
  • the MySqlConnector documentation: mysqlconnector.net;
  • SQL injection, explained by the OWASP: SQL Injection Prevention Cheat Sheet.

docs.title: 15.1. DBMS and MySQL with Laragon
docs.text: In 2008, the course appendices described the installation of SQL Server 2005 Express and MySQL 5, their administration tools (MySQL GUI Tools) and their ODBC drivers, with about thirty screenshots. Chapters 10 and 11 of this document use only MySQL 8, and the easiest way to install it on Windows is to install Laragon, a portable development environment that includes, among other things, MySQL, the graphical client HeidiSQL, a configured terminal, Apache, and PHP. The author also uses it for his PHP courses.

docs.title: 15.1.1. Installation
docs.text:
Laragon can be downloaded from https://laragon.org. The installation is standard; you can keep the suggested installation folder ([C:\laragon]). Laragon provides MySQL 8 (the exact version depends on the Laragon version), with a password-less administrator account ([root]) and a server listening on port 3306 on the local machine. This is the configuration assumed by the examples in this document, where the connection strings are in the form:

Server=localhost;Port=3306;Database=dbarticles;User=root;Password=

If MySQL was installed differently, with a password for [root], you must replace it with [Password=] in the connection strings of the examples ([appsettings.json] files or constants at the top of the programs).

For a system without Laragon, you can also install MySQL Community Server from https://dev.mysql.com/downloads/mysql/, or its open-source derivative, MariaDB. However, the examples have only been tested with MySQL 8: the scripts in Chapter 10 use a collation specific to MySQL 8 ([utf8mb4_0900_ai_ci]), and the examples in Chapter 11 pass a MySQL server version ([MySqlServerVersion]) to Pomelo; with MariaDB, these two points would need to be adjusted.

docs.title: 15.1.2. Starting and Stopping MySQL
docs.text:
The Laragon main window includes a “Start All” button that starts the servers (Apache and MySQL) and a “Stop” button that stops them. Unlike the MySQL 5 installation described in 2008, MySQL is not a Windows service that runs at system startup: it only runs when started from Laragon, which prevents it from consuming resources when not in use. The Laragon menu (right-click in the window) also allows you to start only MySQL and to select its version.

When MySQL is not running, the programs in Chapters 10 and 11 fail with an exception indicating that no connection could be established (“Unable to connect to any of the specified MySQL hosts”): This is the first thing to check if an error occurs.

docs.title: 15.1.3. The Command-Line Client
docs.text:
The Terminal button in Laragon opens a terminal where Laragon commands are available, including the MySQL command-line client [mysql]. To connect to the server, use:

> mysql -u root

then enter SQL commands ending with a semicolon ([show databases;], [use dbarticles;], [select * from articles;]) and [exit] to exit. The client can also run an SQL script, which Chapter 10 does to create its databases:

> cd csharp-oct-2026\10-adonet\sql
> mysql -u root < dbarticles.sql
> mysql -u root < dbtaxes.sql

The scripts completely recreate their database each time they are run: you can rerun them to restore the data to its initial state after testing.

docs.title: 15.1.4. The HeidiSQL graphical client
docs.text:
The Laragon Database button launches the graphical client HeidiSQL, which replaces the 2008 MySQL GUI Tools (now deprecated). Upon first launch, HeidiSQL offers a connection session that is already configured for the Laragon MySQL server (host [127.0.0.1], user [root], blank password, port 3306); simply open it. You’ll see:

  • on the left, the tree view of the server’s databases and their tables;
  • On the right, tabs that display a table's structure, its data (which can be edited directly), and a field for entering SQL queries (the "Query" tab), which are executed by [F9].

To create a database using a script from Chapter 10, open the script (via the “File” menu, using the “Load SQL file” command) in a query tab, then execute it ([F9]). You can also create a database, a user, and user permissions using the menus in HeidiSQL (right-click on the connection / “Create New” / "Database"; "Tools" menu / "User Manager"), but the SQL scripts have the advantage of being reproducible and able to be rerun.

docs.title: 15.1.5. The Databases in This Document
docs.text:
Chapters 10 and 11 use the following databases, all located on the local MySQL server:

DatabaseChapterCreation[dbarticles]10Script [10-adonet/sql/dbarticles.sql]: Table [articles] from the ADO.NET examples[dbtaxes]10script [10-adonet/sql/dbtaxes.sql]: the [brackets] table from version 6 of the [Tax] application and the [admtaxes] user[efarticles], [efshop], [efclients]11created by the programs themselves ([EnsureCreated]) or by migrations from EF Core ([dotnet ef database update])[eftaxes]11created by the migration of the project from version 7 of the application [Tax]

Once testing is complete, a database can be deleted using the SQL command [drop database name;], in the [mysql] client, or in HeidiSQL.

docs.title: 15.2. The NuGet packages used
docs.text:
The following table summarizes the NuGet libraries used by the examples, along with the versions with which the examples were tested. They are downloaded automatically by the [dotnet] command during the first compilation (so Internet access is required at that time).

PackageVersionChapters[Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection]10.0.126, 10, 11, 12[Microsoft.Extensions.Configuration.Json]10.0.126, 10, 11, 12[MSTest]4.0.26, 10[MySqlConnector]2.4.010[Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore]9.0.011[Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore.Relational]9.0.011[Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore.Design]9.0.011[Pomelo.EntityFrameworkCore.MySql]9.0.011[Microsoft.Extensions.Http]10.0.1213

The EF Core migration tool is installed once and for all using the [dotnet tool install --global dotnet-ef --version 9.0.0] command (Chapter 11). ASP.NET Core (Chapters 12 and 13) is part of the SDK and does not require any packages.

docs.title: 9. Asynchronous Programming
docs.text:
The previous chapter introduced threads: we can execute multiple pieces of code “at the same time,” synchronize them, and assign tasks to the thread pool. This chapter, which was not included in the 2008 course, addresses a related but distinct issue: how to write a program that waits a long time (for the disk, the network, or a database) without blocking threads during these waits. The answer in .NET lies in two keywords of the C# language, [async] and [await], and in one type, [Task]. They are everywhere today: the following chapters will use them to access databases ([OpenAsync], [ExecuteReaderAsync], [ToListAsync], [SaveChangesAsync]), to write TCP servers ([AcceptTcpClientAsync]), web clients ([HttpClient]), and web services using ASP.NET Core.

All examples in this chapter are single-file applications ([async-01.cs], [async-02.cs]…) that are run using [dotnet run async-NN.cs] in the [09-async] folder. Many of them measure durations using a stopwatch ([Stopwatch]): the milliseconds displayed vary from one run to another and from one machine to another (the examples were run on a dual-processor machine). It’s the orders of magnitude that matter: 1 second or 3 seconds, 300 ms or 0 ms.

docs.title: 9.1.1. Operations that wait
docs.text:
A program performs two types of work:

  • computational tasks, which occupy the processor: sorting a list, calculating a tax, analyzing a text;
  • input/output (I/O), which essentially consists of waiting for a peripheral device: reading a file from disk, sending a request to a web server and waiting for its response, executing a SQL query on a database server.

The orders of magnitude are very different. A processor executes a few billion instructions per second. A read operation on a disk (SSD) takes on the order of one-tenth of a millisecond; a round trip over a local network takes a fraction of a millisecond; a round trip to a server located on the other side of the country takes a few tens of milliseconds; and a somewhat complex SQL request can sometimes take several seconds. During these waits, the processor could have executed millions of instructions.

When a program reads a line over a network connection using a synchronous (blocking) method, the thread performing this read is blocked: it does nothing, but it still exists. It occupies memory (its stack, on the order of a megabyte), it is recognized by the operating system, and, most importantly, it is no longer available to do anything else. This isn’t a problem in a small console program that does one thing at a time. It’s much more of an issue in two situations:

  • on a server: each client served by a blocked thread ties up that thread. The 2008 course already explained this in the conclusion of its discussion of the asynchronous TCP client: if the thread pool has N threads and all N threads are performing a blocking operation, there are no threads left available for a new client. A modern web server handles thousands of simultaneous requests with just a few dozen threads: this is possible because its threads never get blocked on I/O;
  • in a graphical user interface: a single thread—the UI thread—handles clicks and redraws windows. If it is blocked by a download, the window freezes.

Asynchrony involves initiating the I/O operation, freeing up the thread while it runs (the hardware and operating system do not need it to transfer data), and then resuming work once the operation is complete, possibly on a different thread:

  • In [1], the thread T1 initiates the I/O and remains blocked until it finishes;
  • in [2], the thread T1 initiates the I/O and returns to the thread pool, where it can handle other requests. When the I/O operation completes, the system notifies .NET, which has a thread from the pool—T2 (or T1, if it is available)—execute the rest of the processing.

The [async-01.cs] program measures the difference over 100 operations, each of which waits for one second (the wait simulates I/O). It uses instructions that we will explain later in this chapter ([Task.Run], [Task.Delay], [await]); here, we are only interested in the results.

// why asynchrony: 100 operations that each wait for one second
// (a wait simulates an I/O: disk read, network request, SQL query…)
using System.Diagnostics;

const int nbOperations = 100;
Console.WriteLine($"{nbOperations} operations of one second, {Environment.ProcessorCount} processors");

// 1 - one thread per operation, each thread is blocked during the wait
var stopwatch = Stopwatch.StartNew();
var threads = new Thread[nbOperations];
for (int i = 0; i < nbOperations; i++)
{
    threads[i] = new Thread(() => Thread.Sleep(1000));
    threads[i].Start();
}
Display("1 - one thread per operation", ProcessThreads());
foreach (var thread in threads)
{
    thread.Join();
}
Display("    end");

// 2 - the operations are handed to the thread pool, but they block it
stopwatch.Restart();
var tasks = new Task[nbOperations];
for (int i = 0; i < nbOperations; i++)
{
    tasks[i] = Task.Run(() => Thread.Sleep(1000));
}
Display("2 - thread pool, blocking waits", ProcessThreads());
Task.WaitAll(tasks);
Display("    end");

// 3 - asynchronous waits: no thread is blocked during the wait
stopwatch.Restart();
for (int i = 0; i < nbOperations; i++)
{
    tasks[i] = Task.Delay(1000);
}
Display("3 - asynchronous waits", ProcessThreads());
await Task.WhenAll(tasks);
Display("    end");

// number of threads of the process, half a second after the operations are launched
int ProcessThreads()
{
    if (stopwatch.ElapsedMilliseconds < 500)
    {
        Thread.Sleep(500 - (int)stopwatch.ElapsedMilliseconds);
    }
    using var process = Process.GetCurrentProcess();
    return process.Threads.Count;
}

// display of the elapsed time and, if provided, of the number of threads
void Display(string message, int? nbThreads = null)
{
    string threadsInfo = nbThreads is null ? "" : $", {nbThreads,3} threads in the process";
    Console.WriteLine($"{message,-42} : {stopwatch.ElapsedMilliseconds,5} ms{threadsInfo}");
}

Results:

> dotnet run async-01.cs
100 operations of one second, 2 processors
1 - one thread per operation               :   526 ms, 110 threads in the process
    end                                    :  1012 ms
2 - thread pool, blocking waits            :   501 ms,  13 threads in the process
    end                                    : 24007 ms
3 - asynchronous waits                     :   501 ms,  17 threads in the process
    end                                    :  1002 ms

Comments:

  • Lines 8–21: The solution from the 2008 course, one thread per operation. Each thread executes [Thread.Sleep(1000)]: it is blocked for one second. The 100 waits occur simultaneously, and the entire process takes exactly one second (line 4), but at the cost of 100 additional threads: the process now has more than 100 threads (line 3). With 10,000 operations, 10,000 threads would be required;
  • lines 23–31: the operations are delegated to the thread pool ([Task.Run]), which was introduced in the previous chapter. The pool starts with as many threads as there are processors (2 in this case) and adds more only gradually when they are all busy, since it assumes that its threads are performing computations and that there is no need to have many more than there are processors. But here, its threads are not computing: they are idle. The operations wait for a free thread, and the whole process takes… more than twenty seconds (line 6). This is known as “thread pool starvation,” the most common flaw in servers that combine thread pools with blocking I/O;
  • lines 34–41: the waits are asynchronous ([Task.Delay] instead of [Thread.Sleep]). No thread is blocked during the wait: a system timer will wake up .NET after one second. The entire process lasts one second, and the number of threads does not increase (the threads displayed on line 7 are those that the pool created during step 2; they are idle);
  • line 51: [Process.GetCurrentProcess()] provides access to the currently running process; its property [Threads] is the collection of its threads (those of .NET and those of the system).

Let’s remember the lesson: to wait, you must not block a thread. Asynchrony does not make I/O faster; it allows you to handle many I/O operations simultaneously with few threads, and to keep the threads the application needs available (the GUI thread, the threads in a server’s pool).

docs.title: 9.1.2. Three Successive Models
docs.text:
.NET proposed three ways to write asynchronous code. The first two are still encountered in legacy code and older articles, so it’s useful to recognize them.

ModelOriginPrincipleAPM (“Asynchronous Programming Model”).NET 1.0 (2002)a pair of methods: [BeginXxx] and [EndXxx]. [BeginXxx] initiates the operation and receives a callback method ([AsyncCallback]); the callback method, executed by a thread from the pool at the end of the operation, calls [EndXxx] to retrieve the result or exception. Example: [Socket.BeginConnect] / [EndConnect], used by the asynchronous TCP client from the 2008 course.EAP (“Event-based Asynchronous Pattern”).NET 2.0 (2005)an [XxxAsync] method that initiates the operation and a [XxxCompleted] event triggered upon its completion. Examples: [WebClient.DownloadStringAsync] and [DownloadStringCompleted], the [BackgroundWorker] class (events [DoWork], [ProgressChanged], [RunWorkerCompleted]) studied in the 2008 course.TAP (“Task-based Asynchronous Pattern”).NET 4.0 (2010), C# 5 (2012)a method [XxxAsync] that returns a task ([Task] or [Task<T>]) representing the current operation. The calling code waits for the task using the keyword [await]. This is the current model, the only one used in the rest of the course.

The APM and EAP patterns share the same flaw: the code is broken up into pieces. What naturally reads as “connect, then read, then display” becomes a method that initiates the connection, a callback method that starts reading, and another callback method that displays the data; variables must be shared among these methods, exceptions are handled in different places, and a simple loop (“read as long as there is data”) becomes a callback method that recursively calls itself, like the read method ([lecture]) from the 2008 course. The TAP pattern, along with [async] and [await], allows you to write asynchronous code that takes the form of synchronous code.

The program [async-02.cs] writes the same TCP client according to the two extreme models, APM and TAP. It also contains a small server, run by a thread, that responds to two clients (network programming will be covered in detail in Chapter 12; for now, it suffices to know that a client connects to the server and reads the message the server sends it).

// the same TCP client written with the 2008 APM model then with the current TAP model
using System.Net;
using System.Net.Sockets;
using System.Text;

const int port = 27500;
// a minimal server, executed by a thread: it serves two clients then stops
var listener = new TcpListener(IPAddress.Loopback, port);
listener.Start();
var server = new Thread(() =>
{
    for (int i = 1; i <= 2; i++)
    {
        using Socket service = listener.AcceptSocket();
        // the server takes its time to answer
        Thread.Sleep(500);
        service.Send(Encoding.UTF8.GetBytes($"Hello client no. {i}"));
    }
    listener.Stop();
});
server.Start();
Display("start of the program");

// 1 - the APM model (Asynchronous Programming Model): BeginXxx / EndXxx and callback methods
var end = new ManualResetEventSlim(false);
byte[] buffer = new byte[1024];
var client = new Socket(AddressFamily.InterNetwork, SocketType.Stream, ProtocolType.Tcp);
// we launch the connection, giving the method to call back when it is done
client.BeginConnect(IPAddress.Loopback, port, Connected, client);
Display("APM: connection launched, the program goes on");
// the main thread has nothing left to do: it waits for the signal of the last callback method
end.Wait();

// callback method no. 1: the connection is made
void Connected(IAsyncResult result)
{
    // we retrieve the object passed as the last parameter of BeginConnect
    var socket = (Socket)result.AsyncState!;
    // we end the operation (it is EndConnect that would throw the exception on failure)
    socket.EndConnect(result);
    Display("APM: connected, read launched");
    // we launch the reading of the server's answer with another callback method
    socket.BeginReceive(buffer, 0, buffer.Length, SocketFlags.None, Received, socket);
}

// callback method no. 2: data has arrived
void Received(IAsyncResult result)
{
    var socket = (Socket)result.AsyncState!;
    int nbBytes = socket.EndReceive(result);
    Display($"APM: received [{Encoding.UTF8.GetString(buffer, 0, nbBytes)}]");
    socket.Close();
    // we notify the main thread
    end.Set();
}

// 2 - the TAP model (Task-based Asynchronous Pattern): XxxAsync and await
using (var client2 = new Socket(AddressFamily.InterNetwork, SocketType.Stream, ProtocolType.Tcp))
{
    await client2.ConnectAsync(IPAddress.Loopback, port);
    Display("TAP: connected, read launched");
    int nbBytes = await client2.ReceiveAsync(buffer);
    Display($"TAP: received [{Encoding.UTF8.GetString(buffer, 0, nbBytes)}]");
}
server.Join();

// display prefixed by the number of the thread that executes it
static void Display(string message)
{
    Console.WriteLine($"[thread {Environment.CurrentManagedThreadId,2}] {message}");
}

Results:

> dotnet run async-02.cs
[thread  1] start of the program
[thread  1] APM: connection launched, the program goes on
[thread  6] APM: connected, read launched
[thread  6] APM: received [Hello client no. 1]
[thread  6] TAP: connected, read launched
[thread  6] TAP: received [Hello client no. 2]

Comments:

  • lines 8–21: the server. It listens on port 27500 of the local machine ([IPAddress.Loopback], i.e., 127.0.0.1), accepts two connections one after the other, and sends each client a welcome message after half a second;
  • lines 24–54: The client written according to the APM pattern, as in the 2008 course:
    • line 29: [BeginConnect] initiates the connection and immediately yields control (line 3 of the results). Its last two parameters are the callback method to be invoked at the end of the connection, [Connected], and an arbitrary object that the callback method will find in the [AsyncState] property of its [IAsyncResult] parameter: in this case, the socket itself;
    • line 32: the main thread has nothing left to do. To prevent the program from terminating before the exchange is complete, it waits for a signal that will be sent by the last callback method: a [ManualResetEventSlim] object, whose [Wait] method blocks the thread that calls it until another thread calls its [Set] method (this is a lightweight version of the [AutoResetEvent] barriers seen with threads);
    • lines 35–43: the connection callback method. It must call [EndConnect] with the received parameter: this call terminates the operation and would throw an exception if the connection had failed. It then initiates the read operation with [BeginReceive], specifying a second callback method, [Received];
    • lines 47–54: the read callback retrieves the number of bytes received using [EndReceive], displays the message, closes the socket, and releases the main thread;
    • the results show that the callback methods are executed by a thread other than the main thread (a thread from the pool, not thread 1);
  • lines 57–65: the same client using the TAP model. [ConnectAsync] and [ReceiveAsync] return tasks, and [await] waits for them to finish without blocking the thread: The code reads from top to bottom like synchronous code; the variables are ordinary local variables; there are no callback methods or signals to manage. The thread executing the rest of the code is generally no longer Thread 1: we’ll explain why in the section “Which thread executes the rest?”;
  • Line 68: Each display is prefixed with the number of the thread executing it, [Environment.CurrentManagedThreadId].

It is not necessary to remember the APM pattern. If you need to use an older library that only provides this pattern, the method [Task.Factory.FromAsync] converts a pair [BeginXxx] / [EndXxx] into a method that returns a [Task]; and we will see in the section on [TaskCompletionSource] how to convert an event-based API (EAP model) into a task.

docs.title: 9.2. Tasks: Task and Task<T>
docs.text:
A task is an object that represents an ongoing or completed operation:

  • [Task] represents an operation that does not return a result;
  • [Task<T>] represents an operation that will return a result of type [T]. [Task<T>] derives from [Task].

A task is not a thread. A task can be executed by a thread from the pool (as is the case with tasks created by [Task.Run]), but many tasks are not executed by any thread: the task returned by [Task.Delay(1000)] is simply “completed” by a timer after one second; the task returned by [ReceiveAsync] is completed when the system signals that data has arrived. A task is a promise of a result, which can be queried (is it finished? was it successful?) and waited for.

The program [async-03.cs] demonstrates the main ways to create and wait for a task:

// tasks: creation, wait, status, result, continuation

// 1 - Task.Run hands a processing to the thread pool and returns a Task<T> task
Task<long> task1 = Task.Run(() =>
{
    // a computation of a few tenths of a second
    long sum = 0;
    for (int i = 1; i <= 200_000_000; i++)
    {
        sum += i % 7;
    }
    return sum;
});
Console.WriteLine($"task1 launched, status: {task1.Status}");
// await suspends the program until the end of the task and returns its result
long result = await task1;
Console.WriteLine($"task1 finished, status: {task1.Status}, result: {result}");

// 2 - Task.Delay returns a task that ends after a delay, without occupying a thread
Task task2 = Task.Delay(300);
Console.WriteLine($"task2 launched, status: {task2.Status}");
await task2;
Console.WriteLine($"task2 finished, status: {task2.Status}");

// 3 - tasks that are already finished
Task<int> task3 = Task.FromResult(42);
Task task4 = Task.CompletedTask;
Console.WriteLine($"task3: status {task3.Status}, result {await task3} ; task4: status {task4.Status}");

// 4 - a task that fails: await rethrows its exception
Task<int> task5 = Task.Run(() => int.Parse("abc"));
try
{
    await task5;
}
catch (FormatException e)
{
    Console.WriteLine($"task5: status {task5.Status}, {e.GetType().Name}: {e.Message}");
}

// 5 - the blocking forms Wait() and Result: the current thread is blocked during the wait
Task<string> task6 = Task.Run(() =>
{
    Thread.Sleep(300);
    return "done";
});
task6.Wait();
Console.WriteLine($"task6: Wait() then Result = {task6.Result}");

// 6 - a continuation: what to do when the task is finished
Task<int> task7 = Task.Delay(300).ContinueWith(t => 2 * 21);
Console.WriteLine($"task7: result of the continuation = {await task7}");

// 7 - IsCompleted, IsCompletedSuccessfully, IsFaulted, IsCanceled
Console.WriteLine($"task1: IsCompletedSuccessfully={task1.IsCompletedSuccessfully}, task5: IsCompleted={task5.IsCompleted}, IsFaulted={task5.IsFaulted}");
Console.WriteLine($"task5.Exception: {task5.Exception?.GetType().Name}, {task5.Exception?.InnerException?.GetType().Name}");

Results:

> dotnet run async-03.cs
task1 launched, status: WaitingToRun
task1 finished, status: RanToCompletion, result: 599999998
task2 launched, status: WaitingForActivation
task2 finished, status: RanToCompletion
task3: status RanToCompletion, result 42 ; task4: status RanToCompletion
task5: status Faulted, FormatException: The input string 'abc' was not in a correct format.
task6: Wait() then Result = done
task7: result of the continuation = 42
task1: IsCompletedSuccessfully=True, task5: IsCompleted=True, IsFaulted=True
task5.Exception: AggregateException, FormatException

Comments:

  • Lines 4–12: [Task.Run] assigns a function to the thread pool and immediately returns a task representing its execution. The function returns a [long], so the task is of type [Task<long>]. [Task.Run] is the tool for the calculations to be executed in the background; it must not be used to “make asynchronous” a blocking I/O operation (which is what step 2 of [async-01.cs] did);
  • Line 14: The [Status] property returns the task’s status. Immediately after it is launched, the task waits here for a thread from the pool to take it on ([WaitingToRun]); depending on the machine’s load, you might also see [Running] (running);
  • Line 16: [await task1] waits for the task to finish without blocking the thread and returns its result, which in this case is of type [long]. The expression [await t] is of type [T] if [t] is of type [Task<T>], and has no value if [t] is of type [Task];
