  • line 9: the property [MaxDegreeOfParallelism] of [ParallelOptions] sets the maximum number of concurrent operations (by default, the number of processors). A cancellation token ([CancellationToken]) can also be set here;
  • Lines 10–18: [Parallel.ForEachAsync] receives the collection, the options, and an asynchronous function (an [async] lambda) that is called for each element with the element and a cancellation token, to be passed to the function’s asynchronous operations. [Parallel.ForEachAsync] returns a task that completes when all elements have been processed;
  • lines 13–17: the functions run simultaneously on multiple threads: the counter [inProgress] that they share is modified atomically using the [Interlocked] class from the previous chapter;
  • The results show three waves of three pages: as soon as one page is finished, another begins, and the number of downloads in progress never exceeds 3. The entire process takes 3 seconds instead of 9. When two threads write at nearly the same time, the order of the lines may vary from one execution to another, and a displayed time may even be slightly earlier than that of the previous line;
  • only two or three threads executed all the functions: during wait periods, no thread is busy.

docs.title: 9.11.2. Producer/Consumer: System.Threading.Channels
docs.text:
The previous chapter introduced the producer/consumer pattern using the [BlockingCollection<T>] collection: producer threads enqueue elements into a queue, and consumer threads dequeue them; [Take] (or the enumeration [GetConsumingEnumerable]) blocks a consumer as long as the queue is empty, while [Add] blocks a producer as long as a bounded queue is full. These waits block threads. Channels in the [System.Threading.Channels] namespace (.NET Core 3.0) provide the same service with asynchronous waits:

  • [Channel.CreateBounded<T>(capacity)] creates a bounded channel, [Channel.CreateUnbounded<T>()] creates an unbounded channel;
  • the [Writer] property ([ChannelWriter<T>]) is used by producers: [WriteAsync] publishes an item (waiting asynchronously for space to become available), [TryWrite] attempts to add it immediately, [Complete] indicates that there will be no more elements;
  • The property [Reader] ([ChannelReader<T>]) is used by consumers: [ReadAsync] retrieves an element, while [ReadAllAsync] returns an asynchronous stream of all elements, which ends when the channel is closed by [Complete] and is empty.

The program [async-21.cs] processes orders, generated every 50 ms, using two consumers that each take 400 ms to process an order:

// producer / consumers with a channel (System.Threading.Channels)
using System.Diagnostics;
using System.Threading.Channels;

var stopwatch = Stopwatch.StartNew();
// a bounded channel: it contains at most 2 orders waiting to be processed
Channel<int> channel = Channel.CreateBounded<int>(2);

// the producer and two consumers work at the same time
Task producer = ProduceAsync(channel.Writer, 8);
Task consumer1 = ConsumeAsync("C1", channel.Reader);
Task consumer2 = ConsumeAsync("C2", channel.Reader);
await Task.WhenAll(producer, consumer1, consumer2);
Display("all the orders have been processed");

// the producer: one order every 50 ms
async Task ProduceAsync(ChannelWriter<int> writer, int nbOrders)
{
    for (int i = 1; i <= nbOrders; i++)
    {
        await Task.Delay(50);
        // TryWrite drops the order right away if there is room in the channel
        if (writer.TryWrite(i))
        {
            Display($"P  : order {i} dropped");
        }
        else
        {
            // channel full: WriteAsync waits (without blocking a thread) for a slot to be freed
            Display($"P  : channel full, order {i} waits");
            await writer.WriteAsync(i);
            Display($"P  : order {i} dropped");
        }
    }
    // nothing more will be written: the consumers will leave their loop
    writer.Complete();
    Display("P  : end of the production");
}

// a consumer: processing an order takes 400 ms
async Task ConsumeAsync(string name, ChannelReader<int> reader)
{
    // ReadAllAsync returns an asynchronous stream that ends when the channel is closed and empty
    await foreach (int order in reader.ReadAllAsync())
    {
        Display($"{name} : processing of order {order}");
        await Task.Delay(400);
    }
    Display($"{name} : no more orders");
}

void Display(string message)
{
    Console.WriteLine($"{stopwatch.ElapsedMilliseconds,5} ms : {message}");
}

Results:

> dotnet run async-21.cs
   63 ms : C1 : processing of order 1
   63 ms : P  : order 1 dropped
  130 ms : P  : order 2 dropped
  130 ms : C2 : processing of order 2
  181 ms : P  : order 3 dropped
  233 ms : P  : order 4 dropped
  284 ms : P  : channel full, order 5 waits
  479 ms : P  : order 5 dropped
  479 ms : C1 : processing of order 3
  530 ms : P  : channel full, order 6 waits
  530 ms : C2 : processing of order 4
  530 ms : P  : order 6 dropped
  583 ms : P  : channel full, order 7 waits
  879 ms : C1 : processing of order 5
  879 ms : P  : order 7 dropped
  930 ms : P  : channel full, order 8 waits
  930 ms : C2 : processing of order 6
  930 ms : P  : order 8 dropped
  935 ms : P  : end of the production
 1277 ms : C1 : processing of order 7
 1330 ms : C2 : processing of order 8
 1679 ms : C1 : no more orders
 1731 ms : C2 : no more orders
 1731 ms : all the orders have been processed

Comments:

  • line 7: an integer queue (containing the order numbers) that holds at most 2 pending orders;
  • Lines 10–13: The producer and the two consumers are three asynchronous methods launched simultaneously; the program waits for all three to finish;
  • lines 23–31: the producer attempts to submit each order using [TryWrite]. If the channel is full, it signals this and waits for space to become available with [WriteAsync]: the producer is throttled to the consumers’ pace (lines 8–9), without any thread being blocked. This is the benefit of a bounded channel: a producer that is too fast cannot fill up the memory;
  • line 36: production is complete. The consumers will empty the channel and then exit their loop;
  • lines 44–49: Each consumer processes the asynchronous stream [ReadAllAsync]. An order is delivered to only one consumer: orders are distributed between C1 and C2 based on their availability;
  • As in the previous example, two lines displayed at nearly the same time may appear out of order (the displayed timestamps are therefore not always in ascending order).

Channels are the modern tool for the producer-consumer pattern, both between asynchronous methods and between threads.

docs.title: 9.12. Time: PeriodicTimer and TimeProvider
docs.text:
Two recent classes round out the time-related tools:

  • [PeriodicTimer] (.NET 6) is a timer used with [await]: its method [WaitForNextTickAsync] returns a task that completes at the next “tick.” Unlike [System.Threading.Timer] (used in [async-19.cs]), which calls a callback method on a thread from the pool—possibly while the previous call is still in progress— [PeriodicTimer] is written as a simple loop and never overlaps two executions;
  • [TimeProvider] (.NET 8) is an abstract class that represents the clock: the current time ([GetUtcNow], [GetLocalNow]), timing ([GetTimestamp], [GetElapsedTime]), and the creation of timers. [TimeProvider.System] is the system clock. A class that depends on the time receives a [TimeProvider] instead of using [DateTime.Now] directly: it can then be tested with a controlled clock.

The program [async-22.cs] uses both:

// time: PeriodicTimer and TimeProvider
// 1 - PeriodicTimer: an action every 500 ms, stopped after 2.2 seconds
TimeProvider clock = TimeProvider.System;
long start = clock.GetTimestamp();
using (var timer = new PeriodicTimer(TimeSpan.FromMilliseconds(500)))
using (var stop = new CancellationTokenSource(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(2.2)))
{
    int nbTicks = 0;
    try
    {
        // WaitForNextTickAsync returns true on each tick, false if the timer is stopped by Dispose
        while (await timer.WaitForNextTickAsync(stop.Token))
        {
            nbTicks++;
            Console.WriteLine($"{clock.GetElapsedTime(start).TotalMilliseconds,6:F0} ms : tick no. {nbTicks}");
        }
    }
    catch (OperationCanceledException)
    {
        Console.WriteLine($"{clock.GetElapsedTime(start).TotalMilliseconds,6:F0} ms : timer stopped after {nbTicks} ticks");
    }
}

// 2 - TimeProvider: a class that depends on the time receives its clock instead of reading DateTime.Now
var morning = new FixedClock(new DateTimeOffset(2026, 10, 3, 9, 30, 0, TimeSpan.Zero));
var evening = new FixedClock(new DateTimeOffset(2026, 10, 3, 19, 45, 0, TimeSpan.Zero));
Console.WriteLine(new Welcome(morning).Greet("Pierre"));
Console.WriteLine(new Welcome(evening).Greet("Pierre"));

// a class that depends on the current time
class Welcome(TimeProvider clock)
{
    public string Greet(string name)
    {
        DateTimeOffset now = clock.GetLocalNow();
        string greeting = now.Hour < 18 ? "Hello" : "Good evening";
        return $"[{now:dd/MM/yyyy HH:mm}] {greeting} {name}";
    }
}

// a stopped clock, for the tests: it always gives the same time (in universal time)
class FixedClock(DateTimeOffset instant) : TimeProvider
{
    public override DateTimeOffset GetUtcNow() => instant;
    public override TimeZoneInfo LocalTimeZone => TimeZoneInfo.Utc;
}

Results:

> dotnet run async-22.cs
   507 ms : tick no. 1
  1003 ms : tick no. 2
  1505 ms : tick no. 3
  2001 ms : tick no. 4
  2227 ms : timer stopped after 4 ticks
[03/10/2026 09:30] Hello Pierre
[03/10/2026 19:45] Good evening Pierre

Comments:

  • Lines 5–20: a 500-ms timer and a 2.2-second cancel source. [WaitForNextTickAsync(token)] returns [true] on each clock pulse and [false] if the timer has been cleared ([Dispose]); here, the cancellation stops the loop after 4 ticks;
  • line 4: [GetTimestamp] and [GetElapsedTime] from [TimeProvider] measure a duration, just like the methods of the same name in [Stopwatch];
  • Lines 31–37: The class [Welcome] says “Hello” or “Good evening” depending on the time. It receives its clock in its primary constructor instead of reading from [DateTime.Now]: this is an injected dependency, just as the [dao] layer is injected into the [business] layer in Chapter 6;
  • Lines 42–45: A stopped clock, derived from [TimeProvider], which redefines universal time and the time zone. It allows you to verify the behavior of [Welcome] in the morning and evening without having to wait until nightfall. The NuGet package [Microsoft.Extensions.TimeProvider.Testing] provides a more comprehensive test clock, [FakeTimeProvider], which can be advanced at will, including for delays and timers ([Task.Delay(TimeSpan, TimeProvider)], [new PeriodicTimer(TimeSpan, TimeProvider)]).

docs.title: 9.13. Application: Tax Calculation with Asynchronous I/O
docs.text:
The program [async-23.cs] brings together several tools from this chapter related to the tax calculation that runs through the whole course. It reads the tax brackets from the file [TaxData.txt] (which has already been used) and reads a list of taxpayers from the file [taxpayers.txt]:

y 2 60000
y 3 60000
n 0 60000
n 2 25000
y 5 120000
x 1 20000
y 1 -5

(each line contains: married [y/n], number of children, annual salary), calculates each taxpayer’s tax, and writes the results to the file [results.txt]. All I/O operations are asynchronous, and the entire process is limited to 10 seconds.

// application: the tax calculation with asynchronous input / output
// - the brackets are read from [TaxData.txt], the taxpayers from [taxpayers.txt]
// - the results are written to [results.txt]
using System.Globalization;

using var cancellation = new CancellationTokenSource(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(10));
try
{
    TaxBracket[] brackets = await LoadBracketsAsync("TaxData.txt", cancellation.Token);
    int nbResults = await CalculateTaxesAsync(brackets, "taxpayers.txt", "results.txt", cancellation.Token);
    Console.WriteLine($"{nbResults} lines written to [results.txt]:");
    Console.Write(await File.ReadAllTextAsync("results.txt", cancellation.Token));
}
catch (OperationCanceledException)
{
    Console.WriteLine("processing abandoned: timeout exceeded");
}
catch (Exception e) when (e is IOException or FormatException)
{
    Console.WriteLine($"error: {e.GetType().Name} : {e.Message}");
}

// reads the tax brackets (limit:coeffR:coeffN, decimal point)
static async Task<TaxBracket[]> LoadBracketsAsync(string file, CancellationToken token)
{
    string[] lines = await File.ReadAllLinesAsync(file, token);
    return [.. lines.Where(l => l.Trim() != "").Select(TaxBracket.Parse)];
}

// reads the taxpayers (married children salary), calculates their tax and writes the results
static async Task<int> CalculateTaxesAsync(TaxBracket[] brackets, string input, string output, CancellationToken token)
{
    int nbLines = 0;
    await using var writer = new StreamWriter(output);
    await foreach (string line in File.ReadLinesAsync(input, token))
    {
        string[] fields = line.Split(' ', StringSplitOptions.RemoveEmptyEntries);
        string result = fields switch
        {
            [var m, var c, var s] when m is "y" or "n" && int.TryParse(c, out int children) && children >= 0
                                       && int.TryParse(s, out int salary) && salary >= 0
                => $"tax = {CalculateTax(brackets, m == "y", children, salary)} €",
            _ => "incorrect line",
        };
        await writer.WriteLineAsync($"{line,-12} : {result}");
        nbLines++;
    }
    return nbLines;
}

// the tax calculation (2004 scale on 2003 income, kept for the exercise)
static int CalculateTax(TaxBracket[] brackets, bool married, int nbChildren, int salary)
{
    decimal shares = married ? nbChildren / 2m + 2 : nbChildren / 2m + 1;
    if (nbChildren >= 3)
    {
        shares += 0.5m;
    }
    decimal income = 0.72m * salary;
    decimal quotient = income / shares;
    // the first bracket whose limit exceeds the family quotient, otherwise the last one
    TaxBracket bracket = brackets.FirstOrDefault(t => quotient <= t.Limit, brackets[^1]);
    return (int)(bracket.CoeffR * income - bracket.CoeffN * shares);
}

// a tax bracket
readonly record struct TaxBracket(decimal Limit, decimal CoeffR, decimal CoeffN)
{
    public static TaxBracket Parse(string line)
    {
        string[] fields = line.Split(':');
        return new TaxBracket(decimal.Parse(fields[0], CultureInfo.InvariantCulture),
                                decimal.Parse(fields[1], CultureInfo.InvariantCulture),
                                decimal.Parse(fields[2], CultureInfo.InvariantCulture));
    }
}

Results:

> dotnet run async-23.cs
7 lines written to [results.txt]:
y 2 60000    : tax = 4282 €
y 3 60000    : tax = 2959 €
n 0 60000    : tax = 11519 €
n 2 25000    : tax = 792 €
y 5 120000   : tax = 11109 €
x 1 20000    : incorrect line
y 1 -5       : incorrect line

Comments:

  • line 6: a cancellation source that limits the entire process to 10 seconds. Its token is passed to all asynchronous methods;
  • Lines 24–27: Reading the brackets. The collection expression with spreading [[.. sequence]] converts the LINQ sequence into an array;
  • Lines 31–48: processing of taxpayers. The rows are read one by one using the asynchronous stream [File.ReadLinesAsync], and the results are written using [WriteLineAsync] into a [StreamWriter] released by [await using];
  • Lines 38–43: Validation of a line using a [switch] expression with a three-element list pattern ([[var m, var c, var s]]) and a [when] clause that checks the three fields;
  • lines 52–63: the tax calculation. The [FirstOrDefault] method of LINQ, with a default value, returns the first bracket whose limit is greater than or equal to the family quotient, or the last bracket if none applies (without modifying the data, unlike the 2008 code);
  • lines 14–20: Possible errors are handled in a single location within the main program: time-limit violations, and I/O or format errors (missing file, incorrectly entered number), filtered by [when] with an [or] pattern;
  • The results provide the benchmark values: €4,282 for a married couple with 2 children and a combined income of €60,000; €2,959 with 3 children; and €11,519 for a single person without children.

The calculation itself is synchronous: it performs no I/O and takes a few microseconds. It would be pointless—and even harmful—to make it asynchronous. Only operations that involve waiting are made asynchronous.

docs.title: 9.14. The Golden Rules
docs.text:
Let’s summarize the rules of asynchronous programming with .NET:

  • async all the way: a method that waits for an asynchronous operation becomes asynchronous itself ([async Task]), and so do its callers, all the way back to the entry point ([Main] asynchronous, event handler, controller action ASP.NET Core). Mixing asynchronous code with blocking waits negates the benefits of asynchrony;
  • do not use [.Result], [.Wait()], or [Task.WaitAll] on an unfinished task: use [await], [Task.WhenAll], [Task.WhenAny], or [Task.WhenEach] instead. These blocking forms freeze a thread and can cause permanent deadlocks in graphical applications;
  • Do not use [Thread.Sleep] in asynchronous code: use [await Task.Delay(...)] instead;
  • Do not write [async void] methods, except in GUI event handlers; an asynchronous method should use [Task] or [Task<T>] (in exceptional cases, [ValueTask<T>]);
  • The name of an asynchronous method ends with [Async]: [CalculateTaxesAsync], [ReadRateAsync];
  • A cancelable asynchronous method receives a [CancellationToken] as its last parameter and passes it to all the asynchronous operations it calls; a canceled operation ends with an [OperationCanceledException];
  • [Task.Run] is reserved for calculations that you want to execute in the background (to avoid blocking a GUI thread, for example). Do not wrap a synchronous I/O operation in [Task.Run] to “make it asynchronous”: use the [XxxAsync] version of the operation;
  • start first, then wait: to run multiple independent operations simultaneously, start them all and then wait for them using [Task.WhenAll]; to limit the number of operations, use [Parallel.ForEachAsync] or a channel;
  • [ConfigureAwait(false)] is used in libraries, not in applications;
  • a launched task must be waited for (or explicitly ignored using [_ =], while handling its exceptions): a forgotten task hides its exceptions and may be interrupted by the end of the program.

The following table summarizes the equivalences between the world of threads (previous chapter, 2008 course) and that of tasks:

Threads, blocking waitsTasks, asynchronous waits[Thread.Sleep(1000)][await Task.Delay(1000)][thread.Start()] followed by [thread.Join()][var t = MethodAsync();] then [await t]Wait for multiple threads ([Join] in a loop, [Task.WaitAll])[await Task.WhenAll(...)][Thread.Abort()] (obsolete), [BackgroundWorker.CancelAsync][CancellationTokenSource.Cancel()] and [CancellationToken][BackgroundWorker.ReportProgress] / [ProgressChanged][IProgress<T>.Report][BackgroundWorker.RunWorkerCompleted]The code following [await][BeginXxx] / [EndXxx] and callback methods (APM)[await XxxAsync(...)][Control.Invoke] to return to the interface thread[await], which automatically returns to the synchronization context[BlockingCollection<T>] ([Add] / [GetConsumingEnumerable])[Channel<T>] ([WriteAsync] / [ReadAllAsync])[System.Threading.Timer][PeriodicTimer]

The following chapters will apply these rules: asynchronous database access with ADO.NET (Chapter 10) and Entity Framework Core (Chapter 11), asynchronous multi-client TCP server and [HttpClient] client (Chapter 12), ASP.NET Core web services and their [HttpClient] clients (Chapter 13).

docs.title: 4.1.1. Overview
docs.text:
We will now explore object-oriented programming through examples. An object is an entity that contains data defining its state (referred to as fields, attributes, etc.) and functions (referred to as methods). An object is created based on a template called a class:

public class C1
{
    Type1 p1;          // field p1
    Type2 p2;          // field p2
    ...
    Type3 M3(...)      // method M3
    {
        ...
    }
    Type4 M4(...)      // method M4
    {
        ...
    }
    ...
}

Starting from the previous class [C1], you can create many objects such as [O1], [O2], … All of them will have the fields [p1], [p2], … and the methods [M3], [M4], … However, they will have different values for their [pi] fields, thus each having its own unique state. If [o1] is an object of type [C1], [o1.p1] refers to the field [p1] of [o1], and [o1.M3] refers to the method [M3] of [o1].

Let’s consider an initial object model: the [Person] class.

docs.title: 4.1.2. Creating the C# Project
docs.text:
In the examples from the previous chapter, a program fit into a single source file. From now on, a program may consist of multiple source files: one class per file, plus the main program. These files are grouped together in a project. The 2008 course created projects using the Visual Studio 2008 wizards; here we use the command-line tool [dotnet], which works the same way on Windows, Linux, and macOS. Chapter 2 showed how to open the same project in VS Code or Visual Studio.

In a terminal, navigate to the [04-classes] folder and create a console project named [Persons]:

> dotnet new console -n Persons
The template "Console App" was created successfully.

Processing post-creation actions...
Restoring .../04-classes/Persons/Persons.csproj:
  Determining projects to restore...
  Restored .../04-classes/Persons/Persons.csproj (in 126 ms).
Restore succeeded.

The command creates a folder named [Persons] containing two files. The file [Persons.csproj] describes the project:

<Project Sdk="Microsoft.NET.Sdk">

  <PropertyGroup>
    <OutputType>Exe</OutputType>
    <TargetFramework>net10.0</TargetFramework>
    <ImplicitUsings>enable</ImplicitUsings>
    <Nullable>enable</Nullable>
  </PropertyGroup>

</Project>
  • Line 4: The project produces an executable;
  • line 5: the target program is .NET 10;
  • line 6: a set of common namespaces ([System], [System.IO], [System.Collections.Generic], [System.Linq], …) is implicitly imported into all source files in the project. This is why we can write *[Console.WriteLine] without the ***[using System;]** clause;
  • Line 7: Nullable reference types are enabled. The compiler issues a warning for any reference-type variable (a string, an object) that might take on the value [null] without the program expecting it. We’ll return to this in the section dedicated to these types; for now, just keep in mind that our programs must compile without any warnings.

The second file, [Program.cs], contains the main program. All [*.cs] files in the project folder (and its subfolders) are part of the project: to add a [Person] class, simply create the file [Person.cs] in the [Persons] folder. To run the project, type [dotnet run] in its folder: the command compiles the project, if it has changed, and then runs it.

All the projects in this chapter are grouped into a solution—a file that references a set of projects—which VS Code or Visual Studio can open all at once. The [.slnx] (XML) format, supported by the [dotnet] command since .NET 9 and the default format since .NET 10, replaces the old [.sln] format:

> dotnet new sln --format slnx -n 04-classes
The template "Solution File" was created successfully.

> dotnet sln 04-classes.slnx add Persons/Persons.csproj
Project `Persons/Persons.csproj` added to the solution.

The [dotnet build 04-classes.slnx] command then compiles all projects in the solution.

docs.title: 4.1.3. Definition of the Person class
docs.text:
The definition of the [Person] class in the source file [Person.cs] will be as follows:

namespace Persons;

public class Person
{
    // attributes (fields)
    private string firstName = "";
    private string lastName = "";
    private int age;

    // method
    public void Initialize(string p, string n, int age)
    {
        this.firstName = p;
        this.lastName = n;
        this.age = age;
    }

    // method
    public void Identify()
    {
        Console.WriteLine($"[{firstName}, {lastName}, {age}]");
    }
}
  • Line 1: The class belongs to the [Persons] namespace (the project name). This form, [namespace Persons;]—known as “file scope”—places all types in the file within the namespace. Namespaces are discussed at the end of the chapter;
  • Lines 6–8: The class’s three fields. The two strings are initialized with the empty string; otherwise, they would be set to [null] when the object is created, and the compiler—which has nullable types enabled—would issue a warning;
  • lines 11–15: a method that sets the object’s state;
  • lines 19–21: a method that displays the object’s state.

Here we have the definition of a class, and thus a data type. When we create variables of this type, we call them objects or class instances. A class is therefore a template from which objects are constructed.

The members of a class can be data (fields), methods (functions), or properties. Properties are special methods used to retrieve or set the value of an object’s fields. These members can be accompanied by one of the following keywords:

KeywordAccess[private]A private member is accessible only by the class’s internal methods. This is the default access level[public]A public member is accessible by any method, whether or not it is defined within the class[protected]A protected member is accessible only through the internal methods of the class or a derived class (see the concept of inheritance below)[internal]An internal member is accessible by any method within the same assembly (the same project)

In general, a class’s data is declared private, while its methods and properties are declared public. This means that the user of an object (the programmer):

  • will not have direct access to the object’s private data;
  • can call the object’s public methods, including those that provide access to its private data.

The syntax for declaring a class [C] is as follows:

public class C
{
    private private data, method or property;
    public public data, method or property;
    protected protected data, method or property;
}

The order in which the members [private], [protected], and [public] are declared is arbitrary.

docs.title: 4.1.4. The Initialize method
docs.text:
What is the purpose of the [Initialize] method? Because [lastName], [firstName], and [age] are private members of the [Person] class, the statements:

Person p1;
p1.firstName = "Jean";
p1.lastName = "Dupont";
p1.age = 30;

are invalid. We need to initialize an object of type [Person] using a public method. This is the purpose of the [Initialize] method. We’ll write:

Person p1;
p1.Initialize("Jean", "Dupont", 30);

The notation [p1.Initialize] is valid because [Initialize] is publicly accessible.

docs.title: 4.1.5. The new operator
docs.text:
However, the previous sequence of statements is incorrect. The statement

Person p1;

declares [p1] as a reference to an object of type [Person]. This object does not yet exist, and therefore [p1] is not initialized. When we then write [p1.Initialize("Jean", "Dupont", 30)], we call the method [Initialize] of the object referenced by [p1]. However, this object does not exist, and the compiler reports the error: the local variable [p1] has not been assigned a value. If we write:

Person? p1 = null;
p1.Initialize("Jean", "Dupont", 30);

we explicitly indicate with the keyword [null] that the variable [p1] does not yet reference any object (the question mark in [Person?] indicates that the variable may be set to [null]). The compiler then issues only a warning (dereferencing a null reference), and at runtime, the method call throws a [NullReferenceException] exception. For [p1] to reference an object, you must write:

Person p1 = new Person();

This creates an object of type [Person] that has not yet been initialized: its fields have their default values, in this case the empty string for [lastName] and [firstName], and 0 for [age] (a numeric field without an explicit initial value is 0; a reference-type field is [null]). Now that [p1] references an object, the initialization statement for that object, [p1.Initialize("Jean", "Dupont", 30)], is valid.

docs.title: 4.1.6. The this keyword
docs.text:
Let’s look at the code for the [Initialize] method:

    public void Initialize(string p, string n, int age)
    {
        this.firstName = p;
        this.lastName = n;
        this.age = age;
    }

The statement [this.firstName = p] means that the field [firstName] of the current object ([this]) is assigned the value [p]. The keyword [this] refers to the current object—the one on which the method is being executed. How do we know this? Let’s look at how the object referenced by [p1] is initialized in the calling program:

p1.Initialize("Jean", "Dupont", 30);

It is the method [Initialize] of the object [p1] that is called. When, within this method, the object [this] is referenced, it actually refers to the object [p1]. The method [Initialize] could also have been written as follows:

    public void Initialize(string p, string n, int age)
    {
        firstName = p;
        lastName = n;
        this.age = age;
    }

When a method of an object references a field [A] of that object, the notation [this.A] is implied. It must be used explicitly when there is a conflict of identifiers. This is the case with the statement [this.age = age;], where [age] refers to both a field of the current object and the parameter [age] received by the method. In this case, the ambiguity must be resolved by referring to the field [age] as [this.age].

docs.title: 4.1.7. A Test Program
docs.text:
Here is a short test program. It is written in the source file [Program.cs] of the project:

using Persons;

// a Person object
Person p1 = new Person();
p1.Initialize("Jean", "Dupont", 30);
p1.Identify();
  • Line 1: The main program is written using high-level statements that do not belong to any namespace. To refer to the class [Person] by its name alone, you must import its namespace [Persons] using the clause [using];
  • Line 4: Creation of a [Person] object referenced by [p1];
  • Line 5: Initialize the object;
  • Line 6: Display its status.

Results:

> dotnet run
[Jean, Dupont, 30]

docs.title: 4.1.8. Single-file applications
docs.text:
For a short example, a project is unnecessarily cumbersome. Since version 10, a standalone source file can be executed directly by .NET, without a [.csproj] file: this is a single-file application, which we used in the previous chapter. The project options (nullable types enabled, implicit [using]) are the same as those for a console project. We’ll use this format whenever the example contains only one or two classes.

The file then contains the top-level statements followed by the class declarations: the compiler enforces this order, as the top-level statements must precede any type declarations (class, structure, interface, etc.) in the file. Classes declared in this way do not belong to any namespace, which is irrelevant in a single-file program.

docs.title: 4.1.9. Another Method: Overloading
docs.text:
Let’s continue with the class *[Person] and add a second method, *[Initialize], to it. The program *[classes-01.cs]* is as follows:

// overloading of the Initialize method
Person p1 = new Person();
p1.Initialize("Jean", "Dupont", 30);
p1.Identify();
Person p2 = new Person();
p2.Initialize(p1);
p2.Identify();

// the Person class is declared after the top-level statements
public class Person
{
    // attributes
    private string firstName = "";
    private string lastName = "";
    private int age;

    // initialization from three values
    public void Initialize(string p, string n, int age)
    {
        firstName = p;
        lastName = n;
        this.age = age;
    }

    // initialization from another person
    public void Initialize(Person p)
    {
        firstName = p.firstName;
        lastName = p.lastName;
        age = p.age;
    }

    // identity of the person
    public void Identify()
    {
        Console.WriteLine($"[{firstName}, {lastName}, {age}]");
    }
}
  • lines 2–7: the high-level instructions, i.e., the main program;
  • Line 10: The class [Person] is declared after the high-level statements;
  • lines 18–22: the method [Initialize] from the previous paragraph;
  • lines 26–30: a second method, [Initialize].

We now have two methods named [Initialize]: this is valid as long as they accept different parameters (in number or type). The method [Initialize] is said to be overloaded. The compiler chooses which method to call based on the actual parameters: [p1.Initialize("Jean", "Dupont", 30)] (line 3) calls the first one, and [p2.Initialize(p1)] (line 6) calls the second one.

The parameter of the second method is a reference ([p]) to a person. The fields of the person ([p]) are then assigned to the current object ([this]). Note that the method [Initialize] has direct access to the fields of the object [p] even though they are private (lines 28–30). This is always true: a method of a class [C] has access to the private members of all objects of the same class [C].

Results:

> dotnet run classes-01.cs
[Jean, Dupont, 30]
[Jean, Dupont, 30]

docs.title: 4.1.10. Constructors of the Person class
docs.text:
A constructor is a method that bears the name of the class and is called when the object is created. It is generally used to initialize the object. It is a method that can accept parameters but does not return a value. Its declaration is not preceded by any type (not even [void]).

If a class [C] has a constructor that accepts n parameters, the declaration and initialization of an object of this class can be done as follows:

C obj = new C(arg1, arg2, ... argn);

or

C obj;
...
obj = new C(arg1, arg2, ... argn);

When a class [C] has one or more constructors, one of these constructors must be used to create an object of that class. If a class [C] has no constructors, it has a default constructor, which is the parameterless constructor [public C()]. The object’s fields then retain their initial values. This is what happened in the previous programs, where we had written [new Person()].

The program [classes-02.cs] provides three constructors for the class [Person]:

// constructors of the Person class
Person p1 = new Person("Jean", "Dupont", 30);
p1.Identify();
Person p2 = new Person(p1);
p2.Identify();
Person p3 = new Person();
p3.Identify();

public class Person
{
    // attributes
    private string firstName;
    private string lastName;
    private int age;

    // main constructor
    public Person(string firstName, string lastName, int age)
    {
        this.firstName = firstName;
        this.lastName = lastName;
        this.age = age;
    }

    // copy constructor: it calls the main constructor
    public Person(Person p) : this(p.firstName, p.lastName, p.age)
    {
    }

    // parameterless constructor: it too calls the main constructor
    public Person() : this("?", "?", 0)
    {
    }

    // identity of the person
    public void Identify()
    {
        Console.WriteLine($"[{firstName}, {lastName}, {age}]");
    }
}
  • lines 17–21: the “main” constructor initializes the three fields. Since its parameters have the same names as the fields, the fields are distinguished using [this];
  • line 25: the copy constructor. The notation [: this(p.firstName, p.lastName, p.age)] means that before executing the (empty) body of the constructor, the constructor of the same class that accepts three parameters—[string], [string], [int]—is executed. This is referred to as chained constructors. The initialization code is thus written only once;
  • line 30: the parameterless constructor, which is also chained to the main constructor. Since the class has declared constructors, it no longer has a default constructor: if we want to be able to write [new Person()], we must declare it;
  • Lines 11–14: The two strings are no longer initialized upon declaration. This is no longer necessary: all constructors, either directly or through chaining, assign a value to them, and the compiler verifies this.

The 2008 course had constructors call the [Initialize] method. Chaining with [this(...)] is preferable: with nullable types enabled, the compiler does not inspect the contents of methods called by a constructor and would flag that the fields [firstName] and [lastName] could be set to [null] at the end of construction.

Results:

> dotnet run classes-02.cs
[Jean, Dupont, 30]
[Jean, Dupont, 30]
[?, ?, 0]

docs.title: 4.1.11. Object references
docs.text:
We use the [Person] class from the previous program, omitting its parameterless constructor but including the [Initialize(string, string, int)] method from the beginning of the chapter. The test program becomes the following [classes-03.cs] (we do not reproduce the class):

// object references
// p1
Person p1 = new Person("Jean", "Dupont", 30);
Console.Write("p1="); p1.Identify();
// p2 references the same object as p1
Person p2 = p1;
Console.Write("p2="); p2.Identify();
// p3 references an object that is a copy of the object referenced by p1
Person p3 = new Person(p1);
Console.Write("p3="); p3.Identify();
// we change the state of the object referenced by p1
p1.Initialize("Micheline", "Benoît", 67);
Console.Write("p1="); p1.Identify();
// since p2 = p1, the object referenced by p2 has changed state
Console.Write("p2="); p2.Identify();
// p3 does not reference the same object as p1: the object referenced by p3 has not changed
Console.Write("p3="); p3.Identify();
// are p1 and p2 the same reference? and p1 and p3?
Console.WriteLine($"p1 == p2 : {p1 == p2}, p1 == p3 : {p1 == p3}");

Results:

> dotnet run classes-03.cs
p1=[Jean, Dupont, 30]
p2=[Jean, Dupont, 30]
p3=[Jean, Dupont, 30]
p1=[Micheline, Benoît, 67]
p2=[Micheline, Benoît, 67]
p3=[Jean, Dupont, 30]
p1 == p2 : True, p1 == p3 : False

When the variable [p1] is declared as [Person p1 = new Person("Jean", "Dupont", 30);] (line 3), [p1] refers to the object [Person("Jean", "Dupont", 30)] but is not the object itself. In C, this would be referred to as a pointer—that is, the address of the created object. If we then write [p1 = null;], it is not the object [Person("Jean", "Dupont", 30)] that is modified; rather, it is the reference [p1] that changes its value. The object will be “lost” if it is not referenced by any other variable: the memory it occupies will later be reclaimed by the garbage collector for .NET.

When we write [Person p2 = p1;] (line 6), we initialize the reference [p2]: it “points” to the same object (it refers to the same object) as the reference [p1]. Thus, if the object “pointed to” (or referenced) by [p1] is modified, the object referenced by [p2] is also modified (lines 5–6 of the results).

When [Person p3 = new Person(p1);] is written (line 9), a new object, [Person], is created. This new object will be referenced by [p3]. If the object referenced by [p1] is modified, the object referenced by [p3] (line 7) remains unchanged.

Finally, on line 19, the operator [==], applied to two object references, indicates whether they refer to the same object: [p1] and [p2] refer to the same object, while [p1] and [p3] refer to two different objects, although they have the same content (line 8).

docs.title: 4.1.12. Passing Object Reference Parameters
docs.text:
In the previous chapter, we examined how function parameters are passed when they are simple types ([int], [double], …). Let’s see what happens when the parameter is an object reference. For this, we’ll use the class [StringBuilder] from .NET. A [string] object cannot be modified: an operation such as [s.ToUpper()] returns a new [string] object. An object [StringBuilder], on the other hand, is a mutable string: its method [Append] adds characters to the string without creating a new object.

The program [classes-04.cs] is as follows:

using System.Text;

// passing parameters of object reference type
StringBuilder sb0 = new StringBuilder("test0"), sb1 = new StringBuilder("test1"), sb2 = new StringBuilder("test2");
Console.WriteLine($"In calling function before call: sb0={sb0}, sb1={sb1}, sb2={sb2}");
ChangeStringBuilder(sb0, sb1, ref sb2, out StringBuilder sb3);
Console.WriteLine($"In calling function after call: sb0={sb0}, sb1={sb1}, sb2={sb2}, sb3={sb3}");

// the called function
static void ChangeStringBuilder(StringBuilder sbf0, StringBuilder sbf1, ref StringBuilder sbf2, out StringBuilder sbf3)
{
    Console.WriteLine($"Start of called function: sbf0={sbf0}, sbf1={sbf1}, sbf2={sbf2}");
    sbf0.Append("*****");
    sbf1 = new StringBuilder("test1*****");
    sbf2 = new StringBuilder("test2*****");
    sbf3 = new StringBuilder("test3*****");
    Console.WriteLine($"End of called function: sbf0={sbf0}, sbf1={sbf1}, sbf2={sbf2}, sbf3={sbf3}");
}
  • line 1: the class [StringBuilder] belongs to the namespace [System.Text], which is not part of the implicitly imported namespaces;
  • line 4: three [sb0, sb1, sb2] references to objects of type [StringBuilder];
  • line 6: These are passed to the function [ChangeStringBuilder] with different modes: [sb0] and [sb1] with the default mode, [sb2] with the keyword [ref], and a fourth reference, [sb3], declared within the call itself ([out StringBuilder sb3]), with the keyword [out];
  • lines 10–17: a local function with the formal parameters [sbf0, sbf1, sbf2, sbf3]. The relationships between the formal parameters [sbfi] and the actual parameters [sbi] are as follows:
    • [sbf0] and [sb0] are, when the function starts, two distinct references that point to the same object (references are passed by value);
    • the same applies to [sbf1] and [sb1];
    • [sbf2] and [sb2] are one and the same reference (keyword [ref]);
    • [sbf3] and [sb3] are also the same reference (keyword [out]), which the function must initialize.

Results:

> dotnet run classes-04.cs
In calling function before call: sb0=test0, sb1=test1, sb2=test2
Start of called function: sbf0=test0, sbf1=test1, sbf2=test2
End of called function: sbf0=test0*****, sbf1=test1*****, sbf2=test2*****, sbf3=test3*****
In calling function after call: sb0=test0*****, sb1=test1, sb2=test2*****, sb3=test3*****

Explanations:

  • [sb0] and [sbf0] are two distinct references to the same object. This object was modified via [sbf0] (line 13). This modification is visible via [sb0] (line 5);
  • [sb1] and [sbf1] are two distinct references to the same object. [sbf1] is assigned a new value within the function and now points to a new object (line 14). This does not change the value of [sb1], which continues to point to the original, unmodified object;
  • [sb2] and [sbf2] are the same reference. [sbf2] now points to a new object (line 15). Since [sbf2] and [sb2] are one and the same entity, [sb2] also points to this new object;
  • before the function call, [sb3] had no value. After the call, [sb3] refers to the object created by the function (line 16).

docs.title: 4.1.13. Temporary Objects
docs.text:
In an expression, you can explicitly call an object’s constructor: the object is created, but there is no variable to access it later (to modify it, for example). This temporary object is created for the purpose of evaluating the expression and is then discarded. The memory space it occupied will be automatically reclaimed later by the garbage collector, whose role is to reclaim memory space occupied by objects that are no longer referenced by the program’s data.

Consider the following program, [classes-05.cs], where the constructors of the [Person] class display a message:

// temporary objects
new Person(new Person("Jean", "Dupont", 30)).Identify();

public class Person
{
    // attributes
    private string firstName;
    private string lastName;
    private int age;

    // constructors
    public Person(string firstName, string lastName, int age)
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Constructor Person(string, string, int)");
        this.firstName = firstName;
        this.lastName = lastName;
        this.age = age;
    }

    public Person(Person p)
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Constructor Person(Person)");
        firstName = p.firstName;
        lastName = p.lastName;
        age = p.age;
    }

    // identity of the person
    public void Identify()
    {
        Console.WriteLine($"[{firstName}, {lastName}, {age}]");
    }
}
  • Line 2: The object [Person("Jean", "Dupont", 30)] is constructed and then passed to the copy constructor, which constructs a second object; the method [Identify] is then called on that object. Neither of the two objects is referenced by a variable.

Results:

> dotnet run classes-05.cs
Constructor Person(string, string, int)
Constructor Person(Person)
[Jean, Dupont, 30]

The results show the successive creation of the two temporary objects.

docs.title: 4.1.14. Methods for Reading and Writing Private Fields
docs.text:
We add the necessary methods to the [Person] class to read or modify the state of the objects’ fields ([classes-06.cs]):

// read methods (getters) and write methods (setters) of private attributes
Person p = new Person("Jean", "Michelin", 34);
Console.WriteLine("p=(" + p.GetFirstName() + "," + p.GetLastName() + "," + p.GetAge() + ")");
p.SetAge(56);
Console.WriteLine("p=(" + p.GetFirstName() + "," + p.GetLastName() + "," + p.GetAge() + ")");

public class Person
{
    // attributes
    private string firstName;
    private string lastName;
    private int age;

    // constructor
    public Person(string firstName, string lastName, int age)
    {
        this.firstName = firstName;
        this.lastName = lastName;
        this.age = age;
    }

    // getters
    public string GetFirstName()
    {
        return firstName;
    }

    public string GetLastName()
    {
        return lastName;
    }

    public int GetAge()
    {
        return age;
    }

    // setters
    public void SetFirstName(string firstName)
    {
        this.firstName = firstName;
    }

    public void SetLastName(string lastName)
    {
        this.lastName = lastName;
    }

    public void SetAge(int age)
    {
        this.age = age;
    }
}
  • lines 22–35: the read methods, called getters;
  • lines 38–51: the write methods, called setters.

Results:

> dotnet run classes-06.cs
p=(Jean,Michelin,34)
p=(Jean,Michelin,56)

This approach is typical of the Java language. C# offers a more elegant mechanism: properties.

docs.title: 4.1.15. Properties
docs.text:
There is another way to access a class’s fields: by creating properties. These allow us to manipulate private fields as if they were public.

A property allows you to read ([get]) or set ([set]) the value of a field. A property is declared as follows:

public Type Property
{
    get { ... }
    set { ... }
}

where [Type] is generally the type of the field managed by the property. It may have two methods named [get] and [set]. The method [get] is usually responsible for returning the value of the field it manages (it could return something else; there’s nothing preventing it from doing so). The [set] method receives a parameter named [value], which it normally assigns to the field it manages. It can use this opportunity to verify the validity of the received value and, if necessary, throw an exception if the value is invalid.

Consider the program [classes-07.cs], where the previous accessors and mutators have been replaced by read-write properties:

// properties
Person p = new Person("Jean", "Michelin", 34);
Console.WriteLine("p=(" + p.FirstName + "," + p.LastName + "," + p.Age + ")");
p.Age = 56;
Console.WriteLine("p=(" + p.FirstName + "," + p.LastName + "," + p.Age + ")");
try
{
    p.Age = -4;
}
catch (ArgumentException ex)
{
    Console.WriteLine(ex.Message);
}
// object initializer: parameterless constructor then assignment of the properties
Person p2 = new Person { Age = 7, FirstName = "Arthur", LastName = "Martin" };
Console.WriteLine($"p2=({p2.FirstName},{p2.LastName},{p2.Age})");
try
{
    Person p3 = new Person { FirstName = "Paul", LastName = " " };
}
catch (ArgumentException ex)
{
    Console.WriteLine(ex.Message);
}

public class Person
{
    // attributes
    private string firstName = "";
    private string lastName = "";
    private int age;

    // constructors
    public Person(string firstName, string lastName, int age)
    {
        // we go through the properties to benefit from their checks
        FirstName = firstName;
        LastName = lastName;
        Age = age;
    }

    public Person()
    {
    }

    // properties
    public string FirstName
    {
        get { return firstName; }
        set
        {
            // valid first name?
            if (string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(value))
            {
                throw new ArgumentException($"invalid first name ({value})");
            }
            firstName = value;
        }
    }

    public string LastName
    {
        get { return lastName; }
        set
        {
            // valid last name?
            if (string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(value))
            {
                throw new ArgumentException($"invalid last name ({value})");
            }
            lastName = value;
        }
    }

    public int Age
    {
        get { return age; }
        set
        {
            // valid age?
            if (value < 0)
            {
                throw new ArgumentException($"invalid age ({value})");
            }
            age = value;
        }
    }
}

The [set] methods for the three properties validate the received value (lines 52–57, 66–71, 80–85).

  • Lines 53–55: The method [string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace] returns [true] if the string is [null], empty, or consists solely of spaces. The exception thrown is of type [ArgumentException], the exception defined by .NET to signal an invalid parameter. The 2008 version threw an exception of the general type [Exception], which requires the caller to catch all exceptions;
  • lines 34–39: the constructor initializes the object via properties rather than fields. This allows it to take advantage of the validations performed by the [set] methods, which are implemented in only one place.

How are the methods [get] and [set] called? In the statement on line 3, the program attempts to retrieve the values of the properties [FirstName], [LastName], and [Age] for the person [p]. The [get] method for these properties is then called, and it returns the value of the field they manage. In the [p.Age = 56;] statement (line 4), we want to set the value of the [Age] property. The [set] method of this property is then called. It receives 56 as its [value] parameter.

A property [P] of a class [C] that defines only the method [get] is said to be read-only. If [c] is an object of class [C], the operation [c.P = value] will be rejected by the compiler.

Results:

> dotnet run classes-07.cs
p=(Jean,Michelin,34)
p=(Jean,Michelin,56)
invalid age (-4)
p2=(Arthur,Martin,7)
invalid last name ( )

Line 4 of the results shows that the assignment [p.Age = -4] (line 8) was rejected by the method [set] of the property [Age].

docs.title: 4.1.16. Object initializers
docs.text:
Properties can be used in conjunction with a constructor using the following syntax:

Class obj = new Class(...) { Property1 = val1, Property2 = val2, ... };

This syntax, known as an object initializer, is equivalent to the following code:

Class obj = new Class(...);
obj.Property1 = val1;
obj.Property2 = val2;
...

The order of the properties does not matter. In the previous program [classes-07.cs], the class [Person] has a parameterless constructor that does not initialize anything. Let’s return to the end of the main program:

// object initializer: parameterless constructor then assignment of the properties
Person p2 = new Person { Age = 7, FirstName = "Arthur", LastName = "Martin" };
Console.WriteLine($"p2=({p2.FirstName},{p2.LastName},{p2.Age})");
try
{
    Person p3 = new Person { FirstName = "Paul", LastName = " " };
}
catch (ArgumentException ex)
{
    Console.WriteLine(ex.Message);
}

Line 15: The parameterless constructor is used to create a person, which is then initialized by its properties. We could have written [new Person() { Age = 7, ... }], but parentheses are not required for the parameterless constructor in this syntax. The [set] methods are indeed called: on line 19, the name containing a space is rejected (line 6 of the results).

docs.title: 4.1.17. Automatic properties
docs.text:
In many cases, the methods [get] and [set] of a property simply read from and write to a private field without any further processing. In such cases, you can use an automatic property declared as follows:

public Type Property { get; set; }

The private field associated with the property is not declared; it is automatically generated by the compiler and can only be accessed through its property. Thus, instead of writing the field [firstName] and the property [FirstName] for the program [classes-07.cs], you can write:

    public string FirstName { get; set; } = "";

without declaring the private field [firstName]. The expression [= ""] following the property is the initial value of the hidden field. The difference between the two properties is that the first one validates the first name in [set], while the second one performs no validation.

Is using the automatic property [FirstName] equivalent to declaring a public field [public string FirstName;]? For the user of the class, the syntax is the same. However, declaring a class field as public is not recommended: it violates the concept of encapsulation of an object’s state, which should be private and exposed through public methods. With an automatic property, checks can be added later in [set] without changing the code of the class’s users.

Automatic properties have several variants, as demonstrated by the program [classes-08.cs]:

// automatic, read-only, init and required properties
var p = new Person("Dupont", 30) { FirstName = "Jean", City = "Angers" };
Console.WriteLine(p.Identity);
// FirstName is read / write
p.FirstName = "Jacques";
// Age can only be modified inside the class
p.GrowOlder();
Console.WriteLine(p.Identity);
// the following lines are rejected by the compiler
// p.LastName = "Durand"; // LastName is read-only
// p.Age = 40;           // the set of Age is private
// p.City = "Paris";     // City can only be set when the object is created

// mandatory property (required)
var c = new Contact { Email = "jean.dupont@example.com" };
Console.WriteLine($"Contact: {c.Email}, {c.Phone}");
// var c2 = new Contact();   // rejected: the mandatory property Email is not initialized

public class Person
{
    // constructor
    public Person(string lastName, int age)
    {
        LastName = lastName;
        Age = age;
    }

    // read / write automatic property, with an initial value
    public string FirstName { get; set; } = "";
    // read-only automatic property: set by the constructor
    public string LastName { get; }
    // automatic property whose writing is reserved to the class
    public int Age { get; private set; }
    // init property: set by the constructor or by an object initializer
    public string City { get; init; } = "?";
    // read-only computed property (expression-bodied member)
    public string Identity => $"[{FirstName}, {LastName}, {Age}, {City}]";

    // expression-bodied method
    public void GrowOlder() => Age++;
}

public class Contact
{
    // the property must be initialized when the object is created
    public required string Email { get; init; }
    // optional property
    public string Phone { get; init; } = "unknown";
}
  • line 29: a read-write automatic property with an initial value;
  • line 31: a read-only automatic property—it has no [set] and can only be set by a constructor (line 24);
  • line 33: the [set] method may have more restricted access than the property: here, the [Age] property is readable by everyone but can only be modified by the class’s methods, such as [GrowOlder] (line 40);
  • line 35: a [init] property (C# 9): it can be set by a constructor or an object initializer (line 2), but not afterward. This is a way to create immutable objects while taking advantage of the object initializer syntax;
  • line 37: a read-only property whose value is computed. The notation [=> expression] is a shorthand form of [get { return expression; }]. It also applies to methods (line 40): these are referred to as expression-bodied members;
  • line 46: a required property (C# 11): the keyword [required] requires the code that creates a [Contact] object to initialize the [Email] property in an object initializer (line 15). The compiler rejects line 17 if it is uncommented;
  • lines 10–12: three statements that the compiler rejects, for the reasons given in the comments.

Recall that with the keyword [var] (line 2), the variable’s type is inferred from the expression that initializes it, in this case [Person].

Results:

> dotnet run classes-08.cs
[Jean, Dupont, 30, Angers]
[Jacques, Dupont, 31, Angers]
Contact: jean.dupont@example.com, unknown

Finally, an automatic property can be declared virtual ([public virtual string Prop { get; set; }]) and overridden in a derived class, for example, to add a validation in [set]. The keywords [virtual] and [override] are introduced with inheritance.

docs.title: 4.1.18. The field keyword (C# 14)
docs.text:
Between the automatic property, which does not perform any validation, and the full property in the [classes-07.cs] program, which requires a field to be declared, C# 14 offers an intermediate option: in a property’s accessors, the keyword [field] refers to the field created by the compiler. This allows you to write a validation without declaring a field:

// the field keyword (C# 14)
var p = new Person { FirstName = "  jean ", LastName = "Dupont", Age = 30 };
Console.WriteLine(p.Identity);
try
{
    p.LastName = "";
}
catch (ArgumentException ex)
{
    Console.WriteLine(ex.Message);
}
try
{
    p.Age = -4;
}
catch (ArgumentException ex)
{
    Console.WriteLine(ex.Message);
}
Console.WriteLine(p.Identity);

public class Person
{
    // properties with checks, without a declared field:
    // [field] denotes the field created by the compiler
    public string FirstName
    {
        get;
        set => field = string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(value)
            ? throw new ArgumentException($"invalid first name ({value})")
            : value.Trim();
    } = "";   // initial value of the hidden field

    public string LastName
    {
        get;
        set => field = string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(value)
            ? throw new ArgumentException($"invalid last name ({value})")
            : value.Trim();
    } = "";

    public int Age
    {
        get;
        set
        {
            if (value < 0)
            {
                throw new ArgumentException($"invalid age ({value})");
            }
            field = value;
        }
    }

    // identity
    public string Identity => $"[{FirstName}, {LastName}, {Age}]";
}
  • Lines 26–31: The property [FirstName]. Its method [get] is automatic ([get;]): it returns the value of the hidden field. Its method [set] checks the received value and assigns it—with leading and trailing spaces removed—to the hidden field designated by [field]. The expression [condition ? throw ... : value] uses a throw statement: if the condition is true, an exception is thrown; otherwise, the expression evaluates to [value.Trim()];
  • line 32: the initial value of the hidden field;
  • lines 42–51: a [set] written using a block of statements.

Results:

> dotnet run classes-09.cs
[jean, Dupont, 30]
invalid last name ()
invalid age (-4)
[jean, Dupont, 30]

The first name “jean,” provided surrounded by spaces (line 2 of the program), was stored without them (line 2 of the results).

docs.title: 4.1.19. Class Methods and Attributes
docs.text:
Suppose we want to count the number of [Person] objects created in an application. We could manage a counter ourselves, but we risk overlooking temporary objects that are created here and there. It seems safer to include a statement in the constructors of the [Person] class that increments a counter. This counter cannot be a regular field, since each object has its own fields: it is a field of the class itself, not of a particular instance of that class. We declare it using the keyword [static]:

    private static long nbPersons;

To refer to it, we write [Person.nbPersons] to indicate that it is a field of the [Person] class itself. Here, we have created a private field that cannot be accessed directly from outside the class. We therefore create a public property to provide access to the class field [nbPersons]. To return the value of [nbPersons], the [get] method of this property does not require a specific [Person] object: so we also need a property declared as [static], which will be called from the outside using the syntax [Person.NbPersons]. Here is an example of [classes-10.cs]:

// class members (static)
Person p1 = new Person("Jean", "Dupont", 30);
Person p2 = new Person(p1);
new Person(p1);
Console.WriteLine($"Number of persons created: {Person.NbPersons}");
// a class method
Person p3 = Person.Unknown();
p3.Identify();
Console.WriteLine($"Number of persons created: {Person.NbPersons}");

public class Person
{
    // class attribute
    private static long nbPersons;

    // class property
    public static long NbPersons
    {
        get { return nbPersons; }
    }

    // class method
    public static Person Unknown()
    {
        return new Person("?", "?", 0);
    }

    // instance attributes
    private string firstName;
    private string lastName;
    private int age;

    // constructors
    public Person(string firstName, string lastName, int age)
    {
        this.firstName = firstName;
        this.lastName = lastName;
        this.age = age;
        nbPersons++;
    }

    public Person(Person p) : this(p.firstName, p.lastName, p.age)
    {
    }

    // identity of the person
    public void Identify()
    {
        Console.WriteLine($"[{firstName}, {lastName}, {age}]");
    }
}
  • line 14: the class field. Like any numeric field, it is initialized to 0;
  • lines 17–19: the read-only class property. It could have been written more simply as [public static long NbPersons { get; private set; }];
  • lines 23–25: a class method. It is called using the class name: [Person.Unknown()] (line 7). A class method has no current object: the keyword [this] has no meaning here, and it can only directly access the class members [static];
  • Line 39: The primary constructor increments the counter. The copy constructor, which is chained to the primary constructor, therefore increments it as well.

Results:

> dotnet run classes-10.cs
Number of persons created: 3
[?, ?, 0]
Number of persons created: 4

The program correctly counted the temporary object created on line 4. We have been using class members from the start: [Console.WriteLine], [int.Parse], and [Math.Sqrt] are methods of [static]. [Console] and [Math] are even static classes ([static class]): they contain only members of type [static], and no instances of them can be created.

docs.title: 4.1.20. An array of people
docs.text:
An object is a piece of data like any other, and as such, multiple objects can be grouped together in an array [classes-11.cs]:

// an array of persons
Person[] friends = new Person[3];
friends[0] = new Person("Jean", "Dupont", 30);
friends[1] = new Person("Sylvie", "Vartan", 52);
friends[2] = new Person("Neil", "Armstrong", 66);
// display
foreach (Person friend in friends)
{
    friend.Identify();
}
  • Line 2: creates an array of 3 elements of type [Person]. These 3 elements are initialized here with the value [null], meaning they do not reference any objects. Technically speaking, we refer to this as an “array of objects,” even though it is merely an array of object references. The creation of the array—which is itself an object (as indicated by [new])—does not create any objects of the same type as its elements; this must be done subsequently. Note that the compiler does not flag the fact that the elements of an array of type [Person[]] are equal to [null] immediately after its creation: this is a limitation of nullable type analysis;
  • Lines 3–5: Create 3 objects of type [Person];
  • lines 7–9: display the contents of the table [friends].

The class [Person], declared below, is derived from the program [classes-03.cs], reduced to its three-parameter constructor and its method [Identify]. Results:

> dotnet run classes-11.cs
[Jean, Dupont, 30]
[Sylvie, Vartan, 52]
[Neil, Armstrong, 66]

docs.title: 4.1.21. new() expressions with a target type
docs.text:
When the type of the object to be created is known from the context, C# 9 allows the class name to be omitted after [new]. The program [classes-12.cs] demonstrates this:

// object initializers and target-typed new() expressions
// the type of the created object is inferred from the type of the variable
Person p1 = new("Jean", "Dupont", 30);
Person p2 = new() { FirstName = "Arthur", LastName = "Martin", Age = 7 };
// an array initialized by a collection expression
Person[] friends =
[
    p1,
    p2,
    new("Sylvie", "Vartan", 52),
    new() { FirstName = "Neil", LastName = "Armstrong", Age = 66 },
];
foreach (Person friend in friends)
{
    Console.WriteLine(friend.Identity);
}
// target-typed new() in a method call: the type is that of the parameter
Display(new("Pauline", "Leduc", 12));

// a local function
static void Display(Person p)
{
    Console.WriteLine($"Display: {p.Identity}");
}

public class Person
{
    // constructors
    public Person(string firstName, string lastName, int age)
    {
        FirstName = firstName;
        LastName = lastName;
        Age = age;
    }

    public Person()
    {
    }

    // automatic properties
    public string FirstName { get; set; } = "";
    public string LastName { get; set; } = "";
    public int Age { get; set; }
    // identity
    public string Identity => $"[{FirstName}, {LastName}, {Age}]";
}
  • Line 3: The type of the object created by [new(...)] is that of the variable that receives it, [Person]. This syntax is the opposite of [var]: with [var], the type of the variable is inferred from the expression; with [new()], the type of the object is inferred from the variable;
  • line 4: [new()] with an object initializer;
  • lines 6–11: an array created and populated by a collection expression (C# 12): the elements are enclosed in square brackets and separated by commas. The type of the elements, [Person], is known: [new(...)] is sufficient to create them;
  • line 18: the type of the created object is that of the parameter of the [Display] function.

Results:

> dotnet run classes-12.cs
[Jean, Dupont, 30]
[Arthur, Martin, 7]
[Sylvie, Vartan, 52]
[Neil, Armstrong, 66]
Display: [Pauline, Leduc, 12]

docs.title: 4.2.1. Overview
docs.text:
Here we discuss the concept of inheritance. The purpose of inheritance is to “customize” an existing class so that it meets our needs. Suppose we want to create a class named [Teacher]: a teacher is a specific type of person. They have attributes that other people do not have: the subject they teach, for example. But they also have the attributes common to all people: first name, last name, and age. A teacher is therefore a full member of the class [Person] but has additional attributes. Rather than creating a class [Teacher] from scratch, we prefer to build upon the existing class [Person] and adapt it to the specific characteristics of teachers. The concept of inheritance allows us to do this.

To indicate that the class [Teacher] inherits the properties of the class [Person], we write:

public class Teacher : Person

[Person] is called the parent (or base) class, and [Teacher] is called the derived (or child) class. A [Teacher] object has all the characteristics of a [Person] object: it has the same fields and methods. These fields and methods from the parent class are not repeated in the definition of the child class; we simply specify the fields and methods added by the child class. A C# class can be derived from only one parent class.

The examples in this section are two console projects, [Inheritance1] and [Inheritance2], from the [04-classes.slnx] solution. In the [Inheritance1] project, the [Person] class is defined as follows: [Person.cs]:

namespace Inheritance1;

public class Person
{
    // class property: the number of persons created
    public static long NbPersons { get; private set; }

    // constructor
    public Person(string firstName, string lastName, int age)
    {
        FirstName = firstName;
        LastName = lastName;
        Age = age;
        NbPersons++;
        Console.WriteLine("Constructor Person(string, string, int)");
    }

    // properties
    public string FirstName
    {
        get;
        set => field = Check(value, "first name");
    } = "";

    public string LastName
    {
        get;
        set => field = Check(value, "last name");
    } = "";

    public int Age
    {
        get;
        set => field = value >= 0 ? value : throw new ArgumentException($"invalid age ({value})");
    }

    // identity of the person
    public string Identity => $"[{FirstName}, {LastName}, {Age}]";

    // check of a mandatory string
    private static string Check(string text, string label)
    {
        if (string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(text))
        {
            throw new ArgumentException($"invalid {label} ({text})");
        }
        return text;
    }
}
  • line 6: the person counter from the previous paragraph, this time written as an automatic class property whose definition is reserved for the class;
  • lines 9–15: the constructor initializes the object using its properties and displays a progress message;
  • lines 19–34: three properties that validate their values using the keyword [field]. The validations for the first name and last name, which are identical, are factored into the private class method [Check] (lines 41–47);
  • line 38: the [Identify] method from the previous examples has been replaced by the read-only property [Identity], which returns the person’s identity instead of displaying it.

We are creating a class named [Teacher] that inherits from the class [Person]: [Teacher.cs]:

namespace Inheritance1;

public class Teacher : Person
{
    // constructor
    public Teacher(string firstName, string lastName, int age, int section)
        : base(firstName, lastName, age)
    {
        // we store the section through the Section property
        Section = section;
        // tracing
        Console.WriteLine("Constructor Teacher(string, string, int, int)");
    }

    // Section property
    public int Section { get; set; }

    // Identity property: it hides (new) the one of the parent class
    public new string Identity => $"Teacher[{base.Identity},{Section}]";
}

The [Teacher] class adds to the methods and properties of the [Person] class:

  • line 3: the class [Teacher] derives from the class [Person];
  • line 16: a property [Section], which is the section number to which the teacher belongs within the teaching staff (roughly one section per subject);
  • lines 6–12: a constructor used to initialize all of a teacher’s properties;
  • line 19: a new property, [Identity], which will be discussed in more detail later.

docs.title: 4.2.2. Creating a Teacher Object
docs.text:
A child class does not inherit constructors from its parent class. It must define its own constructors. The constructor for the [Teacher] class is as follows:

    public Teacher(string firstName, string lastName, int age, int section)
        : base(firstName, lastName, age)
    {
        // we store the section through the Section property
        Section = section;
        // tracing
        Console.WriteLine("Constructor Teacher(string, string, int, int)");
    }

The declaration on lines 6–7 specifies that the constructor takes four parameters: [firstName], [lastName], [age], [section], and passes three ([firstName], [lastName], [age]) to its base class, in this case the class [Person]. We know that this class has a constructor, [Person(string, string, int)], which will allow us to create a person using the passed parameters. Once the construction of the [Person] part is complete, the construction of the [Teacher] object continues with the execution of the constructor’s body (line 10).

Note that on the left side of the = sign, the [Section] property is used. If this property performed validity checks, the constructor would benefit from them. This avoids having to place these checks in two different places: the constructor and the property.

In summary, the constructor of a derived class:

  • passes to its base class the parameters it needs to construct itself;
  • uses the remaining parameters to initialize its own members.

We could have chosen to write:

public Teacher(string firstName, string lastName, int age, int section)
{
    this.firstName = firstName;
    this.lastName = lastName;
    this.age = age;
    Section = section;
}

This is impossible, for two reasons. First, the class *[Person] does not have a parameterless constructor: in the absence of ***[: base(...)], the compiler attempts to call this constructor and reports an error. Second, even if the private fields [firstName], [lastName], and [age] existed (here, these are the hidden fields of the properties), only objects of the class [Person] have direct access to them. All other objects, including objects of derived classes as in this case, must access them through public (or protected) members. This would have been different if the class *[Person] had declared these fields as protected (*[protected]*): it would then have allowed derived classes to access them directly. Using the parent class’s constructor is therefore the correct solution and the standard approach: when constructing a child object, first call the parent object’s constructor, then complete the initializations specific to the child object ([Section]* in our example).

If the class [Teacher] did not define a property [Identity], the expression [e.Identity]—where [e] is a teacher—would refer to the property [Identity] inherited from the class [Person]: it is public and, through inheritance, becomes a public property of the class [Teacher]. This would then yield the identity of the [Person] part of the teacher, without its section.

docs.title: 4.2.3. Hiding a property or method: the new keyword
docs.text:
To obtain a teacher’s full identity, the class [Teacher] defines its own property [Identity]:

    // Identity property: it hides (new) the one of the parent class
    public new string Identity => $"Teacher[{base.Identity},{Section}]";

The property [Identity] of class [Teacher] relies on the property [Identity] of its parent class, designated as [base.Identity], to obtain the “Person” portion and then supplements it with the section, which is specific to the class [Teacher].

Consider a teacher object [E]. This object contains a [Person] object:

The property [Identity] is defined in both the class [Teacher] and its parent class [Person]. In the child class [Teacher], the property [Identity] is preceded by the keyword [new] to indicate that a new property, [Identity], is intentionally defined for the class [Teacher] (without [new], the compiler issues a warning). The class [Teacher] now has two properties, [Identity]:

  • one inherited from the parent class [Person];
  • its own.

If [E] is a [Teacher] object, [E.Identity] refers to the property [Identity] of the class [Teacher]. It is said that the property [Identity] of the child class masks (hides) the property [Identity] of the parent class. Generally speaking, if [O] is an object and [M] is a method, to execute the method [O.M], the compiler searches for a method [M] in the following order:

  • in the class of the object [O];
  • in its parent class, if it has one;
  • in the parent class of its parent class, if it exists;
  • and so on.

Inheritance therefore allows the child class to redefine methods and properties with the same names as those in the parent class. This is what enables the child class to be adapted to its own needs.

The test program [Program.cs] for project [Inheritance1] is as follows:

using Inheritance1;

// a teacher
Teacher e = new Teacher("Lucile", "Dumas", 56, 61);
// the Identity property of the Teacher class
Console.WriteLine(e.Identity);
// the Identity property of the Person class is still there
Console.WriteLine(((Person)e).Identity);
// a person
Person p = new Person("Jean", "Dupont", 30);
// the Display method receives a Person or an object of a derived class
Display(e);
Display(p);
// the ToString method inherited from the object class
Console.WriteLine(e.ToString());
Console.WriteLine(p.ToString());
Console.WriteLine($"Number of persons created: {Person.NbPersons}");

// displays the identity of p
static void Display(Person p)
{
    Console.WriteLine(p.Identity);
}
  • line 4: creates a teacher;
  • line 6: displays its identity, that of the class [Teacher];
  • line 8: the conversion operator [(Person)] treats the object [e] as a [Person]: the property [Identity] of the class [Person] is then used;
  • lines 12–13: call to the function [Display] (lines 20–22) with a teacher followed by a person. We’ll return to this in the next paragraph;
  • lines 15–16: call to the [ToString] method on both objects. We’ll also come back to this.

Results:

> dotnet run
Constructor Person(string, string, int)
Constructor Teacher(string, string, int, int)
Teacher[[Lucile, Dumas, 56],61]
[Lucile, Dumas, 56]
Constructor Person(string, string, int)
[Lucile, Dumas, 56]
[Jean, Dupont, 30]
Inheritance1.Teacher
Inheritance1.Person
Number of persons created: 2

We can see that:

  • an object [Person] (line 2) was created before the object [Teacher] (line 3);
  • [e.Identity] provided the teacher's full identity (line 4), and [((Person)e).Identity] provided the identity of its [Person] part (line 5).

docs.title: 4.2.4. Polymorphism
docs.text:
Consider a class hierarchy: C0 ← C1 ← C2 ← … ← Cn, where Ci ← Cj indicates that class Cj is derived from class Ci. This implies that class Cj has all the characteristics of class Ci plus additional ones. Let Oi be objects of type Ci. It is valid to write [Oi = Oj] with j > i. Indeed, by inheritance, class Cj has all the characteristics of class Ci plus additional ones. Therefore, an object Oj of type Cj contains an object of type Ci. The operation [Oi = Oj] causes Oi to be a reference to the object of type Ci contained within the object Oj.

The fact that a variable Oi of class Ci can actually reference not only an object of class Ci but any object derived from class Ci is called polymorphism: the ability of a variable to reference different types of objects.

Let’s take an example and consider the function [Display] from the previous program:

static void Display(Person p)
{
    Console.WriteLine(p.Identity);
}

We can pass it either a *[Person]* or a *[Teacher]: In the latter case, the formal parameter [p], which is of type [Person], receives a value of type [Teacher]. Since the type [Teacher] is derived from the type [Person]*, this is valid.

The property [p.Identity] returns a string identifying the [Person] object [p]. What happens if the parameter passed to the [Display] function is an object of type [Teacher]?
