The previous results show that: the [p.Identity] statement executed the [Identity] property of a [Person] each time, first the person contained in the teacher [e] (line 7), then the person [p] itself (line 8). It did not adapt to the object actually passed as a parameter to [Display]. We would have preferred to have the full identity of the teacher [e]. For that to happen, the notation [p.Identity] would have had to refer to the property [Identity] of the object actually pointed to by [p], rather than the property [Identity] of the “Person” part of that object. With masking ([new]), the property is selected at compile time, based on the declared type of the variable ([Person]).

docs.title: 4.2.5. Redefinition and Polymorphism: virtual and override
docs.text:
It is possible to achieve the desired result by declaring [Identity] as a virtual property ([virtual]) in the base class [Person]. This is what the [Inheritance2] project does; its [Person] class is the same as the one in the [Inheritance1] project, with two changes:

    // identity of the person: virtual property
    public virtual string Identity => $"[{FirstName}, {LastName}, {Age}]";

    // redefinition of the ToString method of the object class
    public override string ToString() => Identity;
  • Line 38: The keyword [virtual] makes [Identity] a virtual property. This keyword can also be applied to methods. Child classes that override a virtual property or method must then use the keyword [override] instead of [new] to qualify their overridden property or method;
  • line 41: a redefinition of the method [ToString], discussed in the following paragraph.

In the class [Teacher], the property [Identity] is redefined as follows:

namespace Inheritance2;

// a sealed class: no class can derive from it
public sealed class Teacher : Person
{
    // constructor
    public Teacher(string firstName, string lastName, int age, int section)
        : base(firstName, lastName, age)
    {
        Section = section;
        Console.WriteLine("Constructor Teacher(string, string, int, int)");
    }

    // Section property
    public int Section { get; set; }

    // Identity property: it redefines (override) the one of the parent class
    public override string Identity => $"Teacher[{base.Identity},{Section}]";
}
  • Line 18: The property [Identity] overrides the one in the parent class;
  • Line 4: The class is sealed ([sealed]), which we’ll explain in more detail later.

With a virtual property or method, the choice of which property is executed by [p.Identity] is made at runtime, based on the actual type of the object referenced by [p]. The program [Program.cs] from the project [Inheritance2] is as follows:

using Inheritance2;

// a teacher
Teacher e = new Teacher("Lucile", "Dumas", 56, 61);
Display(e);
// a person
Person p = new Person("Jean", "Dupont", 30);
Display(p);
// Console.WriteLine(object) displays the result of the object's ToString method
Console.WriteLine(e);
Console.WriteLine(p);
// an array of persons of different types
Person[] persons = [p, e];
foreach (Person person in persons)
{
    Console.WriteLine($"{person.GetType().Name} : {person}");
}

// displays the identity of p
static void Display(Person p)
{
    Console.WriteLine(p.Identity);
}

Results:

> dotnet run
Constructor Person(string, string, int)
Constructor Teacher(string, string, int, int)
Teacher[[Lucile, Dumas, 56],61]
Constructor Person(string, string, int)
[Jean, Dupont, 30]
Teacher[[Lucile, Dumas, 56],61]
[Jean, Dupont, 30]
Person : [Jean, Dupont, 30]
Teacher : Teacher[[Lucile, Dumas, 56],61]

This time, on line 4, the function [Display] correctly displayed the teacher’s full name.

docs.title: 4.2.6. The ToString method
docs.text:
The class [object] (the C# alias for class [System.Object]) is the “parent” class of all C# classes. So when you write:

public class Person

you are implicitly writing:

public class Person : object

The [object] class defines a virtual method, [ToString], which by default returns the full class name of the object. This is what the last two lines of output from the [Inheritance1] project displayed, with the calls to [e.ToString()] and [p.ToString()]: [Inheritance1.Teacher] and [Inheritance1.Person]. Although we did not override the [ToString] method in the [Person] and [Teacher] classes, the [ToString] method of the [object] class was able to display the object’s actual class name.

In the [Inheritance2] project, the [Person] class redefines the [ToString] method (see above):

    public override string ToString() => Identity;

Let’s return to the program [Program.cs] in the project [Inheritance2]:

// Console.WriteLine(object) displays the result of the object's ToString method
Console.WriteLine(e);
Console.WriteLine(p);
// an array of persons of different types
Person[] persons = [p, e];
foreach (Person person in persons)
{
    Console.WriteLine($"{person.GetType().Name} : {person}");
}

In Line 10, the method [WriteLine] of class [Console] has no variant that accepts a parameter of type [Person]. Among the various variants of [WriteLine], there is one that accepts a parameter of type [object]. The compiler will use this method, [WriteLine(object o)], because this signature means that the parameter [o] can be of type [object] or a derived type. Since [object] is the superclass of all classes, any object can be passed as a parameter to [WriteLine]—including an object of type [Person] or [Teacher]. The [WriteLine(object o)] method writes [o.ToString()] to the console. Since the [ToString] method is virtual, the [ToString] method of the actual object is used—in this case, that of the [Person] class. This method returns [Identity], which is also a virtual property: For the teacher [e], it is therefore the property [Identity] of the class [Teacher] that is used, as shown in line 7 of the results. It is therefore unnecessary to redefine [ToString] in the class [Teacher], unlike in the 2008 course.

The same mechanism applies to string interpolation: in [$"{person}"] (line 16), the object [person] is converted to a string by its method [ToString]. The loop on lines 14–16 iterates over an array of references to [Person], which actually point to objects of different types: the method [GetType] (which is also inherited from [object]) returns the actual type of the object, whose property [Name] is the name.

docs.title: 4.2.7. Sealed classes
docs.text:
The class [Teacher] in the [Inheritance2] project is declared as [public sealed class Teacher : Person]. The keyword [sealed] prevents classes from being derived from the class [Teacher]: the declaration [class TeacherResearcher : Teacher] would be rejected by the compiler. A class is sealed when it is not intended to be derived from; the compiler and the runtime can also optimize calls to its virtual methods. The keyword also applies to a redefined method or property: [public sealed override string Identity] would prevent derived classes from redefining it again, without prohibiting derivation from the class.

Conversely, a method or property that is not declared as [virtual], [abstract] (see below), or [override] cannot be overridden with [override]: in C#, unlike in Java, methods are not virtual by default.

docs.title: 4.3. Redefining the meaning of an operator for a class
4.3.1. Introduction
docs.text:
Consider the expression [op1 + op2], where [op1] and [op2] are two operands. It is possible to redefine the meaning of the operator [+]. If the operand [op1] is an instance of class [C1], a static method must be defined in class [C1] with the following signature:

public static Type operator +(C1 operand1, C2 operand2)

When the compiler encounters the expression [op1 + op2], it translates it to [C1.operator +(op1, op2)]. The type returned by the method [operator] is important. In fact, consider the operation [op1 + op2 + op3]. It is translated by the compiler as [(op1 + op2) + op3]. Let [res12] be the result of [op1 + op2]. The next operation performed is [res12 + op3]. If [res12] is of type [C1], it will also be translated to [C1.operator +(res12, op3)]. This allows operations to be chained together.

Unary operators with only one operand can also be redefined. Thus, if [op1] is an object of type [C1], the operation [op1++] can be redefined by a static method of the [C1] class:

public static C1 operator ++(C1 operand1)

What has been stated here applies to most operators, with a few exceptions:

  • Operators [==] and [!=] must be redefined together, as must [<] and [>], [<=] and [>=];
  • the operators [&&], [||], [=], [.], [?:], [??], and [new] cannot be redefined;
  • up to C# 13, the compound assignment operators ([+=], [-=], …) could not be overridden: [a += b] was always compiled to [a = a + b]. C# 14 allows them to be overridden, as we will see.

docs.title: 4.3.2. An example
docs.text:
The [Lists] project in the solution defines a class named [ListOfPersons], which is a list of people. The classes [Person] and [Teacher] in this project are the same as those in the [Inheritance2] project, but without their tracking messages and the person counter. The 2008 course had the class *[ListOfPersons] derived from the class *[ArrayList]*, a list of objects of type *[object], which is now obsolete. We use the generic list [List<Person>] (generic classes are discussed later in this chapter; the class [List<T>] is covered in the next chapter) and, rather than inheriting from it, we place it in a private field of the class. This is referred to as using composition rather than inheritance: the class [ListOfPersons] thus exposes only the operations it has chosen. From the class [List<Person>], we use only the following elements:

  • the method [L.Add(p)], which adds the person [p] to the list [L], and the method [L.AddRange(L2)], which adds all the elements of the list [L2] to it;
  • the property [L.Count], which returns the number of elements in the list [L];
  • The notation [L[i]], which refers to item No. i in the list [L].

The definition of class [ListOfPersons] is as follows: [ListOfPersons.cs]:

namespace Lists;

public class ListOfPersons
{
    // the persons of the list
    private readonly List<Person> persons = [];

    // number of persons in the list
    public int Count => persons.Count;

    // + operator: returns a new list containing the persons of l and the person p
    public static ListOfPersons operator +(ListOfPersons l, Person p)
    {
        ListOfPersons result = new ListOfPersons();
        result.persons.AddRange(l.persons);
        result.persons.Add(p);
        return result;
    }

    // compound assignment operator += (C# 14): adds p to the current list
    public void operator +=(Person p)
    {
        persons.Add(p);
    }

    // indexer by position, read and write
    public Person this[int i]
    {
        get { return persons[i]; }
        set { persons[i] = value; }
    }

    // indexer by last name, read-only: returns the position of the person or -1
    public int this[string lastName]
    {
        get
        {
            // we search for the person
            for (int i = 0; i < persons.Count; i++)
            {
                if (persons[i].LastName == lastName)
                {
                    return i;
                }
            }
            return -1;
        }
    }

    // ToString: returns (person1,person2,...)
    public override string ToString()
    {
        return "(" + string.Join(",", persons) + ")";
    }
}
  • line 6: the list of people. The keyword [readonly] indicates that the field can only be assigned at the time of its declaration or within a constructor: the list itself may change in content, but the field will always refer to the same list. [] is an empty collection expression: the type of the created collection, [List<Person>], is inferred from the field’s type;
  • line 9: the number of people, a read-only property;
  • lines 12–17: definition of the operator [+] for the operation [l + p], where [l] is of type [ListOfPersons] and [p] is of type [Person] or a derived type. The operator creates a new list (line 14), copies the people from [l] into it (line 15), and then adds the person [p] (line 16). As with the [+] operator for numbers or strings, the operands are not modified. Since the list [l] is of the same class, the operator has access to its private field [l.persons]. The resulting list is of type [ListOfPersons], which allows the [+] operators to be chained together as in [l + p1 + p2], interpreted (operator precedence) as [(l + p1) + p2];
  • Lines 21–23: definition of the operator [+=] (C# 14). Unlike the other operators, this is not a static method but an instance method with no return value ([void]): it modifies the current object, in this case by adding the person [p] to it;
  • lines 51–53: we redefine the method [ToString] to display a list of people in the form (person1, person2, ...), where personi is itself the result of the person’s [ToString] method. The static method [string.Join(separator, elements)] concatenates the textual representations of the elements, separating them with the separator. The 2008 course built this string manually using a [StringBuilder] object.

Note that the [ListOfPersons] class has no constructor. It therefore uses the default constructor [public ListOfPersons()], which does nothing other than initialize the [persons] field with the value specified in its declaration. Lines 26–46 are discussed in the following section.

The test program [Program.cs] begins as follows:

using Lists;

// --- the + operator
// a list of persons
ListOfPersons l = new ListOfPersons();
// adding persons
l = l + new Person("jean", "martin", 10) + new Person("pauline", "leduc", 12);
// display
Console.WriteLine("l=" + l);
// l + p returns a new list: l is not modified
ListOfPersons l2 = l + new Person("louis", "durand", 8);
Console.WriteLine("l=" + l);
Console.WriteLine("l2=" + l2);

// --- the += operator (C# 14)
ListOfPersons l3 = l;
// += adds the teacher to the list referenced by l, without creating a new list
l += new Teacher("camille", "germain", 27, 60);
Console.WriteLine("l=" + l);
// l and l3 still reference the same object
Console.WriteLine($"l3=l : {ReferenceEquals(l, l3)}");
  • line 5: creation of an empty list of people [l];
  • line 7: adds two people using the [+] operator;
  • line 11: [l + p] creates a new list [l2]; the list [l] remains unchanged;
  • line 18: adds a teacher using the [+=] operator;
  • Lines 9–13: Concatenating a string and an object uses the [ToString] method, which is redefined from the [ListOfPersons] class.

Results:

> dotnet run
l=([jean, martin, 10],[pauline, leduc, 12])
l=([jean, martin, 10],[pauline, leduc, 12])
l2=([jean, martin, 10],[pauline, leduc, 12],[louis, durand, 8])
l=([jean, martin, 10],[pauline, leduc, 12],Teacher[[camille, germain, 27],60])
l3=l : True

docs.title: 4.3.3. Compound assignment operators (C# 14)
docs.text: Why define the operator [+=] when [l = l + p] produces the same output? If the class does not define [+=], the compiler translates [l += p] to [l = l + p]: a new list is created, all the people from [l] are copied into it, then [l] refers to this new list, and the old one is discarded by the garbage collector. With the operator [+=] defined by the class, the person is added to the existing list without being copied. Line 16 stores a second reference, [l3], to the list [l]; after the [l += ...] statement, both references still point to the same object (line 6 of the results), which proves that the list was not recreated. For a large list, or in a loop, the difference in performance is significant.

docs.title: 4.4. Defining an indexer for a class
docs.text:
Here, we continue to use the class [ListOfPersons]. If [l] is an instance of [ListOfPersons], we want to be able to use the notation [l[i]] to refer to person number i in the list [l], both for reading ([Person p = l[i]]) and writing ([l[i] = new Person(...)]).

To be able to write [l[i]], where [l[i]] refers to an object [Person], we need to define a specific property named [this] in the [ListOfPersons] class:

    // indexer by position, read and write
    public Person this[int i]
    {
        get { return persons[i]; }
        set { persons[i] = value; }
    }

    // indexer by last name, read-only: returns the position of the person or -1
    public int this[string lastName]
    {
        get
        {
            // we search for the person
            for (int i = 0; i < persons.Count; i++)
            {
                if (persons[i].LastName == lastName)
                {
                    return i;
                }
            }
            return -1;
        }
    }

The property [this[int i]] is called an indexer because it gives meaning to the expression [obj[i]], which resembles array notation, whereas [obj] is not an array but an object. The method [get] of the indexer of the object [obj] is called when [variable = obj[i]] is written, and the method [set] is called when [obj[i] = value] is written.

  • Lines 27–30: The position-based indexer. The method [get] returns person No. i from the private list [persons], and the method [set] assigns person [value] to it. The 2008 course, whose class was derived from [ArrayList], had to mask the parent class’s indexer with the keyword [new] and convert the element of type [object] that it returned to [Person]. With a generic list, no more conversion is needed;
  • lines 34–46: we also want to be able to write [int i = l["lastName"]], that is, to index the list [l] not by an element number but by a person’s name. The result of [l[lastName]] is an integer: the position in the list of the person with the name [lastName], or -1 if that person is not in the list. Only the method [get] is defined, thereby preventing the syntax [l["lastName"] = value], which would have required the definition of a method [set]. A class can have multiple indexers, provided their parameters differ.

The test program continues as follows:

// --- indexers
// change of element no. 1
l[1] = new Person("franck", "gallon", 5);
// display of element no. 1
Console.WriteLine("l[1]=" + l[1]);
// display of the list l
Console.WriteLine("l=" + l);
// search for persons by their last name
string[] lastNames = ["martin", "germain", "xx"];
foreach (string lastName in lastNames)
{
    int index = l[lastName];
    if (index != -1)
    {
        Console.WriteLine($"Person({lastName})={l[index]}");
    }
    else
    {
        Console.WriteLine($"Person({lastName}) does not exist");
    }
}
  • line 25: call to the method [set] of the indexer [this[int]];
  • line 27: call to its method [get];
  • Line 34: Call to the [this[string]] indexer;
  • line 37: call to the [this[int]] indexer.

Results:

l[1]=[franck, gallon, 5]
l=([jean, martin, 10],[franck, gallon, 5],Teacher[[camille, germain, 27],60])
Person(martin)=[jean, martin, 10]
Person(germain)=Teacher[[camille, germain, 27],60]
Person(xx) does not exist

docs.title: 4.5.1. Value and Reference
docs.text:
The C# structure is analogous to the C language structure and is very similar to the concept of a class. A structure is defined as follows:

struct StructureName
{
    // fields
    ...
    // properties
    ...
    // constructors
    ...
    // methods
    ...
}

Despite similarities in their declarations, there are significant differences between classes and structures. For example, the concept of inheritance does not exist with structures (a structure can, however, implement interfaces, which are discussed later). If we are writing a class that is not meant to be derived from, what are the differences between a structure and a class that will help us choose between the two? Let’s use the following example to find out: [classes-13.cs]:

// structure and class: value copy, reference copy
// a structure sp1
SPerson sp1;
sp1.Name = "paul";
sp1.Age = 10;
Console.WriteLine("sp1=SPerson(" + sp1.Name + "," + sp1.Age + ")");
// a structure sp2
SPerson sp2 = sp1;
Console.WriteLine("sp2=SPerson(" + sp2.Name + "," + sp2.Age + ")");
// sp2 is modified
sp2.Name = "nicole";
sp2.Age = 30;
// checking sp1 and sp2
Console.WriteLine("sp1=SPerson(" + sp1.Name + "," + sp1.Age + ")");
Console.WriteLine("sp2=SPerson(" + sp2.Name + "," + sp2.Age + ")");

// an object op1
CPerson op1 = new CPerson();
op1.Name = "paul";
op1.Age = 10;
Console.WriteLine("op1=CPerson(" + op1.Name + "," + op1.Age + ")");
// an object op2
CPerson op2 = op1;
Console.WriteLine("op2=CPerson(" + op2.Name + "," + op2.Age + ")");
// op2 is modified
op2.Name = "nicole";
op2.Age = 30;
// checking op1 and op2
Console.WriteLine("op1=CPerson(" + op1.Name + "," + op1.Age + ")");
Console.WriteLine("op2=CPerson(" + op2.Name + "," + op2.Age + ")");

// SPerson structure
struct SPerson
{
    public string Name;
    public int Age;
}

// CPerson class
class CPerson
{
    public string Name = "";
    public int Age;
}
  • lines 33–36: a structure with two public fields: [Name], [Age];
  • lines 40–43: a class with two public fields: [Name], [Age]. Public fields, which are generally discouraged, make this example more readable.

Results:

> dotnet run classes-13.cs
sp1=SPerson(paul,10)
sp2=SPerson(paul,10)
sp1=SPerson(paul,10)
sp2=SPerson(nicole,30)
op1=CPerson(paul,10)
op2=CPerson(paul,10)
op1=CPerson(nicole,30)
op2=CPerson(nicole,30)

This structure does not have a constructor here. It could have one, as we will show later. By default, it always has a parameterless constructor—in this case, [SPerson()]—which sets all its fields to zero ([null] for the references).

The declaration on line 3 creates a structure ([Name], [Age]), and the value of [sp1] is this structure itself. Its fields do not yet have values: the compiler requires that they all be assigned (lines 4–5) before the structure is used (line 6). In the case of a class, the object ([Name], [Age]) must be created explicitly using the [new] operator (line 18). The statement creates a [CPerson] object (roughly equivalent to our structure), and the value of [op1] is then the address (the reference) of that object.

To summarize:

  • in the case of the structure, the value of [sp1] is the structure itself;
  • in the case of the class, the value of [op1] is the address of the created object.

When [SPerson sp2 = sp1;] is written in the program (line 8), a new structure [sp2] ([Name], [Age]) is created and initialized with the value of [sp1], which is the structure itself:

The structure of [sp1] is duplicated in [sp2] (left side of the diagram). This is a value copy. Now let’s consider the instruction [CPerson op2 = op1;] (line 23). In the case of classes, the value of [op1] is copied to [op2], but since this value is actually the object’s address, the object itself is not duplicated (right side of the diagram).

In the case of the structure, changing the value of [sp2] does not change the value of [sp1], as shown by the program (lines 4–5 of the results). In the case of the object, if you modify the object pointed to by [op2], the one pointed to by [op1] is also modified since they are the same (lines 8–9).

We can therefore conclude from these explanations that:

  • the value of a variable of type structure is the structure itself;
  • the value of a variable of type class is the address of the object it points to.

It is said that structures are value types and classes are reference types. The simple types in C# ([int], [double], [decimal], [bool], [char], …) are .NET structures ([System.Int32], [System.Double], …), whereas [string] and arrays are reference types. A structure is suitable for representing a small piece of data (a point, a color, a date, an amount…) that is treated as a value. A structure is not allocated individually on the garbage collector’s heap: a local variable of type structure is generally placed on the stack, and an array of structures contains the structures themselves rather than references to them.

docs.title: 4.5.2. A Structure with Properties and Constructors
docs.text:
Once the fundamental difference between a value and a reference is understood, a structure proves to be very similar to a class, as shown in the following example [classes-14.cs]:

// a structure with constructors, properties and a method
// a person p1
SPerson p1 = new SPerson();
Console.WriteLine($"p1={p1}");
p1.Name = "paul";
p1.Age = 10;
Console.WriteLine($"p1={p1}");
// a person p2
SPerson p2 = p1;
Console.WriteLine("p2=" + p2);
// p2 is modified
p2.Name = "nicole";
p2.Age = 30;
// checking p1 and p2
Console.WriteLine("p1=" + p1);
Console.WriteLine("p2=" + p2);
// a person p3
SPerson p3 = new SPerson("amandin", 18);
Console.WriteLine("p3=" + p3);
// a person p4
SPerson p4 = new SPerson { Name = "x", Age = 10 };
Console.WriteLine("p4=" + p4);
// the default value of a structure: all fields set to zero (null for references)
SPerson p5 = default;
Console.WriteLine("p5=" + p5);
// equality of two structures: comparison of the values of the fields
SPerson p6 = new SPerson("nicole", 30);
Console.WriteLine($"p1.Equals(p2) : {p1.Equals(p2)}, p2.Equals(p6) : {p2.Equals(p6)}");

// SPerson structure
struct SPerson
{
    // constructors
    public SPerson(string name, int age)
    {
        Name = name;
        Age = age;
    }

    public SPerson() : this("?", 0)
    {
    }

    // properties
    public string? Name { get; set; }
    public int Age { get; set; }

    // ToString
    public override string ToString()
    {
        return $"SPerson({Name},{Age})";
    }
}
  • lines 34–37: a constructor with two parameters. The 2008 course explained that a struct constructor could not initialize fields via properties: this restriction has been removed (C# 11);
  • line 40: Since C# 10, a struct can declare its own parameterless constructor, which is chained to the previous one here. It is called by [new SPerson()] (line 3) and by the object initializer on line 21, which then modifies the two properties;
  • lines 45–46: two automatic properties. The property [Name] is declared as type [string?] (a string that could be [null]) because a struct can always be created without using a constructor: this is the case for its default value (line 24), where all fields are set to zero and the name is therefore [null], as well as for the elements of a newly created array of structures;
  • lines 49–51: redefinition of the method [ToString]. A structure implicitly derives from the class [System.ValueType], which itself derives from [object];
  • line 28: The [Equals] method, inherited from [ValueType], compares two structures field by field. The [==] operator, on the other hand, is not defined for a structure unless it is overridden.

Results:

> dotnet run classes-14.cs
p1=SPerson(?,0)
p1=SPerson(paul,10)
p2=SPerson(paul,10)
p1=SPerson(paul,10)
p2=SPerson(nicole,30)
p3=SPerson(amandin,18)
p4=SPerson(x,10)
p5=SPerson(,0)
p1.Equals(p2) : False, p2.Equals(p6) : True

At the end of the program, the structures [p1] and [p2] are different (lines 5–6): with a class, [p1] and [p2] would have referred to the same object.

docs.title: 4.5.3. Immutable Structures and Record Structures
docs.text:
A structure whose state can be modified can lead to unexpected results: since it is copied with every assignment or parameter pass, one often modifies a copy while believing one is modifying the original. Therefore, it is recommended to make structures immutable: once created, they can no longer be modified. The program [classes-15.cs] demonstrates both ways to do this:

// immutable structures (readonly struct) and record structures (record struct)
Point a = new Point(1, 2);
// a.X = 5;   // rejected: the properties of a readonly struct cannot be modified
Point b = a.Move(3, 4);
Console.WriteLine($"a={a}, b={b}");

// a record struct: ToString, Equals, == and != are generated by the compiler
PointR r1 = new PointR(1, 2);
PointR r2 = new PointR(1, 2);
Console.WriteLine($"r1={r1}, r2={r2}");
Console.WriteLine($"r1 == r2 : {r1 == r2}");
// a (non readonly) record struct can be modified
r2.Y = 20;
Console.WriteLine($"r2={r2}, r1 == r2 : {r1 == r2}");
// the with expression creates a modified copy
PointR r3 = r1 with { X = 10 };
Console.WriteLine($"r3={r3}");

// a readonly record struct is immutable
Color red = new Color(255, 0, 0);
Color pink = red with { G = 128, B = 128 };
Console.WriteLine($"red={red}, pink={pink}");
// pink.G = 0;   // rejected: the structure is read-only

// an immutable structure
readonly struct Point
{
    public Point(int x, int y)
    {
        X = x;
        Y = y;
    }

    public int X { get; }
    public int Y { get; }

    // we do not modify the point: we return a new one
    public Point Move(int dx, int dy) => new Point(X + dx, Y + dy);

    public override string ToString() => $"({X},{Y})";
}

// a "positional" record structure: X and Y are public properties
record struct PointR(int X, int Y);

// an immutable record structure
readonly record struct Color(byte R, byte G, byte B);
  • lines 26–40: a structure declared as [readonly] (C# 7.2). The compiler verifies that all its fields and properties are read-only. To “move” a point, the method [Move] returns a new point (line 38);
  • line 44: a record structure (C# 10). This single line declares a structure whose constructor has two parameters, [X] and [Y], and which has two public read-write properties, [X] and [Y]. The compiler also generates a method named [ToString] that displays the structure’s name and its properties, the equality methods and operators [==] and [!=] (line 11), as well as support for the expression [with], which creates a copy of the structure by modifying certain properties (line 16);
  • line 47: an immutable record structure: its properties are read-only (more precisely, [init]: they can only be set at creation), while the expression [with] remains valid (line 21).

Results:

> dotnet run classes-15.cs
a=(1,2), b=(4,6)
r1=PointR { X = 1, Y = 2 }, r2=PointR { X = 1, Y = 2 }
r1 == r2 : True
r2=PointR { X = 1, Y = 20 }, r1 == r2 : False
r3=PointR { X = 10, Y = 2 }
red=Color { R = 255, G = 0, B = 0 }, pink=Color { R = 255, G = 128, B = 128 }

The records ([record]) also exist as classes: we’ll examine them in detail a little later. For now, let’s just note that a [readonly record struct] is the most concise way to declare a small, immutable value-type data item: this is the type we’ll use for the tax brackets in this chapter’s example application.

docs.title: 4.6.1. A First Example
docs.text:
An interface is a set of method or property declarations that forms a contract. A class (or structure) that chooses to implement an interface commits to providing an implementation of all the methods and properties defined in the interface. The compiler verifies this implementation.

For example, here is the definition of the [System.Collections.IEnumerator] interface from .NET:

public interface IEnumerator
{
    // properties
    object Current { get; }
    // methods
    bool MoveNext();
    void Reset();
}

The properties and methods of the interface are defined only by their signatures. They are not implemented (they have no code). It is the classes that implement the interface that provide code for the interface’s methods and properties:

public class C : IEnumerator
{
    ...
    public object Current { get { ... } }
    public bool MoveNext() { ... }
    public void Reset() { ... }
}
  • Line 1: The class [C] implements the interface [IEnumerator]. Note that the symbol [:] used for implementing an interface is the same as the one used for deriving a class;
  • Lines 4–6: The implementation of the methods and properties of the [IEnumerator] interface. They must be public.

By convention, an interface name begins with the letter I. The following examples make up the [Statistics] project in the solution. Consider the following interface, [IStats.cs]:

namespace Statistics;

public interface IStats
{
    // average of a series of values
    double Average { get; }

    // standard deviation of the series
    double StandardDeviation();
}

The [IStats] interface has:

  • a read-only property [Average]: to calculate the average of a series of values;
  • a method [StandardDeviation]: to calculate the standard deviation.

Note that it is not specified anywhere which set of values is being referred to. It could be the average grades of a class, the monthly average sales of a particular product, the average temperature in a given location… This is the principle behind interfaces: they assume the existence of methods in the object but not that of specific data.

A first implementation class for the [IStats] interface could be a class used to store the grades of students in a class for a given subject. A student is characterized by the following [Student] structure: [Student.cs]:

namespace Statistics;

// a student
public readonly record struct Student(string FirstName, string LastName);

The student is identified by their first and last names. The 2008 course defined a structure with two automatic properties; an immutable record structure, as shown in the previous paragraph, is represented in a single line. A grade is characterized by the following structure: [Grade] [Grade.cs]:

namespace Statistics;

// the grade of a student
public readonly record struct Grade(Student Student, double Value)
{
    public override string ToString() => $"[{Student.FirstName},{Student.LastName},{Value}]";
}

The grade is defined by the student being graded and the grade itself. The structure redefines the method [ToString] generated by the compiler to display a grade in the form [firstName,lastName,value].

The grades of all students in a given subject are grouped in the following class [ArrayOfGrades]: [ArrayOfGrades.cs]:

namespace Statistics;

public class ArrayOfGrades : IStats
{
    // properties
    public string Subject { get; }
    public Grade[] Grades { get; }
    public double Average { get; }
    // field
    private readonly double standardDeviation;

    // constructor
    public ArrayOfGrades(string subject, Grade[] grades)
    {
        // storing the data
        Subject = subject;
        Grades = grades;
        // computing the average of the grades
        double sum = 0;
        foreach (Grade grade in Grades)
        {
            sum += grade.Value;
        }
        Average = Grades.Length != 0 ? sum / Grades.Length : -1;
        // computing the standard deviation
        double squares = 0;
        foreach (Grade grade in Grades)
        {
            squares += Math.Pow(grade.Value - Average, 2);
        }
        standardDeviation = Grades.Length != 0 ? Math.Sqrt(squares / Grades.Length) : -1;
    }

    // implementation of the StandardDeviation method of the IStats interface
    public double StandardDeviation()
    {
        return standardDeviation;
    }

    // ToString
    public override string ToString()
    {
        return $"subject={Subject}, grades=({string.Join(",", Grades)})";
    }
}
  • Line 3: The class [ArrayOfGrades] implements the interface [IStats]. It must therefore implement the property [Average] and the method [StandardDeviation]. These are implemented on line 8 ([Average]) and lines 35–37 ([StandardDeviation]);
  • lines 6–8: three read-only automatic properties: the subject for which the object stores grades, the grade array, and the grade average;
  • line 10: a field storing the standard deviation of the grades;
  • lines 13–31: the constructor. Here, we assume that the grades passed to the constructor will not change afterward. Therefore, we use the constructor to immediately calculate the average and standard deviation of these grades and store them. A read-only property such as [Average] can be assigned a value in the constructor (line 24); it cannot be assigned a value afterward. The expressions [condition ? value1 : value2] set the mean and standard deviation of an empty array to -1;
  • lines 41–43: the method [ToString] uses [string.Join] to concatenate the grades, each of which is converted to a string by the method [ToString] of the structure [Grade].

In the previous class, grades were stored in an array. It was not possible to add a new grade after the [ArrayOfGrades] object was created. We now offer a second implementation of the [IStats] interface, called [ListOfGrades], where this time the grades are stored in a list [List<Grade>], with the ability to add grades after the initial creation of the [ListOfGrades] object: [ListOfGrades.cs]:

namespace Statistics;

public class ListOfGrades : IStats
{
    // properties
    public string Subject { get; }
    public List<Grade> Grades { get; }
    // stored average and standard deviation (null: not yet computed)
    private double? average;
    private double? standardDeviation;

    // constructor
    public ListOfGrades(string subject, List<Grade> grades)
    {
        Subject = subject;
        Grades = grades;
    }

    // adding a grade
    public void Add(Grade grade)
    {
        Grades.Add(grade);
        // the average and the standard deviation will have to be recomputed
        average = null;
        standardDeviation = null;
    }

    // average of the grades: computed on first request
    public double Average
    {
        get
        {
            average ??= ComputeAverage();
            return average.Value;
        }
    }

    // standard deviation of the grades: computed on first request
    public double StandardDeviation()
    {
        standardDeviation ??= ComputeStandardDeviation();
        return standardDeviation.Value;
    }

    private double ComputeAverage()
    {
        if (Grades.Count == 0)
        {
            return -1;
        }
        double sum = 0;
        foreach (Grade grade in Grades)
        {
            sum += grade.Value;
        }
        return sum / Grades.Count;
    }

    private double ComputeStandardDeviation()
    {
        if (Grades.Count == 0)
        {
            return -1;
        }
        double m = Average;
        double squares = 0;
        foreach (Grade grade in Grades)
        {
            squares += Math.Pow(grade.Value - m, 2);
        }
        return Math.Sqrt(squares / Grades.Count);
    }

    // ToString
    public override string ToString()
    {
        return $"subject={Subject}, grades=({string.Join(",", Grades)})";
    }
}
  • Line 3: The class [ListOfGrades] implements the interface [IStats];
  • line 7: Grades are now stored in a list rather than an array;
  • lines 20–25: You can now add a grade to those already stored. The mean and standard deviation are no longer calculated in the constructor but on demand, within the interface members themselves: [Average] (lines 29–34) and [StandardDeviation] (lines 39–42). Once calculated, these values are stored so they aren’t recalculated with every request: they are said to be cached. Adding a score invalidates the cache;
  • lines 9–10: the cache. The type [double?] (C# 2) is a nullable value type: a variable of this type contains a [double] or [null], which here means “not yet calculated.” The 2008 course used the value -1 for this;
  • line 33: the [??=] operator (C# 8) only assigns a value to the left-hand variable if it is [null]. The method [ComputeAverage] is therefore called only if the average has not yet been calculated. The property [Value] of a variable [double?] returns the value [double] that it contains.

A test program could look like this: [Program.cs]:

using Statistics;

// a few students and their English grades
Student[] students = [new Student("Paul", "Martin"), new Student("Maxime", "Germain"), new Student("Berthine", "Samin")];
Grade[] grades = [new Grade(students[0], 14), new Grade(students[1], 16), new Grade(students[2], 18)];
// which we store in an ArrayOfGrades object
ArrayOfGrades english = new ArrayOfGrades("english", grades);
// display of average and standard deviation
DisplayStats(english);
// the same grades in a ListOfGrades object
ListOfGrades french = new ListOfGrades("french", new List<Grade>(grades));
DisplayStats(french);
// we add a grade
french.Add(new Grade(new Student("Jérôme", "Jaric"), 10));
DisplayStats(french);
// a variable can have an interface as its type
IStats stats = english;
Console.WriteLine($"English average: {stats.Average}");
stats = french;
Console.WriteLine($"French average: {stats.Average}");

// display of the average and standard deviation of an object implementing IStats
static void DisplayStats(IStats values)
{
    Console.WriteLine($"{values}, Average={values.Average}, Standard deviation={values.StandardDeviation()}");
}
  • line 4: creates an array of students;
  • line 5: creation of an array of grades;
  • line 7: a [ArrayOfGrades] object, whose mean and standard deviation are displayed on line 9;
  • line 11: an object [ListOfGrades], whose mean and standard deviation are displayed on line 12. The class [List<Grade>] has a constructor that accepts a collection of grades, in this case the array [grades];
  • line 14: a new grade is added, followed by a new display;
  • lines 23–25: The function [DisplayStats] takes a [IStats] type as a parameter, which is an interface type. This means that the actual parameter can be any object that implements the [IStats] interface. When using a data object of an interface type, only the methods of the interface implemented by that object are used. The rest is ignored. This property is similar to the polymorphism we saw with classes. If a set of classes Ci that are not related to each other through inheritance (and therefore cannot use inheritance-based polymorphism) share a set of methods with the same signature, it may be useful to group these methods into an interface I that all the relevant classes would implement. Instances of these classes Ci can then be used as actual parameters of functions that accept a formal parameter of type I—that is, functions that use only the methods of the Ci objects defined in the interface I, and not the specific fields and methods of the various Ci classes;
  • lines 17–19: A variable can be of the type of an interface. It can then refer to any object of a class that implements the interface. The compiler allows access only to the members of the interface: the property [Average] and the method [StandardDeviation].

Results:

> dotnet run
subject=english, grades=([Paul,Martin,14],[Maxime,Germain,16],[Berthine,Samin,18]), Average=16, Standard deviation=1,632993161855452
subject=french, grades=([Paul,Martin,14],[Maxime,Germain,16],[Berthine,Samin,18]), Average=16, Standard deviation=1,632993161855452
subject=french, grades=([Paul,Martin,14],[Maxime,Germain,16],[Berthine,Samin,18],[Jérôme,Jaric,10]), Average=14,5, Standard deviation=2,958039891549808
English average: 16
French average: 14,5

Finally, note that interfaces can have multiple implementations; that is, you can write:

public class DerivedClass : BaseClass, I1, I2, ..., In
{
    ...
}

where the Ij are interfaces: a class inherits from only one class, but can implement as many interfaces as it wishes.

docs.title: 4.6.2. Default Interface Methods
docs.text:
Starting with C# 8, an interface can provide a default implementation for some of its methods. A class that implements the interface can then use this implementation or provide its own. This makes it possible, for example, to add a method to an already published interface without requiring all classes that implement it to be modified. The program [classes-16.cs] provides an example:

// default interface methods (C# 8)
IShape[] shapes = [new Square(2), new Circle(1)];
foreach (IShape shape in shapes)
{
    Console.WriteLine(shape.Description());
}
// the default method is only accessible through the interface type
Square square = new Square(3);
// Console.WriteLine(square.Description());   // rejected: Square does not define Description
Console.WriteLine(((IShape)square).Description());

public interface IShape
{
    // method to implement
    double Area();

    // method with a default implementation
    string Description() => $"{GetType().Name} with area {Area():F2}";
}

// Square uses the default implementation of Description
public class Square : IShape
{
    private readonly double side;

    public Square(double side)
    {
        this.side = side;
    }

    public double Area() => side * side;
}

// Circle provides its own implementation of Description
public class Circle : IShape
{
    private readonly double radius;

    public Circle(double radius)
    {
        this.radius = radius;
    }

    public double Area() => Math.PI * radius * radius;

    public string Description() => $"Circle with radius {radius} and area {Area():F2}";
}
  • Lines 12–18: The [IShape] interface declares a method, [Area], to be implemented, and a method, [Description], with a default implementation. This method can use the other members of the interface ([Area]) and those of [object] ([GetType]). The [{Area():F2}] format displays the area with two decimal places;
  • lines 22–31: The class [Square] implements only [Area]; it uses the method [Description] by default;
  • lines 35–46: The class [Circle] provides its own method, [Description];
  • line 10: the default method belongs to the interface, not to the [Square] class: it can only be called through a reference of type [IShape]. The call to [square.Description()] is rejected by the compiler.

Results:

> dotnet run classes-16.cs
Square with area 4,00
Circle with radius 1 and area 3,14
Square with area 9,00

Finally, starting with C# 11, an interface can declare abstract static members that the types implementing it must provide. These are used only with generics: we’ll cover them at the end of the section on generics.

docs.title: 4.7. Abstract Classes
docs.text:
An abstract class is a class that cannot be instantiated. You must create derived classes, which can be instantiated. Abstract classes can be used to refactor the code of a class hierarchy. Let’s examine the following example, which forms the [Users] project of the solution: [User.cs]:

namespace Users;

public abstract class User
{
    // fields
    private readonly string login;
    private readonly string password;
    private readonly string role;

    // constructor
    protected User(string login, string password)
    {
        // we store the information
        this.login = login;
        this.password = password;
        // we identify the user
        string? role = Identify();
        // identified?
        if (role == null)
        {
            throw new UnknownUserException($"[{login},{password}]");
        }
        this.role = role;
    }

    // ToString
    public override string ToString()
    {
        return $"User[{login},{password},{role}]";
    }

    // identification: returns the role of the user or null if they are not recognized
    protected abstract string? Identify();
}
  • line 3: the class is declared abstract using the keyword [abstract];
  • Lines 11–23: the constructor for the [User] class. This class stores information about a web application’s user. The application has various types of users who are authenticated via a username and password (lines 6–7). These two pieces of information are verified against a directory (LDAP) for some users, against a database for others, and so on. The constructor is [protected]: it can only be called by the constructors of derived classes;
  • lines 14–15: the authentication information is stored;
  • line 17: it is verified by a method named [Identify]. Because the authentication method is not known at this level, it is declared abstract (line 33) using the keyword [abstract]. An abstract method has no body: derived classes will provide one. A class that has an abstract method must itself be declared abstract. The method [Identify] returns a string specifying the user’s role (basically, what they are authorized to do), or [null] if the user is not recognized: its return type is therefore [string?];
  • lines 19–21: if the user is not recognized, an exception is thrown;
  • lines 27–29: the method [ToString], which identifies an instance of the class.

We assume here that the developer wants to have control over the construction of instances of the class [User] and its derived classes, perhaps because they want to ensure that an exception of a certain type is thrown if the user is not recognized. Derived classes can rely on this constructor. To do so, they must provide the method [Identify]. Note that the constructor here calls a method overridden by the derived classes even though those classes have not yet executed their own constructors: the method [Identify] must therefore not use any fields of the derived class, which have not yet been initialized. This is a practice that should be used with caution.

The [UnknownUserException] class is as follows:

namespace Users;

public class UnknownUserException : Exception
{
    public UnknownUserException(string message) : base(message)
    {
    }
}
  • Line 3: It derives from the [Exception] class;
  • line 5: it has only one constructor that takes an error message as a parameter. This parameter is passed to the parent class, which has the same constructor.

We now derive the child class [Administrator] from the class [User]:

namespace Users;

public class Administrator : User
{
    // constructor
    public Administrator(string login, string password)
        : base(login, password)
    {
    }

    // identification
    protected override string? Identify()
    {
        // LDAP identification
        // ...
        return "admin";
    }
}
  • lines 6–7: the constructor simply passes the parameters it receives to its parent class;
  • Lines 12–16: The [Identify] method of the [Administrator] class. Suppose an administrator is identified by a directory LDAP. This method overrides the abstract method [Identify] of its parent class: the keyword [override] is required (an abstract method is implicitly virtual). The 2008 course incorrectly stated the opposite. It retains the access specifier [protected] of the method it overrides.

We now derive the child class [Observer] from the class [User]:

namespace Users;

public class Observer : User
{
    // constructor
    public Observer(string login, string password)
        : base(login, password)
    {
    }

    // identification
    protected override string? Identify()
    {
        // identification through a database
        // ...
        return "observer";
    }
}
  • Lines 12–16: the [Identify] method of the [Observer] class. We assume that an observer is identified by verifying their identification data in a database.

Ultimately, the objects [Administrator] and [Observer] are initialized by the same constructor, that of the parent class [User]. This constructor uses the method [Identify] provided by these classes.

A third class, [Unknown], also derives from the [User] class:

namespace Users;

public class Unknown : User
{
    // constructor
    public Unknown(string login, string password)
        : base(login, password)
    {
    }

    // identification
    protected override string? Identify()
    {
        // user not known
        // ...
        return null;
    }
}
  • Line 16: The [Identify] method returns [null] to indicate that the user was not recognized.

A test program for [Program.cs] might look like this:

using Users;

Console.WriteLine(new Observer("observer", "pwd1"));
Console.WriteLine(new Administrator("admin", "pwd2"));
try
{
    Console.WriteLine(new Unknown("xx", "yy"));
}
catch (UnknownUserException e)
{
    Console.WriteLine("Unknown user: " + e.Message);
}
// User u = new User("x", "y");   // rejected: the User class is abstract

Note that in lines 3 and 4, the method [User.ToString()] is called by the method [WriteLine]. On line 7, the constructor throws a [UnknownUserException] exception, which is caught on line 9: the object is not created, and nothing is displayed by [WriteLine]. Line 13, if uncommented, is rejected by the compiler: you cannot create an object of an abstract class.

Results:

> dotnet run
User[observer,pwd1,observer]
User[admin,pwd2,admin]
Unknown user: [xx,yy]

An abstract class is similar to an interface: both declare members that other classes must implement. However, an abstract class can have fields, constructors, and code common to its derived classes; conversely, a class can derive from only one abstract class, whereas it can implement multiple interfaces. The two are often combined: an interface defines the contract, and an abstract class that implements it factors out the code common to multiple implementations. This is what the example application in this chapter will do.

docs.title: 4.8.1. Generic Classes and Methods
docs.text:
Suppose we want to write a method that swaps two integers. This method could look like this:

public static void Swap1(ref int value1, ref int value2)
{
    // we swap the values of value1 and value2
    int temp = value2;
    value2 = value1;
    value1 = temp;
}

Now, if we wanted to swap two references to [Person] objects, we would write:

public static void Swap2(ref Person value1, ref Person value2)
{
    // we swap the references value1 and value2
    Person temp = value2;
    value2 = value1;
    value1 = temp;
}

What distinguishes the two methods is the type T of the parameters: [int] in [Swap1], and [Person] in [Swap2]. Generic classes, interfaces, and methods address the need for code that differs only in the type of certain data. They were introduced with C# 2: prior to that, the type [object] was used, which accepts any type, at the cost of type conversions at runtime and errors detected only at runtime. This is what the [ArrayList] class, mentioned in the section on operators, did.

The program [classes-17.cs] features a generic class, a generic method, and a second, more realistic generic class:

// generic classes and methods
// --- a generic class Generic1<T>
// int
int i1 = 1, i2 = 2;
Generic1<int>.Swap(ref i1, ref i2);
Console.WriteLine($"i1={i1},i2={i2}");
// string
string s1 = "s1", s2 = "s2";
Generic1<string>.Swap(ref s1, ref s2);
Console.WriteLine($"s1={s1},s2={s2}");
// Person
Person p1 = new Person("jean", "clu", 20), p2 = new Person("pauline", "dard", 55);
Generic1<Person>.Swap(ref p1, ref p2);
Console.WriteLine($"p1={p1},p2={p2}");

// --- a generic method Generic2.Swap<T>
Generic2.Swap<int>(ref i1, ref i2);
Console.WriteLine($"i1={i1},i2={i2}");
// the compiler infers T from the type of the actual parameters
Generic2.Swap(ref s1, ref s2);
Console.WriteLine($"s1={s1},s2={s2}");
Generic2.Swap(ref p1, ref p2);
Console.WriteLine($"p1={p1},p2={p2}");

// --- a generic class with a state: a stack of elements of type T
MyStack<Person> stack = new MyStack<Person>();
stack.Push(p1);
stack.Push(p2);
Console.WriteLine($"The stack contains {stack.Count} persons");
Person top = stack.Pop();
Console.WriteLine($"Popped person: {top}, {stack.Count} left");
// stack.Push("x");   // rejected: the stack only accepts Person objects

// a generic class
class Generic1<T>
{
    public static void Swap(ref T value1, ref T value2)
    {
        // we swap the values of value1 and value2
        T temp = value2;
        value2 = value1;
        value1 = temp;
    }
}

// a non-generic class with a generic method
class Generic2
{
    public static void Swap<T>(ref T value1, ref T value2)
    {
        T temp = value2;
        value2 = value1;
        value1 = temp;
    }
}

// a stack of elements of type T
class MyStack<T>
{
    // the elements of the stack
    private readonly List<T> elements = new List<T>();

    // number of elements
    public int Count => elements.Count;

    // adds an element to the top of the stack
    public void Push(T element)
    {
        elements.Add(element);
    }

    // removes the element at the top of the stack
    public T Pop()
    {
        if (elements.Count == 0)
        {
            throw new InvalidOperationException("empty stack");
        }
        T element = elements[^1];
        elements.RemoveAt(elements.Count - 1);
        return element;
    }
}

// a person
class Person
{
    private readonly string firstName;
    private readonly string lastName;
    private readonly int age;

    public Person(string firstName, string lastName, int age)
    {
        this.firstName = firstName;
        this.lastName = lastName;
        this.age = age;
    }

    public override string ToString() => $"[{firstName}, {lastName}, {age}]";
}
  • lines 35–42: The class *[Generic1] is parameterized by a type denoted as *[T]. You can name it whatever you want. This type, [T], is then used within the class just like any other type: for the two parameters to be swapped and for the temporary variable [temp]. The class [Generic1] is said to be a generic class;
  • Line 5: When using a generic class parameterized by the types T1, T2, …, these types must be “instantiated.” Here, we use the static method [Swap] of type [Generic1<int>] to indicate that the references passed to the method [Swap] are of type [int]. Lines 9 and 13: the same applies to the types [string] and [Person];
  • Lines 47–49: The class [Generic2] is not generic, but its static method [Swap] is;
  • line 17: the method [Swap] is called, specifying the type of the parameters between [<>]. In fact, the compiler is able to deduce, based on the type of the actual parameters, which variant of the method [Swap] to use. Therefore, the code on lines 20–22 is valid;
  • lines 58–81: a generic class with a state: a stack of elements of type [T]. Elements are pushed onto the top of the stack and popped from the top. The elements are stored in a generic list of type [List<T>] (line 61), which is itself parameterized by the stack’s type, [T]. The expression [elements[^1]] (line 79) refers to the last element of the list;
  • line 26: a stack of people. The compiler guarantees that it will contain only people: the statement on line 32 would be rejected. The method [Pop] returns an object of type [Person], without conversion.

Results:

> dotnet run classes-17.cs
i1=2,i2=1
s1=s2,s2=s1
p1=[pauline, dard, 55],p2=[jean, clu, 20]
i1=1,i2=2
s1=s1,s2=s2
p1=[jean, clu, 20],p2=[pauline, dard, 55]
The stack contains 2 persons
Popped person: [pauline, dard, 55], 1 left

Note that, to swap two variables, C# 7 now offers a more concise syntax based on tuples: [(a, b) = (b, a);].

docs.title: 4.8.2. Constraints on Generic Parameters
docs.text:
You can place constraints on generic parameters using the keyword [where]. The main ones are as follows:

ConstraintMeaning[where T : struct]T must be a value type (structure), excluding nullable types such as [int?][where T : class]T must be a reference type (class, interface, array, delegate)[where T : notnull]T must be a non-nullable type (value or reference)[where T : new()]T must have a public constructor with no parameters. This constraint comes last[where T : BaseClass]T must be the specified class or a derived class[where T : IInterface]T must implement the specified interface. Multiple interfaces may be specified[where T : U]T must be the type U or a type derived from U, where U is another generic parameter[where T : unmanaged]T must be a value type that contains no references

The program [classes-18.cs] uses two of them:

// constraints on generic parameters
// --- constraint where T : class
string s1 = "s1", s2 = "s2";
Generic3.Swap(ref s1, ref s2);
Console.WriteLine($"s1={s1},s2={s2}");
int i1 = 1, i2 = 2;
// Generic3.Swap(ref i1, ref i2);   // error CS0452: int is not a reference type
Console.WriteLine($"i1={i1},i2={i2}");

// --- constraint where T : IValue
// swapping instances of type RandomValue
for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++)
{
    RandomValue c1 = new RandomValue(), c2 = new RandomValue();
    Console.Write($"Before swap --> c1={c1},c2={c2}");
    Generic4.Order(ref c1, ref c2);
    Console.WriteLine($"   After swap --> c1={c1},c2={c2}");
}
// swapping instances of type StringValue
StringValue c3 = new StringValue("xxxxxxxxxxxxxx"), c4 = new StringValue("xx");
Console.WriteLine($"Before swap --> c3={c3},c4={c4}");
Generic4.Order(ref c3, ref c4);
Console.WriteLine($"After swap --> c3={c3},c4={c4}");

// T must be a reference type
class Generic3
{
    public static void Swap<T>(ref T value1, ref T value2) where T : class
    {
        T temp = value2;
        value2 = value1;
        value1 = temp;
    }
}

// the type T must implement IValue
class Generic4
{
    public static void Order<T>(ref T element1, ref T element2) where T : IValue
    {
        // if the 1st element is greater than the 2nd, we swap the elements
        if (element1.Value() > element2.Value())
        {
            T temp = element2;
            element2 = element1;
            element1 = temp;
        }
    }
}

// an object having an integer value
interface IValue
{
    int Value();
}

// an object having a random value
class RandomValue : IValue
{
    // random number generator shared by all the instances
    // (initialized with a fixed seed so that the results are reproducible)
    private static readonly Random generator = new Random(2026);
    // value of the object
    private readonly int value = generator.Next(100);

    public int Value() => value;

    public override string ToString() => value.ToString();
}

// an object whose value is the length of a string
class StringValue : IValue
{
    private readonly string s;

    public StringValue(string s)
    {
        this.s = s;
    }

    public int Value() => s.Length;

    public override string ToString() => s;
}
  • lines 26–28: the generic method [Swap] requires that the type [T] be a reference type (constraint [where T : class]);
  • line 7: if this line is uncommented, the compiler reports an error because the type [int] is not a class or an interface—it is a structure.

Here is the error message received when compiling the program after line 7 is uncommented:

> dotnet build classes-18.cs
classes-18.cs(7,10): error CS0452: The type 'int' must be a reference type in order to use it as parameter 'T' in the generic type or method 'Generic3.Swap<T>(ref T, ref T)'

The compiler message is displayed in the system language—in this case, English (on a computer configured for French, it would be in French). It lists the filename, the line and column numbers of the error, and the error code ([CS0452]), which can be looked up in the documentation.

Let’s return to the program [classes-18.cs]:

  • Lines 37–39: The type [T] must implement the interface [IValue] (lines 52–54). This interface has a method named [Value], used on line 42, which returns the value of the object of type [T]. Without this constraint, the compiler would reject the call to [element1.Value()]: any object of type [T] does not have a method named [Value]. The two references [element1] and [element2] are swapped only if the value of [element1] is greater than the value of [element2]: the method [Order] sorts the two elements in ascending order by value;
  • lines 58–68: the class [RandomValue] implements the interface [IValue]. The value of an instance is a random number between 0 and 99 (line 64), provided by a random number generator in the [Random] class shared by all instances (line 62). This generator is initialized with a fixed “seed”: it therefore always produces the same sequence of numbers, making the results reproducible. The 2008 course created a generator for each object, initialized with the current time, and had to wait one millisecond between creations to obtain different numbers. When reproducibility is not required, the shared generator [Random.Shared] can be used instead;
  • lines 72–83: the [StringValue] class also implements the [IValue] interface: the value of an instance is the length of the string passed to the constructor;
  • lines 12–17: Instances of type [RandomValue] are sorted;
  • lines 20–23: instances of type [StringValue] are sorted.

Results:

> dotnet run classes-18.cs
s1=s2,s2=s1
i1=1,i2=2
Before swap --> c1=15,c2=28   After swap --> c1=15,c2=28
Before swap --> c1=91,c2=99   After swap --> c1=91,c2=99
Before swap --> c1=91,c2=7   After swap --> c1=7,c2=91
Before swap --> c1=66,c2=85   After swap --> c1=66,c2=85
Before swap --> c1=62,c2=36   After swap --> c1=36,c2=62
Before swap --> c3=xxxxxxxxxxxxxx,c4=xx
After swap --> c3=xx,c4=xxxxxxxxxxxxxx

docs.title: 4.8.3. A generic interface: IComparer<T>
docs.text:
To illustrate the concept of a generic interface, we will sort an array of people first by their names, then by their ages. The method that allows us to sort an array is the static method [Sort] of the class [Array]. It has different signatures (it is overloaded). We will use the following signature:

public static void Sort<T>(T[] array, IComparer<T>? comparer)

[Sort] is a generic method where [T] denotes any type. The method takes two parameters:

  • [T[] array]: the array of elements of type [T] to be sorted;
  • [IComparer<T>? comparer]: a reference to an object that implements the [IComparer<T>] interface.

[IComparer<T>] is a generic interface defined as follows (simplified definition):

public interface IComparer<in T>
{
    int Compare(T? x, T? y);
}

The [IComparer<T>] interface has only one method. The [Compare] method:

  • takes two parameters, [x] and [y], of type [T]. The type [T?] indicates that their values can be [null] (the keyword [in] is a technical detail that we will not explain here);
  • returns a positive number if x > y, 0 if x == y, and a negative number if x < y. It is up to the developer to define the meaning of the operators <, ==, and >. For example, if [p1] and [p2] are two [Person] objects, we can say that p1 > p2 if the name of [p1] comes after the name of [p2] in alphabetical order. This will result in an ascending sort based on the people’s names. If we want to sort by age, we’ll say that p1 > p2 if the age of [p1] is greater than the age of [p2];
  • to sort in descending order, simply reverse the sign of the results.

We now know enough to sort an array of people. The program [classes-19.cs] is as follows:

// the generic interface IComparer<T>: sorting an array of persons
Person[] persons = [new Person("claude", "pollon", 25), new Person("valentine", "germain", 35), new Person("paul", "germain", 32)];
// display
Display("Array to sort", persons);
// sort by last name and first name
Array.Sort(persons, new CompareNames());
Display("Array after sorting by last name and first name", persons);
// sort by age
Array.Sort(persons, new CompareAges());
Display("Array after sorting by age", persons);

// display of an array of persons
static void Display(string text, Person[] persons)
{
    Console.WriteLine(text.PadRight(50, '-'));
    foreach (Person p in persons)
    {
        Console.WriteLine(p);
    }
}

// a person
class Person
{
    public Person(string firstName, string lastName, int age)
    {
        FirstName = firstName;
        LastName = lastName;
        Age = age;
    }

    public string FirstName { get; }
    public string LastName { get; }
    public int Age { get; }

    public override string ToString() => $"[{FirstName}, {LastName}, {Age}]";
}

// comparison of the last and first names of two persons
class CompareNames : IComparer<Person>
{
    public int Compare(Person? p1, Person? p2)
    {
        // we rule out the case of null references
        ArgumentNullException.ThrowIfNull(p1);
        ArgumentNullException.ThrowIfNull(p2);
        // we compare the last names
        int i = string.Compare(p1.LastName, p2.LastName, StringComparison.CurrentCulture);
        if (i != 0)
        {
            return i;
        }
        // equal last names: we compare the first names
        return string.Compare(p1.FirstName, p2.FirstName, StringComparison.CurrentCulture);
    }
}

// comparison of the ages of two persons
class CompareAges : IComparer<Person>
{
    public int Compare(Person? p1, Person? p2)
    {
        ArgumentNullException.ThrowIfNull(p1);
        ArgumentNullException.ThrowIfNull(p2);
        // we compare the ages
        return p1.Age.CompareTo(p2.Age);
    }
}
  • Line 2: the array of people;
  • line 6: sorting the table of people by last name and first name. The second parameter of the generic method [Sort] is an instance of the class [CompareNames], which implements the generic interface [IComparer<Person>];
  • lines 40–54: the class [CompareNames]. Its method [Compare] implements the method [int Compare(T? x, T? y)] of the interface [IComparer<T>], where [T] = [Person]:
    • lines 45–46: Since the parameters are declared as type [Person?], the compiler requires that a null reference be handled before using [p1] and [p2]. The static method [ArgumentNullException.ThrowIfNull] throws an exception if its parameter is [null]; the compiler knows that after it is called, the parameter is not null;
    • line 48: the method [string.Compare] compares two strings in alphabetical order according to the current culture, in this case French;
  • line 9: sorting the array of people by age, using an instance of the [CompareAges] class from lines 59–66. The [CompareTo] method for numeric types returns a negative, zero, or positive number depending on whether the number is less than, equal to, or greater than its parameter: this is exactly what the [Compare] method expects.

Results:

> dotnet run classes-19.cs
Array to sort-------------------------------------
[claude, pollon, 25]
[valentine, germain, 35]
[paul, germain, 32]
Array after sorting by last name and first name---
[paul, germain, 32]
[valentine, germain, 35]
[claude, pollon, 25]
Array after sorting by age------------------------
[claude, pollon, 25]
[paul, germain, 32]
[valentine, germain, 35]

We will see in Chapter 7, which covers delegates, that we can also pass a simple comparison function to [Array.Sort] without writing a class: [Array.Sort(persons, (p1, p2) => p1.Age.CompareTo(p2.Age));].

docs.title: 4.8.4. Abstract Static Members and Generic Mathematics
docs.text:
Can we write a generic method that sums the elements of an array of numbers, regardless of their type ([int], [double], [decimal]…)? We would need to be able to write [sum + value] and have the zero element of type [T]. However, the operator [+] is a static method, and a standard interface constraint only allows the use of instance methods. Since C# 11, an interface can declare abstract static members ([static abstract]), which every type that implements it must provide. .NET 7 has derived “generic mathematics” from this: All numeric types implement the [INumber<T>] interface in the [System.Numerics] namespace, which declares the type’s zero ([T.Zero]), arithmetic operators, and so on. The program [classes-20.cs] demonstrates this:

using System.Numerics;

// static abstract interface members (C# 11) and generic math
Console.WriteLine($"Sum of integers: {Sum([1, 2, 3])}");
Console.WriteLine($"Sum of reals: {Sum([1.5, 2.25])}");
Console.WriteLine($"Sum of decimals: {Sum([10.5m, 0.25m])}");
// an interface of our own
Describe<Cat>();
Describe<Dog>();

// sum of the elements of an array of numbers of type T
// INumber<T> declares static abstract members: T.Zero, the + operator, ...
static T Sum<T>(T[] values) where T : INumber<T>
{
    T sum = T.Zero;
    foreach (T value in values)
    {
        sum += value;
    }
    return sum;
}

// the method uses a static member of the type T
static void Describe<T>() where T : IAnimal
{
    Console.WriteLine($"{typeof(T).Name} : {T.Sound}");
}

interface IAnimal
{
    // static member that each class must implement
    static abstract string Sound { get; }
}

class Cat : IAnimal
{
    public static string Sound => "meow";
}

class Dog : IAnimal
{
    public static string Sound => "woof";
}
  • lines 13–20: The generic method *[Sum] requires that *[T] implement *[INumber<T>]. It can then use the static member [T.Zero] (line 15) and the operator [+] of type [T]* (line 18);
  • lines 4–6: the same method adds together [int], [double], and [decimal]. Collection expressions create arrays of the expected type;
  • lines 29–32: a custom interface that declares an abstract static property [Sound];
  • lines 35–42: two classes implement the static property;
  • Lines 24–26: The generic method [Describe] uses the static member [T.Sound] of type [T], without requiring an instance of that type. [typeof(T)] returns the description of the type [T], whose property [Name] is the name.

Results:

> dotnet run classes-20.cs
Sum of integers: 6
Sum of reals: 3,75
Sum of decimals: 10,75
Cat : meow
Dog : woof

docs.title: 4.9. Namespaces
docs.text:
To write a line on the screen, we use the [Console.WriteLine(...)] statement. If we look at the definition of the class [Console] in the documentation for .NET, we find that it is part of the namespace [System]. This means that the class [Console] should be referred to as [System.Console], and we should actually write [System.Console.WriteLine(...)]. We avoid this by using a [using] clause:

using System;
...
Console.WriteLine(...);

This means that the [System] namespace is imported along with the [using] clause. When the compiler encounters a class name (in this case, [Console]), it searches for it in the various namespaces imported by the [using] clauses. Here, it finds the class [Console] in the namespace [System]. In a recent .NET project, we don’t even need to write [using System;]: this namespace is included in the project’s implicit **using** statements, as we saw at the beginning of the chapter.

The documentation provides a second piece of information about the [Console] class: the assembly that contains it, the [System.Console.dll] file. An assembly is the result of compiling a project: a [.dll] file (library) or an executable. To use the classes in an assembly, the compiler must be aware of it. The 2008 course demonstrated how to pass these references to the [csc] compiler via the command line ([csc /r:fic1.dll /r:fic2.dll prog.cs]). Today, we no longer call the compiler directly: the assemblies of the .NET framework are referenced automatically, and the [.csproj] file references the other libraries, either as packages ([PackageReference]), or as projects ([ProjectReference]), as we will see in Chapter 6, which is devoted to layered architectures.

When creating a class, you can create it within a namespace. The purpose of these namespaces is to avoid name conflicts between classes, for example, when they are distributed. Consider two companies, E1 and E2, distributing packaged classes in the assemblies [e1.dll] and [e2.dll], respectively. Suppose a client C purchases these two sets of classes, in which both companies have defined a class named [Person]. If the client’s program uses the class [Person], the compiler will not know whether to use the class [Person] from [e1.dll] or the one from [e2.dll]. It will report an error. If the company E1 creates its classes in a namespace named [E1] and the company E2 creates its classes in a namespace named [E2], the two classes named [Person] will then be named [E1.Person] and [E2.Person]. The client must use either [E1.Person] or [E2.Person] (or an alias) in its classes, but not [Person]. The namespace resolves this ambiguity.

To create a class in a namespace, the 2008 course stated:

namespace NamespaceName
{
    // class definition
}

This format remains valid (it allows you to include multiple namespaces in a single file), but since C# 10, the file-scope namespace—[namespace NamespaceName;]—placed at the beginning of the file is preferred, as it saves one level of indentation. This is the format we have been using since the beginning of this chapter.

The [Namespaces] project in the solution illustrates these concepts. It contains two classes, [Person], in two different namespaces. The first, [E1/Person.cs]:

// the classes of this file belong to the E1 namespace
namespace E1;

public class Person
{
    private readonly string firstName;
    private readonly string lastName;

    public Person(string firstName, string lastName)
    {
        this.firstName = firstName;
        this.lastName = lastName;
    }

    public override string ToString() => $"E1.Person[{firstName}, {lastName}]";
}

The second, *[E2/Person.cs]*:

// the classes of this file belong to the E2 namespace
namespace E2;

public class Person
{
    public Person(string name)
    {
        Name = name;
    }

    public string Name { get; }

    public override string ToString() => $"E2.Person[{Name}]";
}

Note that a source file’s folder does not determine its namespace; only the declaration *[namespace]* matters. However, it is a useful convention to organize files from a single namespace into a folder with the same name.

The file [GlobalUsings.cs] contains the following clauses [global using] (C# 10):

// imports valid for all the source files of the project
global using E1;
global using System.Text;

A [global using] directive applies to all source files in the project. This is how implicit using statements are implemented: during compilation, the SDK file generates a [obj/Debug/net10.0/Namespaces.GlobalUsings.g.cs] file that contains the lines [global using System;], [global using System.Collections.Generic;], [global using System.IO;], [global using System.Linq;], [global using System.Net.Http;], [global using System.Threading;], and [global using System.Threading.Tasks;]. You can also add a global "using" statement in the file [.csproj]: [<Using Include="E1" />].

The main program, [Program.cs], is as follows:

// namespace aliases and type aliases
using PersonE2 = E2.Person;
using Point = (int X, int Y);

// Person denotes E1.Person: the E1 namespace is imported in GlobalUsings.cs
Person p1 = new Person("Jean", "Dupont");
// PersonE2 is an alias of E2.Person
PersonE2 p2 = new PersonE2("Durand");
// the full name of a class removes any ambiguity
E2.Person p3 = new E2.Person("Martin");
Console.WriteLine($"{p1} {p2} {p3}");
// full name of the types and assembly that contains them
Console.WriteLine($"{typeof(Person).FullName}, {typeof(PersonE2).FullName}");
Console.WriteLine($"{typeof(Console).FullName} is in the assembly {typeof(Console).Assembly.GetName().Name}");
// StringBuilder is known thanks to global using System.Text
StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder("abc");
Console.WriteLine(sb.Append("def"));
// Point is an alias of the tuple type (int X, int Y)
Point origin = (0, 0);
Console.WriteLine($"origin=({origin.X},{origin.Y})");
  • line 2: an alias: in this file, [PersonE2] refers to the class [E2.Person];
  • line 3: Starting with C# 12, an alias can refer to any type; here, it refers to a tuple with two fields named [X] and [Y];
  • line 6: [Person] refers to the class [E1.Person], thanks to the clause [global using E1;]. If the namespace [E2] were also imported, the name [Person] would be ambiguous and the compiler would reject it;
  • line 8: use of the alias;
  • line 10: the fully qualified class name resolves any ambiguity;
  • line 13: the property [FullName] of a type returns its full name, prefixed by its namespace;
  • line 14: the property [Assembly] of a type refers to the assembly that contains it;
  • line 16: the class [System.Text.StringBuilder] is defined via the clause [global using System.Text;];
  • line 19: use of the alias for the tuple type.

Results:

> dotnet run
E1.Person[Jean, Dupont] E2.Person[Durand] E2.Person[Martin]
E1.Person, E2.Person
System.Console is in the assembly System.Console
abcdef
origin=(0,0)

docs.title: 4.10. Records
docs.text:
Many classes serve only to carry data: a person, a grade, a tax bracket… For these, we always write the same code: a constructor that copies its parameters into properties, a [ToString] method that displays these properties, and often comparison methods.
