C# 9 introduced records: the compiler generates this code from a single-line declaration. We’ve already encountered the structure version ([record struct]); here’s the class version ([classes-21.cs]):

// records (C# 9)
Person r1 = new Person("Jean", "Dupont", 30);
Person r2 = new Person("Jean", "Dupont", 30);
// ToString generated by the compiler
Console.WriteLine(r1);
// equality by value: r1 and r2 are two different but equal objects
Console.WriteLine($"r1 == r2 : {r1 == r2}, same object: {ReferenceEquals(r1, r2)}");
// the properties are read-only (init)
// r1.Age = 31;   // rejected
// the with expression creates a modified copy
Person r3 = r1 with { Age = 31 };
Console.WriteLine(r3);
Console.WriteLine($"r1 == r3 : {r1 == r3}");
// deconstruction into variables
var (firstName, lastName, age) = r1;
Console.WriteLine($"first name={firstName}, last name={lastName}, age={age}");

// the same thing with a class
PersonC c1 = new PersonC("Jean", "Dupont", 30);
PersonC c2 = new PersonC("Jean", "Dupont", 30);
Console.WriteLine(c1);
Console.WriteLine($"c1 == c2 : {c1 == c2}");

// a derived record
Teacher e = new Teacher("Lucile", "Dumas", 56, 61);
Console.WriteLine(e);
Console.WriteLine(e.Identity);
// equality takes the type into account: a Person is not equal to a Teacher
Person pe = new Person("Lucile", "Dumas", 56);
Console.WriteLine($"pe == e : {pe == e}");

// a positional record: FirstName, LastName, Age are public properties { get; init; }
record Person(string FirstName, string LastName, int Age)
{
    // members can be added
    public virtual string Identity => $"[{FirstName}, {LastName}, {Age}]";
}

// a record can derive from another record
record Teacher(string FirstName, string LastName, int Age, int Section) : Person(FirstName, LastName, Age)
{
    public override string Identity => $"Teacher[{base.Identity},{Section}]";
}

// an equivalent class... or almost
class PersonC
{
    public PersonC(string firstName, string lastName, int age)
    {
        FirstName = firstName;
        LastName = lastName;
        Age = age;
    }

    public string FirstName { get; init; }
    public string LastName { get; init; }
    public int Age { get; init; }
}
  • Lines 33–36: a positional record. The declaration [record Person(string FirstName, string LastName, int Age)] generates:
    • a constructor with three parameters;
    • three read-only public properties: [FirstName], [LastName], and [Age] ([{ get; init; }]);
    • a method [ToString] that displays the type name and its public properties (line 5);
    • the methods [Equals] and [GetHashCode] and the operators [==] and [!=], which compare property values rather than references;
    • a method [Deconstruct] that breaks the object down into variables (line 15);
    • the expression [with];
    • a record can also, like a class, have additional members; here, the property [Identity];
  • Line 7: [r1] and [r2] are two distinct objects ([ReferenceEquals] returns [false]) but they are equal in the sense of [] because their properties have the same values. For an ordinary class, [] compares the references (line 22);
  • line 11: Since a record is, in principle, immutable, it is not modified (line 9): the expression [with] creates a copy of [r1] in which certain properties have been changed;
  • lines 40–42: A record can be derived from another record (not from an ordinary class). The parameters [FirstName], [LastName], and [Age] are passed to the parent record’s constructor. The property [Identity], declared as [virtual] in [Person], is redefined;
  • line 30: record equality takes into account the actual type of the objects: a [Person] is never equal to a [Teacher], even if their common properties are equal;
  • Lines 46–57: A class that resembles the record [Person]… except that the constructor and properties had to be written, and equality by value, [ToString] and [with] are not provided.

Results:

> dotnet run classes-21.cs
Person { FirstName = Jean, LastName = Dupont, Age = 30, Identity = [Jean, Dupont, 30] }
r1 == r2 : True, same object: False
Person { FirstName = Jean, LastName = Dupont, Age = 31, Identity = [Jean, Dupont, 31] }
r1 == r3 : False
first name=Jean, last name=Dupont, age=30
PersonC
c1 == c2 : False
Teacher { FirstName = Lucile, LastName = Dumas, Age = 56, Identity = Teacher[[Lucile, Dumas, 56],61], Section = 61 }
Teacher[[Lucile, Dumas, 56],61]
pe == e : False

Note that the generated method [ToString] also displays the calculated property [Identity] (line 2), whereas the [ToString] method of the class [PersonC] simply displays the class name (line 7).

Let’s summarize the differences between a class and a record:

ClassRecordEquality: [==], [Equals]same object (equal references)same property values, same type[ToString]type nametype name and public propertiesconstructor and propertiesto be writtenGenerated by the positional declaration, properties [init]modified copyto be writtenexpression [with]inheritancefrom a classfrom a record

A record is used for data defined by its value (a person retrieved from a database, a message exchanged over a network, a tax bracket), and a class is used for an object with an identity and behavior (a computing service, a connection, an editable list). A record is written as [record] (or [record class], which is identical) for a reference type, and [record struct] for a value type.

docs.title: 4.11. Primary constructors
docs.text:
Positional records declare their constructor parameters immediately after their name. Since C# 12, ordinary classes and structures can do the same: this is the primary constructor. The program [classes-22.cs] illustrates this:

// primary constructors (C# 12)
Person p = new Person("Jean", "Dupont", 30);
Console.WriteLine(p.Identity);
p.GrowOlder();
Console.WriteLine(p.Identity);
// another constructor
Person unknown = new Person("Martin");
Console.WriteLine(unknown.Identity);
// a derived class
Teacher e = new Teacher("Lucile", "Dumas", 56, 61);
Console.WriteLine(e.Identity);
// a structure
Point pt = new Point(3, 4);
Console.WriteLine($"pt=({pt.X},{pt.Y}), distance to the origin: {pt.Distance()}");

// a class with a primary constructor
class Person(string firstName, string lastName, int age)
{
    // the parameters firstName and lastName are used to initialize properties
    public string FirstName { get; } = firstName;
    public string LastName { get; } = lastName;
    // the age parameter is used by the methods: it is kept in a hidden field
    public int Age => age;

    // any other constructor must call the primary constructor
    public Person(string lastName) : this("?", lastName, 0)
    {
    }

    public void GrowOlder() => age++;

    public virtual string Identity => $"[{FirstName}, {LastName}, {age}]";
}

// a derived class: it passes three of its parameters to the primary constructor of the parent class
class Teacher(string firstName, string lastName, int age, int section) : Person(firstName, lastName, age)
{
    public int Section { get; } = section;

    public override string Identity => $"Teacher[{base.Identity},{Section}]";
}

// a structure with a primary constructor
readonly struct Point(double x, double y)
{
    public double X { get; } = x;
    public double Y { get; } = y;

    public double Distance() => Math.Sqrt(X * X + Y * Y);
}
  • line 17: the class [Person] has a primary constructor with three parameters. Unlike those of a record, these parameters do not become public properties: they are parameters, visible throughout the entire body of the class;
  • lines 20–21: the parameters [firstName] and [lastName] are used to initialize two read-only properties;
  • line 23: the parameter [age] is used by members of the class: the property [Age], the method [GrowOlder] (line 30), and the property [Identity]. The compiler then stores it in a hidden field, which can be modified ([age++]). It is recommended not to mix these two uses for the same parameter (initializing a property and using it directly), as this may result in two copies of the same data;
  • line 26: a class with a primary constructor may have other constructors, but these must call the primary constructor using [this(...)];
  • line 36: A derived class passes some of the parameters from its primary constructor to the constructor of its parent class: [: Person(firstName, lastName, age)]. This is equivalent to [: base(firstName, lastName, age)] in a traditional constructor;
  • line 44: A structure can also have a primary constructor.

Results:

> dotnet run classes-22.cs
[Jean, Dupont, 30]
[Jean, Dupont, 31]
[?, Martin, 0]
Teacher[[Lucile, Dumas, 56],61]
pt=(3,4), distance to the origin: 5

The primary constructor eliminates repetitive code from constructors that merely store their parameters. It is widely used for classes that receive services during construction, as we will see with dependency injection (Chapter 6).

docs.title: 4.12. Extension Methods and Members
docs.text:
How do you add a method to a class that cannot be modified, such as the class [string] derived from .NET? C# 3 introduced extension methods: static methods that are used as instance methods of the extended type. C# 14 extends this mechanism to properties and static members with extension blocks. The program [classes-23.cs] demonstrates both:

// extension methods (C# 3) and extension members (C# 14)
Person p = new Person("jean", "dupont", 30);
// classic extension methods: they are used like instance methods
Console.WriteLine(p.Initials());
Console.WriteLine("jean".FirstUpper());
// the previous call is translated by the compiler into the following static method call
Console.WriteLine(ClassicExtensions.FirstUpper("jean"));
// extension properties (C# 14)
Console.WriteLine($"{p.FullName} is an adult: {p.IsAdult}");
Console.WriteLine($"\"the weather is nice\" has {"the weather is nice".NbWords} words");
// static extension member (C# 14): it is used with the name of the type
Person unknown = Person.Unknown;
Console.WriteLine($"{unknown.FullName} is an adult: {unknown.IsAdult}");

// a person
record Person(string FirstName, string LastName, int Age);

// classic extension methods: static methods of a static class,
// whose first parameter is preceded by the this keyword
static class ClassicExtensions
{
    public static string Initials(this Person p)
    {
        return $"{char.ToUpper(p.FirstName[0])}.{char.ToUpper(p.LastName[0])}.";
    }

    public static string FirstUpper(this string s)
    {
        return s.Length == 0 ? s : char.ToUpper(s[0]) + s[1..];
    }
}

// extension blocks (C# 14)
static class Cs14Extensions
{
    // instance members added to the Person type: p denotes the extended object
    extension(Person p)
    {
        public bool IsAdult => p.Age >= 18;

        public string FullName => $"{p.FirstName.FirstUpper()} {p.LastName.ToUpper()}";
    }

    // static members added to the Person type
    extension(Person)
    {
        public static Person Unknown => new Person("?", "?", 0);
    }

    // a property added to the string type
    extension(string s)
    {
        public int NbWords => s.Split(' ', StringSplitOptions.RemoveEmptyEntries).Length;
    }
}
  • lines 20–29: Traditional extension methods are static methods of a static class. Their first parameter, preceded by the keyword [this], specifies the extended object:
    • [Initials(this Person p)] extends the type [Person]: it is called [p.Initials()] (line 4);
    • [FirstUpper(this string s)] extends the type [string]: it is called ["jean".FirstUpper()] (line 5). The expression [s[1..]] refers to the substring starting at character #1;
  • line 7: an extension method remains an ordinary static method: the compiler translates ["jean".FirstUpper()] into this call. The method has access only to the public members of the extended object;
  • lines 34–53: the C# 14 extension blocks, also declared within a static class:
    • lines 37–41: the block ***[extension(Person p)] adds the instance members it contains to the type *[Person]. *[p]* refers to the extended object. Properties can now be added ([IsAdult], [FullName]), which was not possible with traditional extension methods;
    • lines 45–47: the block [extension(Person)], with no parameter names, adds static members to the type [Person]: [Person.Unknown] (line 12) is written as if the property had been declared in the record [Person];
    • Lines 51–53: An extension property of type [string], used on line 10.

Results:

> dotnet run classes-23.cs
J.D.
Jean
Jean
Jean DUPONT is an adult: True
"the weather is nice" has 4 words
? ? is an adult: False

Extension methods are ubiquitous in .NET: the operators of LINQ ([Where], [Select], [OrderBy]…), discussed in the next chapter, are extension methods of the [IEnumerable<T>] interface. For an extension to be usable, the namespace of its static class must be imported.

docs.title: 4.13. Pattern Filtering on Objects
docs.text:
The expression [switch] and pattern filtering are not limited to simple values (numbers, strings); they also apply to objects. You can test an object’s type, check the values of its properties, and retrieve the object converted to the correct type—all in a single expression. The program [classes-24.cs] uses a hierarchy of three records:

// pattern matching on objects
object?[] objects =
[
    new Person("Jean", "Dupont", 30),
    new Person("Lise", "Morel", 12),
    new Teacher("Lucile", "Dumas", 56, 61),
    new Teacher("Marc", "Petit", 44, 27),
    new Student("Paul", "Martin", 19, "computer science"),
    "a string",
    42,
    null,
];

// 1 - the type pattern: is Type variable
foreach (object? o in objects)
{
    if (o is Person p)
    {
        // here p is a Person (or an object of a derived class)
        Console.WriteLine($"{p.FirstName} is of type {p.GetType().Name}");
    }
}

// 2 - the property pattern: { Property: pattern }
foreach (object? o in objects)
{
    if (o is Person { Age: >= 18 } adult)
    {
        Console.WriteLine($"{adult.FirstName} is an adult");
    }
}

// 3 - the switch expression on the type and the properties of the object
foreach (object? o in objects)
{
    Console.WriteLine(Describe(o));
}

static string Describe(object? o) => o switch
{
    Teacher { Section: 27 } e => $"{e.FirstName} teaches computer science",
    Teacher e => $"{e.FirstName} teaches in section {e.Section}",
    Student(var firstName, _, _, var major) => $"{firstName} studies {major}",
    Person { Age: < 18 } p => $"{p.FirstName} is a minor",
    Person p => $"{p.FirstName} is {p.Age} years old",
    string s => $"a string of {s.Length} characters",
    int n and > 0 => $"the positive integer {n}",
    null => "the null reference",
    _ => "an unknown object",
};

record Person(string FirstName, string LastName, int Age);
record Teacher(string FirstName, string LastName, int Age, int Section) : Person(FirstName, LastName, Age);
record Student(string FirstName, string LastName, int Age, string Major) : Person(FirstName, LastName, Age);
  • lines 52–54: a [Person] record and two derived records, [Teacher] and [Student];
  • lines 2–11: an array of objects of various types (the type [object?] also accepts [null]);
  • line 17: the pattern of type [o is Person p] is true if [o] references an object of type [Person] or a derived type; in this case, the variable [p], of type [Person], references this object. This avoids the sequence from the 2008 course: testing the type with [is], then converting with [(Person)o]. The pattern is false if [o] is equal to [null];
  • line 27: the property pattern [{ Age: >= 18 }] (C# 8) tests the value of a property of the object, in this case using a relational pattern [>= 18] (C# 9). Multiple properties can be tested by separating them with commas;
  • lines 39–49: the expression [switch] tries the patterns in order and returns the value associated with the first one that matches:
    • line 41: a teacher from section 27;
    • line 42: any other teacher. The order is important: if placed before the previous one, this pattern would have made it inaccessible, which the compiler would have flagged as an error;
    • line 43: a positional pattern: it uses the method [Deconstruct] of the record [Student] to extract its properties in the order they were declared; [_] ignores a property;
    • line 44: a minor;
    • line 47: a positive integer, using the [and] combinator (C# 9); there are also [or] and [not];
    • line 48: the pattern [null];
    • line 49: the pattern [_] accepts everything. Without it, the compiler would report that the expression [switch] does not cover all cases.

Results:

> dotnet run classes-24.cs
Jean is of type Person
Lise is of type Person
Lucile is of type Teacher
Marc is of type Teacher
Paul is of type Student
Jean is an adult
Lucile is an adult
Marc is an adult
Paul is an adult
Jean is 30 years old
Lise is a minor
Lucile teaches in section 61
Marc teaches computer science
Paul studies computer science
a string of 8 characters
the positive integer 42
the null reference

Note that the type pattern also matches derived types: the type pattern loop (lines 2–6) captured the teachers and the student, who are people. Pattern matching is a useful alternative to cascading [if (o is ...)]; however, it should not replace polymorphism: when behavior depends on the object’s type and you have control over the class hierarchy, a virtual method redefined in each class remains the object-oriented solution.

docs.title: 4.14. Nullable reference types
docs.text:
Since the beginning of this chapter, our projects have had nullable reference types enabled ([<Nullable>enable</Nullable>] in [.csproj], an option enabled by default in single-file applications). The principle is as follows:

  • A variable, field, parameter, or reference-type result declared without a question mark—for example, of type [Person]—is never supposed to be equal to [null];
  • if it can be [null], it is declared with a question mark: [Person?];
  • the compiler analyzes the program flow and issues a warning whenever a potentially null value is used without verification, or assigned to a non-nullable variable.

The language does not prohibit anything at runtime: these are compilation warnings, but a program that compiles without warnings is much less prone to the [NullReferenceException] exception, the most common runtime error. The 2008 course, which predates this feature (C# 8, 2019), obviously did not cover it. The program [classes-25.cs] demonstrates the operators associated with nullable types:

// nullable reference types applied to objects
Person[] persons = [new Person("Jean", "Dupont") { MiddleName = "Marie" }, new Person("Paul", "Martin")];
foreach (Person p in persons)
{
    // ?. : returns null if the object on the left is null, otherwise accesses the member
    int? length = p.MiddleName?.Length;
    // ?? : returns the right operand if the left one is null
    Console.WriteLine($"{p.FirstName} : middle name={p.MiddleName ?? "(none)"}, length={length?.ToString() ?? "null"}");
}

// a method that can return null: its return type is Person?
Person? found = Find(persons, "Durand");
Console.WriteLine(found?.FirstName ?? "Durand: person not found");
// after a test, the compiler knows that the reference is not null
found = Find(persons, "Martin");
if (found is not null)
{
    Console.WriteLine($"Martin : {found.FirstName}");
}
// ??= : assigns a value only if the variable (or the property) is null
persons[1].MiddleName ??= "Pierre";
persons[0].MiddleName ??= "Pierre";
Console.WriteLine($"{persons[0].MiddleName}, {persons[1].MiddleName}");
// C# 14: conditional assignment: it is only done if the object is not null
Find(persons, "Dupont")?.MiddleName = "Louise";
Find(persons, "Durand")?.MiddleName = "Louise";
Console.WriteLine(persons[0].MiddleName);
// ! : we assert to the compiler that the reference is not null
Person martin = Find(persons, "Martin")!;
Console.WriteLine(martin.FirstName);
// the following lines cause compiler warnings
// Console.WriteLine(new Person("Lise", "Morel").MiddleName.Length);   // warning
// Person dupond = Find(persons, "Dupond");   // warning
// persons[0] = null;   // warning

// search for a person by last name
static Person? Find(Person[] persons, string lastName)
{
    foreach (Person p in persons)
    {
        if (p.LastName == lastName)
        {
            return p;
        }
    }
    return null;
}

class Person
{
    public Person(string firstName, string lastName)
    {
        FirstName = firstName;
        LastName = lastName;
    }

    // non-nullable properties: they must never be null
    public string FirstName { get; }
    public string LastName { get; }
    // nullable property: null means "no middle name"
    public string? MiddleName { get; set; }
}
  • lines 58–61: The class [Person] has two non-nullable properties, initialized by the constructor, and one nullable property, [MiddleName]: [null] means “no middle name”;
  • line 6: the [?.] operator (C# 6) returns [null] if the object on its left is [null], and accesses the member otherwise. The result is of type [int?];
  • line 8: the operator [??] returns its left operand if it is not [null], and its right operand otherwise;
  • lines 37–46: the function [Find] returns the person being searched for or [null]; its return type is [Person?];
  • line 13: the two operators are combined;
  • lines 16–18: After the [is not null] check, the compiler knows that [found] is not equal to [null]: [found.FirstName] can be written without a warning;
  • lines 21–22: the operator [??=] only assigns a value to the property if it is [null]: Jean’s middle name, “Marie,” is not replaced;
  • lines 25–26: C# 14 allows [?.] on the left side of an assignment: the assignment is performed only if the object is not null. Dupont exists and is given a new middle name; Durand does not exist, and the statement does nothing;
  • line 29: the [!] operator (a “null-forgiving” operator) tells the compiler that we know the value is not null: it does not issue a warning. It’s up to the developer to be sure of this: if the value is null at runtime, an error will occur later on. Use sparingly;
  • lines 32–34: three statements that trigger warnings.

Results:

> dotnet run classes-25.cs
Jean : middle name=Marie, length=5
Paul : middle name=(none), length=null
Durand: person not found
Martin : Paul
Marie, Pierre
Louise
Paul

Let’s uncomment the last three lines of the main program and compile:

> dotnet build classes-25.cs
classes-25.cs(32,19): warning CS8602: Dereference of a possibly null reference.
classes-25.cs(33,17): warning CS8600: Converting null literal or possible null value to non-nullable type.
classes-25.cs(34,14): warning CS8625: Cannot convert null literal to non-nullable reference type.
  • Warning [CS8602]: The property [MiddleName] of a newly created person may be [null]: You cannot use its property [Length] without verification;
  • Warning [CS8600]: The function [Find] may return [null], a value that is assigned to a non-nullable variable of type [Person];
  • Warning [CS8625]: The constant [null] is assigned to an element of type [Person], which is non-nullable.

The program would run despite these warnings, but the first line would throw a [NullReferenceException] exception. In this course, all programs compile without any warnings: we correct the code (by declaring the type as nullable, checking the value, or providing a default value using [??]) rather than ignoring the warning or suppressing it with [!].

docs.title: 4.15. Sample Application - V2
docs.text:
We’ll revisit the tax calculation we covered in the previous chapter (Version 1) and implement it using classes and interfaces. Let’s review the problem. We aim to write a program to calculate a taxpayer’s tax. We’ll consider the simplified case of a taxpayer who has only a single salary to report (using the 2004 tax schedule for 2003 income, kept as-is: this is an exercise):

  • we calculate the employee’s number of tax brackets: shares = nbChildren / 2 + 1 if they are unmarried, nbChildren / 2 + 2 if he is married, where nbChildren is the number of his children;
  • if he has at least three children, he receives an additional half-share;
  • his taxable income R is calculated as R = 0.72 × S, where S is his annual salary;
  • his family quotient is calculated as QF = R / shares;
  • his tax I is calculated using the following table:
thresholdcoeffRcoeffN49620083820.068291.0914,7530.1911,322.9223,8880.2832,668.3938,8680.3744,846.9847,9320.4266,883.6600.4819,505.54

Each row has three fields. To calculate tax I, find the first row where QF ≤ the limit. For example, if QF = 5,000, the row (8,382; 0.068; 291.09) will be found. Tax I is then equal to 0.068 × R - 291.09 × shares. If QF is such that the condition QF ≤ limit is never satisfied, then the coefficients of the last row are used, resulting in tax I = 0.481 × R - 9,505.54 × shares.

The application forms the [TaxV2] project of the solution:

TaxV2/
  TaxBracket.cs        a bracket of the tax scale
  ITax.cs              the tax calculation interface
  AbstractTax.cs       an abstract class implementing ITax
  HardwiredTax.cs      a derived class, with hard-coded data
  Program.cs           the program that dialogues with the user
  TaxV2.csproj

First, we define a type capable of encapsulating a row from the previous array [TaxBracket.cs]:

namespace TaxV2;

// a bracket of the tax scale
public readonly record struct TaxBracket(decimal Limit, decimal CoeffR, decimal CoeffN);

The 2008 course used a structure with three automatic read-write properties. We use an immutable record structure ([readonly record struct]):

  • a structure because a bracket is a small piece of data without an identity, defined solely by its value: an array of brackets directly contains the brackets, without a separate object in memory for each one. With three [decimal] (48 bytes), the structure exceeds the size of approximately 16 bytes usually recommended for a structure; this is not a problem here: there are few brackets, and they are copied only when they are read;
  • immutable ([readonly]) because there is no reason for a tax bracket to be modified once it has been created. The 2008 course, incidentally, modified the limit of the last tax bracket during the calculation—a side effect that we are eliminating;
  • a record ([record]) because the compiler generates the constructor, the properties, [ToString], and the equality operator from a single line.

Then we define an interface [ITax] capable of calculating the tax [ITax.cs]:

namespace TaxV2;

public interface ITax
{
    // tax calculation for a taxpayer
    int Calculate(bool married, int nbChildren, int salary);
}
  • Line 6: The method for calculating the tax based on three pieces of data: the taxpayer’s marital status, the number of children, and annual salary. It returns the tax rounded down to the nearest euro.

Next, we define an abstract class that implements this interface [AbstractTax.cs]:

namespace TaxV2;

public abstract class AbstractTax : ITax
{
    // the tax brackets needed for the calculation come from an external source
    // that only the derived classes know
    protected abstract TaxBracket[] TaxBrackets { get; }

    // tax calculation
    public int Calculate(bool married, int nbChildren, int salary)
    {
        // calculation of the number of shares
        decimal shares = (decimal)nbChildren / 2 + (married ? 2 : 1);
        if (nbChildren >= 3)
        {
            shares += 0.5m;
        }
        // calculation of the taxable income and of the family quotient
        decimal income = 0.72m * salary;
        decimal quotient = income / shares;
        // search for the tax bracket: the last one is used if no limit fits
        TaxBracket[] brackets = TaxBrackets;
        TaxBracket bracket = brackets[^1];
        for (int i = 0; i < brackets.Length - 1; i++)
        {
            if (quotient <= brackets[i].Limit)
            {
                bracket = brackets[i];
                break;
            }
        }
        // tax calculation
        return (int)(income * bracket.CoeffR - shares * bracket.CoeffN);
    }
}
  • Line 3: The class [AbstractTax] implements the interface [ITax];
  • line 7: the scale data, in the form of a protected abstract property. The class [AbstractTax] does not know where this data comes from (written in the code, read from a file, a database, etc.). It leaves this up to the derived classes. This is why it is declared abstract, which prevents it from being instantiated. The 2008 course used a protected field that derived classes had to initialize; the abstract property requires derived classes to provide it: the compiler verifies this;
  • lines 10–33: the implementation of the [Calculate] method of the [ITax] interface. Derived classes will not need to rewrite this method. The [AbstractTax] class thus serves as a factorization class for the derived classes: it contains what is common to all of them;
  • line 13: the number of shares. The conversion [(decimal)nbChildren] is essential: without it, [nbChildren / 2] would be an integer division (3 / 2 = 1). The expression [married ? 2 : 1] equals 2 for a married taxpayer, 1 otherwise;
  • Lines 19–20: taxable income and the family quotient. All calculations are performed using [decimal], a type adapted to the amounts: the suffix [m] of [0.72m] denotes a constant of this type;
  • Lines 22–29: Determining the tax bracket. By default, this is the last bracket ([brackets[^1]], line 23). The loop iterates through all brackets except the last one and stops ([break]) at the first bracket whose limit is greater than or equal to the family quotient;
  • line 33: tax calculation. The conversion [(int)] truncates the result [decimal] to its integer part.

A class that implements the [ITax] interface can be created by deriving it from the [AbstractTax] class. This is what we will now do with [HardwiredTax.cs]:

namespace TaxV2;

public class HardwiredTax : AbstractTax
{
    // tax calculation data (2004 tax scale on 2003 income), hard-coded
    private static readonly decimal[] limits = [4962m, 8382m, 14753m, 23888m, 38868m, 47932m, 0m];
    private static readonly decimal[] coeffR = [0m, 0.068m, 0.191m, 0.283m, 0.374m, 0.426m, 0.481m];
    private static readonly decimal[] coeffN = [0m, 291.09m, 1322.92m, 2668.39m, 4846.98m, 6883.66m, 9505.54m];

    // the tax brackets
    private readonly TaxBracket[] taxBrackets;

    // constructor
    public HardwiredTax()
    {
        // creation and filling of the array of tax brackets
        taxBrackets = new TaxBracket[limits.Length];
        for (int i = 0; i < taxBrackets.Length; i++)
        {
            taxBrackets[i] = new TaxBracket(limits[i], coeffR[i], coeffN[i]);
        }
    }

    // implementation of the abstract property of the parent class
    protected override TaxBracket[] TaxBrackets => taxBrackets;
}
  • Lines 6–8: The class [HardwiredTax] hard-codes the data needed to calculate the tax. These are class fields ([static]) that are read-only ([readonly]): they are shared by all instances and cannot be replaced by other arrays;
  • lines 14–20: the constructor uses this data to build the tax bracket table;
  • line 25: the parent class’s abstract property is implemented: it returns the tax bracket table.

The next chapter will add other classes derived from [AbstractTax], which will read the tax brackets from a text file or JSON: they will only need to provide the [TaxBrackets] property.

A test program might look like the following [Program.cs]:

using TaxV2;

// interactive tax calculation program
// the user types three data items on the keyboard: married nbChildren salary
// the program then displays the tax to pay

const string syntax = """
    syntax: Married NbChildren Salary
    Married: y for married, n for not married
    NbChildren: number of children
    Salary: annual salary in euros
    """;

// creation of an ITax object
ITax tax = new HardwiredTax();

// input loop
while (true)
{
    // we ask for the tax calculation parameters
    Console.Write("Tax calculation parameters in the format: Married (y/n) NbChildren Salary, or nothing to stop: ");
    string parameters = (Console.ReadLine() ?? "").Trim();
    // anything to do?
    if (parameters == "")
    {
        break;
    }
    // checking the number of fields of the typed line
    string[] fields = parameters.Split(' ', StringSplitOptions.RemoveEmptyEntries);
    if (fields.Length != 3)
    {
        Console.WriteLine(syntax);
        continue;
    }
    // checking the validity of the parameters
    // married
    string married = fields[0].ToLower();
    if (married != "y" && married != "n")
    {
        Console.WriteLine(syntax + "\nIncorrect married argument: type y or n");
        continue;
    }
    // nbChildren
    if (!int.TryParse(fields[1], out int nbChildren) || nbChildren < 0)
    {
        Console.WriteLine(syntax + "\nIncorrect NbChildren argument: type a positive or zero integer");
        continue;
    }
    // salary
    if (!int.TryParse(fields[2], out int salary) || salary < 0)
    {
        Console.WriteLine(syntax + "\nIncorrect salary argument: type a positive or zero integer");
        continue;
    }
    // the parameters are correct: we calculate the tax
    Console.WriteLine($"Tax={tax.Calculate(married == "y", nbChildren, salary)} euros");
}

The program above allows the user to perform repeated tax calculation simulations.

  • lines 7–11: the help message is written as a raw string literal (C# 11), delimited by three quotation marks: the string can span multiple lines, and the common indentation of the lines, determined by the position of the closing quotation marks, is removed;
  • Line 15: Creation of a [tax] object that implements the [ITax] interface. This object is obtained by instantiating a type [HardwiredTax], a type that implements the [ITax] interface. Note that the variable [tax] was not assigned the type [HardwiredTax] but rather the type [ITax]. By writing this, we indicate that we are only interested in the [Calculate] method of the [tax] object and not in the rest. To use data from a file, simply change this single line;
  • lines 18–56: the loop for tax calculation simulations;
  • line 22: the three parameters required for the [Calculate] method are requested in a single line entered via the keyboard. [Console.ReadLine] returns [null] if standard input is closed: the operator [??] then replaces [null] with an empty string, which terminates the program;
  • line 29: the method [Split] splits the line into words separated by spaces, with the option [StringSplitOptions.RemoveEmptyEntries] removing empty words caused by consecutive spaces;
  • lines 44–50: the method [int.TryParse] verifies that the last two fields are integers; the declaration [out int nbChildren] creates the variable that receives the number. The 2008 course used [int.Parse] within a [try / catch] block;
  • line 56: call to the [Calculate] method of the [tax] object implementing the [ITax] interface.

Here is an example of the program in action:

The tax amounts are calculated correctly: 4,282 euros for a married taxpayer with two children and an annual salary of 60,000 euros (line 26), and 2,959 euros with three children (line 28). An unmarried taxpayer with no children pays 11,519 euros for the same salary (line 30).

Compared to Version 1, the calculation is now encapsulated in classes behind an interface: the dialog program only recognizes the [ITax] interface. Subsequent versions will build on this separation: Version 3 will change the data source by deriving new classes from [AbstractTax], and Version 4 will organize the application into layers.

docs.title: 5. Commonly Used .NET Classes
docs.text:
Here we present a few frequently used classes from the .NET platform: strings, arrays, collections, files, and regular expressions. We’ll also cover LINQ (Language Integrated Query), which the 2008 course omitted even though it had already been available since C# 3: it is now the most common way to manipulate collections in C#. Before that, we’ll show you how to find information about the thousands of available classes. This guide is indispensable for any C# developer, even experienced ones.

The examples in this chapter—with the exception of the sample application at the end—are single-file applications run by [dotnet run file.cs]. They are located in the [05-classes-dotnet] folder of the course code and run in the French (fr-FR) locale, except for the LINQ and regular-expression examples, which run in the American English locale (en-US).

docs.title: 5.1. Finding Help on .NET Classes
docs.text: The 2008 course provided a detailed description, complete with screenshots, of the MSDN help installed with Visual Studio 2008. This local help is no longer available: the .NET documentation is now online, free of charge, and updated with each new version.

docs.title: 5.1.1. Online Documentation
docs.text:
The starting point is Microsoft’s learn.microsoft.com website. There you’ll find:

  • C# language documentation: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/. It includes an overview of the language, tutorials, the language reference (keywords, operators, statements), and a “What’s New” section that describes each version of C#;
  • the .NET API reference: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/. It describes, namespace by namespace, all classes in .NET: their constructors, properties, and methods, with examples;
  • the API browser, on the same page: a search box where you can type a class or method name ([StringBuilder], [Regex.Match]…). A drop-down list allows you to select the version of .NET (here, .NET 10).

The page for a class, such as System.String, displays:

  • the class’s namespace and the assembly that contains it;
  • its declaration, parent class, and the interfaces it implements;
  • a list of its constructors, properties, and methods, each with a link to a detailed page showing its various overloads, parameters, return values, possible exceptions, and often an example;
  • notes on its usage.

The pages are available in French (machine translation) and English (original text, which is sometimes more precise). You can switch between them by replacing [en-us] with [fr-fr] in the URL. A search on a search engine using the class’s full name (“System.Text.StringBuilder”) usually leads directly to the correct page.

docs.title: 5.1.2. Editor Help
docs.text:
The code editor (Visual Studio, Visual Studio Code with the C# Dev Kit extension, Rider) provides immediate help without having to leave the code:

  • autocompletion (IntelliSense): after typing [aString.], the editor suggests a list of the object’s properties and methods, along with a summary of each;
  • Tooltips: Hovering the mouse over a class, method, or variable name displays its declaration and a summary of its documentation;
  • Parameter help: When you type the opening parenthesis of a call, the editor displays the different overloads of the method and the role of each parameter;
  • Go to Definition (F12 key): Displays the declaration of the class or method. For a .NET class, the editor displays the public declarations reconstructed from the assembly, along with their documentation comments;
  • In Visual Studio, pressing the F1 key on a class or method name opens the corresponding page in the online documentation.

These documentation comments, which are visible when you hover over an element, are the ones used to generate the online reference. You can write similar comments in your own code using the [/// <summary> ... </summary>] syntax placed above a class or method: the editor will display them in the same way.

docs.title: 5.2.1. The System.String class
docs.text:
The C# type [string] is an alias for the [System.String] class. It has numerous properties and methods. Here are a few of them:

Memberrole[public int Length { get; }]number of characters in the string[public char this[int index] { get; }]Character No. [index]: [aString[i]][public bool StartsWith(string value)]returns [true] if the string begins with [value][public bool EndsWith(string value)]returns [true] if the string ends with [value][public bool Contains(string value)]returns [true] if the string contains [value][public bool Equals(string? value)]returns [true] if the string is equal to [value]; equivalent to [aString == value][public int IndexOf(string value)]the first occurrence of [value] in the string, or -1. Another overload starts the search at position [startIndex][public int IndexOf(char value)]the same applies to the character [value][public int LastIndexOf(char value)]same as [IndexOf] but returns the last position instead of the first[public string Insert(int startIndex, string value)]Inserts the string [value] into the string at position [startIndex][public static string Join(string separator, params string[] value)]class method: concatenates the elements of [value], separating them with [separator][public string Replace(char oldChar, char newChar)]returns a copy of the string where the character [oldChar] has been replaced by [newChar]; an overloaded method replaces one string with another[public string[] Split(params char[] separator)]the string is treated as a sequence of fields separated by the characters in [separator]; the result is an array of these fields[public string Substring(int startIndex, int length)]A substring of [length] starting at position [startIndex][public string ToLower()], [public string ToUpper()]converts the string to lowercase, uppercase[public string Trim()]removes leading and trailing spaces from the string ([TrimStart], [TrimEnd]: on one side only)

It is important to note that a string of the type [string] is immutable; it cannot be modified after it is created. When a method returns a string, that string is different from the string to which the method was applied. Thus, [s1.Trim()] returns the string [s2], and [s1] and [s2] are two different strings: [s1] has not changed.

A string [c] can be considered a read-only array of characters:

  • [c[i]] is the i-th character of [c] (the first character is number 0);
  • [c.Length] is the number of characters in [c].

The program [strings-01.cs] is as follows:

// a few methods of the String class
string aString = "the bird flies above clouds";
Display("aString=" + aString);
Display("aString.Length=" + aString.Length);
Display("aString[10]=" + aString[10]);
Display("aString.IndexOf(\"flies\")=" + aString.IndexOf("flies"));
Display("aString.IndexOf(\"x\")=" + aString.IndexOf("x"));
Display("aString.LastIndexOf('a')=" + aString.LastIndexOf('a'));
Display("aString.LastIndexOf('x')=" + aString.LastIndexOf('x'));
Display("aString.Substring(4, 7)=" + aString.Substring(4, 7));
Display("aString.ToUpper()=" + aString.ToUpper());
Display("aString.ToLower()=" + aString.ToLower());
Display("aString.Replace('a', 'A')=" + aString.Replace('a', 'A'));
Display("aString.Insert(9, \"never \")=" + aString.Insert(9, "never "));
// splitting the string into words (separator: spaces)
string[] fields = aString.Split();
for (int i = 0; i < fields.Length; i++)
{
    Display("fields[" + i + "]=[" + fields[i] + "]");
}
Display("string.Join(\":\", fields)=" + string.Join(":", fields));
Display("\"  abc  \".Trim()=[" + "  abc  ".Trim() + "]");
// the original string has not been modified
Display("aString=" + aString);

// a local display method
static void Display(string msg)
{
    Console.WriteLine(msg);
}

Results:

> dotnet run strings-01.cs
aString=the bird flies above clouds
aString.Length=27
aString[10]=l
aString.IndexOf("flies")=9
aString.IndexOf("x")=-1
aString.LastIndexOf('a')=15
aString.LastIndexOf('x')=-1
aString.Substring(4, 7)=bird fl
aString.ToUpper()=THE BIRD FLIES ABOVE CLOUDS
aString.ToLower()=the bird flies above clouds
aString.Replace('a', 'A')=the bird flies Above clouds
aString.Insert(9, "never ")=the bird never flies above clouds
fields[0]=[the]
fields[1]=[bird]
fields[2]=[flies]

"  abc  ".Trim()=[abc]

Comments:

  • line 5: character #10, i.e., the 11th character in the string;
  • Lines 7, 9: An unsuccessful search returns -1;
  • line 10: the 7 characters starting at position 4;
  • line 14: an insertion at position 9, before the word “flies”;
  • line 16: [Split] without parameters splits the string at whitespace characters (space, tab, line break, etc.). The 2008 course used [Split(null)], which amounts to the same thing;
  • line 21: the static method [Join] does the opposite of [Split];
  • Line 23: All of the previous methods returned new strings: [aString] remained unchanged (line 21 of the results);
  • Lines 27–29: a local function, as in Chapter 3.

docs.title: 5.2.2. The Split and Join Methods
docs.text:
The program [strings-02.cs] delves deeper into splitting a string into fields:

// Split and Join
string line = "one:two::three:";
// splitting with the ':' separator
string[] fields = line.Split(':');
for (int i = 0; i < fields.Length; i++)
{
    Console.WriteLine($"fields[{i}]=[{fields[i]}]");
}
// the reverse operation
Console.WriteLine($"join=[{string.Join(":", fields)}]");

// the options of Split: removal of empty fields
fields = line.Split(':', StringSplitOptions.RemoveEmptyEntries);
Console.WriteLine($"RemoveEmptyEntries : {fields.Length} fields [{string.Join("|", fields)}]");

// several separators and removal of the spaces around the fields
string person = " dupont , jean ;  45 ";
fields = person.Split([',', ';'], StringSplitOptions.TrimEntries);
Console.WriteLine($"TrimEntries : {fields.Length} fields [{string.Join("|", fields)}]");

// both options combined
string list = "  red ,, green ,  , blue ";
fields = list.Split(',', StringSplitOptions.RemoveEmptyEntries | StringSplitOptions.TrimEntries);
Console.WriteLine($"both options: {fields.Length} fields [{string.Join("|", fields)}]");

// a separator that is a string
string text = "apple -> pear -> apricot";
fields = text.Split(" -> ");
Console.WriteLine($"string separator: [{string.Join("|", fields)}]");

// Join accepts any collection, not only strings
int[] numbers = [1, 2, 3, 4];
Console.WriteLine($"Join on integers: {string.Join(" + ", numbers)}");

Results:

> dotnet run strings-02.cs
fields[0]=[one]
fields[1]=[two]
fields[2]=[]
fields[3]=[three]
fields[4]=[]
join=[one:two::three:]
RemoveEmptyEntries : 3 fields [one|two|three]
TrimEntries : 3 fields [dupont|jean|45]
both options: 3 fields [red|green|blue]
string separator: [apple|pear|apricot]
Join on integers: 1 + 2 + 3 + 4

Comments:

  • Line 4: The fields are separated by the character [:]. Two consecutive [:] characters, or a single [:] at the end of the string, delimit an empty field: this results in 5 fields, 2 of which are empty (lines 4 and 6 of the results). [Join] reconstructs the original string;
  • the [Split] method has numerous overloads. The 2008 version, [Split(char[] separator)], is now written as [Split(params char[] separator)]: the keyword [params] allows you to process the separators one by one—[Split(':')] or [Split(',', ';')]—without creating an array;
  • Line 13: The enumeration [StringSplitOptions] modifies the field breakdown. [RemoveEmptyEntries] removes empty fields;
  • line 18: [TrimEntries] (.NET 5) removes spaces around each field. The separators are passed here as a collection expression [',', ';'];
  • line 23: the two options are combined using the [|] operator. Spaces are removed before the empty-field check: the field consisting of two spaces between two commas is removed;
  • line 28: the separator can be a string consisting of multiple characters;
  • line 33: [Join] accepts a collection of elements of any type; each element is converted to a string using its [ToString] method.

docs.title: 5.2.3. Searching for and Comparing Strings
docs.text:
String comparison is more subtle than it seems: should uppercase and lowercase letters be distinguished? How should “éclair” be ranked relative to “essay”? The program [strings-03.cs] presents the search and comparison methods:

// searching and comparing strings
string title = "Learning the C# language with .NET";

// Contains, StartsWith, EndsWith: exact comparison by default
Console.WriteLine($"Contains(\"language\") : {title.Contains("language")}");
Console.WriteLine($"Contains(\"LANGUAGE\") : {title.Contains("LANGUAGE")}");
Console.WriteLine($"StartsWith(\"Learning\") : {title.StartsWith("Learning")}");
Console.WriteLine($"EndsWith('T') : {title.EndsWith('T')}");

// the comparison mode is specified with the StringComparison enumeration
Console.WriteLine($"Contains(\"LANGUAGE\", OrdinalIgnoreCase) : {title.Contains("LANGUAGE", StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase)}");
Console.WriteLine($"StartsWith(\"learning\", OrdinalIgnoreCase) : {title.StartsWith("learning", StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase)}");

// equality: the == operator compares the contents of the strings
string answer = "YES";
Console.WriteLine($"answer == \"yes\" : {answer == "yes"}");
Console.WriteLine($"string.Equals(answer, \"yes\", OrdinalIgnoreCase) : {string.Equals(answer, "yes", StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase)}");

// alphabetical order: comparison according to the culture or to the character codes
string a = "éclair", b = "essay";
Console.WriteLine($"Compare(\"{a}\", \"{b}\", CurrentCulture) : {string.Compare(a, b, StringComparison.CurrentCulture)}");
Console.WriteLine($"Compare(\"{a}\", \"{b}\", Ordinal) : {string.Compare(a, b, StringComparison.Ordinal)}");

// empty or blank strings
string? empty = null;
string blank = "   ";
Console.WriteLine($"IsNullOrEmpty(null) : {string.IsNullOrEmpty(empty)}");
Console.WriteLine($"IsNullOrEmpty(\"   \") : {string.IsNullOrEmpty(blank)}");
Console.WriteLine($"IsNullOrWhiteSpace(\"   \") : {string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(blank)}");

// padding
Console.WriteLine($"[{"abc".PadLeft(8)}] [{"abc".PadRight(8, '.')}] [{new string('-', 8)}]");

Results:

> dotnet run strings-03.cs
Contains("language") : True
Contains("LANGUAGE") : False
StartsWith("Learning") : True
EndsWith('T') : True
Contains("LANGUAGE", OrdinalIgnoreCase) : True
StartsWith("learning", OrdinalIgnoreCase) : True
answer == "yes" : False
string.Equals(answer, "yes", OrdinalIgnoreCase) : True
Compare("éclair", "essay", CurrentCulture) : -1
Compare("éclair", "essay", Ordinal) : 132
IsNullOrEmpty(null) : True
IsNullOrEmpty("   ") : False
IsNullOrWhiteSpace("   ") : True
[     abc] [abc.....] [--------]

Comments:

  • lines 5–8: [Contains], [StartsWith], and [EndsWith] perform an exact, character-by-character comparison by default: “LANGUAGE” is not found;
  • Lines 11–12: A parameter of the type [StringComparison] specifies the comparison mode. The most useful values are:
    • [Ordinal]: comparison of character codes;
    • [OrdinalIgnoreCase]: same as above, ignoring case;
    • [CurrentCulture], [CurrentCultureIgnoreCase]: comparison according to the rules of the machine’s language;
    • [InvariantCulture]: comparison based on machine-independent rules;
  • line 16: the operator [] compares the contents of the strings, just like the method [Equals]. This is an important difference from Java, where [] compares references;
  • line 17: the static form of [Equals] also accepts a [StringComparison]. This is the correct way to test a “yes” response entered from the keyboard in uppercase or lowercase;
  • Lines 21–22: [string.Compare] returns a negative, zero, or positive integer depending on whether the first string comes before, is equal to, or comes after the second. In French, “éclair” comes before “essay” (the letter “é” is classified with “e,” line 10 of the results). In ordinal comparison, “éclair” comes after “essay” because the code for the first character, “é” (233), is greater than that of the character “e” (101): the ordinal comparison here returns the difference between the two codes, 132. We will use the cultural order to sort words intended for a user and the ordinal order to compare technical identifiers (file names, keys, etc.);
  • lines 27–29: two static methods for testing a string that is missing ([null]), empty, or contains only spaces;
  • Line 32: [PadLeft] and [PadRight] pad a string to a given length; the constructor [new string('-', 8)] repeats a character.

docs.title: 5.2.4. Interpolation and Formats
docs.text:
String interpolation [$"..."] (C# 6) has been used since the beginning of this course. Like the [string.Format] method, it accepts a width and a format for each expression: [{expression,width:format}]. The program [strings-04.cs] provides examples of this, as well as raw C# 11 strings:

// interpolation, formats and raw strings
string name = "dupont";
int age = 45;
decimal salary = 2345.678m;
double rate = 0.0525;
DateTime date = new(2026, 10, 3, 14, 5, 9);

// simple interpolation
Console.WriteLine($"{name} is {age} years old");
// {expression,width:format}: width > 0 aligns right, < 0 aligns left
Console.WriteLine($"[{name,10}] [{name,-10}] [{age,5}]");
Console.WriteLine($"[{salary,12:F2}] [{salary,-12:F1}] [{salary:N2}] [{salary:C}]");
Console.WriteLine($"[{rate:P2}] [{age:D5}] [{age:X}] [{1234567:N0}]");
Console.WriteLine($"[{date:dd/MM/yyyy}] [{date:HH:mm:ss}] [{date:dddd d MMMM yyyy}]");
// any expression, here a conditional expression in parentheses
Console.WriteLine($"{name} is {(age >= 18 ? "an adult" : "a minor")}");

// the string.Format method and the {n} notation of previous versions of C#
Console.WriteLine(string.Format("{0} is {1} years old and earns {2:F2} euros", name, age, salary));

// an aligned table
string[] products = ["apple", "pear", "apricot"];
decimal[] prices = [2.5m, 3.15m, 12m];
for (int i = 0; i < products.Length; i++)
{
    Console.WriteLine($"{products[i],-10}|{prices[i],8:F2} €");
}

// verbatim string: \ is not an escape character
string path = @"C:\data\course\infos.txt";
Console.WriteLine(path);

// raw string (C# 11): delimited by at least three double quotes, over several lines
string json = """
    {
      "name": "dupont",
      "path": "C:\data"
    }
    """;
Console.WriteLine(json);
// interpolated raw string: with $$, single braces remain literal
string json2 = $$"""{ "name": "{{name}}", "age": {{age}} }""";
Console.WriteLine(json2);

Results:

> dotnet run strings-04.cs
dupont is 45 years old
[    dupont] [dupont    ] [   45]
[     2345,68] [2345,7      ] [2 345,68] [2 345,68 €]
[5,25 %] [00045] [2D] [1 234 567]
[03/10/2026] [14:05:09] [samedi 3 octobre 2026]
dupont is an adult
dupont is 45 years old and earns 2345,68 euros
apple     |    2,50 €
pear      |    3,15 €
apricot   |   12,00 €
C:\data\course\infos.txt
{
  "name": "dupont",
  "path": "C:\data"
}
{ "name": "dupont", "age": 45 }

Comments:

  • line 11: a positive width aligns the value to the right within a 10-character field; a negative width aligns it to the left;
  • Lines 12–14: The most common formats:
formatMeaningexample (fr-FR)[F2]fixed-point number, 2 decimal places2345,68[N2]same as above, with a thousands separator2 345,68[C]monetary amount for the current culture2 345,68 €[P2]percentage (the value is multiplied by 100)5,25 %[D5]5-digit integer or more, padded with zeros00045[X]hexadecimal integer2D[dd/MM/yyyy], [HH:mm:ss]date and time (MM: month, mm: minutes)03/10/2026, 14:05:09[dddd d MMMM yyyy]day and month spelled outsamedi 3 octobre 2026
  • Numbers and dates are formatted according to the current locale, in this case fr-FR: decimal comma, space as a thousands separator, day and month names in French;
  • line 16: a conditional expression placed within an interpolation must be enclosed in parentheses, because the character [:] would introduce a format there;
  • line 19: the notation [{0}], [{1}]… for [string.Format] is the one used in the 2008 course (and [Console.WriteLine], which accepts the same parameters). It is still commonly encountered; the interpolation is more readable;
  • lines 24–26: the widths allow data to be displayed in columns;
  • line 30: a verbatim string [@"..."] does not treat [\] as an escape character. This is useful for Windows paths and regular expressions;
  • lines 34–39: A raw string (C# 11) is delimited by at least three quotation marks. It can span multiple lines and contain unescaped quotation marks and [\]. The indentation of the closing quote is removed from each line: the text JSON is displayed without the 4 spaces from the code margin;
  • Line 42: A raw string can be interpolated. With [$$], an interpolated expression is written between double curly braces [{{name}}], and single curly braces—which are common in a text like JSON—remain ordinary characters.

docs.title: 5.2.5. The System.Text.StringBuilder class
docs.text:
We mentioned that the methods of the [String] class that operate on a string [s1] return another string [s2]. The [System.Text.StringBuilder] class allows you to modify a string without creating a new string for each operation. This improves performance when constructing a string through many successive additions, by avoiding the proliferation of strings with very short lifespans.

The class supports various constructors:

constructorrole[StringBuilder()]default constructor[StringBuilder(string value)]Build and initialize with [value][StringBuilder(string value, int capacity)]Construction and initialization with [value], with an initial capacity of [capacity] characters

A [StringBuilder] object stores its characters in a memory area whose size—its capacity—is automatically adjusted as the text grows. By default, the initial capacity is 16 characters. The third constructor allows you to specify it. The program [strings-05.cs] illustrates this concept of capacity:

using System.Text;

// size and capacity of a StringBuilder
var str = new StringBuilder("test");
Console.WriteLine($"size={str.Length}, capacity={str.Capacity}");
for (int i = 0; i < 10; i++)
{
    str.Append("test");
    Console.WriteLine($"size={str.Length}, capacity={str.Capacity}");
}
// a StringBuilder with initial capacity 10
var str2 = new StringBuilder("test", 10);
Console.WriteLine($"size={str2.Length}, capacity={str2.Capacity}");
for (int i = 0; i < 10; i++)
{
    str2.Append("test");
    Console.WriteLine($"size={str2.Length}, capacity={str2.Capacity}");
}

Results:

> dotnet run strings-05.cs

size=8, capacity=16
size=12, capacity=16
size=16, capacity=16
size=20, capacity=32
size=24, capacity=32
size=28, capacity=32
size=32, capacity=32
size=36, capacity=64
size=40, capacity=64
size=44, capacity=64
size=4, capacity=10
size=8, capacity=10
size=12, capacity=20
size=16, capacity=20
size=20, capacity=20
size=24, capacity=40
size=28, capacity=40
size=32, capacity=40
size=36, capacity=40
size=40, capacity=40
size=44, capacity=80

Comments:

  • line 4: creation of a [StringBuilder] object with an initial capacity of 16;
  • line 5: [Length] is the current number of characters; [Capacity] is the number of characters the object can hold before it needs to expand its memory area;
  • line 8: [Append] adds a string to the end of the text;
  • line 12: creation of an object [StringBuilder] with an initial capacity of 10.

The results show that the capacity doubles when it is insufficient: 16, 32, 64 (lines 6 and 10 of the results), and 10, 20, 40, 80 for the second object. These are the same results as in 2008. If the approximate size of the text is known in advance, setting it at the time of construction avoids successive enlargements.

Here are some of the class’s methods:

methodrole[StringBuilder Append(string value)]Adds [value] to the end of the text. Overridden to accept the types [int], [double], [decimal], [char]…, and an interpolated string[StringBuilder AppendLine()]adds a line break (an overloaded function adds a string followed by a line break)[StringBuilder AppendJoin(string separator, params string[] values)]adds the elements of [values] separated by [separator][StringBuilder Insert(int index, string value)]inserts [value] at the position of [index]; overridden as [Append][StringBuilder Remove(int index, int length)]deletes [length] characters starting at position [index][StringBuilder Replace(string oldValue, string newValue)]replaces [oldValue] with [newValue]; an override replaces a character[string ToString()]converts the text into a string [string]

The program [strings-06.cs] uses them:

using System.Text;

// the methods of StringBuilder return the StringBuilder object itself: they can be chained
var str3 = new StringBuilder("test");
Console.WriteLine(str3.Append("abCD").Insert(2, "xyZT").Remove(0, 2).Replace("xy", "XY"));

// building a string piece by piece
var lines = new StringBuilder();
for (int i = 1; i <= 3; i++)
{
    lines.Append("line ").Append(i).AppendLine();
}
// AppendJoin: the equivalent of string.Join
lines.AppendJoin(", ", "a", "b", "c").AppendLine();
// Append also accepts an interpolated string
int total = 42;
lines.Append($"total={total,6:F1}");
// the final string
string result = lines.ToString();
Console.WriteLine(result);
Console.WriteLine($"{result.Length} characters");

Results:

> dotnet run strings-06.cs
XYZTstabCD
line 1
line 2
line 3
a, b, c
total=  42,0
41 characters

Comments:

  • Line 5: The modification methods return the [StringBuilder] object itself, which allows them to be chained together. Let’s follow the steps: “test” becomes “testabCD” ([Append]), then “texyZTstabCD” ([Insert] in position 2), then “xyZTstabCD” ([Remove] from the first 2 characters), and finally “XYZTstabCD” ([Replace]). [Console.WriteLine] displays the object by calling its method [ToString];
  • lines 9–11: constructing a multi-line text through successive additions: this is the typical use of [StringBuilder];
  • Line 17: [Append] accepts an interpolated string, including width and format;
  • Line 19: The final text is obtained as a [string] string.

For a few concatenations, the [+] operator or interpolation is sufficient: the compiler optimizes them. [StringBuilder] is necessary when the number of additions is large or unknown, typically in a loop.

docs.title: 5.2.6. Views on a string: Span<char>
docs.text:
.NET Core 2.1 (2018) introduced the types [Span<T>] and [ReadOnlySpan<T>]. A [ReadOnlySpan<char>] object is a view into an existing sequence of characters, such as a portion of a string: it does not contain a copy of the characters, only a way to access them. Extracting a portion of a string using a view therefore does not create a new string. The program [strings-07.cs] compares the two ways of parsing a line in the format “last name:first name:age”:

// ReadOnlySpan<char>: a "view" on a part of a string, without copying
string line = "dupont:jean:45";

// with Substring: each field is a new string allocated in memory
int p1 = line.IndexOf(':');
int p2 = line.LastIndexOf(':');
string lastName = line.Substring(0, p1);
int age = int.Parse(line.Substring(p2 + 1));
Console.WriteLine($"Substring : last name={lastName}, age={age}");

// with a view: no intermediate string is created
ReadOnlySpan<char> view = line.AsSpan();
ReadOnlySpan<char> lastNameView = view[..p1];     // characters 0 to p1-1
ReadOnlySpan<char> ageView = view[(p2 + 1)..];    // from p2+1 to the end
// int.Parse accepts a view
age = int.Parse(ageView);
Console.WriteLine($"Span : last name={lastNameView}, age={age}, length of the view={lastNameView.Length}");
// a view can be compared to a string without copying it
Console.WriteLine($"the last name starts with \"du\": {lastNameView.StartsWith("du")}");
// a string is created only if it is really needed
string firstName = view[(p1 + 1)..p2].ToString();
Console.WriteLine($"first name={firstName}");

Results:

> dotnet run strings-07.cs
Substring : last name=dupont, age=45
Span : last name=dupont, age=45, length of the view=6
the last name starts with "du": True
first name=jean

Comments:

  • lines 7–8: Each call to [Substring] creates a new string in memory, even if, as with the age, it is only used for a moment;
  • line 12: [AsSpan] returns a view of the entire string;
  • Lines 13–14: The [start..end] ranges (C# 8), introduced in Chapter 3 for arrays, apply to views: two new views are obtained, without copying;
  • line 16: Many methods in .NET accept a view instead of a string ([Parse], [TryParse], [StartsWith], [Contains], [Equals]…);
  • Line 21: A string is created from a view only if it is actually needed.

Views are an optimization tool used extensively within .NET itself: this is one of the reasons why recent versions are significantly faster than the 2008 .NET Framework. A view can only exist on the execution stack: it cannot, for example, be a field of a class. For an ordinary program, [string] and [Substring] are perfectly suitable: views should only be used in code that has been identified as performance-critical. We will not go any further.

docs.title: 5.3.1. The Array Class
docs.text:
Arrays are derived from the [System.Array] class. This class provides various methods for sorting an array, searching for an element in an array, resizing an array, and more. We’ll present some of its properties and methods. Almost all of them are overloaded, meaning they exist in different variants. Every array inherits these.

Properties:

propertyrole[public int Length { get; }]total number of elements in the array, regardless of the number of dimensions[public int Rank { get; }]Number of dimensions in the array

Methods:

Methodrole[public static int BinarySearch<T>(T[] array, T value)]Returns the position of [value] in [array], which must be sorted; a negative number if [value] is missing[public static void Clear(Array array, int index, int length)]sets the [length] elements of [array] starting at index [index] to their default values: 0 for numbers, [false] for booleans, [null] for references[public static void Copy(Array source, Array destination, int length)]copies the first [length] elements from [source] to [destination][public static void Fill<T>(T[] array, T value)]assigns [value] to all elements of [array][public int GetLength(int dimension)]Number of elements in dimension No. [dimension] of the table[public static int IndexOf<T>(T[] array, T value)]returns the position of [value] within [array], or -1 if [value] is not found; [LastIndexOf] returns the last position[public static void Resize<T>(ref T[]? array, int newSize)]resizes [array] to [newSize] elements; elements already present are retained[public static void Reverse(Array array)]reverses the order of the elements in [array][public static void Sort<T>(T[] array)]sorts [array] according to the natural order of its elements; an overloaded method takes a [IComparer<T>] object that defines the order (Chapter 4)

The program [arrays-01.cs] illustrates the use of certain methods of the [Array] class:

// the Array class: resizing, sorting, searching

// reading the elements of an array typed on the keyboard
double[] elements = Input();
// display of the unsorted array
Display("Unsorted array", elements);
// linear search in the unsorted array
Search(elements, SearchType.Linear);
// sorting the array
Array.Sort(elements);
// display of the sorted array
Display("Sorted array", elements);
// binary search in the sorted array
Search(elements, SearchType.Binary);

// input of the array values: returns the created array
static double[] Input()
{
    // at the start, the array is empty
    double[] elements = [];
    // input loop for the array elements
    while (true)
    {
        Console.Write($"Element (real) {elements.Length} of the array (nothing to finish): ");
        string answer = (Console.ReadLine() ?? "").Trim();
        // end of input if empty string
        if (answer == "")
        {
            break;
        }
        // checking the input
        if (!double.TryParse(answer, out double element))
        {
            Console.WriteLine("Incorrect input, try again");
            continue;
        }
        // one more element: we enlarge the array by one cell
        Array.Resize(ref elements, elements.Length + 1);
        // and we store the new element in it
        elements[^1] = element;
    }
    return elements;
}

// generic method to display the elements of an array
static void Display<T>(string text, T[] elements)
{
    Console.WriteLine(text.PadRight(50, '-'));
    foreach (T element in elements)
    {
        Console.WriteLine(element);
    }
}

// search in the array for elements typed on the keyboard
static void Search(double[] elements, SearchType type)
{
    while (true)
    {
        Console.Write("Element searched for (nothing to stop): ");
        string answer = (Console.ReadLine() ?? "").Trim();
        // finished?
        if (answer == "")
        {
            break;
        }
        // checking
        if (!double.TryParse(answer, out double element))
        {
            Console.WriteLine("Error, try again...");
            continue;
        }
        // we search for the element in the array
        int i = type == SearchType.Binary
            ? Array.BinarySearch(elements, element)    // sorted array
            : Array.IndexOf(elements, element);        // any array
        // display of the answer
        Console.WriteLine(i >= 0 ? $"Found at position {i}" : $"Not in the array ({i})");
    }
}

// type of search
enum SearchType { Linear, Binary }

Comments:

  • Lines 17–42: The method [Input] enters the elements of an array typed from the keyboard. Since the number of elements is not known in advance, the program starts with an empty array (line 20) and expands it by one element for each new entry (line 38). [Resize] actually creates a new array, copies the elements from the old one into it, and stores its reference in the variable passed by [ref]. A more efficient algorithm would allocate space in groups of N elements. An array is not designed to be resized: this scenario is better handled with a list [List<T>], as we will see shortly;
  • line 40: [^1] refers to the last element of the array (indexed from the end, C# 8);
  • In the 2008 course, [Input] was a method with a parameter [out]; the modern version returns the created array, which is more natural;
  • Lines 56–78: The method [Search] searches the array for elements entered from the keyboard. For an unsorted array, a linear search is performed using [IndexOf] (line 76), which examines the elements one by one. For a sorted array, a binary search is performed using [BinarySearch] (line 75), which halves the search range at each step: it finds an element among one million in about twenty comparisons;
  • line 10: the array is sorted. Here, we use a variant of [Sort] that has only one parameter: the array to be sorted. The ordering relation used to compare the array elements is then the implicit one for those elements: in this case, the natural order of numbers;
  • lines 46–51: a generic method that displays an array of elements of any type, [T].

Results:

> dotnet run arrays-01.cs
Element (real) 0 of the array (nothing to finish): 3,6
Element (real) 1 of the array (nothing to finish): 7,4
Element (real) 2 of the array (nothing to finish): -1,5
Element (real) 3 of the array (nothing to finish): x
Incorrect input, try again
Element (real) 3 of the array (nothing to finish): -7
Element (real) 4 of the array (nothing to finish): 
Unsorted array------------------------------------
3,6
7,4
-1,5
-7
Element searched for (nothing to stop): 7,4
Found at position 1
Element searched for (nothing to stop): 0
Not in the array (-1)
Element searched for (nothing to stop): 
Sorted array--------------------------------------
-7
-1,5
3,6
7,4
Element searched for (nothing to stop): 7,4
Found at position 3
Element searched for (nothing to stop): 0
Not in the array (-3)
Element searched for (nothing to stop):

When the element being searched for is absent, [IndexOf] returns -1 and [BinarySearch] returns a negative number (line 27): this is the one’s complement ([~i]) of the position where the element should be inserted to keep the array sorted. Here, [~(-3)] equals 2: the number 0 should be inserted at position 2, between -1.5 and 3.6. Note: [BinarySearch] on an unsorted array returns a meaningless result.

docs.title: 5.3.2. Other methods of the Array class
docs.text:
The program [arrays-02.cs] demonstrates other methods of the [Array] class:

// other methods of the Array class
int[] numbers = [40, 10, 30, 20, 50];
Display("numbers", numbers);

// Reverse: reverses the order of the elements, in place
Array.Reverse(numbers);
Display("after Reverse", numbers);

// Sort on a part of the array: 3 elements starting at index 1
Array.Sort(numbers, 1, 3);
Display("after Sort(numbers, 1, 3)", numbers);

// Copy: copy of 3 elements into another array
int[] copy = new int[5];
Array.Copy(numbers, copy, 3);
Display("copy", copy);

// Fill: fills the array with a value; Clear: resets the elements to their default value
Array.Fill(copy, 7);
Display("after Fill(copy, 7)", copy);
Array.Clear(copy, 1, 2);
Display("after Clear(copy, 1, 2)", copy);

// IndexOf, LastIndexOf on an array of strings
string[] colors = ["red", "green", "blue", "green"];
Console.WriteLine($"IndexOf(green)={Array.IndexOf(colors, "green")}, LastIndexOf(green)={Array.LastIndexOf(colors, "green")}, IndexOf(black)={Array.IndexOf(colors, "black")}");

// sorting an array of strings: alphabetical order of the current culture
Array.Sort(colors);
Display("sorted colors", colors);

// a two-dimensional array: Rank, Length, GetLength
int[,] matrix = new int[2, 3];
Console.WriteLine($"Rank={matrix.Rank}, Length={matrix.Length}, GetLength(0)={matrix.GetLength(0)}, GetLength(1)={matrix.GetLength(1)}");

// display of an array on one line
static void Display<T>(string text, T[] elements)
{
    Console.WriteLine($"{text,-28}: [{string.Join(", ", elements)}]");
}

Results:

> dotnet run arrays-02.cs
numbers                     : [40, 10, 30, 20, 50]
after Reverse               : [50, 20, 30, 10, 40]
after Sort(numbers, 1, 3)   : [50, 10, 20, 30, 40]
copy                        : [50, 10, 20, 0, 0]
after Fill(copy, 7)         : [7, 7, 7, 7, 7]
after Clear(copy, 1, 2)     : [7, 0, 0, 7, 7]
IndexOf(green)=1, LastIndexOf(green)=3, IndexOf(black)=-1
sorted colors               : [blue, green, green, red]
Rank=2, Length=6, GetLength(0)=2, GetLength(1)=3

Comments:

  • line 6: [Reverse] reverses the order of the elements in the array itself;
  • line 10: only 3 elements are sorted starting from position 1: 20, 30, 10 become 10, 20, 30;
  • line 15: copies the first 3 elements of [numbers] into [copy], while the other elements retain their initial value of 0;
  • Lines 19–21: [Fill] fills the array; [Clear] resets 2 elements to 0 starting at position 1;
  • line 29: the strings are sorted in alphabetical order according to the current culture;
  • Line 34: For a two-dimensional array, [Rank] is 2, [Length] is the total number of elements, and [GetLength(i)] is the number of elements in dimension i;
  • Line 39: [string.Join] displays an array on a single line.

LINQ, which we will discuss later, offers other ways to search, sort, or transform the elements of an array.

docs.title: 5.4. Generic Collections
docs.text:
In addition to arrays, there are various classes for storing collections of elements. Generic collections, introduced with .NET 2.0, are located in the [System.Collections.Generic] namespace, which is part of the implicit [using] namespaces. We will first introduce two frequently used collections—the list and the dictionary—and then briefly cover others.

The [System.Collections] namespace contains the older, non-generic versions of these collections, dating back to .NET 1.0: [ArrayList] (a list), [Hashtable] (a dictionary)... The 2008 course still featured [ArrayList]. These classes are now obsolete: they store references of type [object], which requires casting the read elements and boxing the numbers into objects, with associated memory and time costs. Generic collections have none of these drawbacks: a *[List<int>] stores its integers directly in an internal *[int[]] array, and the compiler checks the type of the elements being added. [ArrayList] and [Hashtable] should no longer be used in new code.

docs.title: 5.4.1. The generic class List<T>
docs.text:
The [System.Collections.Generic.List<T>] class allows you to implement collections of [T] objects whose size varies during program execution. An object of type [List<T>] is handled almost like an array. Thus, element i of a [l] list is denoted as [l[i]].

For a list of type [List<T>] where [T] is a class, the list stores references to objects of type [T], like an array of objects; if [T] is a value type ([int], [double], structure…), the values themselves are stored in the list.

Here are some of the properties and methods of generic lists.

Properties:

propertyrole[public int Count { get; }]number of elements in the list[public int Capacity { get; set; }]Number of elements the list can contain before it is expanded. This expansion occurs automatically. This concept of capacity is analogous to that described for class [StringBuilder]

Methods:

Methodrole[public void Add(T item)]adds [item] to the end of the list[public void AddRange(IEnumerable<T> collection)]adds the elements of [collection] to the end of the list[public int BinarySearch(T item)]returns the position of [item] in the sorted list if it is present; otherwise, returns a negative number[public void Clear()]removes all elements from the list[public bool Contains(T item)]returns [true] if [item] is in the list, otherwise [false][public List<T> GetRange(int index, int count)]returns a new list consisting of [count] elements starting from position [index][public int IndexOf(T item)]Returns the position of [item] in the list, or -1 if [item] is not found[public void Insert(int index, T item)]inserts [item] at position [index] in the list[public bool Remove(T item)]removes the first occurrence of [item] from the list; returns [true] if the operation succeeds, [false] otherwise[public void RemoveAt(int index)]removes item No. [index] from the list[public void Reverse()]reverses the order of the items in the list[public void Sort()]sorts the list in natural order; an overloaded version takes a [IComparer<T>][public T[] ToArray()]returns the list elements as an array

Let’s revisit the example we covered earlier with an array and now process it using an object of type [List<double>]. Because the list is similar to an array, the code changes very little. This is the program [collections-01.cs]:

// the List<T> class: the program arrays-01.cs rewritten with a list

// reading the elements of a list typed on the keyboard
List<double> elements = Input();
// number of elements and capacity
Console.WriteLine($"The list has {elements.Count} elements and a capacity of {elements.Capacity} elements");
// display of the unsorted list
Display("Unsorted list", elements);
// linear search in the unsorted list
Search(elements, SearchType.Linear);
// sorting the list
elements.Sort();
// display of the sorted list
Display("Sorted list", elements);
// binary search in the sorted list
Search(elements, SearchType.Binary);

// input of the list values: returns the created list
static List<double> Input()
{
    // at the start, the list is empty
    List<double> elements = new();
    // input loop for the list elements
    while (true)
    {
        Console.Write($"Element (real) {elements.Count} of the list (nothing to finish): ");
        string answer = (Console.ReadLine() ?? "").Trim();
        // end of input if empty string
        if (answer == "")
        {
            break;
        }
        // checking the input
        if (!double.TryParse(answer, out double element))
        {
            Console.WriteLine("Incorrect input, try again");
            continue;
        }
        // one more element in the list: it grows by itself
