    new("jacques", 11, []),
];

// 1 - default serialization: a single line, non-ASCII characters escaped
string json = JsonSerializer.Serialize(persons[1]);
Console.WriteLine($"[default] {json}");

// 2 - options: indentation, accented characters left as they are
var options = new JsonSerializerOptions
{
    WriteIndented = true,
    Encoder = JavaScriptEncoder.Create(UnicodeRanges.All)
};
json = JsonSerializer.Serialize(persons, options);
// writing into a text file
File.WriteAllText("persons.json", json);
Console.WriteLine("[persons.json]");
Console.WriteLine(File.ReadAllText("persons.json"));

// 3 - deserialization: from JSON text to objects
string text = File.ReadAllText("persons.json");
List<Person>? readBack = JsonSerializer.Deserialize<List<Person>>(text);
Console.WriteLine($"[read back] {readBack?.Count} persons");
foreach (Person p in readBack ?? [])
{
    Console.WriteLine($"  {p.Name}, {p.Age} years old, hobbies: [{string.Join(", ", p.Hobbies)}]");
}

// 4 - without attributes: the "Web" options put the property names in camelCase
var web = new JsonSerializerOptions(JsonSerializerDefaults.Web);
string jsonArticle = JsonSerializer.Serialize(new Article("A12", 12.5m), web);
Console.WriteLine($"[Web options] {jsonArticle}");
// and they ignore case when reading
Article? article = JsonSerializer.Deserialize<Article>("""{ "CODE": "B7", "price": 3 }""", web);
Console.WriteLine($"[Web options] {article}");

// 5 - an incorrect JSON document causes a JsonException
try
{
    JsonSerializer.Deserialize<Person>("""{ "name": "x", "age": "twelve" }""");
}
catch (JsonException e)
{
    Console.WriteLine($"[error] {e.GetType().Name} : {e.Message}");
}

// a person; the [JsonPropertyName] attributes set the names of the JSON properties
record Person(
    [property: JsonPropertyName("name")] string Name,
    [property: JsonPropertyName("age")] int Age,
    [property: JsonPropertyName("hobbies")] List<string> Hobbies);

// an article, without attributes
record Article(string Code, decimal Price);

Results:

> dotnet run files-06.cs
[default] {"name":"h\u00E9l\u00E8ne","age":15,"hobbies":["piano","tennis"]}
[persons.json]
[
  {
    "name": "paul",
    "age": 10,
    "hobbies": [
      "football"
    ]
  },
  {
    "name": "hélène",
    "age": 15,
    "hobbies": [
      "piano",
      "tennis"
    ]
  },
  {
    "name": "jacques",
    "age": 11,
    "hobbies": []
  }
]
[read back] 3 persons
  paul, 10 years old, hobbies: [football]
  hélène, 15 years old, hobbies: [piano, tennis]
  jacques, 11 years old, hobbies: []
[Web options] {"code":"A12","price":12.5}
[Web options] Article { Code = B7, Price = 3 }
[error] JsonException : The JSON value could not be converted to Person. Path: $.age | LineNumber: 0 | BytePositionInLine: 30.

Comments:

  • Line 1: A directive for single-file applications. By default, these are configured for native compilation (AOT, "ahead of time"), which produces a standalone executable but disables mechanisms that rely on runtime type discovery (reflection). However, [JsonSerializer] uses reflection by default to discover the properties of objects to be serialized: without this directive, compilation produces warnings and execution fails. A standard [.csproj] project, such as the one in the sample application, does not have this restriction. For a natively compiled application, [System.Text.Json] provides a source generator (a class derived from [JsonSerializerContext]) that generates the serialization code at compile time: we will not cover this here;
  • lines 60–63: the [Person] record to be serialized. Its properties carry the attribute [JsonPropertyName], which sets the property name in the text JSON to [name] instead of [Name]. In a positional record, [property: ...] indicates that the attribute applies to the generated property and not to the constructor parameter;
  • line 17: serialization of an object with default options: the text is written on a single line, and non-ASCII characters are escaped: [é] becomes [\u00E9]. The text remains correct, but it is difficult to read;
  • Lines 21–26: The option [WriteIndented] produces indented text across multiple lines; the option [Encoder] specifies which characters to leave as-is—in this case, all Unicode characters. A list is serialized into an array JSON;
  • line 28: the text JSON is saved to a text file: this is how binary serialization is replaced today;
  • line 34: deserialization reconstructs the list. [Deserialize] creates the [Person] objects by calling the record’s constructor, whose parameters are associated with the JSON properties of the same name. The result is of type [List<Person>?]: the text JSON [null] is a valid document that yields [null];
  • line 42: the “Web” options—which are used by default by ASP.NET Core’s web services—write property names in camelCase format (first letter lowercase): [Code] becomes [code], without an attribute. When parsed, they are case-insensitive: [CODE] is accepted (line 31);
  • line 52: an invalid JSON document—in this case, a string where a number is expected—triggers a [JsonException] exception, whose message indicates the location of the error.

We will use JSON in the following example application and throughout the course.

docs.title: 5.8. Regular Expressions
docs.text:
The [System.Text.RegularExpressions.Regex] class supports the use of regular expressions. These allow you to validate the format of a string. For example, you can verify that a string representing a date is indeed in the dd/mm/yy format. To do this, you use a pattern and compare the string to that pattern. In this example, d, m, and y must be digits. The pattern for a valid date format is therefore [\d\d/\d\d/\d\d], where the symbol [\d] represents a digit. The symbols that can be used in a pattern are as follows:

characterdescription[\]marks the following character as a special character or literal. For example, [n] corresponds to the character n, [ ] corresponds to a newline character, [\] corresponds to \, and [\(] corresponds to ([^]corresponds to the beginning of the string[$]corresponds to the end of the string[*]matches the preceding element zero or more times. Thus, [zo*] matches z or zoo[+]matches the previous element one or more times. Thus, [zo+] matches "zoo," but not "z"[?]matches the preceding element zero or one time. For example, [a?ve?] matches “ve” in “lever”[.]matches any single character, except for a newline character[(pattern)]searches for the pattern and stores the match (a group). The matching substring can be extracted from the [Groups] collection in the result. To find matches with characters in parentheses, use [\(] or [\)][x|y]matches either x or y. For example, [z|foot] matches z or foot; [(z|f)oo] matches zoo or foo[{n}]n is a non-negative integer. Corresponds exactly n times to the previous element. For example, [o{2}] does not correspond to o in Bob, but to the first two o’s in fooooot[{n,}]matches the previous element at least n times. For example, [o{2,}] does not match the 'o' in 'Bob', but matches all the 'o's in 'fooooot'. [o{1,}] is equivalent to [o+], and [o{0,}] is equivalent to [o*][{n,m}]matches the previous element at least n times and at most m times. For example, [o{1,3}] matches the first three “o”s in “foooooot”; [o{0,1}] is equivalent to [o?][xyz]character set: matches one of the specified characters. For example, [abc] matches the letter “a” in “plat”[^xyz]negative character set: matches any character not listed. For example, [^abc] matches "p" in "plat"[a-z]Character range: matches any character in the specified range, in this case a lowercase unaccented letter[^m-z]negative character range: matches any character not between 'm' and 'z'[ ]matches a word boundary, that is, the position between a word character and a non-word character. For example, [er ] matches "er" in "lever," but not "er" in "verb"[\B]corresponds to a position that is not a word boundary. [en*t\B] corresponds to “ent” in “entertain”[\d]corresponds to a digit; is equivalent to [0-9] (along with .NET, also for digits from other Unicode alphabets)[\D]corresponds to a character that is not a digit[ ], [ ], [ ], [ ], [\v]correspond to the characters page break, new line, carriage return, tab, and vertical tab, respectively[\s]corresponds to any whitespace: space, tab, page break, line break… Equivalent to [ \v], plus other Unicode whitespace characters (non-breaking space, etc.)[\S]matches any character that is not a whitespace character[\w]matches any word character: letter (with or without accents), digit, or underscore[\W]matches any character that is not a word character[ um]num is a positive integer: refers to group number num. For example, [(.)\1] matches two consecutive identical characters[\xnn], [\unnnn]corresponds to the hexadecimal character nn (2 digits) or nnnn (4 digits). For example, [\x41] corresponds to A

An element in a template can appear once or multiple times. Let’s look at a few examples using the symbol [\d], which represents a single digit:

templateMeaning[\d]one digit[\d?]0 or 1 digit[\d*]0 or more digits[\d+]1 or more digits[\d{2}]2 digits[\d{3,}]At least 3 digits[\d{5,7}]between 5 and 7 digits

Now let’s imagine a model capable of describing the expected format for a string:

target stringpatterna date in dd/mm/yy format[\d{2}/\d{2}/\d{2}]a time in the hh:mm:ss format[\d{2}:\d{2}:\d{2}]an unsigned integer[\d+]a sequence of spaces, which may be empty[\s*]an unsigned integer that may be preceded or followed by spaces[\s*\d+\s*]an integer that may be signed and preceded or followed by spaces[\s*[+-]?\s*\d+\s*]an unsigned real number that may be preceded or followed by spaces[\s*\d+(\.\d*)?\s*]a real number that may be signed and preceded or followed by spaces[\s*[+-]?\s*\d+(\.\d*)?\s*]a string containing the word "just"[ just ]

The 2008 course used [+|-] for the sign: enclosed in square brackets, the character [|] has no specific meaning, and this format also accepted the | sign before a number. It also used [(.\d*)] for the decimal part: the unescaped period there represents any character. The patterns above have been corrected.

You can specify where to look for the pattern in the string:

patternmeaning[^pattern]the pattern begins the string[pattern$]The pattern ends the string[^pattern$]The pattern starts and ends the string[pattern]The pattern is searched for anywhere in the string, starting from the beginning of the string search stringpatterna string ending with an exclamation point[!$]a string ending with a period[\.$]a string beginning with the sequence //[^//]a string consisting of a single word, possibly preceded or followed by spaces[^\s*\w+\s*$]a string consisting of exactly two words, possibly preceded or followed by spaces[^\s*\w+\s+\w+\s*$]a string containing the word "secret"[ secret ]

Sub sets of a pattern can be “extracted.” Thus, not only can we verify that a string matches a particular pattern, but we can also extract from that string the elements corresponding to the pattern’s sub sets that have been enclosed in parentheses. For example, if you are parsing a string containing a date in the dd/mm/yy format and also want to extract the dd, mm, and yy components of that date, you would use the pattern [(\d\d)/(\d\d)/(\d\d)].

In C# code, a pattern is preferably written as a verbatim string [@"..."]: this way, the numerous [\] characters in the patterns do not need to be doubled. With a regular string, you would have to write ***["\\d+"] instead of ***[@"\d+"].

docs.title: 5.8.1. Check whether a string matches a given template
docs.text:
An object of type [Regex] is constructed as follows:

constructorrole[public Regex(string pattern)]creates a “regular expression” object from a pattern passed as a parameter ([pattern]). A [ArgumentException] exception is thrown if the pattern is incorrect[public Regex(string pattern, RegexOptions options, TimeSpan matchTimeout)]same as above, with options and a timeout (see below)

Once the regular expression has been constructed, it can be compared to character strings using the [IsMatch] method:

methodrole[public bool IsMatch(string input)]true if the string [input] contains a substring that matches the regular expression pattern

The program [regex-01.cs] is as follows:

using System.Text.RegularExpressions;

// checking that a string matches a pattern
string pattern1 = @"^\s*\d+\s*$";
var regex1 = new Regex(pattern1);
// comparing samples with the pattern
foreach (string sample in new[] { "  123  ", "  123a  ", "4567" })
{
    if (regex1.IsMatch(sample))
    {
        Console.WriteLine($"[{sample}] matches the pattern [{pattern1}]");
    }
    else
    {
        Console.WriteLine($"[{sample}] does not match the pattern [{pattern1}]");
    }
}
// the static method Regex.IsMatch avoids creating the Regex object yourself
Console.WriteLine($"Regex.IsMatch(\"18/05/97\", date) : {Regex.IsMatch("18/05/97", @"^\d{2}/\d{2}/\d{2}$")}");
Console.WriteLine($"Regex.IsMatch(\"5/1/01\", date) : {Regex.IsMatch("5/1/01", @"^\d{2}/\d{2}/\d{2}$")}");

Results:

> dotnet run regex-01.cs
[  123  ] matches the pattern [^\s*\d+\s*$]
[  123a  ] does not match the pattern [^\s*\d+\s*$]
[4567] matches the pattern [^\s*\d+\s*$]
Regex.IsMatch("18/05/97", date) : True
Regex.IsMatch("5/1/01", date) : False

Comments:

  • line 4: the pattern for an unsigned integer, optionally surrounded by spaces, that occupies the entire string (anchors [^] and [$]);
  • line 9: the string “123a,” surrounded by spaces, does not match the pattern: the character “a” cannot be a digit or a space. Without the anchors [^] and [$], the string would match, since it contains a number;
  • line 19: The class [Regex] also has static methods that take the pattern as a parameter. .NET stores the most recently used patterns in memory: they can be used in a loop without worrying that the pattern will be parsed on every call.

docs.title: 5.8.2. Find all occurrences of a pattern in a string
docs.text:
The [Matches] method retrieves the elements of a string that match a pattern:

methodrole[public MatchCollection Matches(string input)]returns the collection of elements in the string [input] that match the pattern

The [MatchCollection] class has a property, [Count], which is the number of elements in the collection. If [results] is a [MatchCollection] object, then [results[i]] is the i-th element of that collection; it is of type [Match]. The class [Match] has various properties, including the following:

  • [Value]: the value of the object [Match], i.e., an element matching the pattern;
  • [Index]: the position where the element was found in the explored string.

The program [regex-02.cs] is as follows:

using System.Text.RegularExpressions;

// finding all the occurrences of a pattern in a string
string pattern2 = @"\d+";
var regex2 = new Regex(pattern2);
string sample3 = "  123  456  789 ";
MatchCollection results = regex2.Matches(sample3);
Console.WriteLine($"Pattern=[{pattern2}], sample=[{sample3}]");
Console.WriteLine($"There are {results.Count} occurrences of the pattern in the sample");
foreach (Match m in results)
{
    Console.WriteLine($"[{m.Value}] found at position {m.Index}");
}
// a MatchCollection is a sequence: LINQ applies to it
int sum = results.Sum(m => int.Parse(m.Value));
Console.WriteLine($"sum of the numbers found: {sum}");
// Count counts the occurrences without building the collection
Console.WriteLine($"number of vowels of \"antidisestablishmentarianism\": {Regex.Count("antidisestablishmentarianism", "[aeiouy]")}");

Results:

> dotnet run regex-02.cs
Pattern=[\d+], sample=[  123  456  789 ]
There are 3 occurrences of the pattern in the sample
[123] found at position 2
[456] found at position 7
[789] found at position 12
sum of the numbers found: 1368
number of vowels of "antidisestablishmentarianism": 11

Comments:

  • Line 4: The pattern being searched for is a sequence of digits;
  • line 6: the string in which this pattern is searched for;
  • line 7: all elements of [sample3] that match the pattern [pattern2] are retrieved;
  • Lines 10–12: These are displayed. A [MatchCollection] is traversed with [foreach], like a list;
  • line 15: [MatchCollection] implements [IEnumerable<Match>]: LINQ is applied to it. Here, we sum the numbers found;
  • line 18: the method [Count] (.NET 7) counts the occurrences of the pattern without constructing a collection. The pattern [aeiouy] denotes a vowel.

docs.title: 5.8.3. Retrieving Parts of a Pattern
docs.text:
As mentioned earlier, the parts of a pattern enclosed in parentheses are stored: these are the groups. The program [regex-03.cs] uses them:

using System.Text.RegularExpressions;

// retrieving parts of a pattern: groups
string pattern3 = @"(\d\d):(\d\d):(\d\d)";
var regex3 = new Regex(pattern3);
string sample4 = "It is 18:05:49";
// Match returns the first occurrence of the pattern
Match result = regex3.Match(sample4);
if (result.Success)
{
    Console.WriteLine($"The sample [{sample4}] matches the pattern [{pattern3}]");
    // we display the parenthesized groups
    for (int i = 0; i < result.Groups.Count; i++)
    {
        Console.WriteLine($"groups[{i}]=[{result.Groups[i].Value}] found at position {result.Groups[i].Index}");
    }
}
else
{
    Console.WriteLine($"The sample [{sample4}] does not match the pattern [{pattern3}]");
}

// named groups: (?<name>...)
var regexDate = new Regex(@"(?<day>\d{1,2})/(?<month>\d{1,2})/(?<year>\d{4})");
string text = "Appointment on 3/10/2026, then on 15/11/2026.";
foreach (Match m in regexDate.Matches(text))
{
    // a group is designated by its name rather than by its number
    int day = int.Parse(m.Groups["day"].Value);
    int month = int.Parse(m.Groups["month"].Value);
    int year = int.Parse(m.Groups["year"].Value);
    var date = new DateOnly(year, month, day);
    Console.WriteLine($"[{m.Value}] : day={day}, month={month}, year={year} -> {date:dddd d MMMM yyyy}");
}

// Replace: the groups can be reused in the replacement string
string reversed = regexDate.Replace(text, "${year}-${month}-${day}");
Console.WriteLine($"Replace : {reversed}");

Results:

> dotnet run regex-03.cs
The sample [It is 18:05:49] matches the pattern [(\d\d):(\d\d):(\d\d)]
groups[0]=[18:05:49] found at position 6
groups[1]=[18] found at position 6
groups[2]=[05] found at position 9
groups[3]=[49] found at position 12
[3/10/2026] : day=3, month=10, year=2026 -> Saturday 3 October 2026
[15/11/2026] : day=15, month=11, year=2026 -> Sunday 15 November 2026
Replace : Appointment on 2026-10-3, then on 2026-11-15.

Comments:

  • Line 8: The string [sample4] is compared to the template [regex3] using the method [Match]. This method returns the first occurrence of the template as a [Match] object, which has already been presented. Here, we use two new properties of this class:
    • [Success] (line 9): indicates whether a match was found;
    • [Groups] (line 13): a collection where [Groups[0]] corresponds to the part of the string representing the template, and [Groups[i]] (i >= 1) corresponds to the i-th set of parentheses;
  • if [result] is of type [Match], then [result.Groups] is of type [GroupCollection] and [result.Groups[i]] is of type [Group]. The class [Group] has, like the class [Match], the properties [Value] (the text captured by the group) and [Index] (its position in the parsed string);
  • line 24: a group can be named using the syntax [(?<name>...)]. Here, the pattern recognizes a date in the d/m/yyyy format, with a one- or two-digit day and month;
  • lines 29–31: a named group is referred to by its name rather than its number: the code is more readable and does not depend on the order of the parentheses;
  • line 32: the type [DateOnly] (.NET 6) represents a date without a time. It is displayed in the format [dddd d MMMM yyyy]: the day of the week appears in English;
  • line 37: the [Replace] method replaces each occurrence of the template with a string in which [${name}] (or [$1], [$2]… for numbered groups) denotes the value of a group. Dates are thus reformatted into the year-month-day format.

docs.title: 5.8.4. A Learning Program
docs.text:
Finding the regular expression that verifies whether a string matches a certain pattern can sometimes be a real challenge. The program [regex-04.cs] lets you practice. It takes a pattern and a string as input and indicates whether the string matches the pattern or not.

using System.Text.RegularExpressions;

// a program for learning regular expressions
while (true)
{
    // we ask for the pattern
    Console.Write("Type the pattern to test or nothing to stop: ");
    string pattern = Console.ReadLine() ?? "";
    // finished?
    if (pattern.Trim() == "")
    {
        break;
    }
    // we create the regular expression; an incorrect pattern causes an exception
    Regex regex;
    try
    {
        regex = new Regex(pattern, RegexOptions.None, TimeSpan.FromSeconds(1));
    }
    catch (ArgumentException e)
    {
        Console.WriteLine($"Error: {e.Message}");
        continue;
    }
    // we ask for the samples to compare with the pattern
    while (true)
    {
        Console.Write($"Type the string to compare with the pattern [{pattern}] or nothing to stop: ");
        string input = Console.ReadLine() ?? "";
        // finished?
        if (input.Trim() == "")
        {
            break;
        }
        try
        {
            // we do the comparison
            MatchCollection results = regex.Matches(input);
            if (results.Count == 0)
            {
                Console.WriteLine("I did not find any matches");
                continue;
            }
            // we display the elements matching the pattern
            foreach (Match m in results)
            {
                Console.WriteLine($"I found the match [{m.Value}] at position [{m.Index}]");
                // and its sub-elements (groups 1, 2, ...)
                for (int j = 1; j < m.Groups.Count; j++)
                {
                    Console.WriteLine($"\tsub-element [{m.Groups[j].Value}] at position [{m.Groups[j].Index}]");
                }
            }
        }
        catch (RegexMatchTimeoutException)
        {
            Console.WriteLine("The search was abandoned: it lasted more than one second");
        }
    }
}

Comments:

  • line 18: The regular expression is constructed with a one-second timeout: if a search takes longer than that, it is abandoned and a [RegexMatchTimeoutException] exception is thrown (line 55). We’ll see later why this is useful;
  • line 20: an invalid pattern causes a [ArgumentException] exception (more specifically, [RegexParseException], which is derived from it);
  • lines 45–51: For each match, groups #1 and subsequent groups are displayed, if any.

Here is an example of the output:

> dotnet run regex-04.cs
Type the pattern to test or nothing to stop: \d+
Type the string to compare with the pattern [\d+] or nothing to stop: 123 456 789
I found the match [123] at position [0]
I found the match [456] at position [4]
I found the match [789] at position [8]
Type the string to compare with the pattern [\d+] or nothing to stop: 
Type the pattern to test or nothing to stop: (\d{2}):(\d\d)
Type the string to compare with the pattern [(\d{2}):(\d\d)] or nothing to stop: 14:15 abcd 17:18 xyzt
I found the match [14:15] at position [0]
    sub-element [14] at position [0]
    sub-element [15] at position [3]
I found the match [17:18] at position [11]
    sub-element [17] at position [11]
    sub-element [18] at position [14]
Type the string to compare with the pattern [(\d{2}):(\d\d)] or nothing to stop: 
Type the pattern to test or nothing to stop: ^\s*\d+\s*$
Type the string to compare with the pattern [^\s*\d+\s*$] or nothing to stop:    1456
I found the match [   1456] at position [0]
Type the string to compare with the pattern [^\s*\d+\s*$] or nothing to stop: 
Type the pattern to test or nothing to stop: ^\s*(\d+)\s*$
Type the string to compare with the pattern [^\s*(\d+)\s*$] or nothing to stop: 1456
I found the match [1456] at position [0]
    sub-element [1456] at position [0]
Type the string to compare with the pattern [^\s*(\d+)\s*$] or nothing to stop: abcd 1456
I did not find any matches
Type the string to compare with the pattern [^\s*(\d+)\s*$] or nothing to stop: 
Type the pattern to test or nothing to stop: (a+)+$
Type the string to compare with the pattern [(a+)+$] or nothing to stop: aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa!
The search was abandoned: it lasted more than one second
Type the string to compare with the pattern [(a+)+$] or nothing to stop: 
Type the pattern to test or nothing to stop: (\d+
Error: Invalid pattern '(\d+' at offset 4. Not enough )'s.
Type the pattern to test or nothing to stop:

The templates [^\s*\d+\s*$] and [^\s*(\d+)\s*$] demonstrate the usefulness of groups: the first recognizes the string “1456” preceded by three spaces, including the spaces; the second additionally extracts the number without the spaces. The [(a+)+$] template is examined below.

docs.title: 5.8.5. The Split Method
docs.text:
We have already encountered the [Split] method from the [String] class:

methodrole[public string[] Split(params char[] separator)]The string is treated as a sequence of fields separated by the characters listed in the array [separator]. The result is an array of these fields

The method [Split] of the class [Regex] allows us to specify the separator using a pattern:

methodrole[public string[] Split(string input)]The string [input] is split into fields, which are separated by a separator corresponding to the pattern of the current [Regex] object

Suppose, for example, that a text file contains lines of the form field1, field2, ..., fieldn. The fields are separated by a comma, but this comma may be preceded or followed by spaces. The [\s*,\s*] template describes this separator exactly, as shown by the [regex-05.cs] program:

using System.Text.RegularExpressions;

// Regex.Split: the separator is defined by a pattern
string line = "abc  , def  ,ghi ,   jkl";
// a comma preceded and followed by any number of spaces
var separator = new Regex(@"\s*,\s*");
string[] fields = separator.Split(line);
for (int i = 0; i < fields.Length; i++)
{
    Console.WriteLine($"fields[{i}]=[{fields[i]}]");
}
// several possible separators: ; or | or a sequence of spaces
string[] words = Regex.Split("one;two|three   four", @"[;|]|\s+");
Console.WriteLine($"words=[{string.Join(", ", words)}]");

Results:

> dotnet run regex-05.cs
fields[0]=[abc]
fields[1]=[def]
fields[2]=[ghi]
fields[3]=[jkl]
words=[one, two, three, four]

Comments:

  • line 6: the separator: a comma preceded and followed by any number of spaces. The spaces are removed along with the separator. Note that the option [TrimEntries] from [string.Split], presented above, now allows you to achieve the same result without a regular expression;
  • Line 13: A separator that can take several forms: a semicolon or a vertical bar ([;|]), or ([|]) a sequence of spaces ([\s+]). Here, a regular expression is required.

docs.title: 5.8.6. Generated regular expressions, options, timeout
docs.text:
A [Regex] object parses its template at runtime, then translates it into an internal structure that it interprets, or compiles into executable code if the [RegexOptions.Compiled] option is passed to it. Starting with .NET 7, the [GeneratedRegex] attribute allows this work to be done at compile time: a source generator writes the C# code for the search, which can be viewed in the editor (F12 on the method). The template is validated at compile time, there is no longer any analysis overhead at startup, and the generated code runs as fast as possible. This is now the recommended way to use a template known in advance. The program [regex-06.cs] is as follows:

using System.Diagnostics;
using System.Text.RegularExpressions;

// 1 - regular expressions generated at compile time
Console.WriteLine($"Time(\"It is 18:05:49\") : {Patterns.Time().IsMatch("It is 18:05:49")}");
Match m = Patterns.Time().Match("departure at 07:45:00");
Console.WriteLine($"hours={m.Groups["h"].Value}, minutes={m.Groups["m"].Value}, seconds={m.Groups["s"].Value}");

// 2 - options: here IgnoreCase, set in the attribute
foreach (string answer in new[] { "yes", "YES", "Yes", "no", "yesss" })
{
    Console.Write($"{answer}={Patterns.Yes().IsMatch(answer)} ");
}
Console.WriteLine();
// options are combined with |: Multiline makes ^ and $ match at each start and end of line
string text = "price: 10\nquantity: 3\ntotal: 30";
foreach (Match line in Regex.Matches(text, @"^(\w+): (\d+)$", RegexOptions.Multiline))
{
    Console.Write($"[{line.Groups[1].Value}={line.Groups[2].Value}] ");
}
Console.WriteLine();

// 3 - a timeout protects against patterns with catastrophic backtracking
string input = new string('a', 30) + "!";
try
{
    Console.WriteLine(Patterns.Catastrophic().IsMatch(input));
}
catch (RegexMatchTimeoutException e)
{
    Console.WriteLine($"{e.GetType().Name} : search abandoned after {e.MatchTimeout.TotalMilliseconds} ms");
}
// the same pattern with the non-backtracking engine answers immediately
var stopwatch = Stopwatch.StartNew();
bool found = Regex.IsMatch(input, @"^(a+)+$", RegexOptions.NonBacktracking);
Console.WriteLine($"NonBacktracking : {found}, answer in less than one second: {stopwatch.ElapsedMilliseconds < 1000}");

// the patterns of the program
static partial class Patterns
{
    // a time hh:mm:ss with named groups
    [GeneratedRegex(@"(?<h>\d\d):(?<m>\d\d):(?<s>\d\d)")]
    public static partial Regex Time();

    // yes, whatever the case
    [GeneratedRegex(@"^\s*yes\s*$", RegexOptions.IgnoreCase)]
    public static partial Regex Yes();

    // a pathological pattern, with a timeout of 100 ms
    [GeneratedRegex(@"^(a+)+$", RegexOptions.None, matchTimeoutMilliseconds: 100)]
    public static partial Regex Catastrophic();
}

Results:

> dotnet run regex-06.cs
Time("It is 18:05:49") : True
hours=07, minutes=45, seconds=00
yes=True YES=True Yes=True no=False yesss=False 
[price=10] [quantity=3] [total=30] 
RegexMatchTimeoutException : search abandoned after 100 ms
NonBacktracking : False, answer in less than one second: True

Comments:

  • Lines 39–51: Each template is declared by a partial static method ([partial]) with no body, which generates a [Regex], and is preceded by the attribute [GeneratedRegex]. The source generator writes the method body in another part of the class, which is also declared as [partial]. Starting with C# 13 and .NET 9, you can also declare a partial property: [[GeneratedRegex(...)] private static partial Regex Time { get; }];
  • line 5: the method is used as a regular [Regex] object;
  • line 46: the second parameter of the attribute is a combination of options [RegexOptions]. [IgnoreCase] ignores case: “YES” and “Yes” match the pattern;
  • line 17: the options are used in the same way with the methods of [Regex]. [Multiline] matches [^] and [$] at the beginning and end of each line in the string, rather than just at the beginning and end of the string itself. Other options are useful: [Singleline] ([.] also matches line breaks), [IgnorePatternWhitespace] (spaces in the pattern are ignored, allowing it to be written across multiple lines, including comments), [ExplicitCapture] (only named groups are remembered). These can be combined with the [|] operator;
  • line 50: the pattern [^(a+)+$] is pathological: when applied to a sequence of “a”s ending with another character, the regular expression engine tries every possible way to distribute the “a”s among the group repetitions before concluding that it has failed. The number of possibilities doubles with each additional “a”: with 30 “a”s, there are approximately one billion possibilities. This is known as a catastrophic backtracking. Such a pattern, when applied to strings entered by users, is a security vulnerability: just a few requests are enough to crash a server. The [matchTimeoutMilliseconds] parameter sets a timeout of 100 ms: after that, the search is abandoned with a [RegexMatchTimeoutException] exception (line 6);
  • line 35: the [NonBacktracking] option (.NET 7) uses a different engine, which guarantees a search time proportional to the string’s length. It does not support certain constructs (backward references, such as [\1], for example), but it returns a result immediately in this case.

Note that you must set a timeout or use [NonBacktracking] whenever the pattern or the string being searched comes from outside the program.

docs.title: 5.9. Example Application - V3
docs.text: We’ll revisit the application covered in Chapter 3 (Version 1) and Chapter 4 (Version 2). Remember that this is an exercise: the tax schedule used is the 2004 version (2003 income), which has remained unchanged since the original course.

docs.title: 5.9.1. Data in a File
docs.text:
In version 2, the tax calculation was performed in the abstract class [AbstractTax], which we reproduce here unchanged, except for its namespace:

namespace TaxV3;

public abstract class AbstractTax : ITax
{
    // the tax brackets needed for the calculation come from an external source
    // that only the derived classes know
    protected abstract TaxBracket[] TaxBrackets { get; }

    // tax calculation
    public int Calculate(bool married, int nbChildren, int salary)
    {
        // calculation of the number of shares
        decimal shares = (decimal)nbChildren / 2 + (married ? 2 : 1);
        if (nbChildren >= 3)
        {
            shares += 0.5m;
        }
        // calculation of the taxable income and of the family quotient
        decimal income = 0.72m * salary;
        decimal quotient = income / shares;
        // search for the tax bracket: the last one is used if no limit fits
        TaxBracket[] brackets = TaxBrackets;
        TaxBracket bracket = brackets[^1];
        for (int i = 0; i < brackets.Length - 1; i++)
        {
            if (quotient <= brackets[i].Limit)
            {
                bracket = brackets[i];
                break;
            }
        }
        // tax calculation
        return (int)(income * bracket.CoeffR - shares * bracket.CoeffN);
    }
}

The [Calculate] method uses the tax brackets returned by the abstract property [TaxBrackets] (line 7). The [AbstractTax] class does not know where these brackets come from: it is up to the derived classes to provide them. In version 2, the derived class [HardwiredTax] hard-coded them into its code. A tax bracket is represented, as in version 2, by the record structure [TaxBracket]:

namespace TaxV3;

// a bracket of the tax scale
public readonly record struct TaxBracket(decimal Limit, decimal CoeffR, decimal CoeffN);

and the calculation is described by the interface [ITax]:

namespace TaxV3;

public interface ITax
{
    // tax calculation for a taxpayer
    int Calculate(bool married, int nbChildren, int salary);
}

The new version stores the data in a file, which allows you to change the pay scale without recompiling the program. We write two new classes derived from [AbstractTax]:

  • [FileTax] reads the brackets from a text file [TaxData.txt];
  • [JsonTax] reads them from a JSON file named [TaxData.json].

The text file [TaxData.txt] contains one tax bracket per line, in the format limit:coeffR:coeffN:

4962:0:0
8382:0.068:291.09
14753:0.191:1322.92
23888:0.283:2668.39
38868:0.374:4846.98
47932:0.426:6883.66
0:0.481:9505.54

The 2008 course wrote numbers with a decimal comma (0,068) and read them using [decimal.TryParse] in the machine’s locale: the same file, when read on a British or American machine, would have been rejected or, worse, misinterpreted. A data file must not depend on the language of the machine reading it: we write numbers with a decimal point and read them in the invariant culture ([CultureInfo.InvariantCulture]), which is also used by JSON and most data formats.

The file [TaxData.json] contains the same data, in the form of a JSON array of objects:

[
  { "limit": 4962, "coeffR": 0, "coeffN": 0 },
  { "limit": 8382, "coeffR": 0.068, "coeffN": 291.09 },
  { "limit": 14753, "coeffR": 0.191, "coeffN": 1322.92 },
  { "limit": 23888, "coeffR": 0.283, "coeffN": 2668.39 },
  { "limit": 38868, "coeffR": 0.374, "coeffN": 4846.98 },
  { "limit": 47932, "coeffR": 0.426, "coeffN": 6883.66 },
  { "limit": 0, "coeffR": 0.481, "coeffN": 9505.54 }
]

docs.title: 5.9.2. Errors
docs.text:
Processing these files may fail: missing file, malformed line, incorrect number, etc. As in the 2008 version, we create a special exception class to report these errors. The 2008 course called it [FileTaxException]; we’re naming it [TaxException], since it will also be used for other data sources (the JSON file here, and a database later). It carries an error code:

namespace TaxV3;

// the error codes: powers of 2, which can be combined
[Flags]
public enum ErrorCode
{
    Access = 1,     // the file cannot be read
    Line = 2,       // a line does not have three fields
    Field1 = 4,     // field 1 (limit) is incorrect
    Field2 = 8,     // field 2 (coeffR) is incorrect
    Field3 = 16,    // field 3 (coeffN) is incorrect
    Json = 32       // the JSON document is incorrect
}

// the exception thrown by the classes that read the tax brackets
public class TaxException : Exception
{
    // the error code (a combination of ErrorCode values)
    public int Code { get; init; }

    public TaxException(string message) : base(message) { }
    public TaxException(string message, Exception inner) : base(message, inner) { }
}

Comments:

  • lines 16–22: The class [TaxException] derives from the class [Exception]. It will be used to report any errors that occur while processing the data file. It has two constructors: the first takes an error message, and the second also takes the exception that caused the error, which will be available in the [InnerException] property;
  • Line 19: The property [Code] stores the error code. The keyword [init] allows this to be set only when the object is created, using an object initializer: [new TaxException("...") { Code = 2 }]. It is this form of exception, with an integer code, that subsequent versions of the application will use;
  • lines 4–12: a list of possible error codes:
    • [Access]: error accessing the data file;
    • [Line]: row missing the three expected fields, or file containing no brackets;
    • [Field1], [Field2], [Field3]: Field 1, 2, or 3 in a row is incorrect;
    • [Json]: The document JSON is incorrect.

Some of these errors may occur in combination: all three fields in a row may be incorrect. Therefore, the enumeration [ErrorCode] has been annotated with the attribute [Flags], and its values are powers of 2: each corresponds to a bit of the integer. An error in fields 2 and 3 will result in the code [Field2 | Field3], which is 8 + 16 = 24. Thanks to the [Flags] attribute, the [ToString] method of the enumeration displays such a combination in the form “Field2, Field3.”

docs.title: 5.9.3. The FileTax class
docs.text:
The [FileTax] class provides the brackets read from a text file:

using System.Globalization;
using System.Text.RegularExpressions;

namespace TaxV3;

// the tax brackets read from a text file of limit:coeffR:coeffN lines
public partial class FileTax : AbstractTax
{
    // the field separator: the : character surrounded by optional spaces
    [GeneratedRegex(@"\s*:\s*")]
    private static partial Regex Separator();

    // the tax brackets read from the file
    private readonly TaxBracket[] taxBrackets;

    // implementation of the abstract property of the parent class
    protected override TaxBracket[] TaxBrackets => taxBrackets;

    public FileTax(string fileName)
    {
        // the name of the file, without its path, for the error messages
        string name = Path.GetFileName(fileName);
        // the brackets read; we do not know their number in advance
        List<TaxBracket> brackets = [];
        try
        {
            int lineNumber = 0;
            foreach (string lineRead in File.ReadLines(fileName))
            {
                lineNumber++;
                string line = lineRead.Trim();
                // empty lines are ignored
                if (line == "")
                {
                    continue;
                }
                // the line must have three fields
                string[] fields = Separator().Split(line);
                if (fields.Length != 3)
                {
                    throw new TaxException($"Line no. {lineNumber} is incorrect ({line})")
                    {
                        Code = (int)ErrorCode.Line
                    };
                }
                // three positive or zero decimal numbers, written with a decimal point
                ErrorCode code = 0;
                if (!Read(fields[0], out decimal limit)) code |= ErrorCode.Field1;
                if (!Read(fields[1], out decimal coeffR)) code |= ErrorCode.Field2;
                if (!Read(fields[2], out decimal coeffN)) code |= ErrorCode.Field3;
                if (code != 0)
                {
                    throw new TaxException($"Line no. {lineNumber} is incorrect ({line})")
                    {
                        Code = (int)code
                    };
                }
                // we store the new tax bracket
                brackets.Add(new TaxBracket(limit, coeffR, coeffN));
            }
        }
        catch (Exception e) when (e is IOException or UnauthorizedAccessException)
        {
            // file access error: we wrap it in a TaxException
            throw new TaxException($"Error while reading the file {name}", e)
            {
                Code = (int)ErrorCode.Access
            };
        }
        // at least one bracket is needed
        if (brackets.Count == 0)
        {
            throw new TaxException($"The file {name} does not contain any bracket")
            {
                Code = (int)ErrorCode.Line
            };
        }
        // we transfer the list into the array of brackets
        taxBrackets = brackets.ToArray();
    }

    // conversion of a field into a decimal >= 0, regardless of the culture of the machine
    private static bool Read(string field, out decimal result) =>
        decimal.TryParse(field, NumberStyles.AllowDecimalPoint, CultureInfo.InvariantCulture, out result);
}

Comments:

  • Line 7: The class [FileTax] is derived from the class [AbstractTax], just as the class [HardwiredTax] was in version 2. It is declared as [partial] because it contains a generated regular expression;
  • lines 10–11: the regular expression for the field separator in a limit:coeffR:coeffN line: the character [:], preceded and followed by any number of spaces;
  • lines 14–17: the brackets read, returned by the property [TaxBrackets], which redefines the abstract property of [AbstractTax];
  • line 19: the constructor receives the name of the text file containing the data. Its role is to populate the array [taxBrackets];
  • line 22: the file name without its path, used in error messages. The constructor actually receives a full path, which does not need to be displayed to the user;
  • line 24: Reading a text file is sequential: the number of lines is not known until the entire file has been read. Therefore, the array cannot be sized in advance; the brackets are temporarily stored in a list;
  • line 28: The file is read line by line using [File.ReadLines], which opens and closes the file itself. The 2008 course used [StreamReader];
  • lines 38–43: The line is split into fields using a regular expression; if there are not three fields, a [TaxException] exception with code [Line] is thrown. The 2008 course stored the error in a variable, exited the loop, and then threw the exception after closing the file: throwing it immediately is simpler, and [File.ReadLines] closes the file in any case, since the loop [foreach] releases its counter even when an exception interrupts it;
  • lines 47–55: conversion of the three fields to decimal numbers. Errors are accumulated in the variable [code] using the operator [|=], then reported together;
  • lines 83–84: conversion of a field. [NumberStyles.AllowDecimalPoint] allows only digits and a decimal point: no signs, spaces, or thousands separators. Negative numbers are therefore rejected, which validates the data at the same time as it is converted. [CultureInfo.InvariantCulture] enforces the period as the decimal separator, regardless of the machine’s locale;
  • lines 62–67: file access errors ([IOException] and its variants, such as [FileNotFoundException], or [UnauthorizedAccessException] for insufficient permissions) are wrapped in a [TaxException] with code [Access]. The [when (...)] exception filter (C# 6) intercepts only these exceptions: [TaxException] exceptions thrown within the loop are not intercepted and exit the constructor unchanged. The pattern [e is IOException or UnauthorizedAccessException] is a combined pattern using [or] (C# 9);
  • lines 71–79: an empty file is rejected; otherwise, the list is transferred to the bracket array, which was the purpose of the constructor.

Encapsulating low-level exceptions ([IOException]) into an application-specific exception ([TaxException]) allows the calling code to handle only one type of exception, regardless of the data source: a text file, a JSON file, and, later in the course, a database.

docs.title: 5.9.4. The JsonTax class
docs.text:
The [JsonTax] class provides the brackets read from a JSON file:

using System.Text.Json;

namespace TaxV3;

// the tax brackets read from a JSON file
public class JsonTax : AbstractTax
{
    // "Web" options: property names in camelCase (limit, coeffR, coeffN)
    private static readonly JsonSerializerOptions options = new(JsonSerializerDefaults.Web);

    // the tax brackets read from the file
    private readonly TaxBracket[] taxBrackets;

    // implementation of the abstract property of the parent class
    protected override TaxBracket[] TaxBrackets => taxBrackets;

    public JsonTax(string fileName)
    {
        // the name of the file, without its path, for the error messages
        string name = Path.GetFileName(fileName);
        string json;
        try
        {
            // reading the file
            json = File.ReadAllText(fileName);
        }
        catch (Exception e) when (e is IOException or UnauthorizedAccessException)
        {
            throw new TaxException($"Error while reading the file {name}", e)
            {
                Code = (int)ErrorCode.Access
            };
        }
        TaxBracket[]? brackets;
        try
        {
            // deserialization of the array of brackets
            brackets = JsonSerializer.Deserialize<TaxBracket[]>(json, options);
        }
        catch (JsonException e)
        {
            throw new TaxException($"The file {name} is incorrect: {e.Message}", e)
            {
                Code = (int)ErrorCode.Json
            };
        }
        // at least one bracket is needed, without a negative value
        if (brackets is null || brackets.Length == 0)
        {
            throw new TaxException($"The file {name} does not contain any bracket")
            {
                Code = (int)ErrorCode.Json
            };
        }
        if (brackets.Any(t => t.Limit < 0 || t.CoeffR < 0 || t.CoeffN < 0))
        {
            throw new TaxException($"The file {name} contains a negative value")
            {
                Code = (int)ErrorCode.Json
            };
        }
        taxBrackets = brackets;
    }
}

Comments:

  • Line 9: The “Web” options: the JSON properties [limit], [coeffR], and [coeffN] correspond to the properties [Limit], [CoeffR], and [CoeffN] in the [TaxBracket] structure without needing to modify the latter with attributes. The options are stored in a static field: a [JsonSerializerOptions] object stores information about the types it has processed, and it is recommended to reuse it;
  • lines 25–31: reading the file; an access error is handled as in [FileTax];
  • Line 38: A single instruction converts the text JSON into an array of brackets. [System.Text.Json] knows how to construct a record structure by calling its constructor. An invalid document triggers a [JsonException], encapsulated within a [TaxException] of code [Json];
  • lines 48–57: deserialization checks the document’s format, not the validity of the data: it remains to be verified that there is at least one bracket (the document [null] or [] is a valid JSON) and that no values are negative. The method LINQ [Any] performs this final check in a single line.

Comparing the two classes is instructive: with a structured data format and a library that understands it, parsing the file no longer requires any code.

docs.title: 5.9.5. The main program
docs.text:
The [TaxV3] console project has the following directory structure:

05-classes-dotnet/
  05-classes-dotnet.slnx
  TaxV3/
    AbstractTax.cs
    FileTax.cs
    ITax.cs
    JsonTax.cs
    Program.cs
    TaxBracket.cs
    TaxData.json
    TaxData.txt
    TaxDataInvalid.json
    TaxDataInvalid.txt
    TaxException.cs
    TaxV3.csproj

The project file [TaxV3.csproj] is the one created by [dotnet new console], to which a group of elements has been added:

<Project Sdk="Microsoft.NET.Sdk">

  <PropertyGroup>
    <OutputType>Exe</OutputType>
    <TargetFramework>net10.0</TargetFramework>
    <ImplicitUsings>enable</ImplicitUsings>
    <Nullable>enable</Nullable>
  </PropertyGroup>

  <!-- the data files are copied next to the executable -->
  <ItemGroup>
    <None Update="TaxData*.txt;TaxData*.json" CopyToOutputDirectory="PreserveNewest" />
  </ItemGroup>

</Project>

The element [<None Update="..." CopyToOutputDirectory="PreserveNewest" />] (line 12) specifies that the data files should be copied to the executable’s folder ([bin/Debug/net10.0]) during compilation if they are newer than the existing copy. The character [*] allows you to specify all [TaxData*.txt] and [TaxData*.json] files at once. This is equivalent to the “Copy to Output Directory” property that the 2008 course set in the file properties in Visual Studio.

The [Program.cs] program is as follows:

using TaxV3;

// tax calculation, version 3: the tax brackets are read from a file
// syntax: dotnet run [-- file]; file: TaxData.txt by default, or a .json file

const string syntax = """
    syntax: Married NbChildren Salary
    Married: y for married, n for not married
    NbChildren: number of children
    Salary: annual salary in euros
    """;

// the data file is searched for next to the executable
string fileName = args.Length > 0 ? args[0] : "TaxData.txt";
string path = Path.Combine(AppContext.BaseDirectory, fileName);
Console.WriteLine($"Tax brackets read from [{fileName}]");

// creation of an ITax object; the class depends on the extension of the file
ITax tax;
try
{
    tax = Path.GetExtension(fileName).ToLower() switch
    {
        ".json" => new JsonTax(path),
        _ => new FileTax(path)
    };
}
catch (TaxException e)
{
    // display of the error; the code is displayed as a combination of ErrorCode
    string origin = e.InnerException is null ? "" : $", original exception: {e.InnerException.GetType().Name}";
    Console.WriteLine($"The following error occurred: [Code={(ErrorCode)e.Code}, Message={e.Message}{origin}]");
    // stopping the program
    return 1;
}

// input loop
while (true)
{
    // we ask for the tax calculation parameters
    Console.Write("Tax calculation parameters in the format: Married (y/n) NbChildren Salary, or nothing to stop: ");
    string parameters = (Console.ReadLine() ?? "").Trim();
    // anything to do?
    if (parameters == "")
    {
        break;
    }
    // checking the number of fields of the typed line
    string[] fields = parameters.Split(' ', StringSplitOptions.RemoveEmptyEntries);
    if (fields.Length != 3)
    {
        Console.WriteLine(syntax);
        continue;
    }
    // checking the validity of the parameters
    // married
    string married = fields[0].ToLower();
    if (married != "y" && married != "n")
    {
        Console.WriteLine(syntax + "\nIncorrect married argument: type y or n");
        continue;
    }
    // nbChildren
    if (!int.TryParse(fields[1], out int nbChildren) || nbChildren < 0)
    {
        Console.WriteLine(syntax + "\nIncorrect NbChildren argument: type a positive or zero integer");
        continue;
    }
    // salary
    if (!int.TryParse(fields[2], out int salary) || salary < 0)
    {
        Console.WriteLine(syntax + "\nIncorrect salary argument: type a positive or zero integer");
        continue;
    }
    // the parameters are correct: we calculate the tax
    Console.WriteLine($"Tax={tax.Calculate(married == "y", nbChildren, salary)} euros");
}
return 0;

Comments:

  • line 14: the name of the data file is passed as an argument; by default, it is [TaxData.txt];
  • line 15: the file is searched for in the executable’s folder, [AppContext.BaseDirectory], where it was copied during compilation. Thus, the program finds its data regardless of the folder from which it is launched, which was not the case for the single-file applications in this chapter;
  • Lines 22–25: An expression, [switch] (Chapter 3), selects the class to instantiate based on the file extension. The two branches return different types, [JsonTax] and [FileTax]: the compiler infers the type of the expression using the destination variable [tax], which is of type [ITax] (expression [switch] with target type). The rest of the program only knows the interface [ITax] and is unaware of where the data comes from;
  • lines 28–34: Creating the object may trigger a [TaxException], which is displayed before the program terminates. The code is converted to [ErrorCode] to be displayed in plain text; the original exception, if any, is identified by its type (its message contains the full file path);
  • Lines 37–76: The dialog loop is exactly the same as in version 2.

The values from previous versions are reproduced: 4,282 euros for a married couple with 2 children, 2,959 euros with 3 children, and 11,519 euros for a single person without children, with an annual salary of 60,000 euros. Incorrect entries are flagged as in Version 2.

With the file [TaxData.json]:

> dotnet run -- TaxData.json
Tax brackets read from [TaxData.json]
