There are other cases where information is shared by multiple threads that may want to read or update it at the same time. This raises the issue of the integrity of this information. Suppose the shared information is a structure S containing various pieces of information I1, I2, ..., In:

  • a thread T1 begins updating structure S: it modifies the field I1 and is interrupted before completing the full update of structure S;
  • a thread T2 that acquires the processor then reads structure S to make decisions. It reads a structure in an unstable state: some fields are up to date, others are not.

This situation is called concurrent access to a shared resource—in this case, structure S. It is often difficult to manage. Let’s consider the following example to illustrate the problems that can arise:

  • an application will generate n threads, where n is passed as a parameter;
  • the shared resource is a counter that must be incremented by each generated thread;
  • at the end of the application, the counter’s value is displayed. It should therefore equal n.

The program [threads-06.cs] is as follows:

// unsynchronized concurrent access to a shared resource

// checking the argument: the number of threads to create
const int nbMaxThreads = 100;
if (args.Length != 1 || !int.TryParse(args[0], out int nbThreads) || nbThreads is < 1 or > nbMaxThreads)
{
    Console.Error.WriteLine($"syntax: dotnet run threads-06.cs -- nbThreads (nbThreads between 1 and {nbMaxThreads})");
    return 1;
}

// creation and start of the threads
var threads = new Thread[nbThreads];
for (int i = 0; i < nbThreads; i++)
{
    threads[i] = new Thread(Counter.Increment) { Name = i.ToString() };
    threads[i].Start();
}
// waiting for the end of the threads
foreach (Thread thread in threads)
{
    thread.Join();
}
// display of the counter
Console.WriteLine($"Number of threads generated: {Counter.Value}");
return 0;

// the shared resource
static class Counter
{
    // the thread counter, shared by all the threads
    public static int Value { get; private set; }

    // the method executed by each thread
    public static void Increment()
    {
        // reading the counter
        int value = Value;
        Console.WriteLine($"At {DateTime.Now:HH:mm:ss.fff}, thread {Thread.CurrentThread.Name} read the counter value: {value}");
        // waiting: the thread loses the processor
        Thread.Sleep(1000);
        // incrementing the counter
        Value = value + 1;
        Console.WriteLine($"At {DateTime.Now:HH:mm:ss.fff}, thread {Thread.CurrentThread.Name} wrote the counter value: {Value}");
    }
}

Comments:

  • Lines 4–8: The number of threads is passed as an argument. The condition on line 5 combines all the checks: an argument is required; it is an integer ([int.TryParse]); and it is between 1 and 100 (relational pattern [nbThreads is < 1 or > nbMaxThreads]). The program returns an exit code of 1 if an error occurs, 0 otherwise (line 25);
  • lines 28–43: the shared resource is the static property [Counter.Value]. The counter is encapsulated in a static class, with the method [Increment] executed by each thread. A high-level statement cannot declare a field: therefore, the data shared by the threads are static members of a class;
  • line 37: the counter is read;
  • line 40: the thread pauses for 1 second. It therefore loses the CPU;
  • line 42: the counter is incremented.

The one-second pause is only there to force the thread to lose the processor between reading and writing the counter. In practice, there is no guarantee that a thread will not be interrupted between these two moments, and on a multiprocessor machine, two threads may even read the counter at exactly the same time. The one-second pause merely systematizes this risk.

To pass arguments to a single-file application, place them after [--]:

> dotnet run threads-06.cs -- 5
At 11:36:17.169, thread 3 read the counter value: 0
At 11:36:17.169, thread 4 read the counter value: 0
At 11:36:17.169, thread 2 read the counter value: 0
At 11:36:17.169, thread 0 read the counter value: 0
At 11:36:17.169, thread 1 read the counter value: 0
At 11:36:18.216, thread 3 wrote the counter value: 1
At 11:36:18.216, thread 4 wrote the counter value: 1
At 11:36:18.217, thread 2 wrote the counter value: 1
At 11:36:18.217, thread 1 wrote the counter value: 1
At 11:36:18.217, thread 0 wrote the counter value: 1
Number of threads generated: 1

Looking at these results, it’s clear what’s happening:

  • A first thread reads the counter. It finds 0. It pauses for 1 second and thus loses the CPU;
  • a second thread also reads the counter value. It is still 0 since the previous thread has not yet incremented it. It also pauses for 1 second;
  • in less than a second, all 5 threads have time to read the value 0;
  • when they wake up, they increment the value 0 they read and all write the value 1 to the counter, as confirmed by the last line (line 12).

One might object that the example is artificial. So let’s remove the [Sleep] and use the [++] operator, which gives the illusion of a single instruction. The [threads-07.cs] program is as follows:

// lost updates without Sleep: counter++ is not atomic

// parameters: number of threads, number of increments per thread
int nbThreads = args.Length > 0 && int.TryParse(args[0], out int n) ? n : 4;
int nbIncrements = args.Length > 1 && int.TryParse(args[1], out int m) ? m : 50_000_000;

// we repeat the experiment three times
for (int attempt = 1; attempt <= 3; attempt++)
{
    Counter.Value = 0;
    // creation and start of the threads
    var threads = new Thread[nbThreads];
    for (int i = 0; i < nbThreads; i++)
    {
        threads[i] = new Thread(() =>
        {
            for (int j = 0; j < nbIncrements; j++)
            {
                // read, increment, write: three operations
                Counter.Value++;
            }
        });
        threads[i].Start();
    }
    // waiting for the end of the threads
    foreach (Thread thread in threads)
    {
        thread.Join();
    }
    // result
    int expected = nbThreads * nbIncrements;
    Console.WriteLine($"Attempt {attempt}: expected value {expected:N0}, obtained value {Counter.Value:N0}, lost updates {expected - Counter.Value:N0}");
}

// the shared resource
static class Counter
{
    public static int Value;
}

Comments:

  • Lines 4–5: The number of threads (4 by default) and the number of increments performed by each thread (50 million by default) can be passed as arguments. The expression [args.Length > 0 && int.TryParse(args[0], out int n) ? n : 4] returns the argument if it exists and is valid; otherwise, it returns the default value. The separator [_] makes the constant [50_000_000] readable;
  • line 20: each thread increments the shared counter without any pause;
  • line 38: this time, the counter is a field;
  • line 32: the format [N0] displays an integer with a thousands separator.

Results:

> dotnet run threads-07.cs
Attempt 1: expected value 200,000,000, obtained value 120,818,197, lost updates 79,181,803
Attempt 2: expected value 200,000,000, obtained value 121,419,329, lost updates 78,580,671
Attempt 3: expected value 200,000,000, obtained value 114,583,348, lost updates 85,416,652

Tens of millions of updates were lost, and the number varies from one test to another. The high-level operation [Counter.Value++] is in fact translated into several basic processor instructions: read the value from memory, increment it in a register, and write the result to memory. If two threads read the same value before one of them has written its own, an increment is lost, exactly as in the previous example. It takes many iterations to observe this: with one million increments per thread, each thread has often finished its work before the next one has started, and the result is correct. This is what makes these errors so dangerous: a program can run for months and then fail on the very day the system is under heavier load.

Where does the problem come from? One thread read an outdated value because another thread had been interrupted—or was working simultaneously on another processor—before it had finished its task of updating the counter. This brings us to the concepts of critical resources and critical sections in a program:

  • a critical resource is a resource that can be held by only one thread at a time. Here, the critical resource is the counter;
  • a critical section of a program is a sequence of instructions in a thread’s execution flow during which it accesses a critical resource. We must ensure that, during this critical section, the thread is the only one with access to the resource.

In the program [threads-06.cs], the critical section is the code between reading the counter and writing its new value:

// reading the counter
int value = Value;
// waiting: the thread loses the processor
Thread.Sleep(1000);
// incrementing the counter
Value = value + 1;

To execute this code, a thread must be guaranteed to be the only one running. It may be interrupted, but during that interruption, no other thread must be able to execute this same code. The .NET platform offers various tools to ensure exclusive access to critical sections of code. We’ll look at a few of them now.

docs.title: 8.5.2. The [lock] clause and the [Lock] type
docs.text:
The [lock] clause delimits a critical section as follows:

lock (padlock)
{
    // critical section
}

[padlock] is an object visible to all threads executing the critical section. The [lock] clause ensures that only one thread at a time executes the critical section: a thread that encounters a lock held by another thread is blocked until the lock is released.

Starting with C# 13 and .NET 9, the synchronization object should preferably be an instance of the [System.Threading.Lock] type, which is designed for this purpose. The previous example is rewritten as follows in [threads-08.cs]:

// critical section protected by the lock clause and the System.Threading.Lock type (C# 13 / .NET 9)

// checking the argument: the number of threads to create
const int nbMaxThreads = 100;
if (args.Length != 1 || !int.TryParse(args[0], out int nbThreads) || nbThreads is < 1 or > nbMaxThreads)
{
    Console.Error.WriteLine($"syntax: dotnet run threads-08.cs -- nbThreads (nbThreads between 1 and {nbMaxThreads})");
    return 1;
}

// creation and start of the threads
var threads = new Thread[nbThreads];
for (int i = 0; i < nbThreads; i++)
{
    threads[i] = new Thread(Counter.Increment) { Name = i.ToString() };
    threads[i].Start();
}
// waiting for the end of the threads, in the reverse order of their creation
Thread.CurrentThread.Name = "Main";
for (int i = nbThreads - 1; i >= 0; i--)
{
    Console.WriteLine($"At {DateTime.Now:HH:mm:ss.fff}, thread Main waits for the end of thread {threads[i].Name}");
    threads[i].Join();
    Console.WriteLine($"At {DateTime.Now:HH:mm:ss.fff}, thread Main was notified of the end of thread {threads[i].Name}");
}
// display of the counter
Console.WriteLine($"Number of threads generated: {Counter.Value}");
return 0;

// the shared resource
static class Counter
{
    // the thread counter
    public static int Value { get; private set; }
    // the synchronization object, visible to all threads
    private static readonly Lock padlock = new();

    // the method executed by each thread
    public static void Increment()
    {
        string name = Thread.CurrentThread.Name ?? "?";
        Console.WriteLine($"At {DateTime.Now:HH:mm:ss.fff}, thread {name} waits for permission to enter the critical section");
        // only one thread at a time executes the following block
        lock (padlock)
        {
            // reading the counter
            int value = Value;
            Console.WriteLine($"At {DateTime.Now:HH:mm:ss.fff}, thread {name} read the counter value: {value}");
            // waiting: the thread loses the processor but keeps the lock
            Thread.Sleep(1000);
            // incrementing the counter
            Value = value + 1;
            Console.WriteLine($"At {DateTime.Now:HH:mm:ss.fff}, thread {name} wrote the counter value: {Value}");
        }
        Console.WriteLine($"At {DateTime.Now:HH:mm:ss.fff}, thread {name} left the critical section");
    }
}

Comments:

  • line 36: [padlock] is the object that will enable synchronization of all threads. It is [readonly]: the reference must never change; otherwise, two threads could lock two different objects;
  • Lines 44–53: The critical section of the [Increment] method is enclosed by the [lock] clause. The thread holds the lock while it sleeps for one second: the other threads cannot enter;
  • Lines 20–24: The main thread waits for the threads in the reverse order of their creation.

Results with 3 threads:

> dotnet run threads-08.cs -- 3
At 11:36:23.809, thread Main waits for the end of thread 2
At 11:36:23.809, thread 0 waits for permission to enter the critical section
At 11:36:23.809, thread 1 waits for permission to enter the critical section
At 11:36:23.809, thread 2 waits for permission to enter the critical section
At 11:36:23.855, thread 0 read the counter value: 0
At 11:36:24.855, thread 0 wrote the counter value: 1
At 11:36:24.856, thread 1 read the counter value: 1
At 11:36:24.856, thread 0 left the critical section
At 11:36:25.856, thread 1 wrote the counter value: 2
At 11:36:25.856, thread 1 left the critical section
At 11:36:25.856, thread 2 read the counter value: 2
At 11:36:26.856, thread 2 wrote the counter value: 3
At 11:36:26.856, thread 2 left the critical section
At 11:36:26.857, thread Main was notified of the end of thread 2
At 11:36:26.857, thread Main waits for the end of thread 1
At 11:36:26.857, thread Main was notified of the end of thread 1
At 11:36:26.857, thread Main waits for the end of thread 0
At 11:36:26.857, thread Main was notified of the end of thread 0
Number of threads generated: 3
  • All three threads request entry into the critical section at nearly the same time;
  • only one enters it—in this case, thread 0 (the order of entry is not guaranteed: it is not necessarily the first to arrive that enters first). It reads the counter, sleeps for one second, writes the new value, and exits the critical section;
  • the other two threads are blocked until the first one exits the critical section, then proceed one after the other. Each reads the value written by the previous one;
  • the main thread was waiting for thread 2 to finish. When it is notified, it waits for thread 1 to finish, which has already completed: it is notified immediately. The same applies to thread 0;
  • the number of threads is correct (line 20).

The compiler translates the clause [lock (padlock) { ... }] on a [Lock] object as:

using (padlock.EnterScope())
{
    // critical section
}

[EnterScope] acquires the lock and returns a structure whose method [Dispose]—called upon exiting the [using] block—releases the lock, even if the critical section throws an exception. The type [Lock] also provides the methods [Enter], [TryEnter], and [Exit] for cases where the lock cannot be managed by a block.

Prior to .NET 9, and in much existing code, the lock was a generic object, typically of type [object]:

private static readonly object synchro = new();
...
lock (synchro)
{
    // critical section
}

This form remains valid: any .NET object can serve as a lock. The compiler then translates it into calls to the [Monitor] class, which we will examine later:

bool lockTaken = false;
try
{
    Monitor.Enter(synchro, ref lockTaken);
    // critical section
}
finally
{
    if (lockTaken) Monitor.Exit(synchro);
}

The type [Lock] is more efficient and makes the intent explicit. We always lock a private object: locking an externally visible object ([this], a type with [typeof(...)], a string) would allow external code to acquire the same lock and block ours.

docs.title: 8.5.3. The Mutex Class
docs.text:
The [System.Threading.Mutex] class also allows you to delimit critical sections. It differs from the [lock] clause in terms of visibility:

  • the [lock] clause synchronizes threads within the same application;
  • the [Mutex] class can synchronize threads from different applications (or processes) if given a name.

A [Mutex] is an operating system object: its use is much more resource-intensive than that of a [lock]. For threads within the same process, we therefore prefer to use [lock]; [Mutex] is primarily used between processes. We will use the following constructors and methods:

MemberRole[Mutex()]creates an anonymous Mutex M, usable by the process’s threads[Mutex(bool initiallyOwned, string name)]creates or opens the named mutex [name], shared by all processes that use this name[bool WaitOne()]The thread T1, which is executing [M.WaitOne()], requests ownership of the mutex M. If M is not held by any thread, it is granted to T1. If a thread T2 then attempts the same operation, it is blocked: a mutex can belong to only one thread. T2 will be unblocked when T1 releases M. Thus, multiple threads may be blocked while waiting for M[bool WaitOne(TimeSpan timeout)]Same as above, but the wait is limited to [timeout]. The method returns [false] if the mutex could not be acquired[void ReleaseMutex()]The thread holding M releases it. One of the threads waiting for M then acquires it

Synchronization of a critical section is done as follows:

M.WaitOne();
try
{
    // the thread is the only one to enter here: critical section
}
finally
{
    M.ReleaseMutex();
}

Don't forget to release a mutex; otherwise, the threads waiting on it will remain blocked indefinitely. That is why the release is performed in a [finally] statement, which is executed regardless of whether an exception occurred. The program [threads-09.cs] uses the previous example with a mutex:

// critical section protected by a Mutex

// checking the argument: the number of threads to create
const int nbMaxThreads = 100;
if (args.Length != 1 || !int.TryParse(args[0], out int nbThreads) || nbThreads is < 1 or > nbMaxThreads)
{
    Console.Error.WriteLine($"syntax: dotnet run threads-09.cs -- nbThreads (nbThreads between 1 and {nbMaxThreads})");
    return 1;
}

// creation and start of the threads
var threads = new Thread[nbThreads];
for (int i = 0; i < nbThreads; i++)
{
    threads[i] = new Thread(Counter.Increment) { Name = i.ToString() };
    threads[i].Start();
}
// waiting for the end of the threads
foreach (Thread thread in threads)
{
    thread.Join();
}
// display of the counter
Console.WriteLine($"Number of threads generated: {Counter.Value}");
return 0;

// the shared resource
static class Counter
{
    // the thread counter
    public static int Value { get; private set; }
    // the synchronization object: a Mutex
    private static readonly Mutex synchro = new();

    // the method executed by each thread
    public static void Increment()
    {
        string name = Thread.CurrentThread.Name ?? "?";
        Console.WriteLine($"At {DateTime.Now:HH:mm:ss.fff}, thread {name} waits for permission to enter the critical section");
        // we request ownership of the Mutex
        synchro.WaitOne();
        try
        {
            // reading the counter
            int value = Value;
            Console.WriteLine($"At {DateTime.Now:HH:mm:ss.fff}, thread {name} read the counter value: {value}");
            // waiting
            Thread.Sleep(1000);
            // incrementing the counter
            Value = value + 1;
            Console.WriteLine($"At {DateTime.Now:HH:mm:ss.fff}, thread {name} wrote the counter value: {Value}");
        }
        finally
        {
            // we release the Mutex, exception or not
            Console.WriteLine($"At {DateTime.Now:HH:mm:ss.fff}, thread {name} leaves the critical section");
            synchro.ReleaseMutex();
        }
    }
}

Comments:

  • line 33: the thread synchronization object is now a mutex;
  • line 41: start of the critical section. The thread is blocked until the mutex is free;
  • lines 42–57: Because a mutex must always be released, regardless of whether an exception occurs, the critical section is placed within a [try], whose [finally] clause releases the mutex (line 57).

Results:

> dotnet run threads-09.cs -- 3
At 11:36:28.858, thread 2 waits for permission to enter the critical section
At 11:36:28.906, thread 2 read the counter value: 0
At 11:36:28.858, thread 0 waits for permission to enter the critical section
At 11:36:28.858, thread 1 waits for permission to enter the critical section
At 11:36:29.907, thread 2 wrote the counter value: 1
At 11:36:29.907, thread 2 leaves the critical section
At 11:36:29.907, thread 0 read the counter value: 1
At 11:36:30.907, thread 0 wrote the counter value: 2
At 11:36:30.907, thread 0 leaves the critical section
At 11:36:30.907, thread 1 read the counter value: 2
At 11:36:31.908, thread 1 wrote the counter value: 3
At 11:36:31.908, thread 1 leaves the critical section
Number of threads generated: 3

The results are similar to the previous ones: the threads pass through the critical section one by one, and the final counter value is correct.

The true value of the mutex becomes apparent with a named mutex. The program [threads-10.cs] is run twice, in two different processes, which share a critical section:

// a named Mutex synchronizes threads of different processes

// the name of the Mutex is known to all the processes using it
const string mutexName = @"Global\csharp-course-threads-10";
// the name of the process is passed as an argument
string process = args.Length > 0 ? args[0] : "P";

// we open the named Mutex (it is created if it does not exist yet)
using var mutex = new Mutex(false, mutexName);
Console.WriteLine($"{DateTime.Now:HH:mm:ss.fff}: process {process} requests the Mutex");
// attempt without waiting
if (!mutex.WaitOne(TimeSpan.Zero))
{
    Console.WriteLine($"{DateTime.Now:HH:mm:ss.fff}: the Mutex is held by another process, {process} waits");
    // wait without time limit
    mutex.WaitOne();
}
try
{
    // critical section between processes
    Console.WriteLine($"{DateTime.Now:HH:mm:ss.fff}: process {process} obtained the Mutex, it works for 3 s");
    Thread.Sleep(3000);
    Console.WriteLine($"{DateTime.Now:HH:mm:ss.fff}: process {process} releases the Mutex");
}
finally
{
    mutex.ReleaseMutex();
}

Comments:

  • Line 4: the mutex name. All processes that open a mutex with this name use the same system object. The prefix [Global] specifies that the mutex is visible to all sessions on the machine (the default prefix [Local] limits it to the user’s session);
  • Line 9: The named mutex is created if it does not yet exist; otherwise, it is opened. The first parameter, [false], indicates that the process does not request ownership of it upon creation. The [using] declaration releases the [Mutex] object at the end of the program;
  • line 12: the process attempts to acquire the mutex immediately ([TimeSpan.Zero]). If it fails, it reports the failure and then waits for it indefinitely (line 16);
  • Lines 18–27: the critical section, which lasts 3 seconds, followed by the release of the mutex.

The capture script launches process A, waits 1.5 seconds, and then launches process B. Results for process A:

> dotnet run threads-10.cs -- A
11:36:35.438: process A requests the Mutex
11:36:35.486: process A obtained the Mutex, it works for 3 s
11:36:38.487: process A releases the Mutex

Results of process B:

> dotnet run threads-10.cs -- B
11:36:36.908: process B requests the Mutex
11:36:36.957: the Mutex is held by another process, B waits
11:36:38.487: process B obtained the Mutex, it works for 3 s
11:36:41.487: process B releases the Mutex

Process B found the mutex held by process A and waited. It acquired it the very moment A released it. A common use of a named mutex is to prevent two instances of the same application from being launched: the second instance, unable to acquire the mutex, terminates immediately. If a process terminates without releasing a mutex it holds, the mutex is said to be abandoned: the next process to call [WaitOne] acquires it but throws the exception [AbandonedMutexException] to signal that the protected resource may be in an inconsistent state.

docs.title: 8.5.4. The AutoResetEvent class
docs.text:
An [AutoResetEvent] object is a barrier that allows only one thread to pass at a time. It is constructed as follows:

AutoResetEvent barrier = new AutoResetEvent(state);

The boolean [state] indicates whether the barrier is closed ([false]) or open ([true]). A thread wishing to pass through the barrier indicates this as follows:

barrier.WaitOne();
  • If the barrier is open, the thread passes through and the barrier automatically closes behind it (hence the class name). If multiple threads are waiting, only one passes through;
  • if the barrier is closed, the thread is blocked. Another thread will open it when the time comes. That time depends entirely on the problem being solved. The barrier is opened by the operation:
barrier.Set();

A thread can also close a barrier using [barrier.Reset()]. Unlike a mutex, a barrier does not belong to any specific thread: any thread can open it. If, in the previous example, we replace the mutex with an [AutoResetEvent], the code becomes the following [threads-11.cs]:

// critical section protected by an AutoResetEvent barrier

// checking the argument: the number of threads to create
const int nbMaxThreads = 100;
if (args.Length != 1 || !int.TryParse(args[0], out int nbThreads) || nbThreads is < 1 or > nbMaxThreads)
{
    Console.Error.WriteLine($"syntax: dotnet run threads-11.cs -- nbThreads (nbThreads between 1 and {nbMaxThreads})");
    return 1;
}

// creation and start of the threads
var threads = new Thread[nbThreads];
for (int i = 0; i < nbThreads; i++)
{
    threads[i] = new Thread(Counter.Increment) { Name = i.ToString() };
    threads[i].Start();
}
// we let the threads arrive at the closed barrier
Thread.Sleep(500);
// we open the barrier of the critical section
Thread.CurrentThread.Name = "Main";
Console.WriteLine($"At {DateTime.Now:HH:mm:ss.fff}, thread Main opens the barrier of the critical section");
Counter.Synchro.Set();
// waiting for the end of the threads
foreach (Thread thread in threads)
{
    thread.Join();
}
// display of the counter
Console.WriteLine($"Number of threads generated: {Counter.Value}");
return 0;

// the shared resource
static class Counter
{
    // the thread counter
    public static int Value { get; private set; }
    // the barrier, created closed (false)
    public static readonly AutoResetEvent Synchro = new(false);

    // the method executed by each thread
    public static void Increment()
    {
        string name = Thread.CurrentThread.Name ?? "?";
        Console.WriteLine($"At {DateTime.Now:HH:mm:ss.fff}, thread {name} waits for permission to enter the critical section");
        // passing the barrier: it closes again behind the thread
        Synchro.WaitOne();
        try
        {
            // reading the counter
            int value = Value;
            Console.WriteLine($"At {DateTime.Now:HH:mm:ss.fff}, thread {name} read the counter value: {value}");
            // waiting
            Thread.Sleep(1000);
            // incrementing the counter
            Value = value + 1;
            Console.WriteLine($"At {DateTime.Now:HH:mm:ss.fff}, thread {name} wrote the counter value: {Value}");
        }
        finally
        {
            // we reopen the barrier for another thread
            Console.WriteLine($"At {DateTime.Now:HH:mm:ss.fff}, thread {name} leaves the critical section");
            Synchro.Set();
        }
    }
}

Comments:

  • line 39: the barrier is created in a closed state. It will be opened by the main thread on line 23;
  • line 19: the main thread waits half a second to allow the threads to arrive at the barrier;
  • line 47: the thread responsible for incrementing the counter requests permission to enter the critical section. The various threads accumulate in front of the closed barrier. When the main thread opens it, one of the waiting threads passes through, and the barrier closes again;
  • line 63: when it has finished its work, the thread reopens the barrier, allowing another thread to enter.

Results:

> dotnet run threads-11.cs -- 3
At 11:36:43.413, thread 2 waits for permission to enter the critical section
At 11:36:43.407, thread 0 waits for permission to enter the critical section
At 11:36:43.411, thread 1 waits for permission to enter the critical section
At 11:36:43.914, thread Main opens the barrier of the critical section
At 11:36:43.915, thread 2 read the counter value: 0
At 11:36:44.915, thread 2 wrote the counter value: 1
At 11:36:44.915, thread 2 leaves the critical section
At 11:36:44.915, thread 0 read the counter value: 1
At 11:36:45.916, thread 0 wrote the counter value: 2
At 11:36:45.916, thread 0 leaves the critical section
At 11:36:45.916, thread 1 read the counter value: 2
At 11:36:46.916, thread 1 wrote the counter value: 3
At 11:36:46.916, thread 1 leaves the critical section
Number of threads generated: 3

The results are similar to the previous ones. We see that the three threads wait in front of the barrier until the main thread opens it (line 5).

docs.title: 8.5.5. The classes ManualResetEventSlim and SemaphoreSlim
docs.text:
Two other synchronization tools complement the previous ones.

An object [ManualResetEventSlim] is a barrier that, once opened by [Set], remains open and allows all threads to pass through until it is explicitly closed by [Reset]. This is the “starting signal” for a race. The suffix [Slim] denotes the lightweight versions of the synchronization tools, introduced with .NET 4: they only call upon the operating system if the wait is prolonged and operate only within a process. The program [threads-12.cs] is as follows:

// ManualResetEventSlim: a barrier that lets all the waiting threads through

// the barrier, created closed
using var start = new ManualResetEventSlim(false);

// creation and start of 4 threads
var threads = new Thread[4];
for (int i = 0; i < threads.Length; i++)
{
    threads[i] = new Thread(() =>
    {
        string name = Thread.CurrentThread.Name ?? "?";
        Console.WriteLine($"{DateTime.Now:HH:mm:ss.fff}: runner {name} waits for the start signal");
        // waiting for the barrier to open
        start.Wait();
        Console.WriteLine($"{DateTime.Now:HH:mm:ss.fff}: runner {name} has started");
    })
    { Name = i.ToString() };
    threads[i].Start();
}

// the main thread waits 1 s then gives the start signal
Thread.Sleep(1000);
Console.WriteLine($"{DateTime.Now:HH:mm:ss.fff}: start signal");
// the barrier opens and stays open: all the threads go through
start.Set();
// waiting for the end of the threads
foreach (Thread thread in threads)
{
    thread.Join();
}
Console.WriteLine($"Is the barrier open? {start.IsSet}");

Comments:

  • line 4: the barrier is created in the closed state;
  • line 15: each thread waits for the barrier to open;
  • line 26: the main thread opens the barrier after one second;
  • line 32: The [IsSet] property indicates whether the barrier is open.

Results:

> dotnet run threads-12.cs
11:36:48.866: runner 3 waits for the start signal
11:36:48.865: runner 0 waits for the start signal
11:36:48.866: runner 2 waits for the start signal
11:36:48.865: runner 1 waits for the start signal
11:36:49.865: start signal
11:36:49.865: runner 0 has started
11:36:49.865: runner 1 has started
11:36:49.865: runner 2 has started
11:36:49.865: runner 3 has started
Is the barrier open? True

All four runners started together, to the millisecond, after the starting signal. With an [AutoResetEvent], only one would have started.

A semaphore is a barrier equipped with a counter: it allows at most N threads to enter a section of code at a time. This is useful for limiting the use of a resource available in limited quantities (database connections, concurrent requests to a server, etc.). The program [threads-13.cs] is as follows:

// SemaphoreSlim: at most N threads at a time in a section of code

// a semaphore with 2 slots
using var semaphore = new SemaphoreSlim(2);

// creation and start of 5 threads
var threads = new Thread[5];
for (int i = 0; i < threads.Length; i++)
{
    threads[i] = new Thread(() =>
    {
        string name = Thread.CurrentThread.Name ?? "?";
        Console.WriteLine($"{DateTime.Now:HH:mm:ss.fff}: thread {name} waits for a slot");
        // we request a slot: blocking if there are none left
        semaphore.Wait();
        try
        {
            Console.WriteLine($"{DateTime.Now:HH:mm:ss.fff}: thread {name} obtained a slot (free slots: {semaphore.CurrentCount})");
            // work
            Thread.Sleep(1000);
        }
        finally
        {
            // we give the slot back
            Console.WriteLine($"{DateTime.Now:HH:mm:ss.fff}: thread {name} releases its slot");
            semaphore.Release();
        }
    })
    { Name = i.ToString() };
    threads[i].Start();
}
// waiting for the end of the threads
foreach (Thread thread in threads)
{
    thread.Join();
}

Comments:

  • line 4: the semaphore has 2 slots;
  • line 15: a thread requests a slot. If one is available, it takes it and continues; otherwise, it is blocked until a slot becomes available;
  • line 18: the number of slots still available;
  • line 26: the thread returns its slot, in a [finally] clause.

Results:

> dotnet run threads-13.cs
11:36:51.985: thread 3 waits for a slot
11:36:51.985: thread 1 waits for a slot
11:36:51.985: thread 0 waits for a slot
11:36:51.985: thread 4 waits for a slot
11:36:51.985: thread 2 waits for a slot
11:36:52.035: thread 3 obtained a slot (free slots: 0)
11:36:52.035: thread 2 obtained a slot (free slots: 0)
11:36:53.035: thread 2 releases its slot
11:36:53.037: thread 3 releases its slot
11:36:53.037: thread 1 obtained a slot (free slots: 0)
11:36:53.037: thread 4 obtained a slot (free slots: 0)
11:36:54.037: thread 1 releases its slot
11:36:54.037: thread 4 releases its slot
11:36:54.037: thread 0 obtained a slot (free slots: 1)
11:36:55.037: thread 0 releases its slot

All five threads request a slot; two obtain one immediately, while the other three wait. Each time a thread releases its slot, a waiting thread obtains it. There are never more than two threads in the code section. A single-slot semaphore acts as a lock. The class [SemaphoreSlim] also has a method [WaitAsync] that can be used with [await], which we will encounter in the next chapter; the [Semaphore] class (without [Slim]), which is more resource-intensive, can—like [Mutex]—be named and shared across processes, but only on Windows.

docs.title: 8.5.6. The Interlocked class
docs.text:
The [Interlocked] class makes simple operations on a variable atomic: the operation is executed entirely by the thread, without any other thread being able to observe or modify the variable in the middle of the operation. The previous tools ([lock], [Mutex], [AutoResetEvent]) are all designed to make a group of operations atomic, at the cost of blocking other threads. For simple but frequent operations, the [Interlocked] class avoids this blocking by using special processor instructions. Its main static methods are as follows:

MethodRole[int Increment(ref int x)]Increments [x] by 1 and returns the new value[int Decrement(ref int x)]decrements [x] by 1 and returns the new value[int Add(ref int x, int value)]adds [value] to [x] and returns the new value[int Exchange(ref int x, int value)]assigns [value] to [x] and returns the old value[int CompareExchange(ref int x, int value, int comparand)]assigns [value] to [x] only if [x] is equal to [comparand]; returns the previous value of [x][long Read(ref long x)]atomically reads a 64-bit value (useful on a 32-bit processor)

These methods are available for the types [int], [long], [uint], [ulong], and—for [Exchange] and [CompareExchange]—for other types. The methods [And] and [Or] (.NET 5) atomically perform a bitwise “and” or “or” operation. The parameter is passed by reference ([ref]): [Interlocked] must operate on the variable itself, not on a copy. For this reason, the variable must be a field or a local variable; a property cannot be passed by reference.

The program [threads-14.cs] builds on the experiment from the program [threads-07.cs] and compares three ways to increment the shared counter:

// the Interlocked class: atomic operations without a lock

using System.Diagnostics;

// parameters: number of threads, number of increments per thread
int nbThreads = args.Length > 0 && int.TryParse(args[0], out int n) ? n : 4;
int nbIncrements = args.Length > 1 && int.TryParse(args[1], out int m) ? m : 10_000_000;
Console.WriteLine($"{nbThreads} threads, {nbIncrements:N0} increments per thread, expected value {nbThreads * nbIncrements:N0}");

// three ways to increment the shared counter
Measure("without synchronization", Counter.WithoutSynchronization);
Measure("with lock", Counter.WithLock);
Measure("with Interlocked", Counter.WithInterlocked);

// starts the threads that all execute [increment] nbIncrements times
void Measure(string method, Action increment)
{
    Counter.Value = 0;
    // a barrier so that all the threads start at the same time
    using var start = new ManualResetEventSlim(false);
    var threads = new Thread[nbThreads];
    for (int i = 0; i < nbThreads; i++)
    {
        threads[i] = new Thread(() =>
        {
            start.Wait();
            for (int j = 0; j < nbIncrements; j++)
            {
                increment();
            }
        });
        threads[i].Start();
    }
    // go!
    var stopwatch = Stopwatch.StartNew();
    start.Set();
    foreach (Thread thread in threads)
    {
        thread.Join();
    }
    stopwatch.Stop();
    Console.WriteLine($"{method,-23}: obtained value {Counter.Value,12:N0} in {stopwatch.ElapsedMilliseconds,5} ms");
}

// the shared resource
static class Counter
{
    // a field (and not a property) so that it can be passed by reference
    public static int Value;
    private static readonly Lock padlock = new();

    // read, increment, write: not atomic
    public static void WithoutSynchronization() => Value++;

    // critical section protected by a lock
    public static void WithLock()
    {
        lock (padlock)
        {
            Value++;
        }
    }

    // atomic increment, without a lock
    public static void WithInterlocked() => Interlocked.Increment(ref Value);
}

Comments:

  • line 3: The class [Stopwatch], which measures durations, is in the namespace [System.Diagnostics];
  • lines 11–13: The local function [Measure] is called with three different increment methods, passed as a delegate [Action];
  • lines 16–42: the function [Measure] launches [nbThreads] threads, each of which calls the received method [nbIncrements] times, and measures the total time with a [Stopwatch]. The format [{Counter.Value,12:N0}] right-aligns the value to 12 characters;
  • lines 20–26 and 36: the threads all wait behind a [ManualResetEventSlim] barrier, which opens once they have all been launched. This allows them to begin their work simultaneously, making concurrent access much more likely than with threads launched one after another;
  • line 49: the counter is a field, not a property, so that it can be passed by reference to [Interlocked.Increment];
  • line 53: the unsynchronized increment;
  • lines 56–60: incrementing within a critical section protected by a [Lock];
  • line 65: atomic increment.

Results:

> dotnet run threads-14.cs
4 threads, 10,000,000 increments per thread, expected value 40,000,000
without synchronization: obtained value   26,108,241 in   289 ms
with lock              : obtained value   40,000,000 in  2484 ms
with Interlocked       : obtained value   40,000,000 in   754 ms
  • Without synchronization, the result is incorrect, once again;
  • the other two methods yield the correct result;
  • [Interlocked] is significantly faster than [lock] in this run. The lock is costly here because four threads are constantly competing for the same lock for a tiny operation. The measured times depend heavily on the machine and its load: only their order of magnitude is significant.

The [CompareExchange] method is the building block of “lock-free” algorithms: read the value, calculate the new one, then write it only if the variable has not changed in the meantime; otherwise, start over. The concurrent collections presented later make extensive use of it.

docs.title: 8.6. Concurrent Access to Multiple Shared Resources
8.6.1. Deadlock
docs.text:
In our previous examples, a single resource was shared among the various threads. The situation becomes more complicated if there are multiple resources and they are dependent on one another. In particular, a deadlock can occur: two threads are waiting for each other. Consider the following actions, which occur sequentially:

  • a thread T1 acquires the lock V1 to access a shared resource R1;
  • a thread T2 acquires the lock V2 to access a shared resource R2;
  • Thread T1 requests lock V2. It is blocked;
  • the thread T2 requests the lock V1. It is blocked.

The threads T1 and T2 are waiting for each other indefinitely. Several solutions are possible:

  • request both resources at the same time using a single lock. This isn’t always possible if it results in a long lock on a costly resource;
  • always acquire locks in the same order: if all threads acquire V1 before V2, deadlock is impossible. This is the most commonly used rule;
  • A thread holding V1 that cannot acquire V2 releases V1 to avoid deadlock.

The program [threads-15.cs] causes a deadlock and implements the final solution:

// deadlock: two threads take two locks in a different order

// the two shared resources and their locks
Lock lockR1 = new();
Lock lockR2 = new();

// T1 takes R1 then requests R2; it gives up after 2 s
var t1 = new Thread(() => Work(lockR1, "R1", lockR2, "R2", TimeSpan.FromSeconds(2))) { Name = "T1" };
// T2 takes R2 then requests R1; it waits up to 5 s
var t2 = new Thread(() => Work(lockR2, "R2", lockR1, "R1", TimeSpan.FromSeconds(5))) { Name = "T2" };
t1.Start();
t2.Start();
t1.Join();
t2.Join();
Console.WriteLine("End of Main");

// takes the 1st resource, then tries to take the 2nd during [timeout]
static void Work(Lock first, string firstName, Lock second, string secondName, TimeSpan timeout)
{
    string name = Thread.CurrentThread.Name ?? "?";
    lock (first)
    {
        Console.WriteLine($"{DateTime.Now:HH:mm:ss.fff}: {name} obtained {firstName}");
        // we give the other thread time to take its first resource
        Thread.Sleep(500);
        Console.WriteLine($"{DateTime.Now:HH:mm:ss.fff}: {name} requests {secondName}");
        // request with a maximum waiting time, instead of a lock that would wait indefinitely
        if (second.TryEnter(timeout))
        {
            try
            {
                Console.WriteLine($"{DateTime.Now:HH:mm:ss.fff}: {name} obtained {secondName} and works with {firstName} and {secondName}");
            }
            finally
            {
                second.Exit();
            }
        }
        else
        {
            Console.WriteLine($"{DateTime.Now:HH:mm:ss.fff}: {name} did not obtain {secondName} within {timeout.TotalSeconds} s: it releases {firstName} and gives up");
        }
    }
}

Comments:

  • lines 4–5: the locks on the two resources. These are local variables here, captured by the lambdas in lines 8–10;
  • line 8: the T1 thread acquires R1 and then requests R2; it waits for a maximum of 2 seconds;
  • Line 10: The thread T2 takes R2 and then requests R1—that is, in reverse order; it waits for a maximum of 5 seconds;
  • Line 21: The thread acquires its first resource;
  • line 25: it waits half a second, which gives the other thread time to acquire its own first resource: deadlock is then certain;
  • line 28: instead of a [lock] that would wait indefinitely, the thread requests the second lock with a maximum wait time. [TryEnter] returns [true] if the lock was acquired, or [false] if the timeout expired;
  • line 36: a lock acquired by [TryEnter] must be released by [Exit], within a [finally] clause;
  • Lines 39–41: If the second lock could not be acquired, the thread aborts. Upon exiting the [lock] block, it releases its first resource.

Results:

> dotnet run threads-15.cs
11:37:01.001: T1 obtained R1
11:37:01.001: T2 obtained R2
11:37:01.549: T1 requests R2
11:37:01.549: T2 requests R1
11:37:03.550: T1 did not obtain R2 within 2 s: it releases R1 and gives up
11:37:03.550: T2 obtained R1 and works with R2 and R1
End of Main

Each of the two threads acquired its first resource and then requested the second: they are in a deadlock. After 2 seconds, T1 gives up and releases R1; T2, which was still waiting, immediately obtains R1 and can do its work. Without a wait time, the program would never have finished.

docs.title: 8.6.2. An example: readers and writers
docs.text:
Consider the following example:

  • we have an array into which some threads write data (the writers) and others read it (the readers);
  • the writers are equal to one another but exclusive: only one writer at a time can deposit data into the array;
  • readers are equal to one another but exclusive: only one reader at a time can read the data stored in the array;
  • a reader can only read data from the array when a writer has placed some there, and a writer can only place new data in the array when the data already there has been read by a reader.

There are two types of shared resources:

  • the array being written: only one writer at a time may access it;
  • the array being read: only one reader at a time may access it.

and an order for using these resources:

  • a reader must always follow a writer;
  • a writer must always follow a reader, except the first time.

Access to these two resources can be controlled using two barriers of type [AutoResetEvent]:

  • The [canWrite] barrier controls writers’ access to the array;
  • the barrier [canRead] controls readers’ access to the array;
  • the [canWrite] barrier is created open, allowing the first writer to pass and blocking all others;
  • The [canRead] barrier is created in the closed state, blocking all readers;
  • when a writer has finished their work, they open barrier [canRead] to let a reader in;
  • when a reader has finished their work, they open the barrier [canWrite] to let a writer in.

The program [threads-16.cs] illustrating this synchronization is as follows:

// readers and writers synchronized by two AutoResetEvent barriers

// the number of threads of each kind
const int nbThreads = 2;

// creation and start of the reader threads
for (int i = 0; i < nbThreads; i++)
{
    new Thread(Board.Read) { Name = $"R{i}" }.Start();
}
// creation and start of the writer threads
for (int i = 0; i < nbThreads; i++)
{
    new Thread(Board.Write) { Name = $"W{i}" }.Start();
}
// end of Main: the other threads continue their work
Console.WriteLine("End of Main...");

// the shared resource and its synchronization
static class Board
{
    // the array shared between readers and writers
    private static readonly int[] data = new int[3];
    // signals that the content of data can be read: closed at the start
    private static readonly AutoResetEvent canRead = new(false);
    // signals that data can be written: open at the start
    private static readonly AutoResetEvent canWrite = new(true);

    // read the content of the array
    public static void Read()
    {
        string name = Thread.CurrentThread.Name ?? "?";
        Console.WriteLine($"Method [Read] started by thread {name}");
        // we wait for read permission
        canRead.WaitOne();
        // reading the array
        for (int i = 0; i < data.Length; i++)
        {
            // waiting 0.5 s: the thread loses the processor
            Thread.Sleep(500);
            Console.WriteLine($"{DateTime.Now:HH:mm:ss.fff}: reader {name} read the number {data[i]}");
        }
        // we allow a writer
        canWrite.Set();
        Console.WriteLine($"Method [Read] finished by thread {name}");
    }

    // write into the array
    public static void Write()
    {
        string name = Thread.CurrentThread.Name ?? "?";
        Console.WriteLine($"Method [Write] started by thread {name}");
        // we wait for write permission
        canWrite.WaitOne();
        // writing the array
        for (int i = 0; i < data.Length; i++)
        {
            // waiting 0.5 s
            Thread.Sleep(500);
            // Random.Shared can be used by several threads
            data[i] = Random.Shared.Next(0, 1000);
            Console.WriteLine($"{DateTime.Now:HH:mm:ss.fff}: writer {name} wrote the number {data[i]}");
        }
        // we allow a reader
        canRead.Set();
        Console.WriteLine($"Method [Write] finished by thread {name}");
    }
}

Comments:

  • lines 7–14: creation and launch of two reader threads, followed by two writer threads. No references are kept to the threads: the main thread does not wait for them;
  • line 17: the main thread terminates immediately. The process continues until all four threads—which are foreground threads—have finished;
  • line 23: the array [data] is the shared resource between the reader and writer threads;
  • line 25: The barrier [canRead] signals to the readers that they can read the array. It is opened by the writer who has filled the array. It is created in a closed state: a writer must first fill the array;
  • line 27: The barrier [canWrite] notifies writers that they can write to the array. It is opened by the reader who has read the entire array. It is created open: the array is writable from the start;
  • line 35: a reader waits for a writer to signal that the array has been filled. When this signal arrives, only one of the waiting readers proceeds;
  • lines 37–41: the array is read, with a half-second pause at each element to force the thread to yield the CPU;
  • line 44: the reader notifies the writers that the array has been read and can be filled again;
  • the method [Write] is symmetric to the method [Read];
  • line 61: the written numbers are randomly generated. The property [Random.Shared] (.NET 6) provides a shared generator that can be safely used by multiple threads. The 2008 course shared a regular [Random] object among threads, whose methods are not designed to be called simultaneously by multiple threads.

Results:

> dotnet run threads-16.cs
Method [Read] started by thread R1
Method [Read] started by thread R0
Method [Write] started by thread W0
Method [Write] started by thread W1
End of Main...
11:37:06.185: writer W0 wrote the number 359
11:37:06.719: writer W0 wrote the number 226
11:37:07.219: writer W0 wrote the number 693
Method [Write] finished by thread W0
11:37:07.719: reader R0 read the number 359
11:37:08.220: reader R0 read the number 226
11:37:08.720: reader R0 read the number 693
Method [Read] finished by thread R0
11:37:09.220: writer W1 wrote the number 325
11:37:09.720: writer W1 wrote the number 935
11:37:10.221: writer W1 wrote the number 96
Method [Write] finished by thread W1
11:37:10.721: reader R1 read the number 325
11:37:11.221: reader R1 read the number 935
11:37:11.722: reader R1 read the number 96
Method [Read] finished by thread R1

The following points are worth noting:

  • There is only one reader at a time, although that reader loses the processor in the critical section [Read];
  • there is only one writer at a time, although it loses the processor in the critical section [Write];
  • a reader only reads when there is something to read in the array;
  • a writer writes only when the array has been fully read;
  • however, the order of execution cannot be controlled: there was no reason why writer W0 should come before writer W1, nor why reader R0 should come before reader R1. A different execution may result in a different order.

docs.title: 8.6.3. The Monitor class
docs.text:
In the previous example, when the writers are blocked on the instruction [canWrite.WaitOne()], one of them—any one—is unblocked by the operation [canWrite.Set()]. If you want to open the barrier for a specific writer, things become more complicated.

Consider the analogy of a public service office with service counters. When a customer arrives, they take a numbered ticket from the dispenser and then go sit down. Customers are called by their number over a loudspeaker. While waiting, the customer can do whatever they want: they can read or doze off. They are woken up every time the loudspeaker announces a number. If it’s their number, the customer gets up and goes to the counter; otherwise, they go back to what they were doing. We can operate in a similar way with threads. Let’s take the example of writers:

At the counterWith threadsseveral writers are waiting for the same countertheir threads are blockedthe counter becomes available and the next writer’s number is calledthe thread that was reading from the array notifies the writers that the array is available. Either that thread or another thread has determined which writer should proceedEach writer checks its number; only the one with the called number proceeds to the counter; the others return to the waiting queueEach thread checks to see if it is the one selected. If so, it passes through the barrier; otherwise, it returns to the waiting queue

The [Monitor] class implements this scenario. Its static methods are as follows:

MethodRole[Enter(object token)]Requests the token: the thread obtains it if it is free; otherwise, it is blocked until it becomes free[bool TryEnter(object token, TimeSpan timeout)]Same as above, with a maximum timeout[Exit(object token)]returns the token[bool Wait(object token)]returns the token and blocks the thread until another thread signals a change via [Pulse] or [PulseAll]; the thread must then retrieve the token before continuing[Pulse(object token)]wakes up one of the threads blocked by [Wait] on this token[PulseAll(object token)]wakes up all threads blocked by [Wait] on this token

We will now describe a standard pattern, proposed in the “Threading” chapter of the book by J. and B. Albahari, [C# in a Nutshell], capable of resolving barrier problems with an entry condition.

Threads that share a resource (the counter) access it via an object we’ll call a token. To cross the barrier leading to the counter, you must have the token, and there is only one. The threads must therefore pass the token to one another:

object token = new();

To go to the counter, a thread first requests the token using [Monitor.Enter(token)], or more simply with a [lock] clause. If it obtains the token, it checks that it meets the condition to go to the counter:

lock (token)
{
    while (!iAmTheOneExpected)
    {
        Monitor.Wait(token);
    }
    // going to the counter
    ...
}

If the thread is not the one expected at the counter, it yields its turn by returning the token via [Monitor.Wait(token)] and enters a blocked state. It will be woken up when another thread signals a change in the access condition; it will then retrieve the token and check the condition again. This is why the check is a loop ([while]) rather than a simple [if]. The operation [Monitor.Wait(token)] can only be performed by a thread that holds the token; otherwise, a [SynchronizationLockException] exception is thrown. In this scenario, the token is released only after the operation is completed.

The thread that modifies the access condition for the counter must also hold the token and notify the waiting threads:

lock (token)
{
    // modify the condition for accessing the counter
    ...
    // wake up the threads waiting for the token
    Monitor.PulseAll(token);
}

Waking up the threads means that the waiting threads become candidates for the token; they do not receive it immediately. The token is only available at the end of the [lock] block. All awakened threads will then receive the token in turn, in an indeterminate order, giving them the opportunity to check the access condition again. The first one to satisfy the condition keeps the token and proceeds to the counter.

An important note: the methods [Wait], [Pulse], and [PulseAll] from [Monitor] apply to an object locked by [lock (obj)] or [Monitor.Enter(obj)]. They do not work with the [Lock] type of .NET 9, which has no equivalent. The tokens in this paragraph are therefore objects of type [object].

Armed with this information, we can rewrite the reader/writer application by specifying the order in which readers and writers access their respective counters [threads-17.cs]:

// readers and writers going to the counter in an imposed order: Monitor.Wait / Monitor.PulseAll

// the number of threads of each kind
const int nbThreads = 3;

// the order of the readers: the reverse of the creation order
Board.ReadOrder = [.. Enumerable.Range(0, nbThreads).Select(i => $"R{nbThreads - 1 - i}")];
// the order of the writers: the creation order
Board.WriteOrder = [.. Enumerable.Range(0, nbThreads).Select(i => $"W{i}")];
for (int i = 0; i < nbThreads; i++)
{
    Console.WriteLine($"Reader {Board.ReadOrder[i]} is in position {i}, writer {Board.WriteOrder[i]} is in position {i}");
}

// creation and start of the reader threads then the writer threads
for (int i = 0; i < nbThreads; i++)
{
    new Thread(Board.Read) { Name = $"R{i}" }.Start();
}
for (int i = 0; i < nbThreads; i++)
{
    new Thread(Board.Write) { Name = $"W{i}" }.Start();
}

// write permission
Board.AllowWriting();
// end of Main
Console.WriteLine("End of Main...");

// the shared resource and its synchronization
static class Board
{
    // the array shared between readers and writers
    private static readonly int[] data = new int[3];
    // the access tokens of the read and write counters
    private static readonly object canRead = new();
    private static readonly object canWrite = new();
    // the access conditions of the counters
    private static bool readingAllowed = false;
    private static bool writingAllowed = false;
    private static int nextReader = 0;
    private static int nextWriter = 0;
    // the order of the readers and of the writers
    public static string[] ReadOrder { get; set; } = [];
    public static string[] WriteOrder { get; set; } = [];

    // opens the write counter
    public static void AllowWriting()
    {
        lock (canWrite)
        {
            writingAllowed = true;
            // we wake up all the writers waiting for the token
            Monitor.PulseAll(canWrite);
        }
    }

    // read the content of the array
    public static void Read()
    {
        string name = Thread.CurrentThread.Name ?? "?";
        Console.WriteLine($"Method [Read] started by thread {name}");
        // we request the token of the read counter
        lock (canRead)
        {
            // as long as it is not our turn, we give the token back and wait
            while (!readingAllowed || ReadOrder[nextReader] != name)
            {
                Monitor.Wait(canRead);
            }
            // at the counter: reading the array
            for (int i = 0; i < data.Length; i++)
            {
                Thread.Sleep(500);
                Console.WriteLine($"{DateTime.Now:HH:mm:ss.fff}: reader {name} read the number {data[i]}");
            }
            // next reader
            readingAllowed = false;
            nextReader++;
            // we notify the writers that they can write
            lock (canWrite)
            {
                writingAllowed = true;
                Monitor.PulseAll(canWrite);
            }
            Console.WriteLine($"Method [Read] finished by thread {name}");
        }
    }

    // write into the array
    public static void Write()
    {
        string name = Thread.CurrentThread.Name ?? "?";
        Console.WriteLine($"Method [Write] started by thread {name}");
        // we request the token of the write counter
        lock (canWrite)
        {
            // as long as it is not our turn, we give the token back and wait
            while (!writingAllowed || WriteOrder[nextWriter] != name)
            {
                Monitor.Wait(canWrite);
            }
            // at the counter: writing the array
            for (int i = 0; i < data.Length; i++)
            {
                Thread.Sleep(500);
                data[i] = Random.Shared.Next(0, 1000);
                Console.WriteLine($"{DateTime.Now:HH:mm:ss.fff}: writer {name} wrote the number {data[i]}");
            }
            // next writer
            writingAllowed = false;
            nextWriter++;
            // we notify the readers that they can read
            lock (canRead)
            {
                readingAllowed = true;
                Monitor.PulseAll(canRead);
            }
            Console.WriteLine($"Method [Write] finished by thread {name}");
        }
    }
}

Access to the read counter is conditioned by the following elements:

  • line 36: the token [canRead];
  • line 39: the Boolean [readingAllowed];
  • line 44: the sorted array of reader names. Readers proceed to the reading station in the order specified by this array;
  • line 41: [nextReader] is the index in this array of the next reader authorized to proceed to the counter.

Access to the write counter is similarly controlled by the token [canWrite], the Boolean [writingAllowed], the array [WriteOrder], and the index [nextWriter].

The main program:

  • lines 7–9: readers will proceed to the counter in reverse order of their creation (R2, R1, R0), and writers in the order they were created (W0, W1, W2). The arrays are constructed using a collection expression [.. sequence], which creates an array from a LINQ query;
  • lines 18–22: creation and initialization of readers, followed by writers. They will all be blocked, since neither reading nor writing is permitted;
  • line 26: writing is enabled, and the writers are notified that something has changed (method [AllowWriting], lines 48–54).

The [Read] method:

  • lines 64–86: the entire process at the reading station is controlled by [lock] on token [canRead]. The reader who obtains it keeps it throughout their time at the station;
  • lines 67–69: A reader who has acquired the token returns it if reading is not authorized or if it is not their turn;
  • lines 72–75: passing through the station (reading the table);
  • lines 78–79: the reader changes the access conditions for the read counter. It still holds the read token, and these changes prevent any other reader from accessing the counter;
  • lines 81–84: the reader changes the access conditions for the write counter and notifies all waiting writers that something has changed. To do this, it takes the token [canWrite]: here we see that the thread holds two tokens at the same time. The writers do the same in reverse order (they hold [canWrite] and request [canRead]), which is the deadlock situation described above. However, there is no risk here: a thread requests the second token only at the end of its visit to the counter; the two counters are never occupied at the same time; and the other threads hold a token only long enough to check the access condition, without requesting the other token.

The method [Write] is symmetric to the method [Read]. The 2008 course used, in the main program, [Monitor.Pulse], which wakes up only a single thread: if that thread was not the expected writer, it would go back to sleep, and the expected writer might never be woken up. When using an access condition that specifies a particular thread, you must use [PulseAll].

Here is an example of execution:

11:37:14.240: writer W0 wrote the number 550

11:37:15.790: reader R2 read the number 550
