// the dialog with the user
Dialog.Run(business);
return 0;
  • line 9: the name of the configuration file: [appsettings.json] by default, or the one passed as an argument;
  • lines 16–19: reading the configuration. [ConfigurationBuilder] assembles a configuration from sources: in this case, a single JSON file ([AddJsonFile]), located in the executable’s folder ([SetBasePath]). The parameter [optional: false] (a named parameter, C# 4) makes the file mandatory: its absence causes a [FileNotFoundException];
  • lines 20–21: the configuration is read as a dictionary. The key [Dao:Implementation] refers to the property [Implementation] of the section [Dao]; the level separator is the colon. The indexer returns [null] if the key does not exist: the operator [??] then provides a default value;
  • line 24: the service collection, that is, the list of types that the container can create and how to create them;
  • lines 26–31: the [dao] layer registration. [AddSingleton<ITaxDao>(factory)] indicates that when a [ITaxDao] is requested, the container will call the [factory] function to create it. "Singleton" means that the object will be created only once, upon the first request, and that all subsequent requests will return the same object: there is only one [dao] layer in the application. The factory selects the class based on the configuration, using the expression [switch]; its parameter, the container itself, is not used here, hence the name [_] (“discard”). An unknown implementation results in a [TaxException];
  • line 34: the [business] layer registration: when a [ITaxBusiness] is requested, the container will create a [TaxBusiness] object. To do this, it examines the constructor of the [TaxBusiness] class, sees that it expects a [ITaxDao], and passes it the [dao] layer registered above: this is dependency injection. The [dao] layer is a dependency of the [business] layer;
  • line 37: creation of the container from the collection of services;
  • line 38: the container is asked for the [business] layer. The container creates the [dao] layer, then the [business] layer. [GetRequiredService] throws an exception if the requested type has not been registered. Note that the layer [ui] obtains the layer [business] without specifying the class that implements it;
  • lines 40–44: any configuration or layer creation errors are displayed along with the exception stack trace, and the program terminates;
  • line 48: the user interface, identical to that of version 4.

The 2008 course included the full names of the classes to be instantiated ([Dao.FileTax, TaxV5-dao]) in the configuration file: Spring.NET created them using reflection. We chose instead to define the possible implementations in the factory: the configuration file simply selects from among them, and the compiler verifies that the classes exist and have the required constructors. In both cases, the code for layers [ui] and [business] never specifies the class that implements layer [dao].

docs.title: 6.4.6.3. Executions
docs.text:
With the file [appsettings.json] (implementation [FileTax]):

> dotnet run
Tax calculation parameters in the format: Married (y/n) NbChildren Salary, or nothing to stop: y 2 60000
Tax=4282 euros
Tax calculation parameters in the format: Married (y/n) NbChildren Salary, or nothing to stop: y 3 60000
Tax=2959 euros
Tax calculation parameters in the format: Married (y/n) NbChildren Salary, or nothing to stop: n 0 60000
Tax=11519 euros
Tax calculation parameters in the format: Married (y/n) NbChildren Salary, or nothing to stop:

With the implementation [JsonTax]:

> dotnet run -- appsettings-json.json
Tax calculation parameters in the format: Married (y/n) NbChildren Salary, or nothing to stop: y 2 60000
Tax=4282 euros
Tax calculation parameters in the format: Married (y/n) NbChildren Salary, or nothing to stop:

With the implementation [HardwiredTax]:

> dotnet run -- appsettings-hardwired.json
Tax calculation parameters in the format: Married (y/n) NbChildren Salary, or nothing to stop: y 2 60000
Tax=4282 euros
Tax calculation parameters in the format: Married (y/n) NbChildren Salary, or nothing to stop:

We switched to the [dao] implementation without changing a single line of code or recompiling the application.

With the file [appsettings-error.json], which refers to a nonexistent data file:

> dotnet run -- appsettings-error.json
Exception chain:
----------------------------------------
Entities.TaxException: Error while reading the file TaxDataMissing.txt
----------------------------------------
System.IO.FileNotFoundException: The file [TaxDataMissing.txt] does not exist
----------------------------------------
  • line 6: the original exception, of type [FileNotFoundException], thrown by the class [FileTax];
  • line 4: the [dao] layer encapsulated it in a [TaxException]. It is this exception that was propagated up to the main program via the [GetRequiredService] call.

The .NET container passes through exceptions thrown during object creation without modification. With Spring.NET, the same error produced a chain of eight exceptions, six of which were caused by the framework ([ConfigurationErrorsException], [ObjectCreationException], [TargetInvocationException], etc.), followed by the two exceptions mentioned above. The key takeaway from this chain is that it is often the deepest exception—the last one displayed—that is the most significant.

Dependency injection alone deserves a chapter of its own. We used only the essentials: registering services ([AddSingleton]), building the container ([BuildServiceProvider]), and obtaining a service ([GetRequiredService]). The container can also create a new object for each request ([AddTransient]) or an object per “scope,” such as per request (HTTP) in a web application ([AddScoped]). We’ll see this again in the ASP.NET Core applications, where it is ubiquitous. You can explore this topic further in Microsoft’s documentation: Dependency Injection .NET.

docs.title: 6.5. Conclusion
docs.text:
This chapter has given the [Tax] application the architecture it will retain until the end of the course:

  • a [dao] layer that provides tax brackets through the [ITaxDao] interface;
  • a [business] layer that calculates the tax and interacts with the [dao] layer only through its interface;
  • a layer [ui] that interacts with the user and knows the layer [business] only through its interface [ITaxBusiness];
  • a main program—the only one that knows the implementation classes—which creates the layers and links them, in this case using a dependency injection container and a configuration file;
  • automated unit tests, which verify each layer independently of the others and ensure the application’s non-regression.

The benefits of this architecture will become fully apparent in the following chapters, where the libraries [Tax.Dao], [Tax.Business], and [Tax.Ui] from version 5 will be reused as-is via project references:

  • Version 6 (chapter ADO.NET): A new implementation, [MySqlTax], of the [dao] layer reads the tax brackets from a MySQL database. The layers [business] and [ui] remain unchanged;
  • Version 7 (Entity Framework Core chapter): A [EfTax] implementation of the [dao] layer uses the ORM Entity Framework Core to access the same database;
  • Version 8 (Internet chapter): The [business] layer is installed on a TCP server, which calculates taxes for remote clients; this is therefore a “three-tier” architecture in the strict sense;
  • Version 9 (Web Services chapter): The [business] layer is exposed by a web service REST/JSON written with ASP.NET Core, whose console client uses [HttpClient].

Each time, the work will be limited to writing the new layer and modifying the program that integrates the layers: that is the whole point of layered architecture.

docs.title: 2. Setting Up the Development Environment
docs.text:
In 2008, we installed Visual C# 2008 Express, which included the .NET 3.5 framework, the SQL Compact Server DBMS, and the MSDN documentation, and then created projects using graphical wizards. Today, the development environment consists of two independent components:

  • the .NET SDK (“Software Development Kit”): the compiler, the runtime platform, the libraries, and the [dotnet] command, which allows you to do everything from the command line (create, compile, run, test, and publish a program);
  • an editor or a IDE (integrated development environment): [VS Code] with the [C# Dev Kit] extension, or [Visual Studio 2026], or [JetBrains Rider]. The editor is based on SDK.

This document uses the [dotnet] command for all operations: it works the same way on Windows, Linux, and macOS, regardless of the editor chosen.

docs.title: 2.1.1. Installation
docs.text:
.NET 10 SDK can be downloaded from https://dotnet.microsoft.com/download/dotnet/10.0. On Windows, you can also install it from a terminal (PowerShell or command prompt) using the [winget] package manager:

winget install Microsoft.DotNet.SDK.10

You must select SDK (which contains everything) and not just the “runtime” (which only allows you to run pre-compiled programs). On Linux, SDK is available in the repositories of major distributions (for example, [sudo apt install dotnet-sdk-10.0] on Ubuntu; depending on the distribution version, you may need to add the repository specified in Microsoft’s installation documentation beforehand).

After installation, open a new terminal to verify that the [dotnet] command is available and displays the version of SDK:

> dotnet --version
10.0.112

The command [dotnet --list-sdks] lists the installed SDK versions (multiple versions can coexist):

> dotnet --list-sdks
10.0.112 [C:\Program Files\dotnet\sdk]

The exact version (in this case, [10.0.112]) depends on the installation date: Microsoft releases a hotfix update every month. All versions of SDK and 10.0.x are suitable for this document. The [dotnet --info] command provides more detailed information (operating system, location of SDK, versions of installed runtime platforms).

docs.title: 2.1.2. The dotnet command
docs.text:
The [dotnet] command includes many subcommands. Here are the ones we’ll use:

CommandRole[dotnet run file.cs]compiles and runs a single-file application[dotnet new console -n Name]creates a console project in the [Name] folder (other templates: [classlib], [mstest], [web]…)[dotnet build]compiles the project in the current folder[dotnet run]compiles (if necessary) and runs the project in the current folder[dotnet test]runs the unit tests (Chapter 6)[dotnet new sln]creates a solution (a file that groups multiple projects)[dotnet sln add Project]adds a project to the solution[dotnet add package Name]adds a library NuGet to the project (Chapters 10 and 11)[dotnet add reference ../Other]adds a reference to another project (Chapter 6)[dotnet publish]prepares the program for deployment

Libraries that are not part of the platform are distributed as NuGet packages, downloaded from https://www.nuget.org and stored on the computer in the [%USERPROFILE%\.nuget\packages] folder. In 2008, we copied the DLL files for the libraries (Spring.NET, NUnit, and the MySQL connector) into a [lib] folder within the project; today, the project declares the packages it needs, and the [dotnet] command downloads them.

docs.title: 2.2.1. VS Code
docs.text:
VS Code is a free, cross-platform editor. To program in C#, you add Microsoft’s C# Dev Kit extension (go to the “Extensions” menu and search for “C# Dev Kit”), which also installs the C# extension. This provides:

  • syntax highlighting, code completion, and tooltip help;
  • error detection as you type;
  • code navigation (F12: Go to Definition);
  • a Solution Explorer (“Solution Explorer” view);
  • execution and debugging (F5);
  • running unit tests (the “Testing” view).

In VS Code, open the folder containing the programs (“File / Open Folder”), for example, the [csharp-oct-2026] folder with the examples from this document. The built-in terminal (“Terminal / New Terminal”) allows you to enter [dotnet] commands without leaving the editor.

docs.title: 2.2.2. Visual Studio 2026
docs.text:
On Windows, you may prefer to use Visual Studio 2026, the successor to Visual Studio 2008 used in the original course. Its Community edition is free for individuals, educational institutions, and open-source projects. Install it from https://visualstudio.microsoft.com by selecting the “.NET Desktop Development” workload (and “ASP.NET and web development” for Chapter 13). Visual Studio opens the [.slnx] solutions and [.csproj] projects from the examples directly (“File / Open / Project/Solution”), and runs them using [Ctrl-F5] (without debugging) or [F5] (with debugging), just as in 2008.

A third option is JetBrains Rider, which is free for non-commercial use.

In the rest of this document, the steps are described using the [dotnet] command, which produces the same results regardless of the editor.

docs.title: 2.3. A First Program: A Single-File Application
2.3.1. The program
docs.text:
Starting with .NET 10, a C# program can be a single [.cs] file, without a project file. This is called a "file-based app." Let's create the following [hello.cs] file:

// first C# program: a single-file application
Console.WriteLine("1st try with C# 14 and .NET 10");

and run it:

> dotnet run hello.cs
1st try with C# 14 and .NET 10

Comments:

  • line 1: a comment. Everything following [//] until the end of the line is ignored by the compiler;
  • line 2: the program’s only statement: it prints a line of text to the screen. The program has neither a class nor a method named [Main], unlike its 2008 counterpart; we’ll see in Chapter 3 that the compiler generates them itself;
  • The [dotnet run hello.cs] command compiles the program and then executes it. The first execution takes a few seconds; subsequent executions are almost immediate as long as the file remains unchanged, since the compilation result is stored in a cache.

Single-file applications are suitable for small programs, and we’ll use them for most of the examples. A few directives, placed at the beginning of the file, allow you to create them without a project file:

#:package MySqlConnector@2.4.0
#:property PublishAot=false
#:sdk Microsoft.NET.Sdk.Web
  • the directive [#:package] adds a NuGet library (Chapter 10);
  • the directive [#:property] sets a compilation property (Chapter 5);
  • the [#:sdk] directive selects a different SDK, such as the one for web applications (Chapter 12).

On Windows, if [.cs] files are saved as UTF-8 (which is the default in VS Code), accented characters display correctly in the terminal.

docs.title: 2.3.2. Converting a Single-File Application into a Project
docs.text:
When a single-file application grows (multiple files, tests, references to other projects), it is converted into a project:

> dotnet project convert hello.cs -o hello

The command creates a folder named [hello] containing a copy of the program and a project file named [hello.csproj]:

> dir /s /b (list of files)
hello.cs
hello/hello.cs
hello/hello.csproj

<Project Sdk="Microsoft.NET.Sdk">

  <PropertyGroup>
    <OutputType>Exe</OutputType>
    <TargetFramework>net10.0</TargetFramework>
    <ImplicitUsings>enable</ImplicitUsings>
    <Nullable>enable</Nullable>
    <PublishAot>true</PublishAot>
    <PackAsTool>true</PackAsTool>
    <UserSecretsId>hello-7b9b5da29436665281cfbf4b23ebf4fed6297358227418ac7d456d2e18d162bf</UserSecretsId>
  </PropertyGroup>

</Project>

The project file inherits the default properties of single-file applications (for example, [PublishAot], which prepares for early compilation into native code). You can remove any that are not needed. We will now look at the projects in more detail.

docs.title: 2.4.1. Creating the Project
docs.text:
A project is a folder containing a project file ([.csproj]) and source files. It is created using the command [dotnet new] followed by the name of a template (in this case, [console], a console application):

> dotnet new console -n FirstProgram
The template "Console App" was created successfully.

Processing post-creation actions...
Restoring csharp-oct-2026/02-installation/FirstProgram/FirstProgram.csproj:
  Determining projects to restore...
  Restored csharp-oct-2026/02-installation/FirstProgram/FirstProgram.csproj (in 127 ms).
Restore succeeded.

The command created a folder named [FirstProgram] containing two files. The project file [FirstProgram.csproj] is as follows:

<Project Sdk="Microsoft.NET.Sdk">

  <PropertyGroup>
    <OutputType>Exe</OutputType>
    <TargetFramework>net10.0</TargetFramework>
    <ImplicitUsings>enable</ImplicitUsings>
    <Nullable>enable</Nullable>
  </PropertyGroup>

</Project>
  • Line 1: The project uses SDK [Microsoft.NET.Sdk], the one for console applications and libraries;
  • line 4: the project produces an executable ([Exe]) rather than a library;
  • line 5: the target platform is .NET 10 ([net10.0]);
  • line 6: the most common namespaces ([System], [System.IO], [System.Linq]…) are automatically imported into all files (Chapter 3);
  • line 7: the compiler checks for the use of null references and issues warnings about potential errors (Chapters 3 and 4).

The 2008 file described each source file in the project, library references, and Debug/Release configurations in about a hundred lines. The current project file contains only the settings that differ from the defaults: all [.cs] files in the folder are part of the project.

We replace the contents of the generated [Program.cs] file with the following:

// the main program of the [FirstProgram] project
Console.WriteLine("1st try with a C# 14 / .NET 10 project");

docs.title: 2.4.2. Compilation and Execution
docs.text:
The command [dotnet build], entered in the project folder, compiles the project:

> dotnet build
  Determining projects to restore...
  All projects are up-to-date for restore.
  FirstProgram -> csharp-oct-2026/02-installation/FirstProgram/bin/Debug/net10.0/FirstProgram.dll

Build succeeded.
    0 Warning(s)
    0 Error(s)

Time Elapsed 00:00:01.56
  • Line 2: The command begins by restoring the project, which means downloading the NuGet packages it depends on (there are none here);
  • Line 4: The result of the compilation is a DLL and [FirstProgram.dll] file placed in the project’s [bin/Debug/net10.0] folder. On Windows, the displayed path is a Windows path ([bin\Debug\net10.0\FirstProgram.dll]).

The [bin/Debug/net10.0] folder then contains the following files:

> dir bin\Debug\net10.0 (list of files)
FirstProgram
FirstProgram.deps.json
FirstProgram.dll
FirstProgram.pdb
FirstProgram.runtimeconfig.json
  • [FirstProgram.dll] contains the compiled code (in intermediate code IL);
  • [FirstProgram] (on Windows, [FirstProgram.exe]) is a small launcher that starts the .NET platform and causes it to execute the DLL;
  • [FirstProgram.pdb] contains the information used by the debugger;
  • the two [.json] files describe the program’s dependencies and the version of .NET required to run it.

You can run the launcher directly:

> FirstProgram
1st try with a C# 14 / .NET 10 project

However, the [dotnet run] command is most commonly used; it compiles the project if necessary and then runs it:

> dotnet run
1st try with a C# 14 / .NET 10 project

As in 2008, there are two build configurations: Debug (default, with debug information) and Release (optimized, for production), selected using the option [-c Release]: [dotnet build -c Release] generates the program in the [bin/Release/net10.0] folder. The [obj] folder contains intermediate compilation files. The [bin] and [obj] folders can be safely deleted: they are recreated during the next compilation.

docs.title: 2.5.1. Creating the solution
docs.text:
A solution groups multiple projects together. It allows you to open them together in the editor and compile them together. Let’s create a solution in the folder containing the [FirstProgram] project:

> dotnet new sln -n 02-installation
The template "Solution File" was created successfully.

then let’s add the project to it:

> dotnet sln add FirstProgram
Project `FirstProgram/FirstProgram.csproj` added to the solution.

Let’s add a second project, [TwoHands], whose contents we’ll look at below:

> dotnet sln add TwoHands
Project `TwoHands/TwoHands.csproj` added to the solution.

The command [dotnet sln list] lists the projects in the solution:

> dotnet sln list
Project(s)
----------
FirstProgram/FirstProgram.csproj
TwoHands/TwoHands.csproj

The solution file [02-installation.slnx] is as follows:

<Solution>
  <Project Path="TwoHands/TwoHands.csproj" />
  <Project Path="FirstProgram/FirstProgram.csproj" />
</Solution>

This is a very simple XML file. Since .NET 10, this has been the default format for solutions ([.slnx]). The old [.sln] format, used in Visual Studio 2008, was much more verbose; it is still found in existing projects, and the [dotnet new sln --format sln] command can still be used to create it.

In the solution folder, the command [dotnet build] compiles all projects in the solution. To run a specific project, navigate to its folder and type [dotnet run], or use the [--project] option: [dotnet run --project FirstProgram].

docs.title: 2.5.2. A Project with Multiple Main Methods
docs.text:
The 2008 course demonstrated that a project can contain multiple classes, each with a static method named [Main], and that you must specify which one to execute. This is still possible. The project [TwoHands] contains two classes. The class [P1]:

namespace TwoHands;

class P1
{
    static void Main(string[] args)
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Main of class P1");
    }
}

and the [P2] class:

namespace TwoHands;

class P2
{
    static void Main(string[] args)
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Main of class P2");
    }
}

If you compile the project without taking any further precautions, you’ll get an error:

> dotnet build
...\TwoHands\P1.cs(5,17): error CS0017: Program has more than one entry point defined. Compile with /main to specify the type that contains the entry point.

The compiler does not know which method, [Main], is the program’s entry point. We specify this in the project file using the [StartupObject] property:

<Project Sdk="Microsoft.NET.Sdk">

  <PropertyGroup>
    <OutputType>Exe</OutputType>
    <TargetFramework>net10.0</TargetFramework>
    <ImplicitUsings>enable</ImplicitUsings>
    <Nullable>enable</Nullable>
    <!-- the class whose Main method is executed -->
    <StartupObject>TwoHands.P2</StartupObject>
  </PropertyGroup>

</Project>
  • Line 9: The method [Main] that was executed belongs to the class [TwoHands.P2] (the full class name, including the namespace).

Results:

> dotnet run
Main of class P2

With high-level statements (Chapter 3), the question no longer arises: a single file in a project can contain them, and that file serves as the entry point.

docs.title: 2.6. Examples in this document
docs.text:
To run the examples in this document:

  • download the [csharp-oct-2026] folder (link at the beginning of the document);
  • open it in VS Code (“File / Open Folder”) or, for a specific chapter, open the chapter’s solution ([.slnx]) in Visual Studio;
  • in a terminal located in a chapter’s folder, run a single-file application using [dotnet run name.cs], or a project using [dotnet run] in the project folder.

Chapters 10 and 11 use a MySQL database; the installation of MySQL with [Laragon] is described in the appendix.

docs.title: 3. The Basics of the C# Language
3.1. Introduction
docs.text:
We’ll start by treating C# as a traditional programming language. We’ll cover classes in the next chapter. In a program, there are two main components:

  • data;
  • the instructions that manipulate them.

We generally strive to separate data from instructions:

All the examples in this chapter are single-file applications: a single file, [.cs], without a project file ([.csproj]), which is run using the command [dotnet run basics-01.cs]. This feature, introduced with .NET 10, was covered in the previous chapter. The examples are located in the [03-basics] folder of the course code. They run in the French locale (fr-FR), as on a French Windows machine: real numbers are displayed with a decimal comma.

docs.title: 3.2.1. High-level instructions
docs.text:
The program [basics-01.cs] is as follows:

// minimal program written with top-level statements (C# 9)
// the statements are written directly in the file: no class, no Main method
Console.WriteLine("Hello world!");
// the full name of the Console class is System.Console
System.Console.WriteLine("Number of arguments received: " + args.Length);

Results:

> dotnet run basics-01.cs
Hello world!
Number of arguments received: 0

Comments:

  • The program contains neither classes nor methods: the statements are written directly in the file. These are called high-level statements (C# 9, 2020). A single program file can contain them;
  • Line 3: The [WriteLine] method of the [Console] class prints a line to the screen;
  • line 5: The class [Console] belongs to the namespace [System]. Its full name is [System.Console]. A namespace groups related types, just as a folder groups files;
  • line 5: the program has an array [args] containing the command-line arguments. We’ll come back to this in the “Main Program Arguments” section. The number of elements in the array is [args.Length]. The + operator concatenates a string and a number here: the number is first converted to a string.

With two command-line arguments (everything following [--] is passed to the program):

> dotnet run basics-01.cs -- a0 a1
Hello world!
Number of arguments received: 2

docs.title: 3.2.2. The classic form with a Main method
docs.text:
The 2008 course (C# 3.0) did not cover high-level instructions. The same program was written as follows: [basics-02.cs]:

// the classic form of the same program (the only one possible until C# 8)
using System;

namespace Basics
{
    class Program
    {
        // the Main method is the entry point of the program
        static void Main(string[] args)
        {
            Console.WriteLine("Hello world!");
            System.Console.WriteLine("Number of arguments received: " + args.Length);
        }
    }
}

Results:

> dotnet run basics-02.cs
Hello world!
Number of arguments received: 0

Comments:

  • line 2: the directive [using] imports the namespace [System]. You can then write [Console] instead of [System.Console];
  • Line 4: The class is placed in the [Basics] namespace. Starting with C# 10, you can write [namespace Basics;] (file-scope namespace): the entire file then belongs to this namespace, without curly braces or additional indentation. This is the form we will use from now on;
  • Line 6: In C#, all code belongs to a class. The class here is called [Program];
  • Line 9: The static method [Main] is the program’s entry point: this is the method the system executes upon launch. Its parameter, [args], receives the command-line arguments.

The two programs are equivalent. When it encounters high-level instructions, the compiler generates a class and a method named [Main] that contain these instructions, as well as the parameter [string[] args]. High-level instructions are therefore simply a shorthand form of the standard syntax. They are well-suited for the small programs in this chapter; the standard syntax remains useful when you want to inspect the class that contains [Main].

docs.title: 3.2.3. Implicit using statements
docs.text:
The program [basics-01.cs] uses the class [Console] without the [using System;] directive. This is possible because the .NET SDK automatically adds a generated file containing [global using] directives (C# 10) to every console program, which apply to all files in the program. For [basics-01.cs], this file contains:

// <auto-generated/>
global using System;
global using System.Collections.Generic;
global using System.IO;
global using System.Linq;
global using System.Net.Http;
global using System.Threading;
global using System.Threading.Tasks;

These are the implicit using statements: the most commonly used namespaces are imported automatically. A namespace not included in this list, such as [System.Globalization], must always be imported using a [using] directive at the top of the file. In the program [basics-02.cs], the directive [using System;] is therefore redundant: we left it in to show the 2008 format.

docs.title: 3.3. C# Data
docs.text:
C# uses the following data types:

  • integers;
  • real numbers;
  • decimal numbers;
  • characters and character strings;
  • Booleans;
  • objects.

docs.title: 3.3.1. Predefined data types
3.3.2. Notation for Literal Data
3.3.3.1. Role of declarations
docs.text: A program manipulates data characterized by a name and a type. This data is stored in memory. When the program is compiled, the compiler assigns each piece of data a memory location characterized by an address and a size. It does this based on the declarations made by the programmer. Furthermore, these declarations allow the compiler to detect programming errors. Thus, the operation [x = x * 2;] will be declared invalid if [x] is a character string.

docs.title: 3.3.3.2. Declaring Constants
docs.text:
The syntax for declaring a constant is as follows:

const type name = value;

For example:

const double VatRate = 0.2;

Why declare constants?

  • The program is easier to read if the constant is given a meaningful name;
  • it is easier to modify the program if the “constant” needs to be changed. Thus, if the VAT rate changes to 0.25, the only modification needed will be to the statement that defines its value: [const double VatRate = 0.25;]. If 0.2 had been used explicitly in the program, numerous statements would need to be modified.

The value of a constant must be known at compile time: a number, a string, a Boolean, or an expression that can be calculated from other constants. By convention, in .NET, constant names begin with a capital letter.

docs.title: 3.3.3.3. Variable Declaration
docs.text:
A variable is identified by a name and is associated with a data type. C# distinguishes between uppercase and lowercase letters: the variables [END] and [end] are different.

Variables can be initialized when they are declared. The syntax for declaring one or more variables is:

type variable1 = value1, variable2 = value2, ...;

where [type] is a predefined type or a type defined by the programmer. Initialization is optional; however, C# does not allow the use of a local variable that has not yet been assigned a value.

You can also omit the type of a variable by using the keyword [var] in place of the type:

var variable1 = value1;

The keyword [var] does not mean that the variable has no specific type: it has the type of the value assigned to it, as determined by the compiler. Initialization is required here so that the compiler can deduce the type. We use [var] when the type is obvious from the value.

The program [basics-05.cs] is as follows:

// constants and variables
const double VatRate = 0.2;
const string Currency = "euros";
double priceExclTax = 100;
Console.WriteLine($"Price incl. tax : {priceExclTax * (1 + VatRate)} {Currency}");

// an explicitly typed piece of data
int i = 2;
Console.WriteLine($"Type of int i=2 : {i.GetType().Name},{i.GetType().FullName}");
// implicitly typed data with var
var j = 3;
Console.WriteLine($"Type of var j=3 : {j.GetType().Name},{j.GetType().FullName}");
var today = DateTime.Now;
Console.WriteLine($"Type of var today : {today.GetType().Name},{today.GetType().FullName}");
var x = 3.5;
var y = 3.5F;
var z = 10L;
var name = "dupont";
Console.WriteLine($"x : {x.GetType().Name}, y : {y.GetType().Name}, z : {z.GetType().Name}, name : {name.GetType().Name}");
// several variables declared on the same line
int a = 1, b, c = 3;
b = a + c;
Console.WriteLine($"a={a}, b={b}, c={c}");

Results:

> dotnet run basics-05.cs
Price incl. tax : 120 euros
Type of int i=2 : Int32,System.Int32
Type of var j=3 : Int32,System.Int32
Type of var today : DateTime,System.DateTime
x : Double, y : Single, z : Int64, name : String
a=1, b=4, c=3

Comments:

  • lines 2–3: two constants;
  • line 8: one explicitly typed data item;
  • line 9: [GetType().Name] is the short name of the type, [GetType().FullName] is its full name;
  • Line 11: an implicitly typed value. Because 3 is of type [int], [j] will be of type [int];
  • line 13: Because [DateTime.Now] (the current date and time) is of type [DateTime], [today] will be of type [DateTime];
  • lines 15–18: the inferred type depends on how the literal is written: 3.5 is a [double], 3.5F is a [float], and 10L is a [long];
  • Line 21: three variables declared on the same line; only [a] and [c] are initialized. [b] is assigned a value on the next line.

A variable implicitly typed by the keyword [var] cannot change its type afterward. Thus, after line 13, you could not write:

today = "today";

because [today] is of type [DateTime]. We will see in Chapter 5, with LINQ, that it is possible to create a type “on the fly” within an expression: this is an anonymous type, to which the programmer has not assigned a name. If data of an anonymous type is to be assigned to a variable, the only way to declare that variable is to use the keyword [var].

docs.title: 3.3.4. Nullable Types
docs.text:
A variable of a value type, such as [int], always contains a value. It is sometimes useful to be able to express the absence of a value: an unknown age, an empty field in a database. The type [int?] (C# 2) is the type [int] with the value [null] added to it, which means “no value.” This is referred to as a nullable value type. The principle applies to all value types: [double?], [bool?], [DateTime?], ...

A variable of a reference type, such as [string], can always have the value [null]: this means that it does not reference any object. Attempting to use a member of such a variable—for example, its property [Length]—will result in a runtime error ([NullReferenceException]), one of the most common errors in C#. Starting with C# 8, the compiler can help prevent this: with nullable reference types—enabled by default in projects created using the [dotnet new] command and in single-file applications—

  • the type [string] denotes a string that never evaluates to [null];
  • the type [string?] refers to a string that can be [null].

The compiler tracks the possible values of variables and issues a warning when there is a risk of using the value [null]: assigning [null] to a variable [string], using [Length] on a variable [string?] that has not been tested, etc. Unlike [int?], [string?] does not create a new type at runtime: it is a directive intended for the compiler.

We’ll encounter these types right from the first examples, because the method [Console.ReadLine()], which reads a line typed on the keyboard, returns a [string?]: it returns [null] when there is nothing left to read (end of the input stream). The program [basics-06.cs] is as follows:

// nullable types
// a nullable value type (int?) accepts the null value in addition to integers
int? age = null;
Console.WriteLine($"age.HasValue={age.HasValue}");
age = 23;
Console.WriteLine($"age.HasValue={age.HasValue}, age.Value={age.Value}");
// int? -> int: an explicit conversion is needed (exception if age is null)
int n = (int)age;
Console.WriteLine($"n={n}");

// a nullable reference type (string?) accepts the null value
string? firstName = null;
Console.WriteLine($"firstName is null : {firstName == null}");
// the string type (without ?) is assumed never to be null
string name = "dupont";
Console.WriteLine($"name has {name.Length} characters");

// Console.ReadLine returns a string?: null if the input stream is exhausted
Console.Write("Type a line: ");
string? line = Console.ReadLine();
if (line == null)
{
    Console.WriteLine();
    Console.WriteLine("No line: the input stream is closed");
}
else
{
    // here the compiler knows that line is not null
    Console.WriteLine($"You typed [{line}] : {line.Length} character(s)");
}

Results when entering text via the keyboard:

> dotnet run basics-06.cs
age.HasValue=False
age.HasValue=True, age.Value=23
n=23
firstName is null : True
name has 6 characters
Type a line: hello
You typed [hello] : 5 character(s)

Results when the user presses Ctrl-D (Ctrl-Z followed by Enter on Windows), which closes the input stream:

> dotnet run basics-06.cs
age.HasValue=False
age.HasValue=True, age.Value=23
n=23
firstName is null : True
name has 6 characters
Type a line: 
No line: the input stream is closed

Comments:

  • line 3: [age] does not contain a value;
  • line 4: the [HasValue] property indicates whether the variable contains a value; the [Value] property provides that value;
  • line 8: a [int?] cannot be directly assigned to a [int] since it may be equal to [null]. An explicit conversion is required, which throws an exception if [age] is equal to [null]. We will discuss the safer [??] operator later;
  • line 12: a string that may be equal to [null];
  • line 15: a string that never equals [null]. Writing [name = null;] would trigger a compiler warning;
  • line 20: [Console.ReadLine()] evaluates to [string?]. Declaring [line] as type [string] would trigger a warning;
  • line 21: the value [null] is checked;
  • line 29: in the [else] branch, the compiler knows that [line] is not equal to [null]: it issues no warning for the use of [line.Length].

docs.title: 3.3.5. Conversions between numbers and strings
3.3.6. Data Arrays
docs.text:
A C# array is an object that allows data of the same type to be grouped under a single identifier. It is declared as follows:

Type[] array = new Type[n];

[n] is the number of data elements the array can contain. The syntax [array[i]] refers to data element number i, where i belongs to the range [0, n-1]. Any reference to data item [array[i]] where i is not in the range [0, n-1] causes an exception. Upon creation, each element of the array is assigned the default value for its type: 0 for numbers, [false] for booleans, and [null] for reference types. An array can be initialized at the same time it is declared:

int[] integers = new int[] { 0, 10, 20, 30 };

or, more simply:

int[] integers = { 0, 10, 20, 30 };

or, starting with C# 12, using a collection expression:

int[] integers = [0, 10, 20, 30];

We will use this last form from now on. Arrays have a property [Length], which represents the number of elements they contain.

A two-dimensional array is declared as follows:

Type[,] array = new Type[n, m];

where [n] is the number of rows and [m] is the number of columns. The syntax [array[i, j]] refers to element j in row i. The two-dimensional array can also be initialized at the same time it is declared:

double[,] reals = { { 0.5, 1.7 }, { 8.4, -6 } };

The number of elements in each dimension is obtained using the method [GetLength(i)], where i=0 represents the dimension corresponding to the first index, i=1 represents the dimension corresponding to the second index, and so on. The number of dimensions is obtained using the property [Rank], and the total number of elements using the property [Length].

An array of arrays (also known as a staircase array) is declared as follows:

Type[][] array = new Type[n][];

The declaration above creates an array of n elements. Each element, [array[i]], is a one-dimensional array reference. These references are not initialized by the declaration above; they have the value [null]. Unlike a two-dimensional array, each row can have a different length.

C# 8 introduced two convenient notations:

  • backward indexing: [array[^1]] is the last element, [array[^2]] is the second-to-last, and so on. [array[^1]] is equivalent to [array[array.Length - 1]];
  • the range: [array[1..3]] is a new array consisting of the elements with indices 1 and 2. The start index is included, and the end index is excluded. The bounds can be omitted: [array[2..]] ranges from index 2 to the end, and [array[..^1]] ranges from the beginning to the second-to-last element, inclusive.

The program [basics-08.cs] combines these different arrays:

// arrays
// an initialized 1-dimensional array
int[] integers = new int[] { 0, 10, 20, 30 };
for (int i = 0; i < integers.Length; i++)
{
    Console.WriteLine($"integers[{i}]={integers[i]}");
}

// an initialized 2-dimensional array
double[,] reals = { { 0.5, 1.7 }, { 8.4, -6 } };
for (int i = 0; i < reals.GetLength(0); i++)
{
    for (int j = 0; j < reals.GetLength(1); j++)
    {
        Console.WriteLine($"reals[{i},{j}]={reals[i, j]}");
    }
}
Console.WriteLine($"reals : Rank={reals.Rank}, Length={reals.Length}");

// an array of arrays (jagged array)
string[][] names = new string[3][];
for (int i = 0; i < names.Length; i++)
{
    names[i] = new string[i + 1];
}
// initialization
for (int i = 0; i < names.Length; i++)
{
    for (int j = 0; j < names[i].Length; j++)
    {
        names[i][j] = "name" + i + j;
    }
}
// display
for (int i = 0; i < names.Length; i++)
{
    for (int j = 0; j < names[i].Length; j++)
    {
        Console.WriteLine($"names[{i}][{j}]={names[i][j]}");
    }
}

// an array created without initial values: elements at the default value of the type
bool[] flags = new bool[3];
string?[] strings = new string?[2];
Console.WriteLine($"flags[0]={flags[0]}, strings[0] is null : {strings[0] == null}");

// collection expression (C# 12)
int[] values = [0, 10, 20, 30, 40];
// string.Join joins the elements of an array with a separator
Console.WriteLine($"values=[{string.Join(", ", values)}]");
// index from the end (C# 8): ^1 denotes the last element
Console.WriteLine($"values[^1]={values[^1]}, values[^2]={values[^2]}");
// range (C# 8): the elements at indices 1 and 2 (the end bound is excluded)
int[] slice = values[1..3];
Console.WriteLine($"values[1..3]=[{string.Join(", ", slice)}]");
Console.WriteLine($"values[2..]=[{string.Join(", ", values[2..])}]");
Console.WriteLine($"values[..^1]=[{string.Join(", ", values[..^1])}]");
// the slice is a copy: the original array is not modified
slice[0] = 100;
Console.WriteLine($"slice[0]={slice[0]}, values[1]={values[1]}");

Results:

> dotnet run basics-08.cs
integers[0]=0
integers[1]=10
integers[2]=20
integers[3]=30
reals[0,0]=0,5
reals[0,1]=1,7
reals[1,0]=8,4
reals[1,1]=-6
reals : Rank=2, Length=4
names[0][0]=name00
names[1][0]=name10
names[1][1]=name11
names[2][0]=name20
names[2][1]=name21
names[2][2]=name22
flags[0]=False, strings[0] is null : True
values=[0, 10, 20, 30, 40]
values[^1]=40, values[^2]=30
values[1..3]=[10, 20]
values[2..]=[20, 30, 40]
values[..^1]=[0, 10, 20, 30]
slice[0]=100, values[1]=10

Comments:

  • line 3: a one-dimensional array is initialized;
  • line 4: a loop [for] iterates over indices from 0 to [integers.Length - 1]. The loop [for] is shown below;
  • line 10: a two-dimensional array (2 rows, 2 columns);
  • lines 11–13: [GetLength(0)] is the number of rows, [GetLength(1)] is the number of columns;
  • line 21: an array [names] with 3 elements. Each element is a reference to an array of type [string[]], currently [null];
  • line 24: the 3 elements of the array [names] are initialized. [names[i]] now references an array of i+1 strings;
  • line 31: [names[i][j]] is the jth element of the array referenced by [names[i]]. Since [names[i]] is an array, [names[i].Length] is the number of its elements. The expression “name” + i + j is evaluated from left to right: “name” + i yields a string, to which j is concatenated;
  • lines 44–45: arrays created without initial values. The type [string?[]] is an array whose elements can be [null];
  • line 49: a collection expression;
  • line 51: the method [string.Join] constructs a string using the array’s elements, separated by the string passed as the first parameter;
  • line 53: the last and second-to-last elements;
  • line 55: the elements at indices 1 and 2;
  • lines 60–61: a range creates a copy: modifying [slice] does not modify [values].

docs.title: 3.4. Basic C# Statements
docs.text:
There are:

  • basic statements executed by the computer;
  • instructions that control the flow of the program.

Basic instructions become clear when considering the structure of a microcomputer and its peripherals:

  • 1: reading information from the keyboard;
  • 2: processing information;
  • 3: writing information to the screen.

docs.title: 3.4.1. Writing to the Screen
docs.text:
There are various instructions for writing to the screen:

Console.Out.WriteLine(expression);
Console.WriteLine(expression);
Console.Error.WriteLine(expression);

where [expression] is any data that can be converted to a character string for display on the screen. All C# or .NET objects have a [ToString()] method that is used to perform this conversion. The [Write] method does the same thing as [WriteLine] without wrapping to the next line.

Class [System.Console] provides access to screen-writing operations ([Write], [WriteLine]). It has two properties, [Out] and [Error], which are write streams of type [TextWriter]:

  • [Console.WriteLine()] is equivalent to [Console.Out.WriteLine()] and writes to the stream [Out], which is usually associated with the screen;
  • [Console.Error.WriteLine()] writes to the [Error] stream, which is also usually associated with the screen.

The streams [Out] and [Error] can be redirected to files at runtime, as we will see shortly.

docs.title: 3.4.2. Reading Data Entered via the Keyboard
docs.text:
The data stream from the keyboard is represented by the object [Console.In] of type [TextReader]. This object type allows you to read a line of text using the [ReadLine] method:

string? line = Console.In.ReadLine();

The [Console] class provides a method, [ReadLine], which is associated by default with the [In] stream. Therefore, you can write:

string? line = Console.ReadLine();

The line typed on the keyboard, without the end-of-line character, is stored in the variable [line] and can then be processed by the program. As we have seen, [ReadLine] returns [null] when the input stream is exhausted: this is why the variable is of type [string?]. The stream [In] can be redirected to a file, just like the streams [Out] and [Error].

docs.title: 3.4.3. Example of Input/Output
docs.text:
The program [basics-09.cs] illustrates keyboard/screen input and output operations:

// keyboard / screen input-output

// writing to the Out stream
object obj = new object();
Console.Out.WriteLine(obj);

// writing to the Error stream
int i = 10;
Console.Error.WriteLine("i=" + i);
Console.Error.WriteLine("i={0}", i);

// reading a line typed on the keyboard
Console.Write("Type a line: ");
string? line = Console.ReadLine();
Console.WriteLine($"line={line}");

Results:

> dotnet run basics-09.cs
System.Object
i=10
i=10
Type a line: here I am
line=here I am

Comments:

  • Line 4: [obj] is an object reference;
  • Line 5: [obj] is displayed on the screen. The method [obj.ToString()] is called to retrieve the text to be displayed;
  • line 9: the text is written to the [Error] stream;
  • line 10: the same thing, but with a format. The first parameter, "i={0}", is the display format; the other parameters are the expressions to be displayed. The {n} elements are positional parameters: at runtime, {n} is replaced by the value of the nth expression;
  • lines 13–14: a prompt is displayed without a line break, then the line typed on the keyboard is read;
  • line 15: in an interpolated string, a value like [null] would produce an empty string: no warning is issued.

In the results:

  • line 2: the output generated by line 5 of the code. The method *[obj.ToString()] displayed the type name of the variable *[obj]*: *[System.Object]*. The type [object] is a C# alias for the type .NET [System.Object]*;
  • Lines 3–4: The two entries for the [Error] stream appear on the screen as those for the [Out] stream.

docs.title: 3.4.4. Input/Output Redirection
docs.text:
Windows, Linux, and macOS recognize three standard devices:

  • the standard input device, which by default refers to the keyboard and is numbered 0;
  • the standard output device, which by default refers to the screen and is numbered 1;
  • the standard error device, which is set to the screen by default and is numbered 2.

In C#, the write stream [Console.Out] writes to device 1, the write stream [Console.Error] writes to device 2, and the read stream [Console.In] reads data from device 0.

When you run a program in a command window, you can specify which devices will be 0, 1, and 2 for the program being executed. After the program arguments, you can redirect the standard input and output devices to files:

RedirectionMeaning0<in.txt or <in.txtStandard input stream No. 0 is redirected to the file in.txt. In the program, the stream [Console.In] will therefore read its data from the file in.txt1>out.txt or >out.txtredirects output #1 to the file out.txt. In the program, the stream [Console.Out] will therefore write its data to the file out.txt1>>out.txt or >>out.txtSame as above, but the written data is appended to the current contents of the out.txt file2>err.txtredirects output #2 to the file err.txt. In the program, the stream [Console.Error] will therefore write its data to the file err.txt2>>err.txtSame as above, but the written data is appended to the current contents of the file err.txt1>out.txt 2>err.txtDevices 1 and 2 are both redirected to files

Note that to redirect a program’s input/output streams to files, the program does not need to be modified: the operating system determines the nature of devices 0, 1, and 2. Consider the following program, [basics-10.cs]:

// redirections of the input-output streams
// reading the In stream
string? data = Console.In.ReadLine();
// writing to the Out stream
Console.Out.WriteLine("writing to the Out stream : " + data);
// writing to the Error stream
Console.Error.WriteLine("writing to the Error stream : " + data);

The 2008 course generated an executable using Visual Studio and then ran it in a DOS window. Today, the command [dotnet run] is sufficient: the redirects are applied to the launched program. Here is a session in a Linux terminal (bash):

> echo test > in.txt
> cat in.txt
test
> dotnet run basics-10.cs < in.txt > out.txt 2> err.txt
> cat out.txt
writing to the Out stream : test
> cat err.txt
writing to the Error stream : test
> dotnet run basics-10.cs < in.txt 2> err.txt
writing to the Out stream : test
> dotnet run basics-10.cs < in.txt > out.txt
writing to the Error stream : test

Comments:

  • line 1: the string "test" is placed in the file in.txt;
  • line 2: display the contents of the file in.txt for verification;
  • line 4: run the program. The stream [In] is redirected to the file in.txt, the stream [Out] to the file out.txt, and the stream [Error] to the file err.txt. The execution does not result in any output;
  • lines 5–6: The contents of the file out.txt show that the file in.txt was read and that writing to the stream [Out] was redirected to out.txt;
  • lines 7–8: similar verification for the file err.txt;
  • lines 9–10: only the [Error] stream is redirected: the screen displays only the write operation to the [Out] stream;
  • lines 11–12: only the [Out] stream is redirected: the screen displays only the write operation on the [Error] stream.

It is clear that the streams [Out] and [Error] do not write to the same devices, since they could be redirected separately. The [Error] stream is intended for error messages: this allows you to redirect a program’s output to a file while still seeing its error messages on the screen.

The operators >, >>, and 2> are written the same way in the Windows command prompt ([cmd]), in PowerShell, and in bash. The < operator is recognized by [cmd] and bash, but not by PowerShell, which reserves it for future use: in PowerShell, it is used to send a file to a program’s standard input via a pipe (|). The following commands, provided for illustrative purposes (they were not executed for this course), do on Windows what the bash session above does:

rem Windows command prompt (cmd)
echo test>in.txt
dotnet run basics-10.cs <in.txt >out.txt 2>err.txt
type out.txt
type err.txt

# PowerShell
"test" > in.txt
Get-Content in.txt | dotnet run basics-10.cs > out.txt 2> err.txt
Get-Content out.txt
Get-Content err.txt

docs.title: 3.4.5. Assigning the value of an expression to a variable
docs.text: Here we are interested in the operation [variable = expression;]. The expression can be arithmetic, relational, Boolean, string, etc.

docs.title: 3.4.5.1. Interpretation of the assignment operation
docs.text:
The operation [variable = expression;] is itself an expression that is evaluated as follows:

  • the right-hand side of the assignment is evaluated: the result is a value V;
  • the value V is assigned to the variable;
  • the value V is also the value of the assignment, now viewed as an expression.

Thus, the operation [V1 = V2 = expression] is valid. Since the = operator is evaluated from right to left, we get [V1 = (V2 = expression)]. The expression [V2 = expression] is evaluated and has the value V. Its evaluation caused V to be assigned to V2. The next = operator is then evaluated as [V1 = V]. The value of this expression is still V; its evaluation causes V to be assigned to V1. Thus, the operation [V1 = V2 = expression] is an expression whose evaluation:

  • causes the value of [expression] to be assigned to the variables V1 and V2;
  • returns the value of [expression].

This can be generalized to an expression of the form [V1 = V2 = ... = Vn = expression].

docs.title: 3.4.5.2. Arithmetic Expressions
docs.text:
The operators used in arithmetic expressions are as follows:

OperatorRole+addition-subtraction*multiplication/division: the result is the exact quotient if at least one of the operands is a real number. If both operands are integers, the result is the integer quotient. Thus, 5/2 equals 2 and 5.0/2 equals 2.5%remainder of division (modulo), regardless of the nature of the operands. The remainder has the same sign as the dividend: -5 % 2 equals -1

There are various mathematical functions. Here are a few:

FunctionRole[double Sqrt(double x)]square root[double Cos(double x)], [Sin], [Tan]cosine, sine, tangent (angle in radians)[double Pow(double x, double y)]x to the power of y[double Exp(double x)]exponential[double Log(double x)], [Log10], [Log2]natural logarithm, decimal logarithm, base-2 logarithm[Abs(x)], [Max(x, y)], [Min(x, y)]absolute value, maximum, minimum (for all numeric types)[Floor(x)], [Ceiling(x)], [Truncate(x)]lower integer part, upper integer part, truncation[Round(x)], [Round(x, n)]rounding to the nearest integer, to n decimal places[Math.PI], [Math.E]the constants π and e

All these functions are defined in a .NET class named Math. When using them, you must prefix them with the name of the class in which they are defined. Thus, you would write:

double x, y = 4;
x = Math.Sqrt(y);

The 2008 course included the complete definition of the [Math] class here: Today, it can be found in the online documentation for .NET, learn.microsoft.com/dotnet/api/system.math.

The [basics-11.cs] program is as follows:

// arithmetic expressions
// integer division and real division
Console.WriteLine($"5 / 2 = {5 / 2}, 5.0 / 2 = {5.0 / 2}, 5 / 2.0 = {5 / 2.0}");
// remainder of the division (modulo)
Console.WriteLine($"5 % 2 = {5 % 2}, -5 % 2 = {-5 % 2}, 5.5 % 2 = {5.5 % 2}");
// real division by zero: no error, infinity or NaN (Not a Number)
double zero = 0;
Console.WriteLine($"1 / 0.0 = {1 / zero}, 0 / 0.0 = {0 / zero}");

// some functions of the Math class
double x, y = 4;
x = Math.Sqrt(y);
Console.WriteLine($"Math.Sqrt(4) = {x}");
Console.WriteLine($"Math.Pow(2, 10) = {Math.Pow(2, 10)}");
Console.WriteLine($"Math.Abs(-3.5) = {Math.Abs(-3.5)}, Math.Max(3, 7) = {Math.Max(3, 7)}");
Console.WriteLine($"Math.PI = {Math.PI}, Math.Cos(Math.PI) = {Math.Cos(Math.PI)}");
Console.WriteLine($"Math.Exp(1) = {Math.Exp(1)}, Math.Log(Math.E) = {Math.Log(Math.E)}");
Console.WriteLine($"Math.Floor(-2.5) = {Math.Floor(-2.5)}, Math.Ceiling(-2.5) = {Math.Ceiling(-2.5)}, Math.Truncate(-2.5) = {Math.Truncate(-2.5)}");
// by default Math.Round rounds to the nearest even number
Console.WriteLine($"Math.Round(2.5) = {Math.Round(2.5)}, Math.Round(3.5) = {Math.Round(3.5)}");
Console.WriteLine($"Math.Round(2.5, MidpointRounding.AwayFromZero) = {Math.Round(2.5, MidpointRounding.AwayFromZero)}");
Console.WriteLine($"Math.Round(2.567, 2) = {Math.Round(2.567, 2)}");

// precedence: * / % before + -
Console.WriteLine($"2 + 3 * 4 = {2 + 3 * 4}, (2 + 3) * 4 = {(2 + 3) * 4}, 10 - 4 - 3 = {10 - 4 - 3}");

// assignment is an expression: multiple assignment
int v1, v2;
v1 = v2 = 7 * 6;
Console.WriteLine($"v1={v1}, v2={v2}");

Results:

> dotnet run basics-11.cs
5 / 2 = 2, 5.0 / 2 = 2,5, 5 / 2.0 = 2,5
5 % 2 = 1, -5 % 2 = -1, 5.5 % 2 = 1,5
1 / 0.0 = ∞, 0 / 0.0 = NaN
Math.Sqrt(4) = 2
Math.Pow(2, 10) = 1024
Math.Abs(-3.5) = 3,5, Math.Max(3, 7) = 7
Math.PI = 3,141592653589793, Math.Cos(Math.PI) = -1
Math.Exp(1) = 2,718281828459045, Math.Log(Math.E) = 1
Math.Floor(-2.5) = -3, Math.Ceiling(-2.5) = -2, Math.Truncate(-2.5) = -2
Math.Round(2.5) = 2, Math.Round(3.5) = 4
Math.Round(2.5, MidpointRounding.AwayFromZero) = 3
Math.Round(2.567, 2) = 2,57
2 + 3 * 4 = 14, (2 + 3) * 4 = 20, 10 - 4 - 3 = 3
v1=42, v2=42

Comments:

  • line 3: the division of two integers is an integer division;
  • line 5: the remainder has the same sign as the dividend; the % operator also applies to real numbers;
  • line 8: dividing a real number by zero does not cause an error; it returns infinity (displayed as ∞) or the special value NaN (“Not a Number”) for 0/0. However, dividing an integer by zero throws a [DivideByZeroException] exception;
  • lines 11–12: the example above;
  • Line 18: [Floor] rounds down, [Ceiling] rounds up, [Truncate] rounds to zero;
  • line 20: by default, [Math.Round] rounds a value that is exactly halfway to the nearest even number (“banker’s” rounding): 2.5 becomes 2 and 3.5 becomes 4;
  • line 21: for the rounding method taught in school (2.5 becomes 3), specify the rounding mode;
  • line 25: operator precedence, as shown below;
  • line 29: a multiple assignment.

docs.title: 3.4.5.3. Order of Operations in Evaluating Arithmetic Expressions
docs.text:
The order of operations when evaluating an arithmetic expression is as follows (from highest to lowest priority):

[functions], [( )], [*, /, %], [+, -]

Operators within the same block [ ] have the same precedence. When precedence is equal, evaluation proceeds from left to right: 10 - 4 - 3 evaluates to (10 - 4) - 3 = 3.

docs.title: 3.4.5.4. Relational Expressions
docs.text:
The operators are as follows: <, <=, ==, !=, >, >=. Their precedence is:

  • >, >=, <, <=;
  • ==, !=.

The result of a relational expression is the Boolean [false] if the expression is false, and [true] otherwise.

bool end;
int x = 5;
end = x > 4;

Comparing Two Characters

Let C1 and C2 be two characters. They can be compared using the operators <, <=, ==, !=, >, >=. In this case, it is their Unicode codes—which are numbers—that are compared. According to the Unicode order, the following relationships hold:

space < .. < '0' < '1' < .. < '9' < .. < 'A' < 'B' < .. < 'Z' < .. < 'a' < 'b' < .. < 'z' < .. < 'é'

Comparison of Two Strings

They are compared character by character. The first inequality encountered between two characters results in an inequality of the same direction for the strings. Consider comparing the strings "Cart" and "Cat":

"Cart"    "Cat"
---------------------
'C'   =   'C'
'a'   =   'a'
'r'   <   't'

This last inequality allows us to conclude that "Cart" < "Cat." Consider comparing the strings "Cat" and "Catkin." They are equal until the string "Cat" is exhausted. In this case, the exhausted string is declared the "smaller" one. We therefore have the relation "Cat" < "Catkin."

Functions for Comparing Two Strings

You can use the relational operators == and != to test whether two strings are equal, or the method [Equals] of the class [System.String]. For the relations <, <=, >, and >=, the operators do not apply to strings: you must use the [CompareTo] method of the [System.String] class or the static [string.Compare] method. They return an integer:

  • zero if the two strings are equal;
  • positive if string #1 is greater than string #2;
  • negative if string #1 is less than string #2.

There is a subtlety: [CompareTo] and [string.Compare] do not simply compare Unicode codes. They follow the sorting rules of the current culture, as in a dictionary: in French, “élan” comes before “face,” even though the code for ‘é’ (233) is greater than that for ‘f’ (102). To choose the comparison mode, [string.Compare] and [Equals] accept a parameter of type [StringComparison]:

  • [StringComparison.Ordinal]: character-by-character comparison of Unicode codes. This is the fastest comparison and should be used for identifiers, keywords, and filenames;
  • [StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase]: same as above, ignoring case;
  • [StringComparison.CurrentCulture] (the default for [CompareTo]): follows standard cultural conventions for sorting text intended for users.

The == operator and the [Equals] method without parameters perform an ordinal comparison.

The program [basics-12.cs] is as follows:

// relational expressions and string comparison
int x = 5;
bool end = x > 4;
Console.WriteLine($"x > 4 : {end}, x == 5 : {x == 5}, x != 5 : {x != 5}");

// comparison of characters: their Unicode codes are compared
Console.WriteLine($"'a' < 'b' : {'a' < 'b'}, 'Z' < 'a' : {'Z' < 'a'}, '9' < 'A' : {'9' < 'A'}");
Console.WriteLine($"codes : 'A'={(int)'A'}, 'a'={(int)'a'}, 'é'={(int)'é'}");

// comparison of strings
string string1 = "cat", string2 = "dog";
int n = string1.CompareTo(string2);
bool equal = string1.Equals(string2);
Console.WriteLine($"n={n}, equal={equal}");
Console.WriteLine($"\"dog\"==string1 : {"dog" == string1}, \"dog\"!=string2 : {"dog" != string2}");
Console.WriteLine($"\"Cat\".CompareTo(\"Catkin\") : {"Cat".CompareTo("Catkin")}");

// CompareTo and string.Compare follow the rules of the current culture (fr-FR)
Console.WriteLine($"\"élan\".CompareTo(\"face\") : {"élan".CompareTo("face")}");
Console.WriteLine($"string.Compare(\"Cat\", \"cat\") : {string.Compare("Cat", "cat")}");
// StringComparison.Ordinal: comparison of the Unicode codes, character by character
Console.WriteLine($"Ordinal(\"élan\", \"face\") : {string.Compare("élan", "face", StringComparison.Ordinal)}");
Console.WriteLine($"Ordinal(\"Cat\", \"cat\") : {string.Compare("Cat", "cat", StringComparison.Ordinal)}");
// ignoring case (upper / lower case)
Console.WriteLine($"OrdinalIgnoreCase(\"Cat\", \"cat\") : {string.Compare("Cat", "cat", StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase)}");
Console.WriteLine($"\"Cat\".Equals(\"cat\") : {"Cat".Equals("cat")}");
Console.WriteLine($"\"Cat\".Equals(\"cat\", OrdinalIgnoreCase) : {"Cat".Equals("cat", StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase)}");

Results:

> dotnet run basics-12.cs
x > 4 : True, x == 5 : True, x != 5 : False
'a' < 'b' : True, 'Z' < 'a' : True, '9' < 'A' : True
codes : 'A'=65, 'a'=97, 'é'=233
n=-1, equal=False
"dog"==string1 : False, "dog"!=string2 : False
"Cat".CompareTo("Catkin") : -1
"élan".CompareTo("face") : -1
string.Compare("Cat", "cat") : 1
Ordinal("élan", "face") : 131
Ordinal("Cat", "cat") : -32
OrdinalIgnoreCase("Cat", "cat") : 0
"Cat".Equals("cat") : False
"Cat".Equals("cat", OrdinalIgnoreCase) : True

Comments:

  • line 3: a relational expression;
  • line 7: character comparison;
  • line 8: the [(int)] conversion of a character returns its Unicode code;
  • line 12: the variable [n] is assigned a negative integer because "cat" < "dog";
  • line 13: the variable [equal] has the value [true] if the two strings are equal, [false] otherwise;
  • Line 15: The operators == and != are used to check whether two strings are equal. In a string interpolation, \" represents a quotation mark;
  • line 16: the string that is exhausted first is the shorter one;
  • Lines 19–20: Comparisons based on French conventions: “élan” comes before “face,” and “Cat” comes after “cat” (when the number of letters is the same, lowercase letters come before uppercase ones);
  • lines 22–23: ordinal comparisons: the result here is the difference between the codes of the first differing characters: 233 – 102 = 131 and 67 – 99 = –32;
  • lines 25–27: when case is ignored, “Cat” and “cat” are equal.

docs.title: 3.4.5.5. Boolean expressions
docs.text:
The operators that can be used are AND (&&), OR (||), and NOT (!). The result of a Boolean expression is a Boolean value. Operator precedence:

  • ! ;
  • && ;
  • ||.
double x = 3.5;
bool valid = x > 2 && x < 4;

Relational operators have higher precedence than the && and || operators. These two operators evaluate their right-hand operand only if necessary: in [a && b], b is not evaluated if a is false; in [a || b], b is not evaluated if a is true. This is called “short-circuit evaluation.” Therefore, it is safe to write [text != null && text.Length > 0].

docs.title: 3.4.5.6. Bitwise Operations
docs.text:
Let [i] and [j] be two integers:

OperationRolei << nShifts i n bits to the left. The incoming bits are zerosi >> nShift i n bits to the right. If i is a signed integer ([sbyte], [short], [int], [long]), the sign bit is preservedi >>> nunsigned right shift (C# 11): the incoming bits are zeros, even if i is signedi & jperforms the bitwise logical AND of i and ji | jperforms the bitwise logical OR of i and j~icomplements i to 1i ^ jperforms the EXCLUSIVE OR operation on i and j bit by bit

The program [basics-13.cs] is as follows:

// bit manipulation
short i = 100, j = -13;
ushort k = 0xF123;
Console.WriteLine("i=0x{0:x4}, j=0x{1:x4}, k=0x{2:x4}", i, j, k);
Console.WriteLine("i<<4=0x{0:x4}, i>>4=0x{1:x4}, k>>4=0x{2:x4}", i << 4, i >> 4, k >> 4);
Console.WriteLine("i&j=0x{0:x4}, i|j=0x{1:x4}, i^j=0x{2:x4}, ~i=0x{3:x4}",
    (short)(i & j), (short)(i | j), (short)(i ^ j), (short)~i);
Console.WriteLine("j<<2=0x{0:x4}, j>>2=0x{1:x4}", (short)(j << 2), (short)(j >> 2));
// the same values in binary (B format, .NET 8)
Console.WriteLine($"i={i:B16}, j={j:B16}, i&j={(short)(i & j):B16}");
// unsigned right shift >>> (C# 11): the incoming bits are zeros
int m = -16;
Console.WriteLine($"m={m:B32}, m>>2={m >> 2:B32}, m>>>2={m >>> 2:B32}");

Results:

> dotnet run basics-13.cs
i=0x0064, j=0xfff3, k=0xf123
i<<4=0x0640, i>>4=0x0006, k>>4=0x0f12
i&j=0x0060, i|j=0xfff7, i^j=0xff97, ~i=0xff9b
j<<2=0xffcc, j>>2=0xfffc
i=0000000001100100, j=1111111111110011, i&j=0000000001100000
m=11111111111111111111111111110000, m>>2=11111111111111111111111111111100, m>>>2=00111111111111111111111111111100

Comments:

  • line 4: the format {0:x4} displays parameter #0 in hexadecimal (x) with 4 digits (4);
  • line 7: operations on the bits of a [short] result in a [int]; these are converted back to [short] to display 4 hexadecimal digits. Without conversion, ~i would be displayed as 8 digits (ffffff9b);
  • line 10: the B16 format displays a 16-digit binary integer. We check, bit by bit, the logical AND of i and j;
  • line 13: the [>>] shift preserves the sign bit of m, which is negative; the [>>>] shift fills with zeros.

docs.title: 3.4.5.7. Combination of Operators
docs.text: [a = a + b] can be written as [a += b]; [a = a - b] can be written as [a -= b]. The same applies to the operators /, %, *, <<, >>, >>>, &, |, ^. Thus, [a = a / 2;] can be written as [a /= 2;].

docs.title: 3.4.5.8. Increment and Decrement Operators
docs.text:
The notation [variable++] means [variable = variable + 1] or [variable += 1]. The notation [variable--] means [variable = variable - 1] or [variable -= 1]. When used in an expression, these operators have two forms:

  • [i++] (postfix): the value of the expression is the value of i before the increment;
  • [++i] (prefixed): the value of the expression is the value of i after the increment.

docs.title: 3.4.5.9. The ternary operator ?:
docs.text:
The expression [expr_cond ? expr1 : expr2] is evaluated as follows:

  • The expression [expr_cond] is evaluated. This is a Boolean expression;
  • if it is true, the value of the expression is that of [expr1], and [expr2] is not evaluated;
  • if it is false, the opposite occurs: the value of the expression is that of [expr2], and [expr1] is not evaluated.

The operation [i = (j > 4 ? j + 1 : j - 1);] will assign j+1 to the variable i if j > 4, and j-1 otherwise. This is the same as writing [if (j > 4) i = j + 1; else i = j - 1;], but it is more concise.

docs.title: 3.4.5.10. The operators ??, ??=, and ?.
docs.text:
These operators make it easier to work with values [null]:

  • [a ?? b] (C# 2) evaluates to a if a is not equal to [null], and b otherwise. It is used to provide a fallback value: [string name = Console.ReadLine() ?? "";]. The result is no longer nullable;
  • [a ??= b] (C# 8) assigns b to a only if a is equal to [null];
  • [a?.Member] (C# 6) is [null] if a is [null], otherwise [a.Member]. Thus, [text?.Length] does not cause an error when [text] is equal to [null]; the result is of type [int?].

The program [basics-14.cs] combines these different operators:

// other operators
// boolean expressions
double x = 3.5;
bool valid = x > 2 && x < 4;
Console.WriteLine($"valid={valid}, !valid={!valid}, valid || x > 10 : {valid || x > 10}");

// compound operators
int a = 10;
a += 5;
Console.Write($"a += 5 : {a}");
a *= 2;
Console.Write($", a *= 2 : {a}");
a /= 4;
Console.Write($", a /= 4 : {a}");
a %= 4;
Console.Write($", a %= 4 : {a}");
a <<= 2;
Console.WriteLine($", a <<= 2 : {a}");

// increment and decrement
int i = 5;
int j = i++;    // j receives the old value of i, then i is incremented
int k = ++i;    // i is incremented, then k receives the new value of i
Console.WriteLine($"i={i}, j={j}, k={k}");
i--;
Console.WriteLine($"i={i}");

// ternary operator
int n = 5;
int p = n > 4 ? n + 1 : n - 1;
string parity = n % 2 == 0 ? "even" : "odd";
Console.WriteLine($"p={p}, {n} is {parity}");

// ?? operator: replacement value if the left operand is null
string? input = null;
string name = input ?? "unknown";
int? age = null;
int displayedAge = age ?? -1;
Console.WriteLine($"name={name}, displayedAge={displayedAge}");
// ??= operator: assignment only if the variable is null
string? title = null;
title ??= "Untitled";
title ??= "Other title";
Console.WriteLine($"title={title}");
// ?. operator: access to a member only if the object is not null
string? text = null;
int? length = text?.Length;
Console.WriteLine($"length={length?.ToString() ?? "null"}");
text = "hello";
Console.WriteLine($"length={text?.Length}");

Results:

> dotnet run basics-14.cs
valid=True, !valid=False, valid || x > 10 : True
a += 5 : 15, a *= 2 : 30, a /= 4 : 7, a %= 4 : 3, a <<= 2 : 12
i=7, j=5, k=7
i=6
p=6, 5 is odd
name=unknown, displayedAge=-1
title=Untitled
length=null
length=5

Comments:

  • line 4: a Boolean expression;
  • lines 9–17: combined operators: 10+5=15, 15*2=30, 30/4=7 (integer division), 7%4=3, 3<<2=12;
  • line 22: [j] is assigned 5, then [i] is set to 6;
  • line 23: [i] goes to 7, then [k] receives 7;
  • lines 30–31: two ternary operators;
  • line 36: [input] equals [null]: [name] receives "unknown". The type of [name] is [string], not [string?];
  • line 38: the ?? operator allows you to convert from a [int?] to a [int] without risking an exception;
  • Lines 42–43: The first assignment occurs because [title] is equal to [null]; the second assignment does not occur;
  • line 47: [text] equals [null], so [length] does too;
  • line 48: the operators are combined: if [length] equals [null], the string "null" is displayed.

docs.title: 3.4.5.11. General Operator Precedence
docs.text:
The following table lists the operator precedence, from highest to lowest:

OperatorsAssociativity[x.y] [x?.y] [f(x)] [a[i]] [x++] [x--] [new] [typeof] [checked] [nameof]lr[+x] [-x] [!x] [~x] [++x] [--x] [^x] [(T)x] (type change)rl[x..y] (range)lr[switch] (switch expression)lr[*] [/] [%]lr[+] [-]lr[<<] [>>] [>>>]lr[<] [<=] [>] [>=] [is] [as]lr[==] [!=]lr[&]lr[^]lr[|]lr[&&]lr[||]lr[??]rl[? :] (ternary)rl[=] [+=] [-=] [??=] etc., [=>]rl

lr indicates that, when operators have equal precedence, left-to-right precedence is observed: when an expression contains operators of the same precedence, the operator farthest to the left is evaluated first. rl indicates right-to-left precedence. When in doubt, don’t hesitate to use parentheses: they also make the expression more readable.

docs.title: 3.4.5.12. Type Casting
docs.text:
In an expression, it is possible to temporarily change the representation of a value. This is called “type casting.” The syntax for changing the type of a value in an expression is as follows:

(type) value

The value then takes on the specified type. This results in a change in the value’s representation. We distinguish between:

  • Implicit conversions, performed automatically by the compiler when they do not result in any loss of information: from a [int] to a [long], from a [int] to a [double], from a [char] to a [int], and so on. The conversion from a [long] to a [double] is also implicit, although it may lose precision beyond 2⁵³;
  • explicit conversions, which may result in a loss of information and must be explicitly requested by the programmer using the (type) notation: from a [double] to a [int] (the decimal part is lost), from a [long] to a [int] (the most significant bits are lost), etc.

By default, an overflow in an integer calculation or an integer conversion is not reported: the result is simply false. The keyword [checked], on the other hand, causes an overflow to trigger a [OverflowException] exception. It applies to an expression, [checked(expression)], or to a block of instructions, [checked { ... }].

The program [basics-15.cs] is as follows:

// type changes
int i = 3, j = 4;
float f1 = i / j;
float f2 = (float)i / j;
Console.WriteLine($"f1={f1}, f2={f2}");

// implicit conversions: without loss of information
long l = i;
double d = l;
Console.WriteLine($"l={l}, d={d}");

// explicit conversions (cast): possible loss of information
double real = 3.99;
int truncated = (int)real;
int rounded = (int)Math.Round(real);
Console.WriteLine($"(int)3.99={truncated}, (int)Math.Round(3.99)={rounded}");
long large = 3_000_000_000;
int overflowed = (int)large;
Console.WriteLine($"(int)3000000000={overflowed}");

// characters and integers
char c = (char)65;
int code = 'é';
Console.WriteLine($"(char)65={c}, code of 'é'={code}");

// overflow: silent by default
int max = int.MaxValue;
int next = max + 1;
Console.WriteLine($"int.MaxValue + 1 = {next}");
// checked: the overflow causes an exception
try
{
    int verified = checked(max + 1);
    Console.WriteLine($"verified={verified}");
}
catch (OverflowException e)
{
    Console.WriteLine($"checked(max + 1) : {e.GetType().Name} - {e.Message}");
}
try
{
    checked
    {
        int conversion = (int)large;
        Console.WriteLine($"conversion={conversion}");
    }
}
catch (OverflowException e)
{
    Console.WriteLine($"checked((int)large) : {e.GetType().Name} - {e.Message}");
}

Results:

> dotnet run basics-15.cs
f1=0, f2=0,75
l=3, d=3
(int)3.99=3, (int)Math.Round(3.99)=4
(int)3000000000=-1294967296
(char)65=A, code of 'é'=233
int.MaxValue + 1 = -2147483648
checked(max + 1) : OverflowException - Arithmetic operation resulted in an overflow.
checked((int)large) : OverflowException - Arithmetic operation resulted in an overflow.

Comments:

  • Line 3: [f1] will have the value 0. The division 3/4 is an integer division since both operands are of type [int]; its result, 0, is then converted to [float];
  • Line 4: [(float)i] is the value of [i] converted to [float]. We now have a division between a real number of type [float] and an integer of type [int]: the value of [j] is also transformed into [float], and then the two real numbers are divided. [f2] has a value of 0.75. In the operation [(float)i], [i] is a value encoded exactly as a 4-byte number, while [(float)i] is the same value encoded as an approximate 4-byte real number. This transcoding occurs only during the calculation: the variable [i] always retains its type [int];
  • lines 8–9: implicit conversions;
  • line 14: converting a floating-point number to an integer truncates the decimal part;
  • line 15: to round, we use [Math.Round], which yields a [double], then we convert;
  • line 18: 3 billion does not fit into a [int]: only the least significant 32 bits are retained, and the result no longer makes sense;
  • Lines 22–23: Conversions between characters and Unicode codes; the second is implicit;
  • line 28: the capacity overflow goes unnoticed: the smallest possible [int] is obtained;
  • line 33: with [checked], the overflow triggers a [OverflowException] exception;
  • lines 42–45: a block of [checked]: the conversion of [large] to [int] also throws an exception.

If the overflow occurs in an expression consisting solely of constants, such as [int.MaxValue + 1], the compiler detects it and rejects the program.

docs.title: 3.5.1. Stop
docs.text:
The [Exit] method of the [Environment] class allows you to stop the execution of a program:

Environment.Exit(int status);

[Exit] terminates the current process and returns control to the calling process, which is typically the command interpreter. The value of [status], known as the return code, can be used by the command interpreter. By convention, 0 indicates that the program completed successfully, while any other value indicates an error. On Windows, the return code is available in the [%ERRORLEVEL%] variable at the command prompt and in the [$LASTEXITCODE] variable within PowerShell; on Linux and macOS, it is available in the [$?] variable of the shell. Thus:

Environment.Exit(0);

will terminate the program with a return code of 0. With high-level statements, a [return] statement also terminates the program (return code 0), unless it is located within a function.

The program [basics-16.cs] receives its return code as an argument:

// stopping the program with an exit code
Console.WriteLine("Start of the program");
// the exit code is passed as an argument (see the section on program arguments)
if (args.Length == 0 || !int.TryParse(args[0], out int code))
{
    Console.Error.WriteLine("Syntax : dotnet run basics-16.cs -- exit_code");
    Environment.Exit(1);
    return;
}
Console.WriteLine($"Stopping with exit code {code}");
Environment.Exit(code);
Console.WriteLine("This line is never executed");

Results in a bash terminal:

> dotnet run basics-16.cs -- 3
Start of the program
Stopping with exit code 3
> echo $?
3
> dotnet run basics-16.cs
Start of the program
Syntax : dotnet run basics-16.cs -- exit_code
> echo $?
1

Comments:

  • line 4: We check that an argument has been passed and that it is an integer. The program’s arguments are described later;
  • line 7: if this is not the case, the program terminates with a return code of 1;
  • line 8: this instruction will never be executed, but the compiler does not know that [Environment.Exit] never returns control. Without it, the compiler would assume that the next line could be reached with an uninitialized [code] variable and would reject the program;
  • line 11: terminates with the return code passed as an argument. The following line is not executed;
  • lines 4–9: The command [echo $?] displays the return code of the last program executed: 3, then 1.

docs.title: 3.5.2. Simple decision structure
docs.text:
if (condition)
{
    actions_condition_true;
}
else
{
    actions_condition_false;
}

Notes:

  • the condition is enclosed in parentheses;
  • each action ends with a semicolon;
