<-- <body><h1>Welcome to the test server of the C# course</h1></body>
<-- </html>
bye
  • line 7: the document is announced along with its size, 169 bytes. The client thus knows where it ends;
  • line 16: the document has been fully received, but the server has not closed the connection: in HTTP/1.1, it remains open by default for other requests. The server is waiting for a new request; the user then types [bye] to close the connection.

When the server is unavailable, the connection fails:

> dotnet run internet-06.cs -- localhost 27199
Unable to connect to the service (localhost, 27199): Connection refused

The reader can use this generic TCP client with the echo server, or, if they have an SMTP or POP3 server that accepts unencrypted connections (such as a locally installed test server), to reproduce the sample dialogs shown above.

docs.title: 12.6.4. A generic TCP server
docs.text:
We will now focus on a server:

  • that displays on the screen the lines sent by its clients;
  • which sends back as responses the lines of text typed on the keyboard by a user. The user, therefore, acts as the server.

The program is launched in a command window via [dotnet run internet-07.cs -- port], where [port] is the port to which clients must connect. Service to a client is provided by two processes:

  • the main program:
    • processes clients one after another, not in parallel. Because the console cannot be used by two clients simultaneously, our server processes only one client at a time. Clients who connect during this time have their connection established by the system but must wait for the program to accept them;
    • reads the lines typed by the user on the keyboard and sends them to the client. The user signals with the command [bye] that they are closing the connection with the client;
  • A separate task is dedicated exclusively to reading the lines of text sent by the client.

The server never stops, unless the user presses Ctrl-C on the keyboard.

The program [internet-07.cs] is as follows:

using System.Net;
using System.Net.Sockets;

// generic TCP server
// - displays the lines sent by the client
// - sends it as responses the lines typed on the keyboard by the user
// the clients are served one after the other (a single console)
// call: dotnet run internet-07.cs -- port

const string syntax = "Syntax: dotnet run internet-07.cs -- port";
if (args.Length != 1 || !int.TryParse(args[0], out int port) || port is < 1 or > 65535)
{
    Console.WriteLine(syntax);
    return;
}

// the listening service
var listener = new TcpListener(IPAddress.Any, port);
listener.Start();
Console.WriteLine($"Generic server started on {listener.LocalEndpoint}");

// the keyboard input in progress (it can outlive the connection of a client)
Task<string?>? input = null;
// service loop - the server is stopped by Ctrl-C
while (true)
{
    // wait for a client
    Console.WriteLine("Waiting for the next client...");
    using TcpClient client = await listener.AcceptTcpClientAsync();
    Console.WriteLine($"Client {client.Client.RemoteEndPoint}");
    NetworkStream stream = client.GetStream();
    var writer = new StreamWriter(stream) { AutoFlush = true, NewLine = "\r\n" };
    // a separate task displays the lines sent by the client
    Task reception = ReceiveAsync(new StreamReader(stream));
    // the reading of the responses on the keyboard is done in the main program
    Console.WriteLine("Type your responses (bye to close the connection with the client):");
    try
    {
        while (true)
        {
            // we launch a keyboard input if none is in progress
            input ??= Task.Run(Console.ReadLine);
            // we wait either for a line typed on the keyboard, or for the departure of the client
            if (await Task.WhenAny(input, reception) == reception)
            {
                // the input in progress will serve the next client
                Console.WriteLine("[the client has closed the connection]");
                break;
            }
            string? response = await input;
            input = null;
            // end of the keyboard input (Ctrl-D, Ctrl-Z): server stop
            if (response is null)
            {
                listener.Stop();
                return;
            }
            // end of the connection with this client?
            if (response.Trim().Equals("bye", StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase))
            {
                Console.WriteLine("[connection closed by the server]");
                break;
            }
            // we send the response to the client
            await writer.WriteLineAsync(response);
        }
    }
    catch (IOException ex)
    {
        Console.WriteLine($"The following error occurred while writing: {ex.Message}");
    }
    // we close the connection with the client
    client.Close();
    await reception;
}

// --------------------------------------------------------------------
// displays the lines sent by the client until the connection is closed
static async Task ReceiveAsync(StreamReader reader)
{
    try
    {
        while (await reader.ReadLineAsync() is string request)
        {
            Console.WriteLine($"<-- {request}");
        }
    }
    catch (Exception ex) when (ex is IOException or ObjectDisposedException)
    {
        // the connection was closed during the reading: the task ends
    }
}
  • lines 18–19: the listening service is created and started. It listens on all of the machine’s network interfaces;
  • line 23: current keyboard input. It is declared outside the client loop, for a reason explained below;
  • line 25: infinite loop waiting for clients. The user will stop the server by pressing Ctrl-C;
  • line 29: waiting for a client. When a client arrives, the [TcpClient] instance returned by [AcceptTcpClientAsync] represents the server side of the open connection with that client. The [using] declaration releases it at the end of each loop iteration;
  • line 34: Reading the lines sent by the client is handled by a separate task, as in the generic client;
  • lines 39–65: the loop for entering responses via the keyboard to be sent to the client;
  • Line 42: The [??=] operator (C# 8) initiates a new input only if no input is currently in progress. In fact, when a client closes the connection (line 44), the program moves on to the next client without waiting for an input, and the keyboard input process initiated for the previous client is still in progress: it will be used by the next client. Initiating a second one would cause two input processes to compete for the same keystrokes;
  • line 53: if the standard input is closed, the server stops;
  • line 59: the command [bye] closes the connection with the current client;
  • line 65: the typed line is sent to the client;
  • lines 73–74: Close the connection and wait for the read operation to finish;
  • lines 79–90: the method that continuously displays on the console the lines of text sent by the client. This is similar to what we saw for the generic TCP client.

The 2008 course used this server to simulate a web server queried by a browser. We’ll do the same, replacing the browser with [curl]. The generic server is running on port 27101. In another window, we ask [curl] for the URL [http://localhost:27101/example.html]. [curl] then connects to port 27101 on the [localhost] machine and requests the document [/example.html]. Here is the server window:

> dotnet run internet-07.cs -- 27101
Generic server started on 0.0.0.0:27101
Waiting for the next client...
Client 127.0.0.1:52208
<-- GET /example.html HTTP/1.1
<-- Host: localhost:27101
<-- User-Agent: curl/8.5.0
<-- Accept: */*
<-- 
Type your responses (bye to close the connection with the client):
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Server: generic tcp server
Connection: close
Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8

<html><head><title>Generic server</title></head>
<body><h1>Response of the generic server</h1></body></html>
bye
[connection closed by the server]
Waiting for the next client...
  • line 4: a client has arrived;
  • lines 5–8: we see the HTTP request sent by [curl], ending with a blank line. A browser would send many more headers (supported languages and formats, compression, cookies, etc.): the reader can test this by requesting the same URL from their browser;
  • Lines 10–17: The user at the keyboard is the actual server here, and they craft the response manually. They stick to the bare minimum: a status line, three headers, a blank line, and the HTML document. They do not specify the document size ([Content-Length]) but indicate that they will close the connection after sending it ([Connection: close]). This is sufficient: when the client sees the connection close, it will know that the response is complete;
  • line 19: the user typed [bye]: the server closes the connection with the client;
  • line 20: the server waits for a new client. We stop it with Ctrl-C.

And here is what [curl] displayed:

> curl -v http://localhost:27101/example.html
* Host localhost:27101 was resolved.
* IPv6: ::1
* IPv4: 127.0.0.1
*   Trying 127.0.0.1:27101...
* Connected to localhost (127.0.0.1) port 27101
> GET /example.html HTTP/1.1
> Host: localhost:27101
> User-Agent: curl/8.5.0
> Accept: */*
> 
< HTTP/1.1 200 OK
< Server: generic tcp server
< Connection: close
< Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8
< 
<html><head><title>Generic server</title></head>
<body><h1>Response of the generic server</h1></body></html>
* Closing connection

[curl] received exactly what was typed into the server window (lines 12–18) and detected that the connection was closed (line 19). A browser would have displayed the received HTML page, with the title [Generic server] in the tab.

docs.title: 12.6.5. A web client
docs.text:
In the previous example, we saw the HTTP headers sent by [curl]. We’re going to write a web client that takes a URL as a parameter and displays on the screen everything the server sends it. We’ll assume that the server supports the HTTP/1.1 protocol. Our client will send the following request:

GET /document HTTP/1.1
Host: machine:port
User-Agent: web-client-csharp-course
Connection: close
  • the first line specifies the desired document;
  • the header [Host] identifies the server being queried;
  • the header [User-Agent] identifies our client;
  • the header [Connection] indicates that we want the server to close the connection after responding to us: we will read its response until the end of the stream;
  • the blank line terminates the request.

If, in the first line, we replace [GET] with [HEAD], the server will send us only the HTTP headers from its response, and not the document.

Our web client will be called as follows: [dotnet run internet-08.cs -- URL command], where [URL] is the desired URL and [command] is one of the two keywords [GET] or [HEAD]. The program [internet-08.cs] is as follows:

using System.Net.Sockets;

// web client: requests a URL with an HTTP/1.1 request written "by hand"
// and displays everything the server sends back (HTTP headers and document)
// call: dotnet run internet-08.cs -- URL GET|HEAD

const string syntax = "Syntax: dotnet run internet-08.cs -- http://machine[:port][/document] GET|HEAD";
if (args.Length != 2)
{
    Console.WriteLine(syntax);
    return;
}

// check of the URL: it must be absolute and use the http scheme
if (!Uri.TryCreate(args[0], UriKind.Absolute, out Uri? uri) || uri.Scheme != Uri.UriSchemeHttp)
{
    Console.WriteLine($"Incorrect URL [{args[0]}]. {syntax}");
    return;
}
// check of the command
string command = args[1].ToUpper();
if (command is not ("GET" or "HEAD"))
{
    Console.WriteLine($"The second parameter must be GET or HEAD. {syntax}");
    return;
}

try
{
    // connection to the web server
    using var client = new TcpClient();
    await client.ConnectAsync(uri.Host, uri.Port);
    await using NetworkStream stream = client.GetStream();
    using var reader = new StreamReader(stream);
    // HTTP requires the \r\n line ending (Environment.NewLine is \n under Linux)
    await using var writer = new StreamWriter(stream) { NewLine = "\r\n" };
    // the request: command line, HTTP headers, empty line
    await writer.WriteLineAsync($"{command} {uri.PathAndQuery} HTTP/1.1");
    await writer.WriteLineAsync($"Host: {uri.Authority}");
    await writer.WriteLineAsync("User-Agent: web-client-csharp-course");
    await writer.WriteLineAsync("Connection: close");
    await writer.WriteLineAsync();
    // the request leaves on the network in one go
    await writer.FlushAsync();
    // the response is read until the server closes the connection
    while (await reader.ReadLineAsync() is string line)
    {
        Console.WriteLine(line);
    }
}
catch (SocketException ex)
{
    Console.WriteLine($"The following error occurred: {ex.SocketErrorCode} ({ex.Message})");
}
catch (IOException ex)
{
    Console.WriteLine($"The following error occurred: {ex.Message}");
}

A new feature of this program is the use of the class [Uri] (namespace [System]). The program receives a URL (Uniform Resource Locator), a specific form of URI (Uniform Resource Identifier), in the form [http://server:port/path?param1=val1&param2=val2]. The [Uri] class allows this string to be broken down into its various components:

  • Line 15: [Uri.TryCreate] constructs a [Uri] object from the string [args[0]] and returns [false] if the string is not a valid absolute URI (missing scheme, server, etc.). The 2008 course used the constructor [new Uri(...)] within a [try/catch]; [TryCreate] prevents the exception. We also verify that the scheme is [http]: our client cannot perform the TLS negotiation for [https]. Once the [Uri] object is constructed, we have access to the various elements of the URI. Thus, if the [uri] object was constructed from the string [http://localhost:27110/hello?name=Serge], we have:
    • [uri.Scheme]: http;
    • [uri.Host]: localhost;
    • [uri.Port]: 27110 (80 if the port is not specified in the URL, 443 for HTTPS);
    • [uri.Authority]: localhost:27110 (the port is omitted if it is the scheme's default port);
    • [uri.AbsolutePath]: /hello;
    • [uri.Query]: ?name=Serge;
    • [uri.PathAndQuery]: /hello?name=Serge;
  • line 22: the pattern [not (... or ...)] (C# 9) checks that the command is [GET] or [HEAD];
  • line 32: connects to the server specified by the URL;
  • line 36: HTTP requires \r\n line endings;
  • lines 38–42: the HTTP request;
  • line 44: [AutoFlush] was not used: the request is sent in one go, after being fully written;
  • lines 46–48: the response is displayed until the server closes the connection.

Let’s request only the headers from the root of our test server:

> dotnet run internet-08.cs -- http://localhost:27110/ HEAD
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Length: 169
Connection: close
Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8
Date: Sat, 03 Oct 2026 09:49:51 GMT
Server: Kestrel

We get the status line and the headers, followed by a blank line, but not the document. The header [Content-Length] gives the size the document would have had with the command [GET]. With the command [GET] and a document sent in chunks:

> dotnet run internet-08.cs -- "http://localhost:27110/hello?name=Serge" GET
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Connection: close
Content-Type: text/plain; charset=utf-8
Date: Sat, 03 Oct 2026 09:49:53 GMT
Server: Kestrel
Transfer-Encoding: chunked

c
Hello Serge!
0

Note the quotation marks around the URL in the command: without them, some command interpreters would assign a specific meaning to the character [?]. The document ([Hello Serge!]) is framed by the sizes of its chunks, as we have already seen. Our client displays the raw response; a true HTTP client, on the other hand, must reconstruct the document from the chunks.

A non-existent document:

> dotnet run internet-08.cs -- http://localhost:27110/unknown GET
HTTP/1.1 404 Not Found
Content-Length: 0
Connection: close
Date: Sat, 03 Oct 2026 09:49:54 GMT
Server: Kestrel

A URL that is subject to a redirect:

> dotnet run internet-08.cs -- http://localhost:27110/old GET
HTTP/1.1 302 Found
Content-Length: 0
Connection: close
Date: Sat, 03 Oct 2026 09:49:56 GMT
Server: Kestrel
Location: /hello?name=visitor
  • Line 2: Code 302 indicates a redirect; the requested document is temporarily located at a different address;
  • line 7: this address is provided by the header [Location]. It is relative here: the full address is [http://localhost:27110/hello?name=visitor].

Our client stopped there. A browser, on the other hand, would have automatically requested the new address. That is what our next client will do.

Finally, a request for an [https] URL is rejected:

> dotnet run internet-08.cs -- https://learn.microsoft.com/ GET
Incorrect URL [https://learn.microsoft.com/]. Syntax: dotnet run internet-08.cs -- http://machine[:port][/document] GET|HEAD

docs.title: 12.6.6. A web client that handles redirects
docs.text:
The previous web client does not handle a possible redirect from the URL it requested. The redirect status codes are as follows:

CodeMeaning301 Moved PermanentlyThe document has permanently moved to a new address; a browser can save the new address302 FoundThe document is temporarily located at a different address303 See OtherThe response must be requested from another address using the [GET] method (used after submitting a form)307 Temporary Redirect, 308 Permanent RedirectSame as 302 and 301, but the client must resend the request using the same method ([POST] remains [POST])

In any case, the new address is provided by the [Location] header, either as an absolute or relative URL. The 2008 client detected a redirect based on the presence of the word [moved] in the status line. This is unreliable: the message following the code is arbitrary, and Kestrel responds with [302 Found], without the word [moved]. We rely on the status code itself.

The program [internet-09.cs] is as follows:

using System.Net.Sockets;

// web client that follows the redirections (codes 301, 302, 303, 307, 308)
// call: dotnet run internet-09.cs -- URL GET|HEAD

const string syntax = "Syntax: dotnet run internet-09.cs -- http://machine[:port][/document] GET|HEAD";
if (args.Length != 2)
{
    Console.WriteLine(syntax);
    return;
}
if (!Uri.TryCreate(args[0], UriKind.Absolute, out Uri? uri) || uri.Scheme != Uri.UriSchemeHttp)
{
    Console.WriteLine($"Incorrect URL [{args[0]}]. {syntax}");
    return;
}
string command = args[1].ToUpper();
if (command is not ("GET" or "HEAD"))
{
    Console.WriteLine($"The second parameter must be GET or HEAD. {syntax}");
    return;
}

// the HTTP status codes that signal a redirection
int[] redirectionCodes = [301, 302, 303, 307, 308];
// maximum number of redirections followed
const int maxRedirections = 3;

try
{
    // one iteration per requested URL
    for (int nbRedirections = 0; ; nbRedirections++)
    {
        // we request the URL and get the possible redirection address
        string? location = await RequestAsync(uri, command, redirectionCodes);
        // no redirection: it is finished
        if (location is null)
        {
            break;
        }
        // too many redirections: we give up
        if (nbRedirections == maxRedirections)
        {
            Console.WriteLine($"<-- Giving up: more than {maxRedirections} redirections -->");
            break;
        }
        // the new URL: the redirection address can be absolute or relative to the current URL
        uri = new Uri(uri, location);
        Console.WriteLine($"<-- Redirection to {uri} -->{Environment.NewLine}");
    }
}
catch (SocketException ex)
{
    Console.WriteLine($"The following error occurred: {ex.SocketErrorCode} ({ex.Message})");
}
catch (Exception ex) when (ex is IOException or UriFormatException)
{
    Console.WriteLine($"The following error occurred: {ex.Message}");
}

// --------------------------------------------------------------------
// requests the URL [uri], displays the server's response
// returns the redirection address, or null if there is no redirection
static async Task<string?> RequestAsync(Uri uri, string command, int[] redirectionCodes)
{
    using var client = new TcpClient();
    await client.ConnectAsync(uri.Host, uri.Port);
    await using NetworkStream stream = client.GetStream();
    using var reader = new StreamReader(stream);
    await using var writer = new StreamWriter(stream) { NewLine = "\r\n" };
    // the HTTP request
    await writer.WriteLineAsync($"{command} {uri.PathAndQuery} HTTP/1.1");
    await writer.WriteLineAsync($"Host: {uri.Authority}");
    await writer.WriteLineAsync("User-Agent: web-client-csharp-course");
    await writer.WriteLineAsync("Connection: close");
    await writer.WriteLineAsync();
    await writer.FlushAsync();

    // the status line, for example: HTTP/1.1 302 Found
    string statusLine = await reader.ReadLineAsync() ?? "";
    Console.WriteLine(statusLine);
    string[] fields = statusLine.Split(' ');
    bool redirection = fields.Length >= 2 && int.TryParse(fields[1], out int code)
        && redirectionCodes.Contains(code);

    // the HTTP headers, up to the empty line
    string? location = null;
    while (await reader.ReadLineAsync() is string header && header != "")
    {
        Console.WriteLine(header);
        // the name of an HTTP header is case-insensitive
        if (redirection && header.StartsWith("Location:", StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase))
        {
            location = header["Location:".Length..].Trim();
        }
    }
    Console.WriteLine();
    // the possible document
    while (await reader.ReadLineAsync() is string line)
    {
        Console.WriteLine(line);
    }
    return location;
}

Compared to the previous version, the changes are as follows:

  • line 25: status codes that indicate a redirect;
  • line 27: the maximum number of consecutive redirects. Without a limit, a misconfigured server could trap our client in an infinite loop (browsers give up after about twenty redirects);
  • line 32: the code that was previously executed for a single URL can now be executed successively for multiple URLs;
  • line 35: the [RequestAsync] method requests the current URL, displays the response, and returns the redirect URL—or [null] if there is no redirect;
  • lines 42–44: the process aborts if the maximum number of redirects is reached;
  • line 48: the [Uri(Uri base, string relative)] constructor calculates the new URL. If [location] is an absolute address, it is used as is; if it is relative, it is completed based on the current URL, [uri]. The 2008 course distinguished between the two cases with a test: the compiler handles this;
  • lines 64–103: the request for a URL:
    • line 80: read the status line, for example [HTTP/1.1 302 Found];
    • lines 82–84: extract the code (the second field in the line) and check if it is one of the redirection codes;
    • lines 88–94: read the headers up to the empty line. If there is a redirection, search for the header [Location], ignoring case since the header names in HTTP are case-insensitive. The expression [header["Location:".Length..]] uses a range (C# 8) to extract what follows the header name;
    • lines 98–103: the rest of the response is displayed, then the found redirect URL is returned.

Let’s revisit the URL [/old]:

> dotnet run internet-09.cs -- http://localhost:27110/old GET
HTTP/1.1 302 Found
Content-Length: 0
Connection: close
Date: Sat, 03 Oct 2026 09:50:00 GMT
Server: Kestrel
Location: /hello?name=visitor

<-- Redirection to http://localhost:27110/hello?name=visitor -->

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Connection: close
Content-Type: text/plain; charset=utf-8
Date: Sat, 03 Oct 2026 09:50:00 GMT
Server: Kestrel
Transfer-Encoding: chunked

e
Hello visitor!
0
  • lines 2–7: the temporary redirect to a relative address;
  • line 9: the new URL, supplemented by [new Uri(uri, location)];
  • lines 11–19: the response to the new URL. The document, 0x0e = 14 bytes in size, was sent in chunks.

The URL [/moved] is permanently redirected to an absolute address:

> dotnet run internet-09.cs -- http://localhost:27110/moved GET
HTTP/1.1 301 Moved Permanently
Content-Length: 0
Connection: close
Date: Sat, 03 Oct 2026 09:50:02 GMT
Server: Kestrel
Location: http://localhost:27110/

<-- Redirection to http://localhost:27110/ -->

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Length: 169
Connection: close
Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8
Date: Sat, 03 Oct 2026 09:50:02 GMT
Server: Kestrel

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head><meta charset="utf-8"><title>Test server</title></head>
<body><h1>Welcome to the test server of the C# course</h1></body>
</html>

The URL [/loop] redirects to itself:

> dotnet run internet-09.cs -- http://localhost:27110/loop HEAD
HTTP/1.1 302 Found
Connection: close
Date: Sat, 03 Oct 2026 09:50:04 GMT
Server: Kestrel
Location: /loop

<-- Redirection to http://localhost:27110/loop -->

HTTP/1.1 302 Found
Connection: close
Date: Sat, 03 Oct 2026 09:50:04 GMT
Server: Kestrel
Location: /loop

<-- Redirection to http://localhost:27110/loop -->

HTTP/1.1 302 Found
Connection: close
Date: Sat, 03 Oct 2026 09:50:04 GMT
Server: Kestrel
Location: /loop

<-- Redirection to http://localhost:27110/loop -->

HTTP/1.1 302 Found
Connection: close
Date: Sat, 03 Oct 2026 09:50:04 GMT
Server: Kestrel
Location: /loop

<-- Giving up: more than 3 redirections -->

Our client followed three redirects, then gave up (line 32). With the command [HEAD], no document was sent.

The web server log recorded all requests for the entries [A web client] and [A web client that handles redirects]:

> dotnet run internet-03.cs
Web server started on http://localhost:27110
HEAD / HTTP/1.1 -> 200
GET /hello?name=Serge HTTP/1.1 -> 200
GET /unknown HTTP/1.1 -> 404
GET /old HTTP/1.1 -> 302
GET /old HTTP/1.1 -> 302
GET /hello?name=visitor HTTP/1.1 -> 200
GET /moved HTTP/1.1 -> 301
GET / HTTP/1.1 -> 200
HEAD /loop HTTP/1.1 -> 302
HEAD /loop HTTP/1.1 -> 302
HEAD /loop HTTP/1.1 -> 302
HEAD /loop HTTP/1.1 -> 302

For each redirection, it shows the request that triggered it, followed by the request to the new address (lines 7–8), and the four requests from the interrupted loop (lines 11–14).

Writing an HTTP client based on TCP helps you understand the protocol, but a real client must handle many other things: TLS encryption, chunked transmission, compression, persistent connections, HTTP/2, and HTTP/3… The second part of this chapter introduces the [HttpClient] class from .NET, which handles all of this for us.

docs.title: 12.7. The .NET classes specialized for a protocol
docs.text:
In the previous examples, the HTTP protocol was handled using a TCP client: we had to construct the requests ourselves, parse the status lines and headers, and track redirects. We could have built an SMTP or POP client in the same way. .NET provides classes specialized for the HTTP and SMTP protocols. These classes understand the communication protocol between the client and the server, sparing the developer from having to manage it. We will now present them.

The programs in this second part, like those in the first, are single-file applications in the [12-internet] folder, numbered consecutively ([internet-10.cs] through [internet-19.cs]). The sample application at the end of the chapter constitutes a separate solution, [TaxV8]. The ports used are in the form 272xx.

docs.title: 12.7.1. The classes WebClient and WebRequest, now obsolete
docs.text:
The 2008 course presented two families of classes:

  • Class [WebClient], which requested a document in a single instruction (methods [DownloadString], [DownloadData], [DownloadFile], [OpenRead]) or sent one (methods [UploadString], [UploadValues] for a form…);
  • the classes [WebRequest] / [WebResponse] and their derivatives [HttpWebRequest] / [HttpWebResponse], which were more flexible: they allowed you to choose the HTTP method ([GET], [HEAD], [POST]), add headers, and read the response as it arrives.

These classes still exist in .NET 10 for compatibility, but they have been marked as deprecated since .NET 6. The following small program uses them:

using System.Net;

using var client = new WebClient();
Console.WriteLine(client.DownloadString("http://localhost:27210/"));
var request = WebRequest.Create("http://localhost:27210/");

Compiling it produces the following two warnings (we are reproducing only these two lines from the [dotnet build] output):

> dotnet build webclient.cs
webclient.cs(3,20): warning SYSLIB0014: 'WebClient.WebClient()' is obsolete: 'WebRequest, HttpWebRequest, ServicePoint, and WebClient are obsolete. Use HttpClient instead.' (https://aka.ms/dotnet-warnings/SYSLIB0014)
webclient.cs(5,15): warning SYSLIB0014: 'WebRequest.Create(string)' is obsolete: 'WebRequest, HttpWebRequest, ServicePoint, and WebClient are obsolete. Use HttpClient instead.' (https://aka.ms/dotnet-warnings/SYSLIB0014)

The message is clear: you must use the [HttpClient] class. This class was introduced with .NET 4.5 (2012); it was designed from the outset for asynchronous programming (all of its network methods are asynchronous), supports HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, and HTTP/3, reuses its connections, and can be used by multiple tasks simultaneously. In the current .NET, [WebClient], and [WebRequest] are, in fact, nothing more than facades built on top of [HttpClient]. We will not examine them further and will instead resume with [HttpClient], using the examples that the 2008 course covered with them.

docs.title: 12.7.2.1. A Test Web Server
docs.text:
To illustrate the capabilities of [HttpClient], we need a more feature-rich web server than the one from Part 1 ([internet-03.cs]): it must accept forms, exchange JSON, and be able to handle delays. So we’ll write a second test server, [internet-10.cs], an ASP.NET Core application named “Minimal API,” just like the first one. Again, it’s not necessary to understand this program in detail for now (ASP.NET Core will be covered in the next chapter): all you need to know is what each URL responds with.

#:sdk Microsoft.NET.Sdk.Web
#:property PublishAot=false

// a local web server that will serve as a target for the HttpClient clients
// call: dotnet run internet-10.cs [-- port]
int port = args.Length == 1 && int.TryParse(args[0], out int p) ? p : 27210;

var builder = WebApplication.CreateBuilder(args);
// no ASP.NET log (only the warnings): we write our own
builder.Logging.SetMinimumLevel(LogLevel.Warning);
var app = builder.Build();

// console tracking: each request, the client's port and the status code of the response
app.Use(async (context, next) =>
{
    var request = context.Request;
    string start = $"{request.Method} {request.Path}{request.QueryString} {request.Protocol}"
        + $" (client port {context.Connection.RemotePort})";
    try
    {
        await next(context);
        Console.WriteLine($"{start} -> {context.Response.StatusCode}");
    }
    catch (OperationCanceledException) when (context.RequestAborted.IsCancellationRequested)
    {
        // the client gave up the request before the response
        Console.WriteLine($"{start} -> abandoned by the client");
    }
});

// the consultation URLs accept the GET and HEAD methods
string[] getHead = ["GET", "HEAD"];

// the home page: an HTML document
app.MapMethods("/", getHead, () => Results.Content("""
    <!DOCTYPE html>
    <html lang="en">
    <head><meta charset="utf-8"><title>Test server</title></head>
    <body><h1>Welcome to the HttpClient test server</h1></body>
    </html>

    """, "text/html; charset=utf-8"));

// a text document built from a parameter of the URL
app.MapMethods("/hello", getHead, (string? name) => $"Hello {name ?? "unknown"}!");

// the HTTP headers received by the server, sent back to the client as text
app.MapMethods("/headers", getHead, (HttpRequest request) =>
    string.Join("\n", request.Headers.Select(header => $"{header.Key}: {header.Value}")));

// temporary redirection (302) to a relative address
app.MapMethods("/old", getHead, () => Results.Redirect("/hello?name=visitor"));

// a redirection that loops on itself
app.MapMethods("/loop", getHead, () => Results.Redirect("/loop"));

// a server error (500 Internal Server Error)
app.MapMethods("/error", getHead, () => Results.StatusCode(500));

// a response that takes its time
app.MapGet("/slow", async (int seconds, CancellationToken token) =>
{
    await Task.Delay(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(seconds), token);
    return $"Response obtained after {seconds} s";
});

// a form sent by POST: we describe what was received
app.MapPost("/form", async (HttpRequest request) =>
{
    IFormCollection form = await request.ReadFormAsync();
    string fields = string.Join(", ", form.Select(field => $"{field.Key}=[{field.Value}]"));
    return $"Content-Type received: {request.ContentType}\nFields received: {fields}";
});

// any text sent by POST: we send it back in upper case
app.MapPost("/text", async (HttpRequest request) =>
{
    using var reader = new StreamReader(request.Body);
    string text = await reader.ReadToEndAsync();
    return $"Content-Type received: {request.ContentType}\nText received in upper case: {text.ToUpper()}";
});

// a small "database" of persons, exchanged in JSON format
List<Person> persons = [new(1, "Dupont", 42), new(2, "Durand", 35)];
Lock padlock = new();

// the list of persons
app.MapGet("/api/persons", () =>
{
    lock (padlock)
    {
        return persons.ToList();
    }
});

// a person designated by its number, or 404 if it does not exist
app.MapGet("/api/persons/{id:int}", (int id) =>
{
    lock (padlock)
    {
        return persons.Find(person => person.Id == id) is Person person
            ? Results.Ok(person)
            : Results.NotFound();
    }
});

// addition of a person: the server assigns it a number and answers 201 Created
app.MapPost("/api/persons", (Person newPerson) =>
{
    lock (padlock)
    {
        Person created = newPerson with { Id = persons.Max(person => person.Id) + 1 };
        persons.Add(created);
        return Results.Created($"/api/persons/{created.Id}", created);
    }
});

// any other URL gets the 404 Not Found response (default behaviour)
Console.WriteLine($"Web server started on http://localhost:{port}");
app.Run($"http://127.0.0.1:{port}");

// a person
record Person(int Id, string Name, int Age);

Comments:

  • line 2: Single-file applications are configured by default for native compilation (AOT), which disables reflection-based serialization (JSON). As in Chapter 5, we re-enable it: the server will be able to automatically convert its objects to JSON;
  • Lines 14–27: Each request is logged to the console along with the client’s port and the response status code. The client’s port will allow us to determine whether two requests used the same TCP connection. If the client aborts a request before receiving a response, Kestrel revokes the token [RequestAborted], and the current operation ends with an [OperationCanceledException]: we display this as well;
  • line 35: the URL [/] returns a small HTML document;
  • line 45: URL [/hello?name=xx] generates the text [Hello xx!];
  • line 48: the URL [/headers] returns the HTTP headers from the client’s request to the client as text. This will allow us to see what [HttpClient] sends. The 2008 course used the generic TCP server for this purpose, which the user at the keyboard then had to make respond;
  • lines 52–55: a temporary redirect to [/hello?name=visitor] and a redirect that loops back on itself, as in the server from Part 1;
  • line 58: a 500 response (internal server error);
  • line 61: URL [/slow?seconds=n] does not respond until n seconds have elapsed. The [token] token is canceled if the client aborts the request: the wait is then interrupted;
  • line 68: the URL [/form] receives a form sent via the [POST] method and describe what they received;
  • line 76: URL [/text] receives arbitrary text via [POST] and returns it in uppercase;
  • Lines 84–114: A small “dataset” of people, exchanged in the JSON format. [GET /api/persons] returns the list of people; [GET /api/persons/n] returns person #n (or a 404 response); [POST /api/persons] adds the person sent by the client, assigns them a number, and responds with status code 201 (Created). Since multiple requests can be processed simultaneously by different threads, the list is protected by a lock [Lock] (Chapter 8);
  • line 123: the type [Person], a record ([record]);
  • line 120: the server listens on port 27210 at the loopback address.

The server is launched in a command window and remains there throughout the tests in this section. The requests it has received will be presented at the end of the section.

docs.title: 12.7.2.2. Downloading a document: GetStringAsync
docs.text:
The easiest way to retrieve a document using [HttpClient] is to use one of the following methods:

MethodRoleTask<string> GetStringAsync(string url)requests the URL [url] with the [GET] method and returns the received document as a stringTask<byte[]> GetByteArrayAsync(string url)Same as above, with the document returned as a byte array (an image, for example)Task<Stream> GetStreamAsync(string url)Same as above, with the document returned as a stream to be read as it arrives (a large file, for example)

Each of these also exists with a parameter of type [Uri] and with an additional parameter of type [CancellationToken]. These methods throw an [HttpRequestException] if the server responds with an error code.

The [internet-11.cs] program is as follows:

// first steps with HttpClient: download a document as a string
// the test server [internet-10.cs] must be running on port 27210

// an HTTP client, and the base address of the relative URLs it will be asked for
using var client = new HttpClient { BaseAddress = new Uri("http://localhost:27210/") };

// 1 - a text document
string text = await client.GetStringAsync("hello?name=Serge");
Console.WriteLine($"Document received: {text}");

// 2 - the HTTP headers sent by HttpClient, as the server received them
Console.WriteLine("--- headers sent by default");
Console.WriteLine(await client.GetStringAsync("headers"));

// 3 - we add headers to all the requests of this client
client.DefaultRequestHeaders.UserAgent.ParseAdd("csharp-course-client/1.0");
client.DefaultRequestHeaders.Add("Accept-Language", "en-US");
Console.WriteLine("--- headers after adding User-Agent and Accept-Language");
Console.WriteLine(await client.GetStringAsync("headers"));

// 4 - an HTML document, as an array of bytes
byte[] bytes = await client.GetByteArrayAsync("/");
Console.WriteLine($"--- the home page is {bytes.Length} bytes long");

// 5 - a document that does not exist
try
{
    await client.GetStringAsync("unknown");
}
catch (HttpRequestException ex)
{
    Console.WriteLine($"--- {ex.GetType().Name} : {ex.Message}");
    Console.WriteLine($"Status code: {(int?)ex.StatusCode} ({ex.StatusCode})");
}

Results (with the [internet-10.cs] server having been launched in another window):

> dotnet run internet-11.cs
Document received: Hello Serge!
--- headers sent by default
Host: localhost:27210
--- headers after adding User-Agent and Accept-Language
Host: localhost:27210
User-Agent: csharp-course-client/1.0
Accept-Language: en-US
--- the home page is 163 bytes long
--- HttpRequestException : Response status code does not indicate success: 404 (Not Found).
Status code: 404 (NotFound)

Comments:

  • Line 5: client creation. The [BaseAddress] property sets the address to which the relative URL values used subsequently are linked: [hello?name=Serge] thus refers to [http://localhost:27210/hello?name=Serge]. The trailing slash in the base address is important: without it, the last segment of the path would be replaced by the relative URL;
  • line 8: a single instruction is sufficient to retrieve the document. [HttpClient] built the request, connected, parsed the response, and reconstructed the document sent in chunks ([Transfer-Encoding: chunked]), which our TCP client from the first part displayed as-is;
  • Line 13: In line 3 of the results, we see that [HttpClient] sends only the required header [Host] by default. The 2008 version of [WebClient] added [Connection: Keep-Alive]; this is unnecessary in HTTP/1.1, where the connection is maintained by default. There is also no [User-Agent] header: some public servers reject requests that lack it;
  • Lines 16–17: The [DefaultRequestHeaders] collection contains the headers added to all requests from this client. Common headers have a typed property, such as [UserAgent]; others are added by name, such as [Add]. Lines 7–8 of the results show that they were indeed received by the server;
  • line 22: the document is received as bytes. Note the URL [/]: a relative URL starting with a forward slash denotes the root of the site from the base address;
  • lines 26–33: a non-existent document. [GetStringAsync] throws an [HttpRequestException] whose property [StatusCode] (of type [HttpStatusCode?], .NET 5) returns the received status code. The 2008 course received a [WebException] in this case.

docs.title: 12.7.2.3. Request and response: HttpRequestMessage and HttpResponseMessage
docs.text:
The [GetXxxAsync] methods return only the document. To manage the request (method, headers) or examine the response (status, headers), use the [HttpRequestMessage] and [HttpResponseMessage] classes:

MemberRolenew HttpRequestMessage(HttpMethod method, Uri url)A request. [HttpMethod] has static properties for the following methods: [HttpMethod.Get], [HttpMethod.Head], [HttpMethod.Post]…HttpRequestMessage.Headers, Contentthe request headers and any document that may be sent (method [POST])Task<HttpResponseMessage> SendAsync(HttpRequestMessage request)The [HttpClient] method sends the request and returns the response. [GetAsync(url)] is a shortcut for a [GET] requestHttpResponseMessage.StatusCode, ReasonPhrase, Versionstatus line: code (enumeration [HttpStatusCode]), message, and version of HTTPHttpResponseMessage.IsSuccessStatusCodetrue if the status code is between 200 and 299HttpResponseMessage.EnsureSuccessStatusCode()throws an [HttpRequestException] if the status code is not between 200 and 299HttpResponseMessage.Headersthe headers of the response itself ([Date], [Server], [Location]…)HttpResponseMessage.Contentthe received document ([HttpContent]): its own headers ([Content.Headers]: [Content-Type], [Content-Length]…) and the methods [ReadAsStringAsync], [ReadAsByteArrayAsync], [ReadAsStreamAsync] for reading itHttpResponseMessage.RequestMessagethe request to which the response corresponds: in the event of a redirect, this is the last request sent

We’ll use these classes to implement the web client from Part 1 ([internet-08.cs], [internet-09.cs]), which was called using a URL and the [GET] or [HEAD] method. The 2008 course did the same with the classes [HttpWebRequest] / [HttpWebResponse]. The program [internet-12.cs] is as follows:

using System.Net.Http.Headers;

// web client based on HttpClient: displays the status, the headers and the document received
// call: dotnet run internet-12.cs -- URL GET/HEAD

const string syntax = "Syntax: dotnet run internet-12.cs -- URL GET/HEAD";
if (args.Length != 2)
{
    Console.WriteLine(syntax);
    return;
}
// the URL must be an absolute http or https URL
if (!Uri.TryCreate(args[0], UriKind.Absolute, out Uri? uri) || (uri.Scheme != "http" && uri.Scheme != "https"))
{
    Console.WriteLine($"Incorrect URL [{args[0]}]: give a URL of the form http://machine[:port]/document");
    return;
}
// the HTTP method
string command = args[1].ToUpper();
if (command is not ("GET" or "HEAD"))
{
    Console.WriteLine(syntax);
    return;
}

// the handler that does the network work: at most 3 redirections followed
var handler = new SocketsHttpHandler { MaxAutomaticRedirections = 3 };
// the HTTP client: 10 seconds at most to get a response
using var client = new HttpClient(handler) { Timeout = TimeSpan.FromSeconds(10) };
try
{
    // the request: method, URL, headers
    using var request = new HttpRequestMessage(new HttpMethod(command), uri);
    request.Headers.UserAgent.ParseAdd("csharp-course-client/1.0");
    // we send it and wait for the response
    using HttpResponseMessage response = await client.SendAsync(request);
    // the status line
    Console.WriteLine($"The server {response.RequestMessage?.RequestUri} answered: "
        + $"HTTP/{response.Version} {(int)response.StatusCode} {response.ReasonPhrase}");
    // the headers of the response, then those of the document
    Console.WriteLine("--- headers");
    DisplayHeaders(response.Headers);
    DisplayHeaders(response.Content.Headers);
    // a status code outside the 200-299 range throws an HttpRequestException
    response.EnsureSuccessStatusCode();
    // the document
    Console.WriteLine("--- document");
    Console.WriteLine(await response.Content.ReadAsStringAsync());
}
catch (HttpRequestException ex)
{
    Console.WriteLine($"{ex.GetType().Name} [{ex.HttpRequestError}] : {ex.Message}");
}
catch (TaskCanceledException ex) when (ex.InnerException is TimeoutException)
{
    Console.WriteLine("The server did not answer within the allotted time");
}

// displays a collection of headers: a name can have several values
static void DisplayHeaders(HttpHeaders headers)
{
    foreach ((string name, IEnumerable<string> values) in headers)
    {
        Console.WriteLine($"{name}: {string.Join(", ", values)}");
    }
}

Comments:

  • Line 13: As in [internet-08.cs], the system verifies that the URL is valid. The scheme [https] is accepted this time: [HttpClient] is capable of performing the TLS negotiation;
  • Line 27: An [HttpClient] delegates network processing to a handler—by default, a [SocketsHttpHandler] object created for it. We create it ourselves to set one of its properties: [MaxAutomaticRedirections] limits the number of followed redirects to 3 (50 by default). The handler also manages the connection pool, cookies ([UseCookies]), decompression ([AutomaticDecompression]), and the proxy ([Proxy]);
  • line 29: the [Timeout] property sets the maximum time to receive a response (100 seconds by default);
  • lines 33–34: the request, including the requested method and a [User-Agent] header specific to this request. The 2008 course did not figure out how to make a [HEAD] request using [WebClient]: with [HttpRequestMessage], you simply need to choose the method;
  • Line 36: The request is sent; the response is available once its headers and, by default, its document have been received. [HttpResponseMessage] is [IDisposable]: the [using] declaration releases its resources;
  • lines 38–39: the status line. [response.RequestMessage.RequestUri] is the URL from the last request: in the event of redirection, it differs from the requested URL;
  • lines 42–43: [HttpClient] organizes the headers into two collections: those from the response and those describing the document;
  • line 45: if the status code does not indicate success, an [HttpRequestException] is thrown;
  • line 48: the document is read as a character string. The character set specified by the [Content-Type] ([charset=utf-8]) header is used to decode the received bytes;
  • line 50: starting at .NET 8, the [HttpRequestError] property of the exception indicates the nature of the error in the form of an enumeration: [ConnectionError], [NameResolutionError], [SecureConnectionError]… It is set to [Unknown] for an error status code;
  • line 54: For historical reasons, a timeout results in a [TaskCanceledException], whose internal exception is a [TimeoutException]; the [when] filter checks for this;
  • lines 60–64: A header name can have multiple values; each element of the [HttpHeaders] collection is a pair (name, values) that is parsed in the [foreach].

Let’s request the site’s root:

> dotnet run internet-12.cs -- http://localhost:27210/ GET
The server http://localhost:27210/ answered: HTTP/1.1 200 OK
--- headers
Date: Sat, 03 Oct 2026 10:18:56 GMT
Server: Kestrel
Content-Length: 163
Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8
--- document
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head><meta charset="utf-8"><title>Test server</title></head>
<body><h1>Welcome to the HttpClient test server</h1></body>
</html>

We find the information we obtained by analyzing the response ourselves using the TCP client: the status line, the response headers [Date] and [Server], and then the document headers [Content-Length] and [Content-Type].

A URL that is being redirected:

> dotnet run internet-12.cs -- http://localhost:27210/old GET
The server http://localhost:27210/hello?name=visitor answered: HTTP/1.1 200 OK
--- headers
Date: Sat, 03 Oct 2026 10:18:58 GMT
Server: Kestrel
Transfer-Encoding: chunked
Content-Type: text/plain; charset=utf-8
--- document
Hello visitor!

The redirection was handled automatically: the response received is that of URL [/hello?name=visitor] (line 2). Let’s compare this with the first part: the client [internet-09.cs] had to read the status line, extract the code, look for the header [Location], calculate the new URL, and start over, in a loop limited to three redirects. Here, all of this is handled by the handler [SocketsHttpHandler]. The document, sent in chunks (line 6), has been reconstructed. To handle the redirects yourself, simply set [AllowAutoRedirect = false] on the handler: the 302 response is then returned as-is.

A non-existent document:

> dotnet run internet-12.cs -- http://localhost:27210/unknown GET
The server http://localhost:27210/unknown answered: HTTP/1.1 404 Not Found
--- headers
Date: Sat, 03 Oct 2026 10:19:00 GMT
Server: Kestrel
Content-Length: 0
HttpRequestException [Unknown] : Response status code does not indicate success: 404 (Not Found).

The 404 code is included in the response, along with its headers. It was [EnsureSuccessStatusCode] that threw the exception. In the 2008 course, with [HttpWebRequest], a [WebException] was obtained directly, and the response had to be retrieved from the exception; with [HttpClient], only the methods [GetStringAsync], [GetByteArrayAsync], and [GetStreamAsync] throw an exception for an error code; [SendAsync] and [GetAsync] return the response, and it is up to the program to decide.

The URL [/loop], which redirects to itself:

> dotnet run internet-12.cs -- http://localhost:27210/loop HEAD
The server http://localhost:27210/loop answered: HTTP/1.1 302 Found
--- headers
Date: Sat, 03 Oct 2026 10:19:02 GMT
Server: Kestrel
Location: /loop
HttpRequestException [Unknown] : Response status code does not indicate success: 302 (Found).

After three redirects, the handler gives up and returns the last response received, a 302 response. Since it is not in the 200–299 range, [EnsureSuccessStatusCode] throws an exception.

A server error:

> dotnet run internet-12.cs -- http://localhost:27210/error HEAD
The server http://localhost:27210/error answered: HTTP/1.1 500 Internal Server Error
--- headers
Date: Sat, 03 Oct 2026 10:19:04 GMT
Server: Kestrel
HttpRequestException [Unknown] : Response status code does not indicate success: 500 (Internal Server Error).

A port on which no server is listening:

> dotnet run internet-12.cs -- http://localhost:27299/ GET
HttpRequestException [ConnectionError] : Connection refused (localhost:27299)

The property [HttpRequestError] is equal to [ConnectionError]: the server could not be reached. Finally, an [https] URL sent to our server, which only speaks HTTP in plain text:

> dotnet run internet-12.cs -- https://localhost:27210/ GET
HttpRequestException [SecureConnectionError] : The SSL connection could not be established, see inner exception.

The TLS negotiation failed ([SecureConnectionError]). On a machine connected to the Internet, a URL request, like [https://learn.microsoft.com/], would normally be served as HTTP/2 or HTTP/3, depending on the server’s capabilities.

One final note on proxies. The 2008 course devoted a paragraph to HTTP proxies—the machines through which workstations on a corporate network must pass to access the Web. By default, [HttpClient] uses the proxy configured for the system (Windows settings, environment variables [HTTP_PROXY] and [HTTPS_PROXY] on Linux, and macOS). You can specify a different one using the [Proxy] property of the handler, [new SocketsHttpHandler { Proxy = new WebProxy("proxy.example.org:3128") }], or use none at all with [UseProxy = false].

docs.title: 12.7.2.4. Sending data to the server: GET and POST
docs.text:
A client can send information to the server in two ways:

  • using the [GET] method, the information is part of the URL: [/document?param1=value1&param2=value2];
  • using the [POST] method, the information forms the document attached to the request, following the blank line that ends the headers. The [Content-Type] header specifies its format. For an HTML form, the document has the same format as the parameters section of a URL: [param1=value1&param2=value2], with the type [application/x-www-form-urlencoded].

In both cases, the values must be encoded: certain characters (spaces, [&], [=], [?], accented letters, etc.) cannot appear as-is in a URL or in a form. The 2008 course used the [HttpUtility.UrlEncode] method for this purpose; today we use [Uri.EscapeDataString] for a value to be placed in a URL, and the [FormUrlEncodedContent] class itself encodes a form.

The [HttpClient] methods for sending data are [PostAsync], [PutAsync], and [PatchAsync]. They receive a URL and the document to be sent, an object derived from [HttpContent]:

ClassSent DocumentFormUrlEncodedContenta form, constructed from a collection of (name, value) pairsStringContenttext, with its encoding and type ([text/plain], [application/json]…)ByteArrayContent, StreamContentarbitrary bytes, a stream (a file, for example)MultipartFormDataContenta form containing files ([multipart/form-data])JsonContentan object transformed into JSON (namespace [System.Net.Http.Json])

The program [internet-13.cs] is as follows:

using System.Text;

// send data to the server: URL parameters (GET), form and text (POST)
// the test server [internet-10.cs] must be running on port 27210

using var client = new HttpClient { BaseAddress = new Uri("http://localhost:27210/") };

// 1 - GET: the parameters are part of the URL; they must be encoded in it
string name = "Jean & Marie";
string url = $"hello?name={Uri.EscapeDataString(name)}";
Console.WriteLine($"--- GET {url}");
Console.WriteLine(await client.GetStringAsync(url));

// 2 - POST of a form: the parameters form the document sent to the server
var form = new FormUrlEncodedContent(
[
    new("name", "Jean & Marie"),
    new("age", "42"),
    new("city", "Angers"),
]);
// the document as it will be sent
Console.WriteLine($"--- POST form, document sent: {await form.ReadAsStringAsync()}");
using (HttpResponseMessage response = await client.PostAsync("form", form))
{
    response.EnsureSuccessStatusCode();
    Console.WriteLine(await response.Content.ReadAsStringAsync());
}

// 3 - POST of any text, with its type
var text = new StringContent("summer and winter", Encoding.UTF8, "text/plain");
Console.WriteLine("--- POST text");
using (HttpResponseMessage response = await client.PostAsync("text", text))
{
    response.EnsureSuccessStatusCode();
    Console.WriteLine(await response.Content.ReadAsStringAsync());
}

Results:

> dotnet run internet-13.cs
--- GET hello?name=Jean%20%26%20Marie
Hello Jean & Marie!
--- POST form, document sent: name=Jean+%26+Marie&age=42&city=Angers
Content-Type received: application/x-www-form-urlencoded
Fields received: name=[Jean & Marie], age=[42], city=[Angers]
--- POST text
Content-Type received: text/plain; charset=utf-8
Text received in upper case: SUMMER AND WINTER

Comments:

  • Lines 9–10: The value [Jean & Marie] is placed inside the URL. Without encoding, the character [&] would be interpreted as the separator between two parameters, and the server would receive the parameter [name] with the value [Jean]. In line 2 of the results, we see that the space has become [%20] and the character [&] has become [%26]: this is the hexadecimal code for the character, preceded by [%];
  • Lines 15–19: The form is constructed from a collection of pairs, [KeyValuePair<string, string>]; since the type of each element is known, [new(...)] is sufficient;
  • line 22: to verify this, we read the document that will be sent: on line 4 of the results, we find the format [name=value&name=value]. In a form, a space is encoded as [+];
  • line 23: the form is sent using the method [POST] to the URL [/form]. The server indicates (lines 5–6) that it has received a document of type [application/x-www-form-urlencoded] and that it has extracted and decoded the three fields from it;
  • line 30: text, encoded as UTF-8, of type [text/plain]. The server returns it in uppercase (line 9).

Note the [using (...) { ... }] blocks: we could not use a [using] declaration here, because there are two [response] variables in the same code block. The difference between [GET] and [POST], noted in the 2008 course, remains true: a browser displays the parameters of a [GET] request in its address bar, not those of a [POST] request; furthermore, a [GET] request should only be used to retrieve information, while a [POST] request is used to send information or modify the server’s state.

docs.title: 12.7.2.5. Exchanging Objects in JSON Format
docs.text:
Applications currently exchange most of their data in the JSON format, described in Chapter 5. The [System.Net.Http.Json] namespace adds extension methods to [HttpClient] and [HttpContent] that, in a single statement, perform the HTTP request and the conversion between objects and JSON using [System.Text.Json]:

MethodRoleTask<T?> GetFromJsonAsync<T>(string url)retrieves the URL via [GET] and converts the received JSON document into an object of type [T]Task<HttpResponseMessage> PostAsJsonAsync<T>(string url, T object)sends the object, converted to JSON, via [POST] (type [application/json]) and returns the response. [PutAsJsonAsync] does the same with the [PUT] methodTask<T?> ReadFromJsonAsync<T>()Method of [HttpContent]: converts the JSON document from a response into an object of type [T]

The [internet-14.cs] program is as follows:

#:property PublishAot=false
using System.Net.Http.Json;

// exchange objects in JSON format with a web server
// the test server [internet-10.cs] must be running on port 27210

using var client = new HttpClient { BaseAddress = new Uri("http://localhost:27210/") };

// 1 - the list of persons: the JSON document is directly turned into objects
List<Person>? persons = await client.GetFromJsonAsync<List<Person>>("api/persons");
Console.WriteLine("--- list of persons");
foreach (Person person in persons ?? [])
{
    Console.WriteLine(person);
}

// 2 - a person
Person? durand = await client.GetFromJsonAsync<Person>("api/persons/2");
Console.WriteLine($"--- person no. 2: {durand}");

// 3 - addition of a person: the object is sent in JSON format
var martin = new Person(0, "Martin", 25);
using (HttpResponseMessage response = await client.PostAsJsonAsync("api/persons", martin))
{
    Console.WriteLine($"--- addition of {martin}");
    Console.WriteLine($"Status: {(int)response.StatusCode} {response.ReasonPhrase}, Location: {response.Headers.Location}");
    // the JSON document received, raw then as an object
    Console.WriteLine($"JSON received: {await response.Content.ReadAsStringAsync()}");
    Person? created = await response.Content.ReadFromJsonAsync<Person>();
    Console.WriteLine($"Person created: {created}");
}

// 4 - a person who does not exist
try
{
    await client.GetFromJsonAsync<Person>("api/persons/99");
}
catch (HttpRequestException ex)
{
    Console.WriteLine($"--- person no. 99: {ex.GetType().Name} : {ex.Message}");
}

// a person: the same type as on the server side
record Person(int Id, string Name, int Age);

Results:

> dotnet run internet-14.cs
--- list of persons
Person { Id = 1, Name = Dupont, Age = 42 }
Person { Id = 2, Name = Durand, Age = 35 }
--- person no. 2: Person { Id = 2, Name = Durand, Age = 35 }
--- addition of Person { Id = 0, Name = Martin, Age = 25 }
Status: 201 Created, Location: /api/persons/3
JSON received: {"id":3,"name":"Martin","age":25}
Person created: Person { Id = 3, Name = Martin, Age = 25 }
--- person no. 99: HttpRequestException : Response status code does not indicate success: 404 (Not Found).

Comments:

  • Line 1: As with the server, we re-enable JSON serialization via reflection. The other solution, discussed in Chapter 6 for the [dao] layer of Version 5, is a serialization context generated at compile time ([JsonSerializerContext]): each of the methods above has an overload that accepts it;
  • Line 10: the list of people. The JSON document [[{"id":1,"name":"Dupont","age":42},...]] sent by the server is directly converted into a list of [Person] objects. The result is of type [List<Person>?]: the JSON document could be [null];
  • line 12: if that is the case, an empty list is traversed;
  • line 18: a single person;
  • line 23: the object [martin] is converted to JSON and sent to the server. The server responds with status code 201 (Created) and the header [Location], which provides the URL for the new resource (line 7 of the results);
  • line 28: the received JSON document: the property names are in the format “camelCase” ([id], [name], [age]), following web conventions. The methods of [System.Net.Http.Json] use the options [JsonSerializerDefaults.Web], which perform the conversion using the C# properties [Id], [Name], and [Age];
  • line 29: the same document, converted to an object. Note that the document may have been read twice: [HttpClient] kept it in memory, since the request was made without the [HttpCompletionOption.ResponseHeadersRead] option, which we will discuss later;
  • lines 34–40: Like [GetStringAsync], [GetFromJsonAsync] throws an [HttpRequestException] if the status code indicates an error.

We will revisit these methods in the next chapter, where the tax calculation server will become a JSON web service.

docs.title: 12.7.2.6. Timeout, Cancellation, and Client Reuse
docs.text:
The program [internet-15.cs] illustrates three important points for using [HttpClient] in a real-world application:

using System.Diagnostics;

// timeout, cancellation and reuse of an HttpClient
// the test server [internet-10.cs] must be running on port 27210

// 1 - a single HttpClient instance for the whole application
//     timeout of 2 seconds for each request
var client = new HttpClient
{
    BaseAddress = new Uri("http://localhost:27210/"),
    Timeout = TimeSpan.FromSeconds(2),
};

// 2 - successive requests: the same TCP connection is reused
Console.WriteLine("--- three successive requests");
for (int i = 1; i <= 3; i++)
{
    Console.WriteLine(await client.GetStringAsync($"hello?name=trial{i}"));
}

// 3 - a response obtained within the timeout, then a response that is too slow
foreach (int seconds in (int[])[1, 3])
{
    Console.WriteLine($"--- response in {seconds} s expected");
    try
    {
        Console.WriteLine(await client.GetStringAsync($"slow?seconds={seconds}"));
    }
    catch (TaskCanceledException ex) when (ex.InnerException is TimeoutException)
    {
        Console.WriteLine($"{ex.GetType().Name} : {ex.Message}");
    }
}

// 4 - a request cancelled by the program after half a second
Console.WriteLine("--- cancellation after 0.5 s");
using (var cancellation = new CancellationTokenSource(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(0.5)))
{
    try
    {
        Console.WriteLine(await client.GetStringAsync("slow?seconds=1", cancellation.Token));
    }
    catch (TaskCanceledException ex) when (cancellation.IsCancellationRequested)
    {
        Console.WriteLine($"Request cancelled ({ex.GetType().Name})");
    }
}

// 5 - four simultaneous requests with the same client
Console.WriteLine("--- four simultaneous requests of one second each");
var stopwatch = Stopwatch.StartNew();
string[] responses = await Task.WhenAll(
    Enumerable.Range(1, 4).Select(_ => client.GetStringAsync("slow?seconds=1")));
foreach (string response in responses)
{
    Console.WriteLine(response);
}
Console.WriteLine($"Total duration: {stopwatch.Elapsed.TotalSeconds:F1} s");

Results:

> dotnet run internet-15.cs
--- three successive requests
Hello trial1!
Hello trial2!
Hello trial3!
--- response in 1 s expected
Response obtained after 1 s
--- response in 3 s expected
TaskCanceledException : The request was canceled due to the configured HttpClient.Timeout of 2 seconds elapsing.
--- cancellation after 0.5 s
Request cancelled (TaskCanceledException)
--- four simultaneous requests of one second each
Response obtained after 1 s
Response obtained after 1 s
Response obtained after 1 s
Response obtained after 1 s
Total duration: 1.0 s

Comments:

  • Line 8: A single instance of [HttpClient] is used by the entire program. This is the rule: an [HttpClient] object manages a pool of connections and reuses them from one query to the next; it is designed to be long-running and can be used by multiple tasks simultaneously. Creating an [HttpClient] for each request, within a [using], is a classic mistake: each instance opens its own connections, which the system then keeps in reserve for some time after they are closed (TIME_WAIT status of TCP); a program that makes many queries eventually exhausts the available ports. We included [using] in the previous programs because they made only a few requests before terminating;
  • line 11: each request must receive a response within 2 seconds at most;
  • lines 16–18: three successive requests. We’ll see in the server log that they used the same connection (TCP);
  • lines 22–29: a response that arrives in 1 second, followed by a response that would take 3 seconds: after 2 seconds, the request is abandoned and a [TaskCanceledException] is thrown (line 9 of the results). The expression [(int[])[1, 3]] assigns a type to the collection expression, which does not have one on its own;
  • lines 37–45: a cancellation initiated by the program. All methods of [HttpClient] accept a cancellation token, just like the asynchronous methods discussed in Chapter 9. Here, the token is automatically canceled after half a second (constructor [CancellationTokenSource(TimeSpan)]); in an interactive application, it would be canceled by a [Cancel] button or by Ctrl-C. The exception is again a [TaskCanceledException]; it is the [when (cancellation.IsCancellationRequested)] filter that distinguishes between cancellation and a timeout;
  • Lines 51–58: Four requests launched simultaneously on the same client, then processed together by [Task.WhenAll] (Chapter 9). Each request took one second to process; the total took one second (line 17): the requests were processed in parallel.

The log for server [internet-10.cs] shows all requests received since the beginning of this section:

> dotnet run internet-10.cs
Web server started on http://localhost:27210
GET /hello?name=Serge HTTP/1.1 (client port 45988) -> 200
GET /headers HTTP/1.1 (client port 45988) -> 200
GET /headers HTTP/1.1 (client port 45988) -> 200
GET / HTTP/1.1 (client port 45988) -> 200
GET /unknown HTTP/1.1 (client port 45988) -> 404
GET / HTTP/1.1 (client port 45996) -> 200
GET /old HTTP/1.1 (client port 46006) -> 302
GET /hello?name=visitor HTTP/1.1 (client port 46006) -> 200
GET /unknown HTTP/1.1 (client port 46018) -> 404
HEAD /loop HTTP/1.1 (client port 56222) -> 302
HEAD /loop HTTP/1.1 (client port 56222) -> 302
HEAD /loop HTTP/1.1 (client port 56222) -> 302
HEAD /loop HTTP/1.1 (client port 56222) -> 302
HEAD /error HTTP/1.1 (client port 56230) -> 500
GET /hello?name=Jean%20%26%20Marie HTTP/1.1 (client port 56262) -> 200
POST /form HTTP/1.1 (client port 56262) -> 200
POST /text HTTP/1.1 (client port 56262) -> 200
GET /api/persons HTTP/1.1 (client port 39124) -> 200
GET /api/persons/2 HTTP/1.1 (client port 39124) -> 200
POST /api/persons HTTP/1.1 (client port 39124) -> 201
GET /api/persons/99 HTTP/1.1 (client port 39124) -> 404
GET /hello?name=trial1 HTTP/1.1 (client port 39138) -> 200
GET /hello?name=trial2 HTTP/1.1 (client port 39138) -> 200
GET /hello?name=trial3 HTTP/1.1 (client port 39138) -> 200
GET /slow?seconds=1 HTTP/1.1 (client port 39138) -> 200
GET /slow?seconds=3 HTTP/1.1 (client port 39138) -> abandoned by the client
GET /slow?seconds=1 HTTP/1.1 (client port 39140) -> abandoned by the client
GET /slow?seconds=1 HTTP/1.1 (client port 39156) -> 200
