GET /slow?seconds=1 HTTP/1.1 (client port 39172) -> 200
GET /slow?seconds=1 HTTP/1.1 (client port 39170) -> 200
  • lines 3–7: the five requests from [internet-11.cs] arrived over the same connection (same client port): the client kept it open between requests;
  • lines 9–10: the redirected request from [internet-12.cs] and the request to the new address, made automatically over the same connection;
  • lines 12–15: the initial request and the three redirects that followed before the connection was closed;
  • Lines 24–28: The successive requests from [internet-15.cs] all used the same connection. The request that took too long was abandoned by the client (line 28): [HttpClient] closed the connection, and the server saw its token [RequestAborted] revoked;
  • line 29: the request canceled by the program had to open a new connection, since the previous one had been closed;
  • the last four lines: the four simultaneous requests used four different connections, opened specifically for this purpose. In HTTP/1.1, a connection carries only one request at a time; HTTP/2 would allow all of them to be sent over a single connection.

A program that remains active for a long time (a server, a system service) must take one final point into account: a single [HttpClient] retains its connections indefinitely and therefore does not detect changes in the IP addresses of the servers it queries, which the DNS would reveal. To address this, a maximum connection lifetime is set using the [PooledConnectionLifetime] property of the [SocketsHttpHandler] handler (for example, two minutes). In applications based on the the .NET Generic Host ([Microsoft.Extensions.Hosting]) and in ASP.NET Core, the [HttpClient] objects are instead obtained via the [IHttpClientFactory] interface: Declared with [services.AddHttpClient()] (package [Microsoft.Extensions.Http]), this factory provides configured clients (base address, headers, timeout) and manages their handlers and lifetimes itself. Readers will find it in the ASP.NET Core documentation.

docs.title: 12.7.3. Application: A proxy client for a web translation service
docs.text: We will now demonstrate how [HttpClient] enables the use of web resources, even when those resources were not intended for use by a program.

docs.title: 12.7.3.1. The application
docs.text:
The 2008 course used the [trans.voila.fr] translation site. Users would type in text, select a translation direction (“French to English,” etc.) from a drop-down list, click a button, and receive an HTML page containing the translation. The course created a [TranslationService] class that performed the same task programmatically: it constructed the URL for the request, sent it to the site, and extracted the translation from the received HTML page using a regular expression. A Windows Forms GUI relied on this class; this is referred to as a “proxy” client: the [TranslationService] class acts as a substitute for the website and hides it from the user.

That website no longer exists, and our test machine does not have Internet access. We’re keeping the concept by replacing the website with a small local site that mimics it: it has the same form (a text box, a drop-down list of translation directions written like the one on the 2008 website) and displays the translation in the same location on its page. Its “translations” are done word-for-word using small dictionaries: it’s the client’s technique that interests us, not the quality of the translation. The graphical interface is replaced by a console test program, like the one from the 2008 course. The architecture is as follows:

docs.title: 12.7.3.2. The translation site
docs.text:
The program [internet-16.cs] is as follows:

#:sdk Microsoft.NET.Sdk.Web
using System.Net;
using System.Text;
using System.Text.RegularExpressions;

// a small word-for-word "translation" website, which imitates the site queried by the 2008 course
// call: dotnet run internet-16.cs [-- port]
int port = args.Length == 1 && int.TryParse(args[0], out int p) ? p : 27220;

// the translation directions: code -> (label, dictionary)
var translationDirections = new Dictionary<string, (string Label, Dictionary<string, string> Words)>
{
    ["fe"] = ("French → English", new()
    {
        ["ce"] = "this", ["chien"] = "dog", ["est"] = "is", ["perdu"] = "lost", ["malade"] = "sick",
        ["l'"] = "the ", ["été"] = "summer", ["sera"] = "will be", ["chaud"] = "hot",
    }),
    ["ef"] = ("English → French", new()
    {
        ["my"] = "mon", ["tailor"] = "tailleur", ["is"] = "est", ["rich"] = "riche",
        ["this"] = "ce", ["dog"] = "chien", ["lost"] = "perdu",
    }),
    ["fs"] = ("French → Spanish", new()
    {
        ["ce"] = "este", ["chien"] = "perro", ["est"] = "está", ["perdu"] = "perdido",
        ["l'"] = "el ", ["été"] = "verano", ["sera"] = "será", ["chaud"] = "caliente",
    }),
};

var builder = WebApplication.CreateBuilder(args);
builder.Logging.SetMinimumLevel(LogLevel.Warning);
var app = builder.Build();

// console tracking of the requests
app.Use(async (context, next) =>
{
    await next(context);
    var request = context.Request;
    Console.WriteLine($"{request.Method} {request.Path}{request.QueryString} -> {context.Response.StatusCode}");
});

// the translation page: the form, followed by the translation if a text was provided
app.MapGet("/translation", (string? direction, string? text) =>
{
    var page = new StringBuilder();
    page.Append("""
        <!DOCTYPE html>
        <html lang="en">
        <head><meta charset="utf-8"><title>Translator of the C# course</title></head>
        <body>
        <h1>Translation of texts</h1>
        <form action="/translation" method="get">
        <textarea name="text" rows="4" cols="60"></textarea>
        <select name="direction">

        """);
    // the list of translation directions, written as in 2008: unclosed <option> tags
    foreach ((string code, (string label, _)) in translationDirections)
    {
        page.Append($"    <option value='{code}'>{label}\n");
    }
    page.Append("""
        </select>
        <input type="submit" value="Translate">
        </form>

        """);
    // the translation, if there is a text to translate
    if (!string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(text))
    {
        if (direction is not null && translationDirections.TryGetValue(direction, out var translator))
        {
            // word-for-word translation; an unknown word is left as is
            string translation = Regex.Replace(text.Trim().ToLower(), @"\w+'?",
                word => translator.Words.GetValueOrDefault(word.Value, word.Value));
            page.Append($"<strong>Translated text: </strong><div class=\"txtTrans\">{WebUtility.HtmlEncode(translation)}</div>\n");
        }
        else
        {
            page.Append("<p>Unknown translation direction</p>\n");
        }
    }
    page.Append("</body>\n</html>\n");
    return Results.Content(page.ToString(), "text/html; charset=utf-8");
});

Console.WriteLine($"Translation service started on http://localhost:{port}/translation");
app.Run($"http://127.0.0.1:{port}");

Comments:

  • Lines 11–26: the three proposed translation directions, along with their codes ([fe] for French → English, as on the 2008 website), their labels, and their dictionaries. The labels contain HTML entities ([→] for [→]), just like those on the original website;
  • line 43: the site’s single page, [/translation], may receive two parameters: the translation direction [direction] and the text [text];
  • lines 58–60: the drop-down list. As on the 2008 site, the [<option>] tags are not closed: the HTML on actual sites is not always very clean, and our client will have to work around this;
  • lines 74–75: the word-for-word translation. The regular expression [\w+'?] matches a word, possibly followed by an apostrophe ([l'], [d']); each word is replaced with its translation, or left as is if it is unknown;
  • line 76: the translation is placed within a [<div class="txtTrans">] tag, as on the 2008 website. It is encoded with [WebUtility.HtmlEncode]: characters that have a meaning in HTML ([<], [&]…) and, using this method, accented letters are replaced by entities;
  • Line 80: An unknown translation direction results in a page with no translation.

Here is the page generated with [curl] for the translation of [l'été sera chaud] into Spanish; note the text encoding in URL:

> curl "http://localhost:27220/translation?direction=fs&text=l%27%C3%A9t%C3%A9%20sera%20chaud"
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head><meta charset="utf-8"><title>Translator of the C# course</title></head>
<body>
<h1>Translation of texts</h1>
<form action="/translation" method="get">
<textarea name="text" rows="4" cols="60"></textarea>
<select name="direction">
    <option value='fe'>French → English
    <option value='ef'>English → French
    <option value='fs'>French → Spanish
</select>
<input type="submit" value="Translate">
</form>
<strong>Translated text: </strong><div class="txtTrans">el verano será caliente</div>
</body>
</html>

To write the client, we need, just as in 2008:

  • know what the site expects: a [GET /translation?direction=code&text=encoded text] request. On a real website, you can find this by looking at the URL displayed by the browser after a translation, or the [action] attribute of the form;
  • know where, within the received pages, the information we’re interested in is located: the translation directions are in the [<option value='code'>label] tags of the drop-down list (line 10 of the page above), and the translation is in the [<div class="txtTrans">] tag (line 16). You can find this by viewing the page’s source code in the browser.

Two regular expressions (Chapter 5) can be used to extract this information:

  • [<option[^>]*value='(\w+)'>([^<\r\n]+)]: an [<option] tag, followed by characters other than [>], [value='], the code (first group), [>], and then the label—that is, the characters that follow until the next [<] or the end of the line (second group);
  • [<div class="txtTrans">(.*?)</div>]: the translation is the text (first group) between the opening tag and the first [</div>] tag that follows. The quantifier [*?] is “lazy”: it takes as few characters as possible.

docs.title: 12.7.3.3. The TranslationService client
docs.text:
The 2008 course divided the client into two projects: a library for the [TranslationService] class and its interface, and a Windows Forms application for the graphical user interface, configured by Spring.NET. To keep things brief, we’re combining the [ITranslationService] interface, its implementation [TranslationService], the exception [TranslationException], and the test program into a single application file. The program [internet-17.cs] is as follows:

using System.Net;
using System.Text.RegularExpressions;

// "proxy" client of a translation web service: the TranslationService class
// hides from the program the HTTP dialog and the parsing of the HTML pages of the translation site
// call: dotnet run internet-17.cs [-- siteUrl]   (by default http://localhost:27220/)

string siteUrl = args.Length == 1 ? args[0] : "http://localhost:27220/";
using var client = new HttpClient { BaseAddress = new Uri(siteUrl), Timeout = TimeSpan.FromSeconds(10) };
try
{
    // creation of the translation service: it queries the site to know the translated languages
    ITranslationService service = await TranslationService.CreateAsync(client);
    Console.WriteLine("Translation directions offered by the site:");
    foreach ((string code, string label) in service.TranslatedLanguages)
    {
        Console.WriteLine($"  {code} : {label}");
    }
    // a few translations
    (string Text, string Direction)[] trials =
    [
        ("ce chien est perdu", "fe"),
        ("l'été sera chaud", "fs"),
        ("my tailor is rich", "ef"),
        ("xx", "ef"),
        ("", "fe"),
        ("bonjour", "fx"),
    ];
    foreach ((string text, string direction) in trials)
    {
        try
        {
            string translation = await service.TranslateAsync(text, direction);
            Console.WriteLine($"Translation [{service.TranslatedLanguages[direction]}] of [{text}]: [{translation}]");
        }
        catch (TranslationException e)
        {
            Console.WriteLine($"The following error with code {e.Code} occurred: {e.Message}");
        }
    }
}
catch (TranslationException e)
{
    Console.WriteLine($"The following error with code {e.Code} occurred: {e.Message}");
    if (e.InnerException is Exception cause)
    {
        Console.WriteLine($"Cause: {cause.GetType().Name} : {cause.Message}");
    }
}

// --------------------------------------------------------------------
// the interface presented to the program
interface ITranslationService
{
    // the translation directions: code -> label, for example fe -> French → English
    IReadOnlyDictionary<string, string> TranslatedLanguages { get; }
    // translation of a text in the direction given by its code
    Task<string> TranslateAsync(string text, string direction);
}

// the exception specific to the translation service
class TranslationException : Exception
{
    public int Code { get; init; }
    public TranslationException(string message) : base(message) { }
    public TranslationException(string message, Exception inner) : base(message, inner) { }
}

// the implementation: an HTTP client of the translation site
partial class TranslationService : ITranslationService
{
    // the HTTP client, provided by the program
    private readonly HttpClient client;
    public IReadOnlyDictionary<string, string> TranslatedLanguages { get; }

    // private constructor: we go through the factory method CreateAsync
    private TranslationService(HttpClient client, Dictionary<string, string> languages)
    {
        this.client = client;
        TranslatedLanguages = languages;
    }

    // the options <option value='fe'>French → English of the form
    [GeneratedRegex(@"<option[^>]*value='(\w+)'>([^<\r\n]+)")]
    private static partial Regex OptionRegex();

    // the translation: <div class="txtTrans">...</div>
    [GeneratedRegex("""<div class="txtTrans">(.*?)</div>""")]
    private static partial Regex TranslationRegex();

    // creation of the service: the translation directions are read from the site's form
    public static async Task<TranslationService> CreateAsync(HttpClient client)
    {
        string page;
        try
        {
            page = await client.GetStringAsync("translation");
        }
        catch (Exception e) when (e is HttpRequestException or TaskCanceledException)
        {
            throw new TranslationException("The translation site is unreachable", e) { Code = 11 };
        }
        var languages = new Dictionary<string, string>();
        foreach (Match option in OptionRegex().Matches(page))
        {
            // the HTML entities (→...) are decoded
            languages[option.Groups[1].Value] = WebUtility.HtmlDecode(option.Groups[2].Value.Trim());
        }
        if (languages.Count == 0)
        {
            throw new TranslationException("The site gives no translation direction") { Code = 13 };
        }
        return new TranslationService(client, languages);
    }

    // translation
    public async Task<string> TranslateAsync(string text, string direction)
    {
        // is the requested translation possible?
        if (!TranslatedLanguages.ContainsKey(direction))
        {
            throw new TranslationException($"The translation direction [{direction}] is not recognized") { Code = 10 };
        }
        // the URL to request: the text must be encoded
        string url = $"translation?direction={direction}&text={Uri.EscapeDataString(text)}";
        try
        {
            // we only wait for the headers of the response: the document will be read progressively
            using HttpResponseMessage response = await client.GetAsync(url, HttpCompletionOption.ResponseHeadersRead);
            response.EnsureSuccessStatusCode();
            using var reader = new StreamReader(await response.Content.ReadAsStreamAsync());
            // we look for the translation line after line, and stop as soon as we have found it
            while (await reader.ReadLineAsync() is string line)
            {
                Match result = TranslationRegex().Match(line);
                if (result.Success)
                {
                    return WebUtility.HtmlDecode(result.Groups[1].Value.Trim());
                }
            }
        }
        catch (Exception e) when (e is HttpRequestException or TaskCanceledException or IOException)
        {
            throw new TranslationException("Error encountered during the translation", e) { Code = 11 };
        }
        // the page did not contain a translation
        throw new TranslationException("The server did not send back a translation") { Code = 12 };
    }
}

Let’s start with the interface and the exception:

  • lines 53–58: the interface presented to the program. The property [TranslatedLanguages] is the dictionary of translation directions accepted by the site, consisting of entries of the form [fe] → [French → English]; the method [TranslateAsync] translates the text [text] into the direction with code [direction]. In 2008, the method was synchronous; it is now asynchronous, like the methods of [HttpClient] that it uses;
  • lines 62–66: the service-specific exception, with an error code, modeled after [TaxException] (Chapter 6).

The [TranslationService] class:

  • line 70: the class is partial ([partial]) because the code for its regular expressions is generated at compile time (attribute [GeneratedRegex], Chapter 5);
  • line 73: the service does not create its own [HttpClient]; it receives it from the program, which determines its configuration (base address, timeout) and its lifetime;
  • line 77: the constructor is private. The service can only be created after querying the site, which is an asynchronous operation; however, a constructor cannot be asynchronous. Therefore, a static construction method, [CreateAsync], is used;
  • lines 84–89: the two regular expressions presented above. The first is a verbatim string literal [@"..."] (no escape sequences), the second a raw string literal [""" ... """] (C# 11), which allows the quotation marks in [class="txtTrans"] to be written without doubling them;
  • lines 92–113: creating the service. The 2008 course stored the list of translation keys in the Spring configuration file. We read it from the website itself, which ensures that it is up to date:
    • line 97: we request the form page, without any parameters;
    • line 99: a communication error is encapsulated in a [TranslationException] with code 11;
    • lines 104–107: each [<option>] tag found by the regular expression provides a code (group 1) and a label (group 2). [WebUtility.HtmlDecode] replaces the HTML entities with the characters they represent: [French → English] becomes [French → English];
  • lines 117–147: the translation:
    • lines 120–122: the system verifies that the requested translation direction exists. The 2008 code contained an error here: [String.Format] was called without the value to be inserted into the message; string interpolation makes this type of error impossible;
    • Line 125: the request URL, in which the text is encoded;
    • Line 129: [GetAsync] returns the response as soon as its headers arrive, without waiting for the document. The 2008 course preferred [HttpWebRequest] over [WebClient] so that the page could be read line by line and stop as soon as the translation was found; the [ResponseHeadersRead] option allows you to do the same with [HttpClient];
    • lines 131–138: the document is read as it arrives, line by line, and the translation is searched for in each line. As soon as it is found, it is returned, decoded; the [using] statements close the stream and release the response, and the rest of the page is never read;
    • line 142: a communication error throws a code 11 exception;
    • line 147: if the page has been read in its entirety without finding a translation, a code 12 exception is thrown.

The test program:

  • line 8: the website address can be passed as an argument;
  • line 9: the application’s HTTP client;
  • line 13: creation of the service. The program then interacts with the service only through its interface [ITranslationService];
  • lines 20–27: the test cases from the 2008 course, plus two error cases: an empty text and an unknown translation direction. The array is an array of named tuples (C# 7);
  • line 29: each tuple is deconstructed into two variables.

Results, with the [internet-16.cs] site having been launched in another window:

> dotnet run internet-17.cs
Translation directions offered by the site:

The following error with code 12 occurred: The server did not send back a translation

  • line 9: an unknown word is rendered as-is, just as the 2008 site did;

docs.title: 12.7.3.4. Conclusion
docs.text:
This application demonstrated that [HttpClient] allows us to leverage web resources. The technique is the same each time:

  • determine which URL to query. It is usually preconfigured;
  • query it;
  • find what we’re looking for in the server’s response using regular expressions.

This technique, now known as “web scraping,” is fragile: over time, the URL being queried or the page’s structure may change, and the regular expression that used to find the result may no longer work. It’s a good idea to store this information in a configuration file, but that isn’t always enough; moreover, the terms of use for many sites prohibit it. A robust analysis of an HTML page would, in fact, be better performed using a specialized library (AngleSharp, HtmlAgilityPack) rather than regular expressions. In the next chapter, we’ll see that there are more stable resources on the Web, designed for use by programs: web services. Current translation services, for example, all offer an interface of this type, which accepts and returns JSON.

docs.title: 12.7.4. An SMTP client with the SmtpClient class
docs.text:
An SMTP client is a client of an SMTP server—a mail-sending server—whose protocol we described in Part 1. The [SmtpClient] class in the [System.Net.Mail] namespace encapsulates the requirements of such a client: the developer does not need to know the details of the SMTP protocol or those of the MIME message format. It is accompanied by the classes [MailMessage] (a message), [MailAddress] (an email address), and [Attachment] (an attachment).

The [SmtpClient] class still exists in .NET 10 and has not been declared obsolete, but its documentation states that Microsoft does not recommend it for new developments: it does not support modern authentication protocols (OAuth 2.0, which major email providers are increasingly requiring) and will no longer be updated. The documentation recommends the open-source library MailKit (the [MailKit] NuGet package), which also supports reading email in POP3 and IMAP. Since this package is not available in the course environment, we will present [SmtpClient], whose basic principles (a message, addresses, attachments, and a client that sends it) are identical to those in MailKit.

The 2008 course presented [SmtpClient] in a Windows Forms application that sent the email to port 25 of a real SMTP server, after asking the user to disable their antivirus protection. We’ll keep it simpler and safer: the email will be sent to a small SMTP test server written in C# and running on the local machine, which will display everything it receives and forward nothing. For real-world use, there are full-featured test servers, such as Mailpit or smtp4dev, which also offer a web interface for viewing received messages.

docs.title: 12.7.4.1. An SMTP test server
docs.text:
Our SMTP server follows the structure of the echo server from Part 1: an asynchronous loop waiting for clients, one task per client, and a cancellation token triggered by Ctrl-C. The service provided to each client is the minimal SMTP dialog presented in Part 1. The program [internet-18.cs] is as follows:

using System.Net;
using System.Net.Sockets;
using System.Text;

// test SMTP server: it plays the minimal SMTP dialog and displays the messages received,
// without ever delivering them to their recipients
// call: dotnet run internet-18.cs [-- port]   (port 27225 by default); stop with Ctrl-C
int port = args.Length == 1 && int.TryParse(args[0], out int p) ? p : 27225;

// Ctrl-C cancels the token: the server stops cleanly
using var cancellation = new CancellationTokenSource();
Console.CancelKeyPress += (_, e) =>
{
    e.Cancel = true;
    cancellation.Cancel();
};

// the server only accepts clients from the local machine
var listener = new TcpListener(IPAddress.Loopback, port);
var services = new List<Task>();
int clientNumber = 0;
try
{
    listener.Start();
    Console.WriteLine($"Test SMTP server started on {listener.LocalEndpoint}");
    while (true)
    {
        TcpClient client = await listener.AcceptTcpClientAsync(cancellation.Token);
        services.Add(ServeAsync(client, clientNumber++, cancellation.Token));
        services.RemoveAll(service => service.IsCompleted);
    }
}
catch (OperationCanceledException)
{
    Console.WriteLine("Server stop requested");
}
finally
{
    listener.Stop();
}
await Task.WhenAll(services);

// --------------------------------------------------------------------
// the SMTP dialog with a client: C: lines received from the client, S: lines sent by the server
static async Task ServeAsync(TcpClient client, int clientNumber, CancellationToken token)
{
    Console.WriteLine($"--- start of the dialog with client {clientNumber} ({client.Client.RemoteEndPoint})");
    try
    {
        using (client)
        {
            NetworkStream stream = client.GetStream();
            using var reader = new StreamReader(stream, Encoding.UTF8);
            // SMTP requires \r\n line endings
            await using var writer = new StreamWriter(stream, new UTF8Encoding(false)) { AutoFlush = true, NewLine = "\r\n" };

            // sending of a response line, also displayed on the console
            async Task ReplyAsync(string response)
            {
                Console.WriteLine($"S: {response}");
                await writer.WriteLineAsync(response);
            }

            // the envelope of the current message: sender and recipients
            string? sender = null;
            List<string> recipients = [];
            // welcome message
            await ReplyAsync("220 smtp.test ESMTP test server of the C# course");
            while (await reader.ReadLineAsync(token) is string command)
            {
                Console.WriteLine($"C: {command}");
                // the verb: the first four characters, case-insensitive
                string verb = command.Length >= 4 ? command[..4].ToUpperInvariant() : command;
                switch (verb)
                {
                    case "EHLO":
                        // multi-line response: 250-... then 250 ...
                        await ReplyAsync("250-smtp.test hello");
                        await ReplyAsync("250-SIZE 10485760");
                        await ReplyAsync("250 8BITMIME");
                        break;
                    case "HELO":
                        await ReplyAsync("250 smtp.test hello");
                        break;
                    case "MAIL":
                        // MAIL FROM:<address>
                        sender = command[(command.IndexOf(':') + 1)..].Trim();
                        recipients.Clear();
                        await ReplyAsync("250 2.1.0 Ok");
                        break;
                    case "RCPT":
                        // RCPT TO:<address>
                        recipients.Add(command[(command.IndexOf(':') + 1)..].Trim());
                        await ReplyAsync("250 2.1.5 Ok");
                        break;
                    case "DATA" when sender is null || recipients.Count == 0:
                        await ReplyAsync("503 5.5.1 Give the sender and the recipients first");
                        break;
                    case "DATA":
                        await ReplyAsync("354 End data with <CR><LF>.<CR><LF>");
                        // the message: all the lines up to a line reduced to a dot
                        int nbLines = 0;
                        while (await reader.ReadLineAsync(token) is string line && line != ".")
                        {
                            Console.WriteLine($"C: {line}");
                            nbLines++;
                        }
                        Console.WriteLine("C: .");
                        Console.WriteLine($"[message from {sender} to {string.Join(", ", recipients)}: {nbLines} lines]");
                        await ReplyAsync("250 2.0.0 Ok: message accepted");
                        sender = null;
                        recipients.Clear();
                        break;
                    case "RSET":
                        sender = null;
                        recipients.Clear();
                        await ReplyAsync("250 2.0.0 Ok");
                        break;
                    case "NOOP":
                        await ReplyAsync("250 2.0.0 Ok");
                        break;
                    case "QUIT":
                        await ReplyAsync("221 2.0.0 Goodbye");
                        return;
                    default:
                        await ReplyAsync("502 5.5.2 Command not recognized");
                        break;
                }
            }
        }
    }
    catch (OperationCanceledException)
    {
        Console.WriteLine($"Dialog with client {clientNumber} interrupted by the server stop");
    }
    catch (IOException ex)
    {
        Console.WriteLine($"The following error occurred with client {clientNumber}: {ex.Message}");
    }
    finally
    {
        Console.WriteLine($"--- end of the dialog with client {clientNumber}");
    }
}

We will comment only on what is new compared to the echo server:

  • Line 19: The server listens only on the loopback address: only programs on the same machine can connect to it;
  • line 55: SMTP requires \r\n line endings, regardless of the system;
  • lines 58–61: a local function (C# 7) that sends a response line to the client and displays it on the console, preceded by [S:]. Lines received from the client are displayed preceded by [C:], as in the sample dialogs from Part 1;
  • lines 65–66: the header of the current message: the sender identified by [MAIL FROM] and the recipients identified by [RCPT TO];
  • line 68: the greeting message: in SMTP, the server speaks first;
  • line 73: the command verb consists of its first four characters ([EHLO], [MAIL], [RCPT]…), the case of which is unknown;
  • Lines 76–80: The response to [EHLO] consists of several lines. In these lines, the server specifies its capabilities: the maximum message size ([SIZE]) and support for 8-bit encoded characters ([8BITMIME]);
  • line 96: a [case] clause may be supplemented by a [when] condition: the [DATA] command is rejected if the sender or recipients have not been specified;
  • lines 99–110: the message itself. The server prompts the client to send it (code 354), then reads and displays all lines up to a line reduced to a single dot, and acknowledges receipt (code 250);
  • lines 122–124: the client has finished; the server responds and closes the connection, exiting the method;
  • line 126: any other command is rejected.

This server does not perform many checks and does not support the [STARTTLS] and [AUTH] extensions: it is sufficient to observe what [SmtpClient] sends.

docs.title: 12.7.4.2. The SMTP client
docs.text:
The [internet-19.cs] program prompts the user via the keyboard for the email elements that the 2008 graphical application used to have users enter into its form, then sends them to the SMTP server specified as an argument:

using System.Net.Mail;
using System.Net.Mime;
using System.Text;

// sending an e-mail with the SmtpClient class
// call: dotnet run internet-19.cs -- smtpServer port
// the attachments are looked for in the current folder

const string syntax = "Syntax: dotnet run internet-19.cs -- smtpServer port";
if (args.Length != 2 || !int.TryParse(args[1], out int port) || port is < 1 or > 65535)
{
    Console.WriteLine(syntax);
    return;
}
string server = args[0];

// input of the elements of the mail
string sender = Input("Sender");
string recipients = Input("Recipients (separated by commas)");
string copies = Input("Copy to (Cc)");
string blindCopies = Input("Blind copy to (Bcc)");
string subject = Input("Subject");
string attachments = Input("Attachments (separated by commas)");
// the text: several lines, ended by an empty line
Console.WriteLine("Text of the message (ended by an empty line):");
var text = new StringBuilder();
while (Console.ReadLine() is string line && line != "")
{
    text.AppendLine(line);
}

try
{
    // the message
    using var message = new MailMessage
    {
        From = new MailAddress(sender),
        Subject = subject,
        Body = text.ToString(),
        // the text is encoded in UTF-8 and transported as is (8 bits)
        BodyEncoding = Encoding.UTF8,
        BodyTransferEncoding = TransferEncoding.EightBit,
    };
    // the addresses: Add accepts a list of addresses separated by commas
    message.To.Add(recipients);
    if (copies != "")
    {
        message.CC.Add(copies);
    }
    if (blindCopies != "")
    {
        message.Bcc.Add(blindCopies);
    }
    // the attachments, designated by their path
    foreach (string file in attachments.Split(',', StringSplitOptions.TrimEntries | StringSplitOptions.RemoveEmptyEntries))
    {
        message.Attachments.Add(new Attachment(file));
    }

    // the SMTP client: it knows the SMTP protocol and the MIME format of the messages
    using var client = new SmtpClient(server, port);
    await client.SendMailAsync(message);

    // summary of the sending
    Console.WriteLine("Sending successful...");
    Console.WriteLine($"Subject: {message.Subject}");
    Console.WriteLine($"Recipients: {message.To}");
    Console.WriteLine($"Cc: {message.CC}");
    Console.WriteLine($"Bcc: {message.Bcc}");
    Console.WriteLine($"Attachments: {string.Join(", ", message.Attachments.Select(attachment => attachment.Name))}");
}
catch (Exception ex) when (ex is FormatException or SmtpException or IOException)
{
    Console.WriteLine($"The following error occurred: {ex.GetType().Name} : {ex.Message}");
    if (ex.InnerException is Exception cause)
    {
        Console.WriteLine($"Cause: {cause.GetType().Name} : {cause.Message}");
    }
}

// input of a line on the keyboard
static string Input(string label)
{
    Console.Write($"{label}: ");
    return Console.ReadLine()?.Trim() ?? "";
}

Comments:

  • lines 18–23: entry of the email elements, using the local function [Input];
  • lines 26–29: the message text, spanning multiple lines, ending with a blank line;
  • lines 35–42: the message, created with an object initializer:
    • [From]: the sender, a [MailAddress] object. The constructor of [MailAddress] checks the address format and throws a [FormatException] if it is incorrect;
    • [Subject], [Body]: the subject and body of the message;
    • [BodyEncoding], [BodyTransferEncoding]: the text is encoded in UTF-8 and transmitted as-is, using 8 bits (the server indicated that it accepts this format). Without these two properties, [SmtpClient] would choose its own encoding (base64 or quoted-printable), which would make the text difficult to read when displayed by the server;
  • Lines 45–52: the recipients, those in the “Cc” (Carbon Copy) field, and those in the “Bcc” (Blind Carbon Copy) field. Recipients in the “Bcc” field receive the message, but the other recipients are not aware of this. The [Add] method from the [To], [CC], and [Bcc] collections accepts a comma-separated list of addresses; the 2008 version parsed the list itself using a regular expression;
  • lines 55–57: attachments, identified by their file path. A relative path is relative to the current directory; in our tests, the file [attachment.txt] is located in the [12-internet] directory, from which the program is launched;
  • line 61: the SMTP client, with the server name and port. For a real server, we would also specify [EnableSsl = true] (encryption by [STARTTLS]) and the connection credentials, [Credentials = new NetworkCredential("username", "password")];
  • line 62: asynchronous message transmission. The 2008 course used the synchronous method [Send];
  • lines 65–70: a summary of the transmission;
  • Line 72: An invalid address causes a [FormatException] error; a sending issue causes a [SmtpException] error; an attachment not found causes a [FileNotFoundException] error, derived from [IOException].

The SMTP test server is launched in a command window on port 27225. In another window, a message is sent to two recipients, with one recipient in carbon copy, one in blind carbon copy, and an attachment:

> dotnet run internet-19.cs -- localhost 27225
Sender: alice@example.org
Recipients (separated by commas): bob@example.com, carole@example.com
Copy to (Cc): david@example.com
Blind copy to (Bcc): eve@example.com
Subject: Minutes of the meeting at the café
Attachments (separated by commas): attachment.txt
Text of the message (ended by an empty line):
Hello,
here are the minutes of the meeting at the café.
Best regards,
Alice

Sending successful...
Subject: Minutes of the meeting at the café
Recipients: bob@example.com, carole@example.com
Cc: david@example.com
Bcc: eve@example.com
Attachments: attachment.txt

The file [attachment.txt] contains two lines of text. Here is what the server displayed:

> dotnet run internet-18.cs
Test SMTP server started on 127.0.0.1:27225
--- start of the dialog with client 0 (127.0.0.1:53546)

S: 250 2.1.5 Ok
C: RCPT TO:<carole@example.com>
S: 250 2.1.5 Ok
C: RCPT TO:<eve@example.com>
S: 250 2.1.5 Ok
C: RCPT TO:<david@example.com>
S: 250 2.1.5 Ok
C: DATA
S: 354 End data with <CR><LF>.<CR><LF>
C: MIME-Version: 1.0
C: From: alice@example.org
C: To: bob@example.com, carole@example.com
C: Cc: david@example.com
C: Date: 3 Oct 2026 12:20:36 +0200
C: Subject: =?utf-8?B?TWludXRlcyBvZiB0aGUgbWVldGluZyBhdCB0aGUgY2Fmw6k=?=
C: Content-Type: multipart/mixed;
C:  boundary=--boundary_0_40431766-5e35-4c3f-a18f-31531f8834df
C: 
C: 
C: ----boundary_0_40431766-5e35-4c3f-a18f-31531f8834df
C: Content-Type: text/plain; charset=utf-8
C: Content-Transfer-Encoding: 8bit
C:

C: here are the minutes of the meeting at the café.
C: Best regards,
C: Alice

C: ----boundary_0_40431766-5e35-4c3f-a18f-31531f8834df

C: Content-Transfer-Encoding: base64
C: Content-Disposition: attachment
C: 
C: VGhpcyBpcyB0aGUgYXR0YWNobWVudCBvZiB0aGUgdGVzdCBtYWlsLgpJdCBjb250YWlu
C: cyB0d28gbGluZXMuCg==
C: ----boundary_0_40431766-5e35-4c3f-a18f-31531f8834df--

[message from <alice@example.org> to <bob@example.com>, <carole@example.com>, <eve@example.com>, <david@example.com>: 29 lines]
S: 250 2.0.0 Ok: message accepted
C: QUIT

Server stop requested

Comments:

  • line 5: [SmtpClient] appears with the machine name;
  • lines 9–17: the message envelope: the sender, followed by all recipients, including the blind carbon copy (BCC) recipient ([eve@example.com]). The envelope determines to whom the message is delivered;
  • lines 21–28: the message headers, which make up what the recipients will see. They include the recipients [To] and [Cc], but not the blind-carbon-copy recipient: this is how the blind carbon copy remains hidden. The subject line contains an accented character; since the headers can only contain ASCII characters, it was encoded according to the RFC 2047 standard: [=?utf-8?B?...?=] means “UTF-8 text encoded in Base64”;
  • line 27: the message is in MIME format (Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions, RFC 2045 and following): it consists of several parts, separated by a delimiter line ([boundary]) chosen at random by [SmtpClient];
  • lines 32–38: the first part, the message text, in 8-bit UTF-8: it is readable as is;
  • lines 41–46: the second part, the attachment, encoded in Base64. Base64 encodes arbitrary bytes using 64 characters from the ASCII set; the recipient’s mail server does not need to know the nature of the attachment;
  • line 50: the end of the message;
  • line 51: our server received a message for four recipients;
  • lines 53–54: [SmtpClient] ends the exchange;
  • line 56: the server was stopped with Ctrl-C after the tests.

An invalid address is rejected before any message is sent:

> dotnet run internet-19.cs -- localhost 27225

docs.title: 12.8. A generic asynchronous TCP client
docs.text:
The 2008 course devoted an entire section here to a generic asynchronous TCP client, featuring a Windows Forms graphical interface: a field for the server name and port, a [Connect] / [Disconnect] button, a text box for entering the lines to be sent, and two lists displaying connection events and server communication. Graphical user interfaces are no longer part of this course, and this example has lost most of its relevance: its purpose was to demonstrate asynchronous programming, which has undergone a complete transformation since 2008.

The 2008 client worked directly with a [Socket] object and used the asynchronous model of the time, called APM (Asynchronous Programming Model): each operation was divided into a [BeginXxx] method, which initiated the operation and returned control immediately, and a [EndXxx] method, called within a callback method executed by a thread from the pool at the end of the operation. The connection was written as follows:

// starting the connection: the connected method will be called back at the end of the operation
client.BeginConnect(Dns.GetHostEntry(serverName).AddressList[0], port, connected, client);
...
// the callback method
private void connected(IAsyncResult result)
{
    Socket client = result.AsyncState as Socket;
    // end of the operation: throws an exception if the connection failed
    client.EndConnect(result);
    // starting the asynchronous reading of the data sent by the server
    client.BeginReceive(data, 0, bufferSize, SocketFlags.None, read, client);
}

The [read] callback method for the receive operation had to in turn call [BeginReceive] to read the rest of the data, reconstruct the lines from the received byte blocks (since a line could be split between two blocks) and, since it ran on a thread in the pool, call the form’s [Invoke] method to update the GUI. The code was lengthy, and the dialog logic was scattered across several methods.

The APM model was replaced by the task-based model (TAP, Task-based Asynchronous Pattern, introduced with .NET 4 in 2010) and by the keywords [async] / [await] (C# 5, 2012), presented in Chapter 9. The generic TCP client from the first part ([internet-06.cs]) is already an asynchronous client: [ConnectAsync] replaces the pair [BeginConnect] / [EndConnect]; a receive task that calls [ReadLineAsync] in a loop replaces the callback chain of [BeginReceive]; and [StreamReader] is responsible for reconstructing the lines. The code reads in the order in which it executes, like synchronous code. In a current graphical application (WPF, WinUI, .NET MAUI), [await] also resumes execution on the interface thread, eliminating the need for calls to [Invoke].

The conclusion from the 2008 course still holds true: asynchrony offers little benefit to a client with only one connection, other than an interface that remains responsive; it is, however, essential for a server. A server that serves its clients with blocking operations ties up one thread per client; with asynchronous operations, just a few threads are enough to serve a large number of clients. This is what the server in the following example application does.

docs.title: 12.9. Sample Application, Version 8: Tax Calculation Server
12.9.1. The Architecture of the New Version
docs.text:
We’ll revisit the tax calculation application. In version 5 (Chapter 6), it consisted of three layers, each in its own library: [dao] (tax brackets), [business] (the calculation), and [ui] (the console dialog), assembled via dependency injection; versions 6 and 7 replaced the [dao] layer with database access. The 2008 course started with version 7 (data in a database, graphical interface); we are starting with version 5, which is simpler to run: the new version would work the same way with the [dao] layer from versions 6 and 7.

We will distribute this architecture across two machines:

  • A [server] machine hosts the [business] and [dao] layers from version 5. A [server] layer is built to allow clients on the network to query the tax calculation service using a text-based TCP protocol;
  • a machine [client] hosts the [ui] layer of version 5. A new [business] layer, which acts as a client to the server (TCP), enables the client to query the tax calculation service.

The architecture is changing significantly: Version 5 was a single-user application; Version 8 becomes a client/server application, and the server will be able to serve multiple clients simultaneously. However, we will write only two new classes, [TaxServer] and [TaxBusinessTcp], and two main programs: everything else is reused without modification.

The [TaxV8] solution consists of two console projects that reference the projects from version 5:

12-internet/TaxV8/
  TaxV8.slnx
  Tax.Server/
    Tax.Server.csproj          references to Tax.Dao and Tax.Business (V5)
    appsettings.json           configuration of the [dao] layer and of the server
    Program.cs                 integration of the layers, launch of the server
    TaxServer.cs               the [server] layer
  Tax.Client/
    Tax.Client.csproj          references to Tax.Business and Tax.Ui (V5)
    TaxBusinessTcp.cs          the [business] layer of the client: a TCP client
    Program.cs                 integration of the layers, dialog

docs.title: 12.9.2. The Communication Protocol
docs.text:
We are retaining the 2008 server protocol. Once the client is connected, the server sends it a welcome message, then accepts the following commands, one per line, case-insensitive:

CommandServer Responsehelpa list of accepted commands, on four linestax married nbChildren annualSalarythe tax for a married person (married is [y]) or an unmarried person ([n]) with [nbChildren] children and an annual salary of [annualSalary] euros, for example, [4282] in response to [tax y 2 60000]; or an error message, on a linegoodbyethe message [Goodbye...]; the server then closes the connection

Any other command receives the response [Command not recognized. Use the help command.]

docs.title: 12.9.3.1. The project
docs.text:
The file [Tax.Server.csproj] is as follows:

<Project Sdk="Microsoft.NET.Sdk">

  <PropertyGroup>
    <OutputType>Exe</OutputType>
    <TargetFramework>net10.0</TargetFramework>
    <ImplicitUsings>enable</ImplicitUsings>
    <Nullable>enable</Nullable>
  </PropertyGroup>

  <ItemGroup>
    <!-- the [dao] and [business] layers of version 5, reused as they are -->
    <ProjectReference Include="../../../06-architectures/TaxV5/Tax.Dao/Tax.Dao.csproj" />
    <ProjectReference Include="../../../06-architectures/TaxV5/Tax.Business/Tax.Business.csproj" />
  </ItemGroup>

  <ItemGroup>
    <!-- dependency injection container and reading of a JSON configuration file -->
    <PackageReference Include="Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection" Version="10.0.12" />
    <PackageReference Include="Microsoft.Extensions.Configuration.Json" Version="10.0.12" />
  </ItemGroup>

  <ItemGroup>
    <!-- the configuration file is copied next to the executable -->
    <None Update="appsettings.json" CopyToOutputDirectory="PreserveNewest" />

</Project>
  • Lines 12–13: The layers [dao] and [business] from version 5 are referenced by their projects. The data files [TaxData.txt] and [TaxData.json] from the [Tax.Dao] project are copied to the server’s output folder;
  • lines 18–19: the dependency injection container and the reading of a JSON configuration file, as in version 5;
  • line 24: the configuration file is copied next to the executable.

The configuration file [appsettings.json]:

{
  "Dao": {
    "Implementation": "FileTax",
    "File": "TaxData.txt"
  },
  "Server": {
    "Port": 27200,
    "Echo": true
  }
}
  • Lines 2–4: The configuration for the [dao] layer, identical to that in version 5: tax brackets are read from the text file [TaxData.txt];
  • Lines 6–8: The server’s listening port and the echo of the dialogue with clients in the server log. The 2008 server had an administration console (commands [start port], [stop], [echo start], [echo stop], [status], [quit]); we opted for a configuration file and shutdown via Ctrl-C, which are simpler and more in line with how modern servers operate.

docs.title: 12.9.3.2. The main program
docs.text:
The server’s [Program.cs] file is as follows:

using Dao;
using Entities;
using Business;
using Microsoft.Extensions.Configuration;
using Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection;
using Server;

// the TCP tax calculation server: configuration, integration of the layers, execution
TaxServer server;
try
{
    // reading the configuration, next to the executable
    IConfiguration config = new ConfigurationBuilder()
        .SetBasePath(AppContext.BaseDirectory)
        .AddJsonFile("appsettings.json", optional: false)
        .Build();
    string implementation = config["Dao:Implementation"] ?? "HardwiredTax";
    string file = config["Dao:File"] ?? "";
    int port = int.TryParse(config["Server:Port"], out int p) ? p : 27200;
    bool echo = bool.TryParse(config["Server:Echo"], out bool e) && e;

    // registration of the layers in the container
    var services = new ServiceCollection();
    // the [dao] layer: the implementation is chosen by the configuration (as in version 5)
    services.AddSingleton<ITaxDao>(_ => implementation switch
    {
        "HardwiredTax" => new HardwiredTax(),
        "FileTax" => new FileTax(file),
        "JsonTax" => new JsonTax(file),
        _ => throw new TaxException($"Unknown implementation [{implementation}] of the [dao] layer")
    });
    // the [business] layer of version 5
    services.AddSingleton<ITaxBusiness, TaxBusiness>();
    // the [server] layer: the container will pass it the [business] layer and its options
    services.AddSingleton(new ServerOptions(port, echo));
    services.AddSingleton<TaxServer>();

    // creation of the server, and therefore of the [business] and [dao] layers
    ServiceProvider provider = services.BuildServiceProvider();
    server = provider.GetRequiredService<TaxServer>();
}
catch (Exception ex)
{
    // display of the exception chain and stop
    Console.WriteLine("The following error occurred during the initialization of the server:");
    for (Exception? cause = ex; cause != null; cause = cause.InnerException)
    {
        Console.WriteLine($"{cause.GetType().Name} : {cause.Message}");
    }
    return 1;
}

// Ctrl-C cancels the token: the server stops cleanly
using var cancellation = new CancellationTokenSource();
Console.CancelKeyPress += (_, e) =>
{
    e.Cancel = true;
    cancellation.Cancel();
};
// execution of the server until the requested stop
await server.RunAsync(cancellation.Token);
return 0;

This is clearly the main program from version 5:

  • lines 13–20: reading the configuration. The values are character strings: the port and echo are converted using [TryParse], with default values provided;
  • lines 25–33: the layers [dao] and [business] are stored in the container exactly as in version 5;
  • lines 35–36: the new feature. The server options (port, echo) are stored as a pre-built object, followed by the [server] layer itself. The constructor of [TaxServer] expects an [ITaxBusiness] and a [ServerOptions]: the container will provide them;
  • Line 40: Creating the server triggers the creation of the [business] layer, which in turn triggers the creation of the [dao] layer; this is when the [TaxData.txt] file is read. An error (file missing, malformed) is displayed and the program terminates (lines 42–50);
  • lines 54–58: Ctrl-C cancels the token [cancellation], as in the echo server;
  • line 61: the server runs until the token is canceled.

docs.title: 12.9.3.3. The [server] layer
docs.text:
The [TaxServer] class is as follows:

using System.Net;
using System.Net.Sockets;
using Business;

namespace Server;

// the options of the server: listening port and echo of the dialog in the log
public record ServerOptions(int Port, bool Echo);

// the [server] layer: it makes the [business] layer accessible through a TCP protocol of text lines
public class TaxServer(ITaxBusiness business, ServerOptions options)
{
    // the fixed responses of the protocol
    private const string Welcome = "Welcome to the tax calculation server";
    private const string Help = "Accepted commands\n1-help\n2-tax married(Y/N) nbChildren annualSalary\n3-goodbye";
    private const string Goodbye = "Goodbye...";
    private const string IncorrectCommand = "Command not recognized. Use the help command.";
    private const string IncorrectCalculation = "Incorrect calculation command. Use the help command.";

    // execution of the server until the token is cancelled
    public async Task RunAsync(CancellationToken token)
    {
        var listener = new TcpListener(IPAddress.Any, options.Port);
        // the service tasks in progress
        var services = new List<Task>();
        int clientNumber = 0;
        try
        {
            listener.Start();
            Log($"Tax calculation server started on port {options.Port}");
            while (true)
            {
                // wait for a client
                TcpClient client = await listener.AcceptTcpClientAsync(token);
                // it is served by a task that we do not wait for: we go back to waiting for the next client
                services.Add(ServeAsync(client, clientNumber++, token));
                services.RemoveAll(service => service.IsCompleted);
            }
        }
        catch (OperationCanceledException)
        {
            Log("Server stop requested");
        }
        catch (SocketException ex)
        {
            Log($"The following error occurred on the server: {ex.SocketErrorCode} ({ex.Message})");
        }
        finally
        {
            listener.Stop();
        }
        // we wait for the end of the services in progress
        await Task.WhenAll(services);
        Log("Server stopped");
    }

    // the service provided to a client
    private async Task ServeAsync(TcpClient client, int clientNumber, CancellationToken token)
    {
        Log($"Start of service to client {clientNumber} ({client.Client.RemoteEndPoint})");
        try
        {
            using (client)
            {
                NetworkStream stream = client.GetStream();
                using var reader = new StreamReader(stream);
                await using var writer = new StreamWriter(stream) { AutoFlush = true };

                // sending of a response to the client, with possible echo in the log
                async Task WriteAsync(string response)
                {
                    if (options.Echo)
                    {
                        Log($"---> client {clientNumber} : {response}");
                    }
                    await writer.WriteLineAsync(response);
                }

                // welcome message
                await WriteAsync(Welcome);
                // loop read request / write response, until the goodbye command
                while (await reader.ReadLineAsync(token) is string request)
                {
                    if (options.Echo)
                    {
                        Log($"<--- client {clientNumber} : {request}");
                    }
                    // the request split into fields
                    string[] fields = request.Trim().ToLower().Split(' ', StringSplitOptions.RemoveEmptyEntries);
                    if (fields is ["goodbye"])
                    {
                        await WriteAsync(Goodbye);
                        break;
                    }
                    // the response according to the command
                    string response = fields switch
                    {
                        ["help"] => Help,
                        ["tax", ..] => CalculateTax(fields),
                        _ => IncorrectCommand,
                    };
                    await WriteAsync(response);
                }
            }
        }
        catch (OperationCanceledException)
        {
            Log($"Service to client {clientNumber} interrupted by the server stop");
        }
        catch (IOException ex)
        {
            Log($"The following error occurred while serving client {clientNumber}: {ex.Message}");
        }
        finally
        {
            Log($"End of service to client {clientNumber}");
        }
    }

    // the command tax married nbChildren annualSalary: returns the tax or an error message
    private string CalculateTax(string[] fields)
    {
        // 4 fields are needed: tax, y or n, two integers
        if (fields is not [_, "y" or "n", var children, var salary]
            || !int.TryParse(children, out int nbChildren)
            || !int.TryParse(salary, out int annualSalary))
        {
            return IncorrectCalculation;
        }
        try
        {
            // the calculation is handed to the [business] layer
            return business.CalculateTax(fields[1] == "y", nbChildren, annualSalary).ToString();
        }
        catch (Exception ex)
        {
            // the message of the exception, on a single line: the protocol is made of text lines
            return ex.Message.ReplaceLineEndings(" ");
        }
    }

    // the server's log: each line is timestamped
    private static void Log(string message) => Console.WriteLine($"{DateTime.Now:HH:mm:ss} {message}");
}
  • line 8: the server options, a positional record (C# 9);
  • line 11: the class receives the [business] layer and its options via its primary constructor (C# 12). It knows only the [business] layer’s [ITaxBusiness] interface and knows nothing about the [dao] layer;
  • lines 14–18: the protocol’s fixed responses. The response to the [help] command contains \n: it will be received by the client as four lines, as in 2008;
  • lines 21–54: the client wait loop. This is the same as the echo server from the first part: each client is served by an asynchronous task that is not blocked (line 36), canceling the token ends a client’s wait (line 40), and the server waits for ongoing services to complete before shutting down (line 53). The 2008 server assigned each client to a thread from a pool limited to 10 threads, which remained blocked for the duration of the service; here, no thread is held up by a client that is taking its time;
  • lines 58–116: the service provided to a client:
    • lines 70–76: a local function that sends a response to the client and also writes it to the log if logging is enabled;
    • line 80: Once the client is connected, the server sends it a welcome message;
    • line 82: the command-reading loop, which stops if the client closes the connection or if the server is shut down;
    • line 89: the command, converted to lowercase, is parsed into fields. The 2008 course used [Regex.Split] with the [\s+] pattern; the [RemoveEmptyEntries] option of [Split] similarly removes empty fields caused by multiple consecutive spaces;
    • line 90: a list pattern (C# 11): the command consists solely of the word [goodbye]. The server responds and exits the loop: the connection is closed upon exiting the [using (client)] block;
    • lines 96–100: a [switch] expression with list patterns selects the response: [["help"]] recognizes the command [help] on its own, while [["tax", ..]] recognizes a command beginning with [tax], followed by any number of fields (slice pattern [..]). The 2008 server would close the connection upon receiving an empty line; it now receives the response [Command not recognized];
  • Lines 121–138: Calculation of the tax:
    • Lines 124–128: A single list pattern checks that the command has four fields, that the second field is either [y] or [n], and assigns the last two fields to the variables [children] and [salary]; it then checks that these are integers. The 2008 code performed these checks in four successive tests;
    • line 133: the calculation is requested from the [business] layer. A single instance of [TaxBusiness] serves all clients, potentially simultaneously, from different threads: this is possible because this class does not modify any data after it is constructed (its tax bracket array is read-only);
    • line 138: if the [business] layer throws an exception (for example, due to a negative number of children), its message is returned to the client. This message may contain line breaks: these are replaced with spaces, since the protocol requires a single-line response;
  • line 143: the server log, displayed on the console: each line is preceded by the time, which allows you to see the sequence of concurrent services. [Console.WriteLine] can be called without any special precautions from multiple threads: its writes do not interfere with one another.

docs.title: 12.9.4. The tax calculation server client
docs.text: The 2008 course used the graphical interface from version 7; we are using the console interface from version 5—the class [Ui.Dialog]—without modifying it.

docs.title: 12.9.4.1. The [business] layer of the client
docs.text:
The [ui] layer communicates with a [business] layer, of which it knows only the [ITaxBusiness] interface:

namespace Business;

// the interface of the [business] layer
public interface ITaxBusiness
{
    int CalculateTax(bool married, int nbChildren, int salary);
}

All that is needed, therefore, is to provide it with another implementation of this interface, which, instead of calculating the tax, requests it from the server. This is the [TaxBusinessTcp] class:

using System.Net.Sockets;
using Entities;
using Business;

namespace Client;

// the [business] layer of the client: it implements ITaxBusiness by delegating the calculation to the TCP server
public class TaxBusinessTcp : ITaxBusiness, IDisposable
{
    // the connection to the server, open for the whole lifetime of the object
    private readonly TcpClient client;
    private readonly StreamReader reader;
    private readonly StreamWriter writer;

    // connection to the server (machine, port)
    public TaxBusinessTcp(string machine, int port)
    {
        try
        {
            client = new TcpClient(machine, port);
            NetworkStream stream = client.GetStream();
            reader = new StreamReader(stream);
            writer = new StreamWriter(stream) { AutoFlush = true };
            // the server speaks first: we read (and ignore) its welcome message
            ReadResponse();
        }
        catch (Exception e) when (e is SocketException or IOException)
        {
            throw new TaxException($"Unable to connect to the server ({machine}, {port})", e) { Code = 21 };
        }
    }

    // tax calculation: one request, one response
    public int CalculateTax(bool married, int nbChildren, int salary)
    {
        string response;
        try
        {
            writer.WriteLine($"tax {(married ? "y" : "n")} {nbChildren} {salary}");
            response = ReadResponse();
        }
        catch (IOException e)
        {
            throw new TaxException("Error communicating with the server", e) { Code = 22 };
        }
        // the server returns the tax, or an error message
        return int.TryParse(response, out int tax)
            ? tax
            : throw new TaxException($"The server answered: {response}") { Code = 23 };
    }

    // reading of a response line; null means that the server has closed the connection
    private string ReadResponse() =>
        reader.ReadLine() ?? throw new TaxException("The server has closed the connection") { Code = 24 };

    // end of the connection: we take leave of the server, if it is still there
    public void Dispose()
    {
        try
        {
            writer.WriteLine("goodbye");
            reader.ReadLine();
        }
        catch (IOException)
        {
            // the connection is already cut: there is nothing left to do
        }
        client.Dispose();
    }
}
  • Line 8: The class implements [ITaxBusiness]. It also implements [IDisposable]: it maintains a network connection, which must be closed;
  • lines 11–13: the connection to the server and its read and write streams. The 2008 class opened a new connection for each calculation; we open a single connection, used for all calculations in a session: this is more efficient, and the server sees one client per user session;
  • lines 16–29: the constructor connects to the server and reads its welcome message (line 25). A connection error is encapsulated in a [TaxException], the application exception;
  • lines 34–49: the tax calculation. The command [tax y 2 60000] is sent to the server (line 39) and its response is read. If the response is an integer, that is the tax amount; otherwise, it is a server error message, which is returned in a [TaxException] (line 49). The 2008 code directly converted the response to an integer and asked the reader to improve it: a server error message caused a conversion exception that masked the true cause of the error;
  • line 53: [ReadLine] returns [null] when the server has closed the connection; a [TaxException] is then thrown;
  • Lines 57–68: End of the connection. The client logs off from the server using the [goodbye] command, then closes the connection. If the server has already terminated the connection, the resulting [IOException] is ignored.

This raises a question: why does this class use the synchronous methods [TcpClient(machine, port)], [ReadLine], and [WriteLine], when the rest of this chapter uses their asynchronous versions? Because the [ITaxBusiness] interface in version 5 is synchronous: [CalculateTax] returns an [int], not a [Task<int>], and the [ui] layer calls it without [await]. To use [ReadLineAsync], you would either have to wait for its result in a blocking manner ([ReadLineAsync().Result])—which Chapter 9 advised against—or make the interface asynchronous, and thus modify the [business] and [ui] layers from version 5. For a console program that serves only one user, synchronous methods are perfectly suited: the main thread has nothing else to do but wait for the response. Asynchrony is essential on the server side, which must serve many clients, not on the client side. When we write new layers in the next chapter, we will equip them with asynchronous interfaces.

docs.title: 12.9.4.2. The client’s main program
docs.text:
Project [Tax.Client.csproj] references layers [business] and [ui] from Version 5:

<Project Sdk="Microsoft.NET.Sdk">

  <PropertyGroup>
    <OutputType>Exe</OutputType>
    <TargetFramework>net10.0</TargetFramework>
    <ImplicitUsings>enable</ImplicitUsings>
    <Nullable>enable</Nullable>
  </PropertyGroup>

  <ItemGroup>
    <!-- the interface of the [business] layer and the [ui] layer of version 5 -->
    <ProjectReference Include="../../../06-architectures/TaxV5/Tax.Business/Tax.Business.csproj" />
    <ProjectReference Include="../../../06-architectures/TaxV5/Tax.Ui/Tax.Ui.csproj" />
  </ItemGroup>

  <ItemGroup>
    <!-- dependency injection container -->
    <PackageReference Include="Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection" Version="10.0.12" />
  </ItemGroup>

</Project>

The [Tax.Ui] project is a console application: a project can reference another executable project to use its public classes—in this case, [Ui.Dialog]. The [Program.cs] file is as follows:

using Client;
using Entities;
using Business;
using Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection;
using Ui;

// the console client of the tax calculation server
// call: dotnet run [-- machine port]   (by default: localhost 27200)
string machine = args.Length > 0 ? args[0] : "localhost";
int port = args.Length > 1 && int.TryParse(args[1], out int p) ? p : 27200;

// the [business] layer is now a TCP client of the tax calculation server
var services = new ServiceCollection();
services.AddSingleton<ITaxBusiness>(_ => new TaxBusinessTcp(machine, port));
// the container releases (Dispose) the objects it created: the connection will be closed at the end of the program
using ServiceProvider provider = services.BuildServiceProvider();
try
{
    ITaxBusiness business = provider.GetRequiredService<ITaxBusiness>();
    Console.WriteLine($"Connected to the tax calculation server ({machine}, {port})");
    // the [ui] layer of version 5, unchanged
    Dialog.Run(business);
}
catch (TaxException e)
{
    Dialog.DisplayError(e);
    return 1;
}
return 0;
  • lines 9–10: the server’s machine and port, passed as arguments, with default values;
  • line 14: the [business] layer registered in the container is now [TaxBusinessTcp]. Since its constructor expects two parameters that the container does not know, a creation function is provided for it;
  • line 16: the container is declared with [using]. When it is released at the end of the program, it in turn releases the [IDisposable] objects it created: the [Dispose] method of [TaxBusinessTcp] will be called, and the connection will be closed properly;
  • line 19: creation of the [business] layer, i.e., the connection to the server;
  • line 22: the Version 5 dialog, unchanged. The [ui] layer is unaware that the tax is calculated by a remote server;
  • Lines 24–27: A connection or communication error is displayed by the [DisplayError] method from version 5.

The dialog is exactly the same as in Version 5: it includes the validation values (4282 and 2959 for a married person with 2 or 3 children and a salary of 60,000 euros, 11519 for an unmarried person with no children), and the same error messages for incorrect entries. These messages are generated by the client’s [ui] layer, which validates the input before requesting the calculation: incorrect entries never reach the server.

Now let’s launch two clients, A and B, in two windows, with B starting while A is still connected. Each performs two calculations. In client A’s window:

To see the server’s responses to incorrect commands, you need a client that sends the commands exactly as they are typed: the generic TCP client from the first part works perfectly. The server speaks first, which this client can handle:

  • line 2: the welcome message, which arrived even before the client’s prompt;
  • lines 5–8: the response to the command [help], spanning four lines;
  • line 11: the command’s case is ignored;
  • lines 13–15: two malformed calculation commands;
  • line 18: the command is well-formed, but the [business] layer rejects a negative number of children; the exception message (in English: it comes from .NET) was returned on a single line;
  • line 20: an unknown command;
  • lines 21–23: after the command [goodbye], the server closed the connection.

The server is then terminated with Ctrl-C while one last client is still connected. This client performed an initial calculation before the termination and sent its second request afterward:

2-tax married(Y/N) nbChildren annualSalary
3-goodbye
12:22:03 <--- client 3 : tax y 2 60000
12:22:03 ---> client 3 : 4282
12:22:04 <--- client 3 : TAX N 0 60000
12:22:04 ---> client 3 : 11519
12:22:05 <--- client 3 : tax x 2 60000
12:22:05 ---> client 3 : Incorrect calculation command. Use the help command.
12:22:06 <--- client 3 : tax y 2
12:22:06 ---> client 3 : Incorrect calculation command. Use the help command.
12:22:07 <--- client 3 : tax y -2 60000
12:22:07 ---> client 3 : nbChildren ('-2') must be a non-negative value. (Parameter 'nbChildren') Actual value was -2.
12:22:08 <--- client 3 : calculation
12:22:08 ---> client 3 : Command not recognized. Use the help command.

12:22:09 ---> client 3 : Goodbye...
12:22:09 End of service to client 3
12:22:12 Start of service to client 4 (127.0.0.1:52306)
12:22:12 ---> client 4 : Welcome to the tax calculation server
12:22:17 <--- client 4 : tax y 2 60000
12:22:17 ---> client 4 : 4282
12:22:17 Server stop requested
12:22:17 Service to client 4 interrupted by the server stop
12:22:17 End of service to client 4
12:22:17 Server stopped
  • Lines 3–13: the client from the first run. With the echo output, we can see all the commands received and all the responses sent. Note the command [goodbye] (line 11), sent by the [Dispose] method of [TaxBusinessTcp] when the user finished: the session was closed properly;
  • lines 14–31: clients A (client 1) and B (client 2). Client 2 arrived (line 16) while client 1 was still being served, and their requests were processed alternately as they arrived: the server does indeed serve multiple clients simultaneously;
  • lines 32–53: the session for the generic TCP client;
  • Lines 54–61: The last client, being served at the time of the shutdown. Ctrl-C canceled the token; the two operations that were waiting for it—reading a command from client 4 and waiting for a new client—ended with an [OperationCanceledException], in an order that depends on the thread scheduling. The server waited for the current service to finish before shutting down.

docs.title: 12.9.6. Conclusion
docs.text:
Once again, we were able to reuse existing code without modifying it: the [dao] and [business] layers from the server-side version 5, and the [ui] layer on the client side. This was made possible by the systematic use of interfaces and dependency injection: to deploy the application across two machines, all that was needed was to add a [server] layer on top of the [business] layer and provide the [ui] layer with a different implementation of [ITaxBusiness]. If version 1 had combined tax calculation and user interaction within the same program, none of this would have been reusable. Note that the [ui] layer has no knowledge of the fact that a remote server calculates the tax amount.

Our in-house protocol does, however, have its limitations: we must write the server, manage connections, parse commands, convert responses, and a client written in another language would need to be familiar with this specific protocol. Version 9, in the next chapter, will replace the TCP server with a web service: the protocol will be HTTP, data will be exchanged using JSON, and the client will use [HttpClient].

docs.title: 12.10. Conclusion
docs.text:
This chapter introduced Internet programming with .NET, starting with the fundamentals and progressing to high-level classes:

  • the first part reviewed how Internet protocols work (IP, TCP, UDP, DNS) and text-based application protocols (HTTP, SMTP, POP, FTP), then introduced the classes [IPAddress] and [Dns], as well as the classes [TcpClient] and [TcpListener], which are used asynchronously. Using these, we wrote servers that serve multiple clients simultaneously, generic TCP clients, and a web client that communicated with HTTP “manually”;
  • The second part introduced classes specialized for a protocol. For HTTP, the [HttpClient] class replaces the obsolete [WebClient] and [WebRequest]: it accomplishes in a single statement what our TCP client used to do in fifty lines; it handles redirects, forms, JSON, timeouts, and cancellation, and is intended to be reused across requests. For SMTP, the [SmtpClient] class remains usable, though the MailKit library is preferred for new developments;
  • the sample application has become a client/server application, without any changes to its existing layers.

The principles of asynchronous programming discussed in Chapter 9 have found their primary application here: an asynchronous server serves a large number of clients using a few threads, and an asynchronous client waits for responses from the network without blocking a thread. However, writing a TCP server and inventing its own protocol remains the exception: most distributed applications today communicate via HTTP, using web services that exchange JSON data. This is the subject of the next chapter.

docs.title: 13.1. Introduction
docs.text:
In the previous chapter, we presented several TCP/IP client-server applications. Since the clients and the server exchange lines of text, they can be written in any language. The client simply needs to know the communication protocol expected by the server.

Web services are also server applications (TCP/IP). They have the following characteristics:

  • they are hosted by web servers, and the client-server exchange protocol is HTTP (HyperText Transfer Protocol), a protocol built on top of TCP/IP, which we explored in the previous chapter;
  • the web service has a standard communication protocol, regardless of the service provided. A web service offers various services: S1, S2…, Sn. Each of these services expects parameters provided by the client and returns a result to the client. For each service, the client needs to know:
    • how to specify the service Si;
    • the list of parameters to be provided and their types;
    • the type of result returned by the service. Once these elements are known, the client-server dialogue follows the same format, regardless of which web service is being queried. This standardizes client communication;
  • To protect against attacks from the Internet, many organizations open only certain ports on their servers to the outside world: primarily ports 80 (HTTP) and 443 (HTTPS) for the web service. All other ports are locked. Consequently, client-server applications such as those described in the previous chapter are generally restricted to the organization’s private network (intranet). Hosting a service on a web server makes it accessible to the entire Internet community;
  • the web service can be viewed as a remote object: the services it offers then become methods of that object. A client can use this remote object as if it were local, through an intermediary object called a proxy, which hides all network communication. This allows us to build a client that is independent of this layer: if the layer changes, the rest of the client does not need to be modified;
  • As with the TCP/IP client-server applications from the previous chapter, the client and server can be written in any programming language. They exchange lines of text consisting of two parts: the headers required by the HTTP protocol and the message body, whose format is agreed upon between the client and the server.

The architecture of a web service-based client-server application is as follows:

This is an extension of the layered architecture from Chapter 6, to which specialized network communication layers are added: the client-side web service client and the web service itself on the server side. We have already encountered a similar architecture with the TCP tax calculation server (version 8) from the previous chapter.

docs.title: 13.1.1. Yesterday: SOAP and WSDL
docs.text: In 2008, this course used the SOAP web services from the .NET Framework: [.asmx] files created with Visual Web Developer, whose public methods were marked with the [[WebMethod]] attribute. The client sent an HTTP POST request whose body was an XML document in SOAP (Simple Object Access Protocol) format: an “envelope” containing the method name and its parameters. The server responded with another XML envelope containing the result.
